I pace the length of the walk-in freezer, the sub-zero air doing nothing to cool the prickle of sweat at the back of my neck. My thumb swipes down on my phone screen, reloading the local dining page for the seventeenth time in ten minutes. The headline, "Bistro Noir's Bitter Disappointment," glares back at me. I chew the inside of my cheek until I taste iron. Did table four cancel? I need to ask the host, but my legs feel like lead. I lean against a rack of chilled pork shoulders, my chest rising and falling in rapid, shallow bursts. Every time the heavy metal door clicks open, I flinch, expecting my sous chef to walk in with today's reservation numbers. I stare at the screen again, my finger hovering over the power button, but I just swipe down one more time.

Elias gripped the plating tweezers so tightly his knuckles turned a translucent white. The delicate micro-greens hovered over the seared scallop, but his hand vibrated like a plucked guitar string, sending a tiny green leaf tumbling onto the pristine white porcelain. He squeezed his eyes shut, exhaling a breath that hitched in his throat. The critic’s words—"a clumsy, heavy-handed catastrophe"—flashed behind his eyelids like neon signage. He snatched a towel, wiping the empty space on the rim until the cloth threatened to polish away the glaze. "Chef? Table seven needs that," Maria whispered. Elias snapped his head up, his pulse drumming a frantic rhythm behind his ears. He swallowed the dry lump in his throat, nodded sharply, and grabbed a fresh scallop. His chest felt constricted, wrapped in tight iron bands as he reached for the greens again.

He stood at the farmer's market, staring at a crate of heirloom tomatoes, the critic’s damning phrase "bland, uninspired produce" ringing in his ears. Marcus picked up a heavy, bruised Brandywine, turning it over and over. He put it down. He picked up another. His foot tapped a relentless staccato against the damp asphalt. Was this one too firm? Too soft? He pressed his thumbnail into the skin, his breath catching as the juice bled out. "You buying, Chef?" the stall owner asked. Marcus jumped, dropping the fruit back into the crate. He wiped his damp palms on his jeans, suddenly hyper-aware of the sounds of the bustling market, the overlapping voices pressing in on him. He pulled out a crumpled twenty-dollar bill, his fingers trembling as he thrust it toward the vendor. "All of them," he blurted, shifting rapidly from heel to toe.

I stare at the reflection of my face in the polished stainless steel of the pass. The kitchen is quiet, prep complete, but the silence rings in my ears like a siren. Tonight is the first service since the review called my tasting menu "a misguided vanity project." I adjust my apron string, pulling it tight, then untying it, then pulling it tight again. The knot digs into my spine. My stomach churns, rolling over itself like boiling water. I pick up my clipboard, but the daily prep list dances in front of my eyes, the ink blurring into meaningless shapes. Someone drops a pan in the dish pit, and I jolt, the clipboard clattering out of my slick hands onto the tiles. I scramble to pick it up, breathing fast, refusing to meet the eyes of the line cooks staring at me.

Clara dipped her tasting spoon into the simmering beurre blanc. She brought it to her lips, closing her eyes. She reached for the kosher salt, tossing in a heavy pinch. She tasted again. She grabbed the lemon wedge, squeezing until the rind broke against her knuckles. The critic had called her sauces "muddy and confused." Dipping a third spoon, she brought it up to her mouth, but her hand shook, splashing hot butter over her wrist. She didn't register the burn. She stared into the bubbling pot, shifting her weight from side to side. Did it need white pepper? More wine? She pulled a handful of chives from her station and chopped them at lightning speed, the knife blade a blur that narrowly missed her fingertips. Her chest rose and fell in quick, ragged spasms. She threw the herbs out and started chopping another bunch.

The reservation book lies open on the hostess stand, a vast expanse of blank white lines. I drum my fingers against the polished oak, keeping a frantic, irregular beat. Three tables booked for a Friday night. I bite down on my thumbnail, tearing away a ragged strip of cuticle. The taste of copper fills my mouth. The phone rings, and my breath hitches in my throat. I freeze, staring at the flashing red light on the receiver as if it might explode. What if it’s another cancellation? What if they read the Sunday paper, saw the words "overpriced mediocrity," and decided to go elsewhere? The phone rings a second time, louder now. My palms leave damp smudges on the wood. I reach out, my hand hovering an inch above the plastic handset, unable to pick it up, unable to walk away.

The ceiling fan clicked with every rotation. Click. Swoosh. Click. Swoosh. David lay flat on his back, staring into the dark room. He kicked the heavy duvet off his legs, only to pull the thin sheet up to his chin a second later. He rolled onto his side, pressing his face into the pillow, but the glossy magazine spread burned into his retinas. "A tragedy of flavors," the bold font read. He flipped to his back, clutching the mattress edges. He heard his own heartbeat thudding against his ribs in a rapid, hollow drum. Sitting up suddenly, he gasped for air as if the room had emptied of oxygen. He swung his legs over the bed, feet hitting the cold floorboards, and began pacing the narrow carpet strip by the dresser, his hands opening and closing at his sides.

The phone feels slippery against my ear. The investor on the other line is talking about "restructuring" and "rebranding," but the words just sound like buzzing static. I nod into the empty office, my knee bouncing violently under the desk. "Right. Absolutely," I force out, my voice cracking on the second syllable. I clear my throat, dragging a sweaty palm down the leg of my chef pants. The crumpled newspaper clipping sits in the wastebasket, the headline mocking me from the garbage. I push my rolling chair backward, stand up, and immediately sit back down. "We can bounce back from this review," I say, but the sentence rushes out in a breathless tumble. I squeeze my eyes shut and press my fingertips hard against my temples, willing the frantic fluttering in my chest to slow down before it cracks my ribs apart.

When the waiter brought the plate back into the kitchen, Julian stopped breathing. The half-eaten duck breast sat under the harsh fluorescent lights. "Table four says it's too tough," the waiter mumbled, sliding the plate onto the stainless counter. Julian stepped back, knocking a stack of mixing bowls onto the floor with a deafening crash. He didn't bend down to pick them up. His eyes darted from the duck to the ticket, then to the dining room doors. Was the critic back in disguise? He wiped his damp forehead with the back of his sleeve, leaving a smudge of flour on his brow. His jaw locked tight, muscles bulging under his ears. He grabbed the tongs, poking at the meat. His hand trembled so violently the tongs clattered against the ceramic plate. "Fire another duck," he rasped, his voice barely a whisper.

The dining room is dark, save for the streetlight bleeding through the front windows. I scrub the copper sauté pan over the deep sink. The metal is already gleaming, but I press the steel wool down harder, scraping it in tight, aggressive circles. "Pretentious," the reviewer had written. "Lacking soul." I scrub until my shoulders ache and my breathing turns ragged. I drop the pan, the clang echoing through the empty restaurant, making me flinch. I grip the edge of the sink, hanging my head as cold sweat breaks out across my collarbones. I dry my hands on my apron, but they remain damp. Walking to the walk-in fridge, I check the lock, turn away, and immediately spin around to rattle the heavy handle again. I do this three times before I finally step toward the back exit, my keys jangling uncontrollably.

A flash went off in the dining room. Chef Lin peeked through the small porthole window of the kitchen door, rising onto his tiptoes. A customer was photographing the salmon crudo. Lin chewed his bottom lip, tasting blood. The reviewer had decimated the plating of this exact dish just two days ago, comparing it to "a toddler's finger painting." Lin stepped away from the door, paced in a tight circle around the plating station, and returned to the window. He rubbed the back of his neck, slick with perspiration, leaving damp handprints on the door frame. His foot tapped a frantic rhythm against the anti-fatigue mat. The customer took a bite. Lin held his breath, his chest tightening as if wrapped in cellophane. He stared unblinking, waiting to see if the diner's jaw would slow, if their brow would furrow in disgust.

The article from yesterday’s gazette sits folded in my breast pocket, heavy as a stone. I cross out the venison on the spring menu. The paper tears under the pressure of my red pen. I cross out the beet salad. I scribble furiously over the truffle risotto until ink bleeds through to the wooden table of the corner booth. My leg bounces, shaking the entire booth. I have to change everything before tonight's service. Flipping the page to the desserts, my vision swims, letters scrambling into meaningless black shapes. I take a short, gasping breath, trying to fill my lungs, but the air stops dead in the back of my throat. I drop the pen. It rolls off the table onto the floor, and I just stare at it, completely frozen, my ears ringing with the phantom sound of a ticking clock.

I re-tied my shoelaces for the fourth time, pulling the loops so tight the nylon dug into my fingers. The roster sheet on my desk seemed to vibrate under the fluorescent lights. Julian was a good kid, first to arrive, last to leave, but his jump shot just wasn't varsity material. I checked my watch. 3:14 PM. He’d be knocking on the door at 3:15. I stood up, walked to the window, and wiped my sweaty palms on my khakis. I sat back down, then stood right back up. I picked up the red pen, capped it, uncapped it, and threw it into the drawer. How do you look a teenager in the eye and crush his dream? The clock ticked. A soft, hesitant rap sounded against the frosted glass of my office door. My stomach plummeted to my shoes, and I swallowed hard against a throat that felt like sandpaper. "Come in," I rasped.

Coach Miller paced the length of the touchline, his cleats tearing little divots into the turf. He checked his phone. Screen dark. He tapped it against his thigh in a rapid, staccato rhythm. Maya sat on the bench, dutifully lacing her boots for a practice she wouldn't play in. Miller rubbed the back of his neck, feeling a cold prickle of sweat despite the crisp autumn air. He cleared his throat, taking a step toward her, but stopped, abruptly spinning around to inspect the goal net instead. He tugged at the mesh, his jaw clenched so tightly his teeth ached. Maya had the heart of a lion but the footwork of a beginner, and league rules limited the squad to eighteen. He squeezed his eyes shut, inhaling a shallow, jagged breath. Turning back to the bench, he forced his heavy, leaden feet to move forward one agonizing step at a time.

My cleats clicked against the concrete tunnel, echoing too loudly in the empty stadium. Coach had called me in early. I couldn't stop bouncing on the balls of my feet as I stood outside his office, my heart drumming a frantic beat against my ribs. I wiped my hands on my jersey, leaving damp streaks across the fabric. Through the half-open door, I could see him holding the finalized roster, my name conspicuously absent from the starting lineup sheet we’d practiced with yesterday. I gnawed on the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper. Every time I breathed in, my chest felt tight, like someone had wrapped a heavy iron band around my lungs. Just knock, I told myself, but my fist hovered an inch from the wood, trembling. I pulled my hand back, ran it through my hair, and swallowed a lump the size of a baseball.

Elena’s fingers hovered over her mechanical keyboard, trembling just enough to make the RGB lights reflect in a blurry wave. She needed to send the Discord message to David. One simple sentence: We need to talk. She typed the 'W', then furiously hit backspace. She bit her lower lip, peeling away a tiny strip of dry skin. David was the soul of the guild, but his reaction times had plummeted, costing them the qualifiers. Elena minimized the chat window, maximized it, then minimized it again. The steady hum of her PC fan sounded deafening in the quiet room. She grabbed her water bottle, but her grip fumbled, spilling cold droplets onto her mousepad. She cursed under her breath, hastily wiping the mess with her sleeve. Her chest felt tight, her breaths coming in short, shallow puffs as she finally clicked the voice call button, squeezing her eyes shut as it rang.

The chalk dust in the air usually smelled like victory, but today it just made me nauseous. I rolled the small clipboard between my palms, the plastic edge leaving deep red creases in my skin. Sarah was currently on the beam, executing a flawless back handspring, completely unaware that the funding cuts meant we only had room for five girls. I couldn't stop shifting my weight from my left foot to my right, my knees feeling like they were filled with water. I checked my stopwatch, even though I hadn't started it. Five minutes left of practice. I rubbed my temples, trying to push away the pounding headache that had been building since I woke up at 3 AM. I walked toward the mats, stopped, and retreated to the uneven bars. I pulled my whistle off my neck, the cord tangling in my shaky fingers, and put it in my pocket.

Leo sat on the cold tile edge of the pool, his legs dangling in the chlorinated water. Coach Vance had asked him to stay behind. Leo’s right leg bounced uncontrollably, splashing tiny waves against the gutter. He gripped the edge of the pool deck so hard his knuckles turned stark white. Every time Vance glanced up from his clipboard, Leo’s stomach performed a violent flip. He peeled off his swim cap, twisting the silicone tightly around his index finger until the tip throbbed purple, then quickly unraveled it to do it again. The echoing shouts of his teammates leaving the locker room faded into a suffocating silence. Leo kept swallowing, but his mouth was completely dry. He stared at the blue line painted on the bottom of the pool, his breathing turning rapid and shallow. Vance’s heavy footsteps approached, echoing wetly on the tiles, and Leo squeezed his eyes shut.

I poured a third cup of black coffee, though my stomach was already churning acid. The gym echoed with the thud of volleyballs, but all I could hear was the erratic thumping in my own ears. I held the final roster tightly against my chest, shielding the paper as if someone might read it from across the court. Emma was laughing with the setter, her smile bright and infectious. I shifted my gaze to the floorboards, tracing the painted lines with my eyes over and over again. My jaw ached from clenching it all morning. I walked toward the bleachers, then veered off toward the equipment closet, entirely forgetting why I was moving. I grabbed a deflated ball, turning it over in my slick, sweaty hands. Emma was a senior. This was her last chance. I took a deep, jagged breath, tasting the bitter coffee, and forced myself to turn around.

I sat in the plastic chair outside Coach's office, my cleats tapping a frantic rhythm on the linoleum. Thump-thump-thump-thump. The sound was driving me crazy, but I couldn't command my leg to stop bouncing. My hands rested on my knees, completely clammy, smudging dirt onto my game pants. Through the thin drywall, I could hear him shifting papers. My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird trying to escape. I leaned forward, resting my head in my hands, taking quick, uneven breaths that failed to fill my lungs. Yesterday, I dropped three passes. Today, he asked to see me alone. I gnawed on my thumbnail, tearing away a ragged strip of cuticle. A drop of blood welled up, but I barely felt it. The doorknob clicked and slowly turned. I jolted upright, my throat instantly closing up as I stared at the widening gap.

Coach Harris stood behind the plexiglass, scratching furiously at the frost on the glass with his thumbnail. He had completely shredded the edge of his game program. Out on the ice, Tyler was running drills, his skates carving crisp lines into the rink. Harris checked the clock above the scoreboard every ten seconds. He unzipped his heavy jacket, felt a rush of cold air, and immediately zipped it back up to his chin. His stomach roiled, heavy and sour. He reached into his pocket for a piece of gum, but his hand was shaking too much to unwrap the foil, so he shoved it back. Management had demanded a roster trim before the playoffs. Tyler’s brother had just passed away. Harris rubbed his face violently with both hands, leaving red marks across his cheeks. He blew his whistle to end practice, the shrill sound making him flinch.

Mia stood at the edge of the red rubber track, her spikes sinking into the spongy surface. Coach Reynolds had called her over right after the hurdles heat. She wrapped her arms tightly around her torso, her fingertips digging into her own ribs. She shifted her weight from foot to foot, unable to stand still as she watched Reynolds slowly walk toward her, a manila folder clutched in his hand. Mia’s breath hitched in her throat, coming out in tiny, visible white puffs in the cold morning air. She pulled her bottom lip between her teeth and bit down hard. She tried to focus on the distant mountains, but her vision kept snapping back to the folder. Her chest felt like it was encased in a tightening vise. Reynolds stopped two feet away, offering a tight, sorrowful smile, and Mia’s knees suddenly felt as weak as wet paper.

I paced the length of the baseline, picking up stray tennis balls and dropping them into the hopper. One. Two. Three. I counted them aloud, desperate for a distraction. The yellow fuzz felt rough against my damp palms. Across the net, Julian was packing his rackets into his duffel bag. I needed to walk over there before he zipped it up. I took a step forward, but my feet felt encased in concrete. I adjusted my visor, took it off, wiped my forehead, and jammed it back on. My heart pounded a relentless rhythm against my sternum. Julian looked up, catching my eye, and offered a weary wave. I swallowed thickly, my throat clicking in the silence of the empty courts. I grabbed the metal handle of the hopper, my knuckles turning white as I dragged it forward, dreading the conversation waiting for me at the net.

Coach Davies stood on the dock, the wooden planks groaning under his shifting weight. He pulled his stopwatch from his pocket, stared at the blank digital screen, and shoved it back. The eight-man shell glided toward the boathouse, oars lifting in perfect unison. He rubbed his temples in slow, firm circles. Liam was in the bow seat, beaming with exertion. Davies walked to the edge of the dock, then hastily backed away, nearly tripping over a mooring cleat. His stomach twisted into a tight, agonizing knot. The board of directors had cut the scholarship funding, and Liam was the last one in. Davies picked at the skin around his thumbnail until it stung. The crew docked, their laughter echoing over the water. Davies took a sharp, shallow breath, trying to steady his trembling hands by burying them deep into his windbreaker pockets as Liam hopped out onto the wood.

I knew exactly how I had left the little blue leather book on my desk: perfectly aligned with the edge of my laptop. Now, it sat at a crooked angle, the ribbon bookmark dangling outside instead of tucked within the pages. My stomach dropped to the floor, leaving a hollow, echoing cavern behind. Did Chloe read the entry about her boyfriend? My palms grew clammy as I wiped them roughly on my jeans. I paced the narrow gap between our twin beds, chewing on my thumbnail until I tasted copper. Every time the hallway doorknob rattled, a jolt shot up my spine, making me flinch. I rehearsed my defense, the words tangling in my throat. When Chloe finally walked in, carrying two iced coffees and smiling, I could only stare at her, my breathing shallow and fast, waiting for the polite mask to slip.

Marcus stared at the folded piece of notebook paper left carelessly on Liam’s bed. Written in Liam’s scrawl was a quote Marcus recognized instantly—it was a line from his own journal, an entry he had penned at 2 AM about dropping out of pre-med. Marcus’s chest tightened as if a heavy iron band had clamped around his ribs. He immediately dropped to his knees, pulling his storage bin from under the bed. The padlock on his diary was scratched. His hands shook so violently he dropped the key twice before finally testing the lock. It clicked open too easily. He swallowed hard, his mouth tasting like cotton, and backed into the corner of the dorm room. Liam would be back from chemistry lab in ten minutes. Marcus pulled his knees to his chest, tapping his heel against the linoleum at a frantic, erratic tempo.

The dog-eared page was a dead giveaway. I never fold the corners of my journal. I shut the bathroom door, locked it, and sat on the closed toilet lid with the book pressed tightly against my sternum. My heartbeat hammered a frantic rhythm against the cardboard cover. Sarah was out in the living room, humming a pop song while chopping vegetables. Did she see the pages about my eating habits? About the debts? I rubbed the back of my neck, feeling the prickle of sweat at my hairline. I needed a hiding place. Under the mattress was too obvious. Inside a textbook? No, she borrowed those. I looked wildly around the cramped bathroom, my breath coming in short, sharp gasps. I carefully pried off the air vent cover, shoving the book into the dusty shaft before scrubbing my trembling hands under the faucet with scalding water.

Elena watched from the library window as her roommate, Maya, crossed the quad. Maya was holding Elena’s distinct velvet-covered diary, gesturing with it while talking to a friend. A cold rush flooded Elena’s veins, making her fingertips go entirely numb. She backed away from the glass, bumping hard into a bookshelf. The heavy thud made a few students shush her, but Elena couldn’t focus on them. Her eyes darted toward the library exit. She had to intercept Maya. But what would she say? Her mind raced through a dozen excuses, none of them making sense. She grabbed her backpack, the zipper snagging as she yanked it with uncoordinated, jerky movements. Taking the stairs two at a time, Elena’s chest heaved. She bit down hard on her lower lip, tasting salt, praying she could reach the courtyard before Maya opened the book again.

The digital clock flashed 3:14 AM. I lay perfectly rigid on my top bunk, staring at the glow-in-the-dark stars plastered to the ceiling. Below me, Greg snored softly, entirely at peace. I gripped the edge of my blanket, twisting the fabric around my knuckles until they turned white. Before turning out the lights, I had noticed a smudge of blue ink on Greg’s index finger. It was the exact shade of the fountain pen I used exclusively in my private notebook—the notebook I kept hidden in my sock drawer. My throat felt incredibly tight. Every time Greg shifted in his sleep, my heart leaped into my throat, convinced he was waking up to confront me about the things I had written. I spent the hours counting my own rapid, shallow breaths, desperately mapping out a plan to switch dorms by the end of the week.

"You know," Julian said, casually stirring his ramen, "sometimes you just have to embrace the 'beautiful disaster' of it all." Sam froze, his spoon hovering inches from his mouth. That exact phrase—beautiful disaster—was the title of yesterday’s journal entry, an entry about Sam’s estranged father. Sam’s stomach lurched violently, as if he had just crested the peak of a roller coaster. He slowly lowered his spoon, suddenly nauseous. He stared intensely at the grain of the cheap wooden desk, afraid to meet Julian’s eyes. A cold prickle spread down Sam’s arms. He tapped his left foot against the chair leg in a rapid, involuntary staccato. "Yeah," Sam managed to squeak out, his voice cracking midway. He abruptly pushed his chair back, the legs screeching against the floor, and grabbed his jacket. "I need some air," he muttered, practically sprinting out the door.

I was packing my duffel bag for winter break when I saw it. My leather-bound diary was sitting on top of Jenna’s laundry pile, far from my own desk. My ears started ringing, a high-pitched whine that drowned out the upbeat holiday music playing from our shared speaker. I snatched the book up, my hands fluttering like trapped birds. The clasp was undone. She had read it. She knew everything. I shoved the diary deep into my bag, zipping it shut with aggressive force. I began pacing the tiny dorm, my mind spinning a hundred miles a minute. I checked my phone—Jenna would be back from her final exam in twenty minutes. I couldn't face her. I grabbed my coats, stuffed my electronics haphazardly into my tote bag, and fled down the hallway, glancing over my shoulder every few seconds until I reached the safety of my car.

When Clara flipped open her moleskine to write her evening reflection, a neon pink sticky note fell into her lap. "We need to talk about page 42," the handwriting read. It was unmistakably her roommate’s looping script. Clara stopped breathing. Page forty-two detailed her intense crush on her roommate’s brother. A wave of heat rushed to her face, followed instantly by an icy chill that made her teeth chatter. She clutched the sticky note, crumpling it into a tiny ball until her fingernails dug painfully into her palm. She stood up, then sat down again, entirely unable to keep still. Her eyes darted to the dorm room door, expecting the handle to turn at any second. Clara began to gather her things, tossing clothes wildly into a laundry basket, desperate for any excuse to be out of the room when the inevitable knock came.

We were sitting across from each other in the study lounge. Mark was highlighting his biology text, while I pretended to read my sociology notes. Earlier, I had found a stray blonde hair—Mark’s hair—pressed neatly between the pages of my private logbook. Now, the silence between us felt thick and suffocating, like breathing through a heavy wool blanket. I kept shifting in my seat, crossing and uncrossing my legs, unable to find a comfortable position. Every time Mark sighed or turned a page, my muscles coiled tighter, bracing for impact. I chewed the inside of my cheek until it felt raw and tasted like blood. I needed to use the restroom, but leaving meant turning my back on him. I just kept my eyes glued to the blurry text of my textbook, waiting for the bomb to drop, my leg bouncing incessantly under the table.

Through the crack in the door, Aisha saw her roommate, Beth, sitting cross-legged on the floor, deeply engrossed in a familiar green spiral notebook. Aisha’s breath hitched. She shrank back into the dim hallway corridor, pressing her spine flat against the cinderblock wall. Her hands were slick with cold perspiration. She rubbed them furiously against her thighs, leaving damp streaks on her sweatpants. Beth was reading the entry about the stolen exam answers. Aisha felt a sudden, intense urge to vomit. She squeezed her eyes shut, fighting a wave of dizziness, and tried to regulate her jagged, uneven breathing. She crept quietly backward, her sneakers squeaking faintly on the linoleum, terrified that the slight noise would alert Beth. Aisha reached the stairwell and bolted downward, desperately putting distance between herself and the dorm room before Beth could turn another page.

I unlocked the door to our suite and stopped dead in my tracks. My private, leather-bound journal was sitting wide open on Tyler’s desk. Tyler was in the shower; I could hear the water running. My pulse thumped against my temples so hard it gave me an instant headache. I tiptoed closer, wincing at every creak of the floorboards. It was open to the page where I confessed my struggles with my mental health. A profound coldness washed over me. I grabbed the book, my hands trembling violently, and fumbled to shove it into my backpack. The shower turned off. My heart hammered wildly against my ribs. I practically ripped the zipper of my bag closed, my breath coming in rapid, shallow gasps. I threw myself onto my bed, pretending to be asleep, squeezing my eyes shut as Tyler walked into the room.

The bass from the speakers vibrated through the floorboards, but Leo barely felt it. His roommate, Derek, was standing by the keg, telling a group of girls a "funny hypothetical story" that matched Leo’s most secretive diary entry down to the finest detail. Leo stood frozen by the chips, a plastic cup of soda crumpling under his tightening grip. Liquid spilled over his knuckles, but he didn't wipe it away. His chest rose and fell in rapid, shallow bursts. He desperately scanned the crowded room for the nearest exit, but the front door was blocked by a throng of dancing students. He wiped his sweaty forehead with the back of his trembling arm. If Derek mentioned the ending of the story, everyone would know. Leo abandoned his drink, pushed roughly past a couple making out, and practically broke into a run toward the back patio.

My fork scraped against the porcelain plate, a sound that seemed to echo in the sudden vacuum of the dining room. Elias had just set down his glass of water and quietly mentioned his shahada. I kept my eyes fixed on my half-eaten mashed potatoes, tracing a little moat in them with the tines of my fork. My foot tapped a frantic rhythm against the leg of my chair. What would Dad say? I sneaked a glance at the head of the table, my throat suddenly tight and completely devoid of moisture. Would there be shouting? Would Elias be asked to leave? I pressed my thumb hard into my index finger, focusing on the sharp pinch to stop the room from spinning. The silence stretched out, thin and brittle like spun sugar, ready to shatter into a million jagged pieces at the slightest breath.

Claire’s breath hitched, caught somewhere between her ribs. Her mother sat gracefully on the edge of the floral sofa, hands folded, calmly explaining the refuge ceremony she attended last week. Claire gripped the hem of her sweater, her thumb relentlessly rubbing the frayed wool until the friction burned her skin. She scanned the living room—the crucifix above the mantle, the heavy family Bible resting on the coffee table. Her heart hammered against her sternum like a trapped bird. How was Grandma going to react at Easter? The thought triggered a sudden wave of heat rushing up the back of Claire's neck. She tried to swallow, but her mouth tasted like pennies. She nodded at her mother's serene smile, but beneath her ribs, a swarm of agitated bees buzzed relentlessly, making it impossible to sit entirely still. She crossed and uncrossed her legs, staring at the floorboards.

Mark’s hands were steady as he held his latte, explaining the mikveh and his weekly meetings with the rabbi. Meanwhile, I was tearing my paper napkin into progressively smaller shreds, piling the white confetti onto the small wooden table. My pulse drummed a rapid, frantic beat in my ears, drowning out the ambient jazz playing overhead. If he became observant, what did that mean for us? For the future we had outlined on a napkin just like the one I was currently destroying? I forced myself to take a breath, but it only reached the top of my chest. My jaw ached from how hard I was clenching my teeth. I wanted to ask a dozen questions, but the words bottlenecked in my throat. I just kept nodding, my eyes darting from his calm face to the pile of torn paper, my leg bouncing under the table.

The windshield wipers slapped back and forth, a metronome to the drumming of David’s fingers on the steering wheel. In the passenger seat, Chloe held up her new silver pentacle necklace, cheerfully discussing her solstice plans. David felt a cold bead of sweat slide down his spine. He checked the rearview mirror, then the side mirror, then the speedometer, unable to let his gaze rest in one place. His stomach churned as if he had swallowed a handful of gravel. Would the school administration give her trouble? What about his conservative parents coming for Thanksgiving next month? He gripped the steering wheel so tightly his knuckles turned a stark, bloodless white. Every time Chloe paused, waiting for his validation, David swallowed hard against a lump in his throat, offering a clipped, breathless response while his eyes darted frantically across the slick, rain-soaked asphalt ahead.

The wooden porch swing creaked rhythmically, though I felt anything but peaceful. Grandpa handed me the beautifully bound copy of the Bhagavad Gita, his eyes twinkling with a newfound lightness. I took the book, my palms uncomfortably damp against the cover. I found myself repeatedly adjusting my glasses, pushing them up the bridge of my nose every few seconds. Our family had been staunchly Presbyterian for five generations. My mind raced ahead to Sunday service, visualizing the empty space in the third pew, imagining Pastor Miller’s pointed questions. I tapped my heel against the wooden deck, a rapid thumping that I couldn't seem to control. A sour, heavy sensation settled deep in my gut. I tried to formulate a supportive sentence, but I just kept licking my dry lips, my eyes darting toward the screen door to see if anyone else had heard him.

A plate slipped from Sarah’s hands, clattering loudly against the sink basin, though thankfully it didn't break. "Rome?" she squeaked, her voice an octave higher than normal. Leo leaned against the counter, calmly explaining the RCIA classes. Sarah grabbed a dish towel, aggressively drying the same already-dry mug over and over again. Her chest rose and fell in quick, shallow bursts. She thought of their fiercely Protestant grandmother, whose portrait hung in the hallway, practically glaring at them. A faint ringing started in Sarah’s ears. She paced the length of the narrow kitchen, her bare feet slapping against the linoleum. Four steps to the fridge, four steps to the oven. Turn. Repeat. She bit the inside of her cheek until she tasted the metallic tang of blood, desperately trying to map out a strategy to keep Leo and Aunt Martha in separate rooms during the upcoming Christmas dinner.

Maya sat cross-legged on her dorm bed, showing me the silver Kara she now wore on her wrist. I sat at my desk, violently clicking my pen. Click-click. Click-click. The sound mirrored the erratic thumping against my ribs. "So, you're going to the Gurdwara every week?" I asked, my voice cracking slightly. I spun my chair back and forth, unable to keep my body still. Mom and Dad were visiting this weekend. They expected us both at Sunday mass. My mouth felt full of cotton. I imagined the impending dinner conversation, the silence, the dropped silverware. I rubbed my hands up and down my denim-clad thighs, trying to wipe away the clammy sweat. My breathing was so fast I felt lightheaded. I kept staring at the polished steel bracelet, my mind spinning a chaotic web of impending family arguments and shattered holiday traditions.

Elena stared at the laptop screen, her son’s bearded face pixelating slightly as he proudly displayed his new prayer rope. She gripped the edge of the mahogany desk, her fingernails biting into the polished wood. Her heart fluttered uncomfortably in her throat, making it difficult to swallow. "That's... beautiful, sweetheart," she managed to say, though her chest felt tight, as if invisible bands were wrapped around her ribs. She glanced quickly at the door, ensuring her husband hadn't walked in. Her leg jiggled under the desk, vibrating the floorboards. She reached for her water, but her hand was trembling so much that the ice clinked noisily against the glass. She quickly set it back down. What would the rest of their congregation say? She bit her lower lip, tasting her lipstick, her eyes darting across the screen without truly focusing on her son's smiling face.

The crisp autumn air usually settled my mind, but today I couldn't stop shivering, and it wasn't from the cold. Jake sat beside me on the park bench, explaining his recent baptism into the LDS church. I dug my hands deep into my coat pockets, balling them into tight fists until my fingernails dug half-moons into my palms. I nodded along, but a loud buzzing filled my ears. I kept scanning the park, watching a pigeon peck at the concrete, unable to hold eye contact with him for more than a second. My breath puffed out in rapid, shallow white clouds. Our family was fiercely protective of their traditions. Aunt Sylvia was going to lose her mind. I bounced my knee relentlessly against the wooden slats of the bench. I wanted to leap up and start walking, anything to burn off the sudden, electric energy coursing uncomfortably through my veins.

Arthur paced the length of the sterile waiting room corridor, exactly twelve steps from the water cooler to the vending machine. Turn. Twelve steps back. His brother sat calmly in the plastic chair, having just announced his refusal of future blood transfusions due to his new faith. Arthur rubbed his temples, where a sharp, pulsing headache had suddenly blossomed. His stomach flipped, acidic and hot. He checked his watch, though he had just looked at it thirty seconds prior. He unbuttoned his collar, feeling as though the room had lost half its oxygen. Every time a nurse walked past, Arthur flinched, his heart galloping against his ribs. He imagined medical emergencies, forms, arguments with doctors. He stopped pacing and leaned against the cool cinderblock wall, closing his eyes tightly. He took short, ragged gasps of air, his hands buried deep in his pockets, fingers endlessly twisting his car keys.

Sarah pulled a small quartz crystal from her purse, placing it delicately next to her wine glass. As she talked about energy alignment and her new spiritual guide, I shredded my paper coaster into microscopic pieces. My chest felt like it had been strapped tightly in a corset. I glanced around the crowded restaurant, inexplicably convinced that the people at the next table were eavesdropping. I took a gulp of my ice water, but the lump in my throat wouldn't budge. My heel tapped a frantic, silent rhythm on the carpeted floor. What if she wanted to change our daily routines? What if she expected me to join her? A cold sweat prickled along my hairline. I kept adjusting my watch strap, loosening it, then tightening it again. I forced a smile, but my jaw was clamped so tight my teeth ground together.

When her father announced he was taking precepts at the Zen center, Jenna accidentally snapped the stem of her wine glass. The delicate crystal shattered onto the patio stones. She dropped to her knees, gathering the jagged shards with reckless speed, ignoring his gentle insistence to let him get a broom. Her pulse pounded so loudly in her ears it drowned out the evening cicadas. She scraped her knees against the rough concrete, her breath coming in tiny, hitched gasps. How was Mom going to handle this? Mom, who led the church choir every Sunday? Jenna’s hands shook so violently that a piece of glass slipped, slicing a neat red line across her thumb. She didn't feel the sting. She just kept staring at the blood, her chest rising and falling rapidly as she envisioned the explosive argument bound to echo through the house tonight.

I watched my brother trace the ornate mahogany of Grandpa’s grandfather clock, his eyes calculating a price tag. My leg bounced under the dining table, the heel of my shoe tapping a rapid, erratic rhythm against the hardwood. "It would pay for the roof," he said casually. I swallowed hard, but my mouth felt like it was stuffed with cotton. My fingers shredded a paper napkin into microscopic confetti, my pulse hammering so loudly in my ears I could barely hear the clock’s familiar ticking. If he sold it, the house would be completely silent. I pictured the empty corner in the hallway, the gaping void where our history had stood for eighty years, and a cold sweat broke out across my neck. "Let's just... let's look at the budget again," I managed to say, my voice cracking on the last syllable.

Elena paced the parlor, her slippers wearing a familiar path into the Persian rug. On the velvet settee, her aunt held the sapphire pendant to the afternoon light, murmuring about auction houses. Elena’s fingernails dug into her palms, leaving deep crescent-moon indentations. She couldn't sit down. Every time she tried, a tight coil in her chest wound a fraction tighter, making it difficult to draw a full breath. She kept glancing at the front door, then back to the gleaming blue stone. What if the appraiser arrived today? What if they took it right out of her aunt's hands? She adjusted the collar of her blouse, feeling as though the room had grown ten degrees hotter. "Are you absolutely certain we have to do this right now?" she asked, her words rushing out in a breathless tumble.

My sister slapped the hood of Dad’s 1969 Mustang, a bright smile on her face as she talked to the guy from the dealership. I stood ten feet away, violently chewing the inside of my cheek until I tasted the sharp tang of copper. The keys were heavy in my pocket, burning against my thigh. I kept shifting my weight from left to right, unable to lock my knees. Every time the dealer nodded, my stomach did a sickening flip. I ran a hand through my hair, realizing I’d already done it so many times my scalp was tender. If she signed the title over, it was gone forever. I took a shallow breath, feeling a flutter in my ribcage like a trapped bird. "Just one more week," I blurted out, stepping between them. "Give me one week to find the money."

Marcus stared at the laptop screen over his husband’s shoulder, watching the cursor hover over the 'List Item' button. His mother’s vintage lace wedding gown lay perfectly pressed in its preservation box on the bed behind them. Marcus’s knee jackhammered up and down, rattling the small desk. He kept wiping his damp palms on his jeans, leaving dark streaks across the denim. "It’s just taking up space," David reasoned gently, but Marcus barely heard him over the rush of blood in his ears. He imagined a stranger cutting the delicate French lace, altering the bodice, erasing his mother's memory. He swallowed, but his throat was bone dry. He reached out, his hand hovering over David’s, his fingers trembling slightly. "Wait," Marcus croaked, his eyes darting wildly between the glowing screen and the white box. "Don't click it yet. Please, just don't click it."

I kept refreshing my email, pulling the screen down with a sweaty thumb every three seconds. My cousin had taken our great-grandfather’s WWII diary to a rare book dealer downtown, and I was waiting for the verdict. My foot tapped a rapid beat against the subway floor, drawing an annoyed look from the woman beside me. I couldn't stop picking at the cuticle of my thumb until it bled. The thought of those fragile, tear-stained pages being bartered away made my chest feel like it was bound in tight iron bands. I typed a text to him: Did you do it? Then I deleted it. Then I typed it again. My breathing grew shallow and rapid, the stale air of the train car suddenly feeling impossibly thin. Every time my phone buzzed with a spam notification, I jumped, my heart leaping into my throat.

Sarah watched her father lay the deed to the lakeside cabin on the oak table. She immediately began twisting her silver ring round and round her finger, the metal biting into her skin. She couldn’t keep her eyes on the document, her gaze darting to the window, the floor, the ticking clock, and back to the paper. "The developers are offering double," her father said. Sarah’s stomach clenched into a hard, cold knot. She took a sip of water, but couldn't force it past the lump in her throat. She stood up, then immediately sat back down, smoothing her skirt with jerky, uncoordinated movements. The walls of the dining room seemed to inch closer together. "But the summers," she whispered rapidly, her words stumbling over one another. "What about the summers? Where will we go? You can't just sign it."

The appraisers were walking around my grandmother’s Steinway, making notes on their clipboards. My aunt stood by the fireplace, proudly discussing its mint condition. I pressed my back hard against the hallway wall, trying to ground myself, but my knees felt like water. I dug my fingernails into the plaster, my gaze locked on the piano keys. I kept imagining the lid slamming shut for the last time. A wave of nausea rolled through me, and I pressed the heel of my hand against my forehead, which was suddenly slick with cold perspiration. I wanted to scream, to throw myself over the mahogany lid, but my jaw was locked completely tight. My pulse pounded against my temples in a rapid rhythm. I took a half-step forward, my chest heaving with quick, shallow gasps, eager to interrupt them before they finalized a number.

Liam hovered near the doorway of his brother's study, watching him polish the silver hilt of the Revolutionary War cavalry sword. Liam’s hands were stuffed deep in his pockets, his fists clenched so tightly his knuckles ached. He rocked back and forth on his heels, shifting his weight constantly. "A collector from Boston wants it," his brother murmured without looking up. Liam felt a sudden drop in his gut, like stepping off a stair that wasn't there. He paced three steps to the left, then three steps to the right. He wanted to speak, but he avoided it, knowing his voice would betray the violent tremor shaking his chest. He rubbed his face vigorously with both hands, trying to rub away the image of the sword leaving the house in a cardboard shipping tube. "Are you absolutely sure?" Liam asked, his voice cracking horribly.

"It's just an old blanket," my daughter said, folding the patchwork quilt into a plastic bin. "The boutique owner will pay five hundred for it." I watched her hands move, my own hands trembling so violently I had to sit on them to hide the shaking. The quilt had been made from the scraps of my mother's dresses. A cold prickle washed over my scalp. I bit my lower lip until I tasted blood, staring blindly at the plastic lid as she snapped it shut. Each click of the container felt like a physical blow to my ribs. I couldn't drag enough air into my lungs. My eyes darted around the living room, searching for something else I could offer her to sell instead. "I'll write you a check," I blurted, my voice shrill and way too loud. "I'll write you a check right now."

Chloe watched her uncle snap the gold pocket watch shut. The tiny metallic click echoed in the quiet pawn shop. Chloe’s heart hammered against her ribs like a trapped moth. She gripped the edge of the glass display counter, her knuckles turning bone-white under the fluorescent lights. The pawnbroker pulled out a stack of hundred-dollar bills, and Chloe’s breath hitched. She shifted her weight from foot to foot, her eyes darting between the cash and her grandfather’s watch. She wanted to snatch the timepiece and run. A drop of sweat rolled down the back of her neck, and her stomach twisted into a series of tight, agonizing knots. She chewed furiously on the inside of her cheek. When her uncle reached out to take the money, Chloe gasped, her hand shooting out to grab his wrist with a sudden, crushing grip.

My uncle pointed at the oil painting of our great-grandmother, negotiating a price with the gallery curator. I stood by the door, picking mercilessly at a loose thread on my sweater until the hem began to unravel. My mouth tasted like dry chalk. I tried to take a deep breath, but my chest felt completely rigid, locked in place by a heavy, invisible weight. I kept checking my watch, though I had nowhere to be. The seconds ticked by agonizingly slow. If that painting left our family, the last visual link to our heritage vanished with it. My legs felt hollow, like they might buckle at any second. I paced to the window, stared blindly at the street, and paced back to the door. "Can we just wait a day?" I interrupted, the words tumbling out of my mouth in a hurried, breathless rush.

In the bright kitchen, Rosa’s sister was photographing their grandmother’s leather-bound recipe book for an online auction. Rosa stood at the island, rapidly tearing a paper towel into tiny, identical squares. Her gaze flickered repeatedly to the flashing camera lens. Every bright burst of light made her flinch, sending a jolt of electricity down her spine. She kept swallowing, trying to clear the severe tightness in her throat. The thought of a stranger owning the handwritten notes and flour-dusted pages made her head spin dizzily. She gripped the edge of the marble counter to steady herself, her palms leaving sweaty handprints on the stone. She wanted to yell at her sister to stop, but her mind was racing too fast to form a coherent sentence. Rosa squeezed her eyes shut, her breathing shallow and ragged, listening to the relentless clicking of the camera shutter.

The flashlight beam trembled against the dusty floorboards, casting long, erratic shadows across the attic. Arthur stood frozen before the stack of unmarked trunks tucked beneath the eaves. He wiped a damp palm on his jeans, leaving a streak of dust, and swallowed hard against the lump forming in his throat. The previous owners were supposed to have cleared everything out. Why hadn't they? He took half a step back toward the pull-down stairs, his pulse thrumming loudly in his ears. What if there was a reason they abandoned these heavy wooden crates? His eyes darted to the small, rusted padlock on the nearest trunk. A sharp creak sounded from the house settling below, and Arthur flinched, almost dropping the flashlight as his breath hitched. He couldn't bring himself to step any closer.

I chewed on the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper, staring down at the scatter of black-and-white photographs covering the attic floor. I only came up here to check the insulation. Now, I found myself pacing the narrow space between the exposed joists, my heart hammering a frantic rhythm against my ribs. The faces in the pictures all had the eyes scratched out with violent, deep grooves. I checked my phone—no signal. I checked it again three seconds later. Nothing. The air up here felt entirely too thin, and the dust coated my throat like sandpaper. Why would the Millers leave this behind? Did they know it was up here? I rubbed my temples, trying to slow the relentless spinning of my thoughts, but the scratching sound of a branch against the roof made me jump out of my skin.

Maya’s fingernails dug crescents into the wooden frame of the attic hatch. She stood halfway up the ladder, her knuckles entirely white, staring at the dozen porcelain dolls arranged in a perfect semi-circle around a child’s rocking chair. A bead of cold sweat trailed slowly down the back of her neck. She had asked the real estate agent three times if the house was completely empty, and he had promised it was. Her breathing grew shallow and rapid, each inhale catching high in her chest. The glassy eyes of the dolls seemed to catch the faint sliver of moonlight filtering through the cracked vent. She didn’t climb the rest of the way up. Instead, she kept her gaze locked on the rocking chair, lowering herself down one excruciatingly slow rung at a time, convinced that if she blinked, something in the shadows might move.

The rolled-up parchment slipped from my clammy fingers and snapped back into a tight tube. I pressed the heels of my hands against my eyes, taking quick, uneven breaths, but the image of the map was already burned into my brain. The previous tenants had left a detailed schematic of the neighborhood, and my new house was circled heavily in red ink, with arrows pointing toward the crawlspace and the attic where I currently crouched. I stood up too quickly, cracking my skull against a low beam, but I barely felt the pain over the loud rushing sound in my ears. I scrambled toward the trapdoor, nearly tripping over a loose floorboard. I needed to get downstairs. I needed to check the deadbolts. Were the windows locked? I couldn't remember if I had secured the latch on the kitchen window before coming upstairs.

Elias knelt in the suffocating heat of the attic, staring at the vintage leather suitcase tucked into the darkest corner. He hadn't touched it yet. He just hovered his hand an inch above the brass latches, his fingers trembling so violently that they blurred in the dim light. A rhythmic, muffled sound echoed from inside the leather casing. Tick. Tick. Tick. He yanked his hand back, pressing it flat against his chest to feel the frantic drumming of his own heart. He looked over his shoulder, ensuring the path to the ladder was clear. "Just an old clock," he whispered to the empty room, but his voice cracked, betraying him. He shifted his weight, and the floorboards groaned underfoot. The ticking seemed to grow louder, matching the rapid, shallow gasps escaping his lips as he retreated toward the square of light in the floor.

I kept tapping my foot against the top rung of the ladder, unable to force myself fully into the attic. Lined up along the exposed beams were dozens of mason jars filled with murky, dark liquid. I pulled my phone out of my pocket, dialed my sister's number, then hung up before it even rang. I dialed it again. Hung up again. What was I supposed to say? My throat felt incredibly tight. The air up here smelled metallic and sweet, like old rust and rotting fruit, making my stomach churn in tight circles. I shoved my hands into my pockets to hide their shaking, keeping my eyes fixed on the jars. Were those teeth at the bottom of the third one? My knee started bouncing uncontrollably. I needed to shut the hatch. I needed to seal it, nail it shut, and pretend I never opened it.

The soft hiss of static crackled through the dusty air. Clara froze, the cardboard box of Christmas decorations slipping from her grasp and spilling onto the floorboards. Tucked behind the chimney breast sat a massive, ancient radio transmitter. The green light on its dial glowed faintly, illuminating the dark corner. Clara gnawed on the edge of her thumbnail, her eyes darting from the glowing dial to the single wire trailing up toward the roof. The previous owners moved out six months ago. The power to the attic was supposed to be cut. She took two quick, jerky steps backward, her chest rising and falling in rapid succession. The static suddenly shifted, replaced by a low, rhythmic scratching noise broadcasting through the speaker. Clara spun around, abandoning the decorations entirely, and scrambled toward the staircase, her footfalls loud and frantic against the wood.

The moment the flashlight beam hit the garment bag hanging from the rafter, a cold shiver violently rocketed down my spine. I squeezed my eyes shut, counted to three, and opened them again, but the shape was still there. I took a hesitant step closer, my boots feeling like they were cast in lead. Inside the translucent plastic was a wedding dress heavily stained with black soot, alongside a tiny, ash-covered baby blanket. I backed away, my shoulder blades hitting a wooden support beam. The air conditioning wasn't routed up here, yet I couldn't stop my teeth from chattering. I wrapped my arms tightly around my torso, rubbing my elbows, trying to generate some kind of warmth. Why would anyone leave this? I backed blindly toward the stairs, never taking my eyes off the plastic bag, wishing I had never bought this house.

Marcus rubbed the back of his neck, his fingers slick with sweat despite the drafty chill of the attic. A heavy iron safe sat in the center of the room, completely out of place among the scattered insulation and dust bunnies. He unzipped his jacket, zipped it back up, and then aggressively ran a hand through his hair. The real estate listing mentioned the house was sold as-is from an estate after a sudden disappearance. He walked a tight circle around the heavy iron box, his gaze fixed on the dial. Every time he stopped moving, his foot began a rapid, involuntary tapping against the floorboards. He licked his lips, but his mouth was completely dry. If he called a locksmith, what exactly would they find inside? His chest felt like it was wrapped in tight iron bands just looking at the rusted combination lock.

I clamped my hand over my own mouth to stifle the sound of my breathing. Tucked behind a stack of old storm windows was a sleeping bag, rumpled and flattened. Beside it sat three empty cans of soup and a crumpled candy bar wrapper. The wrapper looked shiny. New. Not something left behind by the couple who sold me the house two years ago. My eyes strained against the dim lighting, darting wildly toward the shadowed corners of the pitched roof. I slowly lowered the flashlight, sure that the beam would act as a beacon. The floorboards above the master bedroom groaned—a sound I usually blamed on the house settling. My knees felt entirely weak, like water. I didn't turn my back to the shadows as I slid toward the trapdoor, feeling blindly with my heel for the first rung of the ladder.

The bare bulb hanging from the ceiling flickered, casting a sickly yellow glow over the far wall. Leo dropped the box of books he was carrying. The cardboard hit the floor with a heavy thud, bursting open, but he didn't even glance down. He stared at the wooden planks of the attic wall, which were plastered with hundreds of printed photographs and newspaper clippings. His pulse pounded fiercely in his temples, almost deafening him. He stumbled forward, his hands flying to his head, fingers pulling rigidly at his hair. Every single photograph was of him. Walking his dog, getting coffee, sitting on his previous apartment's balcony. He spun around in a full circle, his chest heaving, scanning the empty, dusty space. He rushed toward the stairs, practically throwing himself down the ladder, his hands slipping on the rungs as he scrambled for the safety of the ground floor.

My thumb smeared the dusty ink on the final page of the leather-bound journal. I couldn't stop flipping the pages, reading the erratic, messy handwriting faster and faster. The previous owner had filled three notebooks detailing how the architecture of the house seemed to shift when no one was looking, how the hallways stretched in the dark. I slammed the book shut, dropping it onto the floorboards as if it had burned my fingers. I wiped my sweaty palms violently against my jeans. The silence of the attic pressed heavily against my ears, thick and suffocating. I stared at the doorframe leading back to the stairs. Did it look narrower than when I climbed up here? I swallowed the dry lump in my throat, my chest rising and falling in quick, shallow hitches. I practically lunged for the exit, needing to see if the staircase remained unchanged.

The neighbor’s casual comment about "what happened in the master bath" echoed in my head. I sat on the edge of the sofa, peeling a hangnail until it bled. The digital clock blinked 2:14 AM. Every time the ice maker dropped a cube, my shoulders hitched toward my ears. I kept my eyes fixed on the hallway leading to the bathroom, my breathing shallow and quick. I hadn't gone in there since the conversation over the fence. My bladder ached, but the thought of crossing that threshold made my stomach twist into tight knots. I wrapped the throw blanket around my shoulders, shivering despite the thermostat reading seventy-two degrees, and waited for the sunrise.

Elias pressed his forehead against the cold glass of the living room window, his fingers drumming a frantic, irregular beat on the sill. The yellowed newspaper clipping he had found beneath the attic floorboards sat on the coffee table, its bold headline burning into his mind. He turned away, walking briskly to the front door to jiggle the deadbolt for the fourth time in ten minutes. Satisfied it was locked, he marched to the back door, testing that one too. The floorboards creaked under his slippers, a sound he had found charming yesterday, but now made the hair on his arms stand upright. He wiped a bead of sweat from his upper lip, his eyes darting toward the basement stairs.

The true crime documentary played softly, but the narrator’s voice felt like a physical blow. That was my kitchen island on the screen. Those were my custom cabinets. The remote slipped from my clammy palms, clattering onto the hardwood. My heart battered against my ribs like a trapped bird. I swallowed hard, but my mouth was entirely devoid of moisture. Slowly, my gaze drifted from the television to the exact spot on the rug where the chalk outline had been drawn in the broadcast. I pulled my knees to my chest, wrapping my arms tightly around my shins. The refrigerator hummed, and I flinched, my eyes wide, scanning the empty corners of the room for shadows that shouldn't be there.

"It’s amazing how well they cleaned up the basement after the tragedy," the plumber muttered, packing up his wrenches. Sarah watched him leave, her jaw clamped so tightly her teeth ached. The moment his van pulled out of the driveway, she sprinted to the kitchen and grabbed the largest chef’s knife from the block. Her chest heaved, taking in rapid, insufficient gulps of air. She crept toward the basement door, her bare feet silent on the linoleum. Pressing her ear against the painted wood, she strained to listen over the rushing sound of blood in her own ears. The washing machine beeped from downstairs, and Sarah leaped backward, dropping the knife with a loud clatter, clutching her chest.

I typed my new address into the search engine on a whim, expecting property value history. Instead, the first result was a ten-year-old police report. I slammed the laptop shut so hard the hinge cracked. I pushed my chair back, the legs screeching against the floor, and began pacing the length of the study. My thumbnail found its way between my teeth, and I gnawed on it, tasting copper. The house, usually so peaceful, suddenly felt entirely too large. A draft brushed the back of my neck, raising goosebumps along my spine. I darted to the hallway, flipping every light switch I could find until the entire ground floor blazed with artificial daylight, but the shadows still seemed to cling to the baseboards.

The historical society representative handed Marcus the brass plaque, cheerfully explaining the grisly events of 1892 that earned the cottage its landmark status. Marcus took the heavy metal plate, his hands vibrating so much the edges blurred. He thanked the woman, closing the door and leaning his full weight against it. His chest rose and fell in jerky, staccato movements. He stared at the dark stain on the original oak floorboards near the fireplace—a stain the realtor had assured him was just water damage from a leaky roof. He rubbed his hands up and down his forearms, feeling a sudden, icy chill. He walked backward into the kitchen, refusing to turn his back on the fireplace.

The letter was addressed to 'The Estate of the Butcher.' I dropped the envelope onto the welcome mat like it was searing hot. I wiped my palms vigorously against my jeans, trying to scrub away an invisible grime. Backing into the entryway, I locked the door and slid the chain into place. My pulse thumped heavily in the hollow of my throat. I stood frozen in the foyer, straining to catch any sound from the upper floor. A floorboard settled overhead with a sharp pop. I gasped, pressing my back flat against the wall. I reached blindly into my pocket for my phone, my fingers fumbling with the screen, ready to dial emergency services if the stairs even creaked.

Elena scrubbed the bathtub grout with a toothbrush, her knuckles white around the plastic handle. The elderly neighbor had mentioned the previous owner’s gruesome end just twenty minutes ago over the hedge. Elena scrubbed faster, the bristles fraying against the porcelain. She couldn't catch her breath; the bathroom suddenly felt like a sealed box. She stopped, staring at a faint, rusty discoloration near the drain. Her stomach pitched forward, acid rising in her throat. She scrambled backward on her hands and knees until her back hit the bathroom door. She pulled her phone from her pocket with trembling fingers, dropping it twice on the bathmat before finally opening a hotel booking app.

I was just trying to plant some hydrangeas when my trowel hit the yellow police tape buried six inches deep. I left the trowel in the dirt and stumbled backward, tripping over the garden hose. I scrambled to my feet, brushing soil off my knees with erratic, jerky sweeps of my hands. I rushed inside, locking the sliding glass door and yanking the curtains shut so violently the rod nearly snapped. I paced between the kitchen island and the sofa, my teeth chattering despite the summer heat. Every few seconds, I peeked through a tiny slit in the blinds, staring at the freshly dug hole in the yard, expecting something to crawl out of the loose earth.

The detective stood on the porch, flipping through a small notebook, asking if anyone had come by looking for the "evidence." David shook his head, his vocal cords paralyzed. As the officer drove away, David locked the deadbolt, the chain, and the new sliding bolt he had installed yesterday. He walked through the house, double-checking the locks on the windows, testing each latch with a firm tug. His palms left sweaty prints on the glass. He sat in the armchair facing the front door, a heavy iron fireplace poker resting across his lap. The grandfather clock ticked loudly, and David flinched at each chime, his eyes wide and unblinking in the fading evening light.

Discovering the truth about the basement changed the air in the house. It felt thicker now. I stood at the top of the cellar stairs, my hand hovering an inch over the light switch. I needed to do laundry, but my feet felt encased in concrete. I swallowed, but there was nothing there. I took one step down, and the wooden tread groaned. I launched myself backward, scrambling onto the safety of the kitchen linoleum. My chest heaved as I slammed the door shut, leaning my forehead against the cool wood. I dragged a heavy oak dining chair across the floor and wedged it under the doorknob, stepping back with short, rapid breaths.

A casual Google search brought up the crime scene photos. They were taken right where Chloe's bed now stood. She sat in the living room, chewing the inside of her cheek until she tasted iron. The sun dipped below the horizon, casting long, reaching shadows across the carpet. She refused to turn on the lamps, shrinking into the corner of the sectional sofa. Her knees were pulled tight to her chin, her arms locked around her legs. The wind rattled the windowpane, and she let out a sharp, involuntary squeak. She kept her gaze fixed firmly on the staircase, listening intensely to the silence of the second floor, completely unwilling to go upstairs.

The familiar opening chords echoed through the smoky room of The Blue Note, and my knee instantly started bouncing against the underside of the tiny wooden table. I peeled the wet paper label off my beer bottle, stripping it into microscopic shreds. Up on the stage, the velvet-voiced singer leaned into the microphone to deliver the lyrics I had scribbled on a napkin three years ago. I swallowed hard, the rough fabric of my collar suddenly feeling like a tightening noose. My eyes darted around the dim room, scanning the shadowy faces of the audience. Were they listening? Did they notice the tempo was dragging? I pressed my thumb into the condensation on the glass, leaving a deep print, my chest tight as the chorus approached. If she missed the high note, I wasn’t sure I could stay in my seat.

Marcus stood in the wings of the massive stadium, his fingers aggressively fraying the edges of his AAA backstage pass. The crowd of fifty thousand roared as the pop idol center-stage struck the opening chord on an acoustic guitar. It was Marcus’s chord progression. He bit down hard on the inside of his cheek, tasting a faint metallic tang of copper, and shifted his weight from his left foot to his right, over and over. He checked his phone screen—blank—then shoved it back into his pocket. The singer approached the bridge, the section Marcus had obsessed over for six sleepless nights. Marcus squeezed his eyes shut and stopped breathing entirely, his hands balled into tight fists at his sides. He waited for the beat drop, the pulsing blood in his ears almost drowning out the stadium speakers.

Elias adjusted his tie for the fifth time in three minutes, sitting rigidly in the folding chair of the high school gymnasium. On the polished floor ahead, the youth symphony raised their instruments. The conductor brought his baton down, and the sweeping melody of Elias’s early sonata filled the room. Elias’s jaw locked. He leaned forward, his elbows digging sharply into his knees, and rubbed his damp palms briskly up and down the fabric of his trousers. The woodwinds were coming up. They always rushed the woodwinds. He pinched the bridge of his nose, his foot tapping a rapid, silent rhythm against the linoleum that completely ignored the conductor's actual tempo. Every slight scratch of a bow or wavering flute note sent a sharp jolt straight up his spine. He fixed his gaze firmly on the exit doors.

I was halfway down the subway stairs when I heard it. The acoustic strumming was unmistakable, followed by the raspy melody of my latest indie release bouncing off the tiled walls. I froze mid-step, my hand gripping the cold metal handrail so hard my knuckles turned a blotchy white. My heart kicked violently against my ribs. I ducked behind a grime-covered concrete pillar, pressing my back flat against it so the busker wouldn't see me. I peeked around the edge, my breath coming in short, shallow hiccups. Commuters were walking by, some tossing coins into the open guitar case. I pulled my beanie down lower over my face and chewed furiously on my bottom lip. Should I go say something? Should I turn around and take the bus? My stomach did a slow, uncomfortable flip as he started the second verse.

In the dimly lit control room, Sarah clicked her ballpoint pen. Click-click, click-click, click-click. The sound engineer shot her a sharp sideways glance, but she couldn’t stop her thumb from pressing the plastic button. On the other side of the soundproof glass, a legendary session guitarist was tuning up to play the solo for her title track. Sarah swallowed a dry lump in her throat and began picking aggressively at a loose hangnail on her index finger until it stung. She dragged a hand through her hair, tangling her fingers in the curls, and paced three steps to the left, then three steps to the right. The engineer hit the playback. As the heavy bassline rolled into the studio, Sarah held her breath, her eyes blown wide, staring fixedly at the guitarist's hands, bracing herself for the first slide down the fretboard.

I slid down lower in the worn leather armchair, pulling the collar of my flannel shirt up to my chin. The guy at the front of the coffee shop had just adjusted the mic stand and announced the title of his next cover—my song. I grabbed my half-empty paper cup, squeezing the cardboard until hot black coffee splashed over the rim and burned my fingers. I didn’t let go. My eyes darted to the barista, then to the couple by the window, cataloging every slight movement they made. The guy started strumming, and he was using a different picking pattern. I squeezed my eyes tightly shut, a sudden wave of heat prickling across the back of my neck. I kept swallowing, but my mouth was completely devoid of moisture. I stared fiercely at the ground, silently counting the floorboards until the chorus ended.

Arthur sat stiffly in the center of the plush theater row, his wooden cane held upright between his knees. Up on the brilliantly lit stage, a glittering pop star was delivering a modern, synthesized rendition of his folk anthem. Arthur’s hands were clamped so tightly over the rounded top of his cane that his weathered skin looked nearly translucent. He blinked rapidly, his jaw muscles visibly pulsing beneath his gray beard. With every modernized pop-drop, Arthur gave a small, involuntary flinch. He cleared his throat quietly, unbuttoning his jacket, then immediately buttoning it back up again. His eyes flicked to the left, watching the younger audience members sway to the electronic beat. He wiped a thin layer of sweat from his upper lip with his trembling hand, counting down the measures until the final chord would put an end to it.

The auditorium was silent, save for the faint rustling of programs. I sat entirely rigid in the front row, my fingernails digging sharp half-moons into the soft flesh of my palms. Up on the grand piano bench sat Chloe, my ten-year-old student, her small fingers poised over the keys to play the sonata I had composed for her. My leg shook violently, rattling the shared armrest between me and a bewildered parent. I leaned so far forward I was practically hovering over the seat cushion. C sharp, I chanted silently in my head, staring unblinking at her right hand. Please remember the C sharp. My chest felt as tight as a coiled spring, and a single bead of perspiration rolled slowly down my temple. I gnawed on the inside of my cheek, waiting for her hands to finally drop and strike the opening chord.

The bass vibrated straight through the mud of the festival grounds, shaking the plastic cup of water crushed in Leo’s hand. Up in the glowing neon booth, the headlining DJ transitioned into a new track. Leo recognized the distorted vocal sample immediately—it was his unreleased bootleg. He dropped his cup, the water spilling onto his sneakers, and grabbed the hair at the back of his head, pulling hard enough to hurt. He spun around, scanning the sea of dancing bodies packed into the tent. His breathing turned rapid and shallow as he watched their faces. Would they dance? Would they leave for another stage? He started chewing aggressively on his thumbnail, his eyes darting rapidly from the flashing strobe lights to the crowd. He shifted his weight from side to side, bouncing on his toes, incapable of standing still for a single second.

I hovered my cursor over the thumbnail for the sixth time. The video title clearly named my acoustic ballad, but the view count sat at two million. I pushed my rolling desk chair violently away from the monitor, springing to my feet. I paced the length of my tiny bedroom, taking exactly four steps to the door, spinning around, and taking four steps back. I grabbed a throw pillow off the bed and hugged it tightly against my chest, crushing it to my collarbone. My heart drummed a chaotic, rapid rhythm against my ribs. I picked up my phone, unlocked it, locked it, and threw it onto the mattress. Slowly, I crept back toward the computer desk. I held my breath, squeezed my eyes half-shut as if preparing for a physical blow, and blindly tapped the spacebar to hit play.

High in the darkened balcony, Julian pressed his back hard against the plush velvet seat. Down below, the lead actress stepped into the spotlight to sing the finale he had spent two years writing. Julian began twisting his silver wedding band furiously around his finger, pulling it up over the knuckle and shoving it back down until his skin grew red and irritated. He swallowed constantly, his throat parched, but the bottle of water at his feet felt a thousand miles away. As she approached the modulation, Julian pulled his knees together and tucked his hands securely between his thighs to stop their violent trembling. He kept his eyes fixed on the ornate ceiling molding, entirely unable to look at the stage. Every intake of her breath echoed loudly in his ears, making his stomach twist into tight, uncomfortable knots.

I stood near the open bar, furiously tearing a cocktail napkin into tiny confetti. The wedding band had just finished a classic rock cover, and the frontman announced they were slowing things down with a local favorite. The unmistakable bassline of my old high school band’s anthem filled the banquet hall. My face flushed burning hot. I stared intensely at the pile of shredded paper on the high-top table, avoiding eye contact with any of the guests. I took a massive gulp of my club soda, nearly choking as the carbonation hit my dry throat. My foot tapped out a rapid, double-time beat against the brass rail of the bar. Someone at a nearby table pointed at me and whispered. I quickly turned my back to them, hunching my shoulders up toward my ears and staring fixedly at the bartender cleaning glasses.

When Greg from next door knocked, I was already chewing my lower lip. He pointed at the massive oak straddling our property line, suggesting we split the cost of removing it. My heart instantly kicked into a rapid, uneven rhythm against my ribs. I stared at the tree, then at Greg, then back at the tree. If it falls, will it crush the roof? If we hire someone, what if they drop a branch on his car and I'm liable? I rubbed my sweaty palms against the sides of my jeans, leaving dark streaks on the denim. "I, uh, I need to look into it," I stammered, my voice sounding thin and reedy. I stepped back, my hand gripping the edge of the door so tightly my knuckles turned stark white, already running through a dozen disastrous scenarios involving lawyers and crushed shingles.

Mrs. Higgins stood perfectly rigid on her porch as the new neighbor, a burly man named Tom, casually mentioned taking down the silver birch between their lots. Her right hand flew to the base of her throat, fingers pressing into her collarbone as her breathing grew shallow and erratic. She watched Tom’s calloused hands gesture toward the delicate white trunk. Her mind spiraled, visualizing heavy machinery tearing up her prize-winning hydrangeas, the deafening roar of woodchippers shattering her quiet mornings, and the glaring afternoon sun that would mercilessly bake her living room. She shifted her weight from her left foot to her cane, her jaw clenched so tight her teeth ached. "Well," she managed to whisper, clearing her throat twice to find her voice. "We must check the deeds first." She didn't wait for his reply, backing into her hallway and hastily turning the deadbolt.

I watched through the blinds for twenty minutes before forcing myself to walk out to the fence. Sarah was leaning against the chain-link, eyeing the overgrown pine. When she mentioned hiring a crew to cut it down, all the moisture vanished from my mouth. I tried to swallow, but my throat felt like sandpaper. I began twisting my wedding band, spinning it frantically around my finger. What if the roots have entwined with my plumbing? If they grind the stump, will it burst the water main? My gaze darted from the towering green needles to Sarah’s expectant smile, unable to maintain eye contact for more than a second. A cold prickle of sweat broke out across the back of my neck.
