The words "The surprise party is all set for 7 PM!" beamed brightly on my screen, directly beneath my mother’s contact photo. The very person I was surprising. I instantly dropped the phone onto the rug as if it had burned my fingers. My hands flew to my hair, gripping the roots tight. "No, no, no," I muttered to the empty living room, my voice a hushed whisper. I dropped to my knees, hovering over the screen without daring to touch it. I watched the little "Delivered" text turn into "Read" within seconds. My pulse throbbed painfully in my temples. I scrambled to formulate a lie—a joke, a typo, anything—but my fingers shook so violently I kept hitting the wrong keys. I held my breath, waiting for her reply, feeling as though the walls were slowly inching inward, compressing the air out of the room.

Marcus gnawed on his lower lip until he tasted a faint metallic tang. The attachment sent to his biggest corporate client wasn't the Q3 financial report. It was the invoice for his upcoming bachelor party, complete with an itemized list of embarrassingly juvenile expenses. He clicked his mouse furiously, trying to recall the email, but the server had already processed it. He pushed his office chair back, the wheels screeching against the plastic mat, and stood up abruptly. He loosened his silk tie, suddenly feeling as though the collar was choking him. He walked to the window, staring blankly at the city traffic below, his right foot tapping a relentless rhythm against the carpet. Every time his Outlook notification chimed from the desk behind him, Marcus flinched, his shoulders hiking up toward his ears as he braced himself for the professional ruin waiting in his inbox.

I stared at the name at the top of the chat thread, blinking rapidly hoping the letters would rearrange themselves. "Chloe" stared back at me. I had just sent "She never does her dishes and it's driving me insane" directly to Chloe, my roommate. I shoved the phone deep into my coat pocket, squeezing my eyes shut. I was standing in the grocery store aisle, but the bright fluorescent lights suddenly felt blinding, and the ambient music sounded distorted. I leaned heavily against the handle of my shopping cart, my chest rising and falling in shallow, rapid breaths. I could hear her footsteps echoing in our apartment in my mind. Would she pack her things? Would she scream? I abandoned my half-full cart next to the cereal boxes and fast-walked toward the exit, my heart hammering a wild, erratic beat against my ribs with every step.

Julian’s thumb froze in mid-air. He had just forwarded a detailed description of his bizarre rash to his neighborhood carpool group instead of his doctor. He felt the blood drain entirely from his face, leaving a cold, prickling sensation in his cheeks. He rapidly pressed the power button, plunging the screen into darkness, only to immediately unlock it again. The message was already accumulating confused reactions. Julian’s stomach performed a violent somersault. He tossed the phone onto his bed and began to pace the length of his bedroom, his hands rubbing furiously up and down his face. He imagined facing Mrs. Higgins tomorrow morning during the school run. A wave of nausea washed over him. He sat on the edge of the mattress, bouncing his knee at a breakneck speed, staring at the device as if it were a venomous snake preparing to strike.

"The hiring manager is an absolute nightmare," I read aloud, my voice cracking. I looked at the recipient. It wasn't my wife. It was the hiring manager, who had texted me directions just ten minutes prior. I slammed the laptop shut and shoved my phone under a sofa cushion. The silence in my living room was suddenly suffocating. I started pacing, pulling at the loose threads of my sweater until they unraveled in my sweating palms. What was I supposed to do? Apologize? Pretend my phone was hacked? I retrieved the phone from under the cushion, my hand trembling so badly I dropped it twice. The screen lit up with a new text. I squeezed my eyes shut, my teeth grinding together so hard my jaw ached. I couldn't bring myself to read the response, feeling a cold sweat prickle along the back of my neck.

Elena’s grip on her phone tightened until her knuckles turned white. The photo of her two prohibited kittens, snuggled on the couch, had successfully sent to "Mr. Davis - Landlord." She inhaled sharply, a high-pitched wheeze escaping her throat. She immediately tried holding down the message to unsend, but her clammy fingers kept slipping against the glass screen. "Delete for me," she accidentally tapped. The message vanished from her view, leaving her utterly blind to his read receipts. She groaned, burying her face in her hands. She stood up and began hurriedly gathering the cat toys scattered across the rug, tossing them blindly into a closet. Every creak of the hallway floorboards outside her apartment door made her jump. She stood frozen in the center of the living room, barely breathing, her eyes darting between the front door and the silent, dark rectangle of her phone.

I hit send on "Bring the vodka, I've got the house to myself tonight!" and immediately realized my mistake. The recipient read "Mrs. Gable - AP Chem." My throat closed up instantly. I threw the phone onto the passenger seat of my parked car, gripping the steering wheel so tightly my forearms cramped. The streetlights outside seemed to glare at me accusingly. I leaned forward, resting my forehead against the cold leather of the wheel, trying to take deep breaths, but the air felt thin and useless. My academic record, my college recommendations, the impending call to my parents—it all flashed behind my closed eyelids in a dizzying montage. A loud ding echoed in the quiet car. I jolted upright, my heart slamming into my throat. I stared at the phone sitting innocently on the seat, completely unable to extend my arm to turn it over.

Sam stood perfectly still in the mall concourse, oblivious to the crowds rushing past him. He had just texted a picture of the diamond engagement ring to his girlfriend, Claire, instead of her sister. His mouth went completely dry. He stared at the 'Delivered' notification, his chest feeling as though a tight iron band had been clamped around it. He typed 'IGNORE THAT!' but deleted it, then typed 'Wrong person!' and deleted that too. His thumb hovered over the keyboard, shaking visibly. He dragged a trembling hand through his hair, tugging at the roots. The element of surprise, planned for six months, was evaporating before his eyes. Three animated dots appeared on the screen. Claire was typing. Sam’s stomach plummeted as if he were cresting the peak of a rollercoaster, his breathing growing shallow as he watched those three little dots dance on the glowing screen.

I pace the length of the sidewalk, my thumbnail caught hard between my teeth. Where the grand oak used to be, there’s only a jagged yellow circle of exposed wood. I pull my phone out, unlock the screen, forget what I meant to look for, and lock it again. The sawdust is still fresh, scattered across the manicured grass. Was it diseased? Did the new owners think it was a hazard? My chest tightens, and I take three shallow breaths, rubbing my cold, clammy palms against my jeans. I walk closer, then back away, my eyes darting toward the front window of the house. If they come out, what do I say? I check my watch, though time doesn't matter. The sap smells sharp, almost chemical, and I can't stop bouncing my heel against the pavement.

Elias rubbed his temples in rapid, tight circles. The community garden was supposed to be protected, yet the space where his silver maple stood was a barren patch of turned earth. He dropped to his knees, his fingers digging frantically through the loose soil as if he might find the roots and somehow glue them back together. "Where is it? Where did it go?" he muttered to nobody, his voice thin and raspy. He stood up, turning in a full circle, scanning the passing pedestrians, then the construction vehicles parked on the street. He pulled his collar away from his neck to let the air in, but the tight band around his ribs remained. He jogged toward a city worker leaning against a backhoe, his hands trembling so badly he had to shove them deep into his pockets before speaking.

My knee bounces beneath the steering wheel, the engine idling while I stare through the chain-link fence. The plaque is still there in the dirt, reading "Class of '98," but the cherry blossom is just... gone. I chew the inside of my cheek until I taste iron. Why did they cut it? Are they expanding the parking lot? I reach for the door handle, then pull my hand back. I shouldn't go out there. But what if they took the wood somewhere? I grab my keys, drop them, and curse under my breath as my hands fumble in the dark footwell. Every shadow seems to stretch toward the empty space by the playground. I finally grasp the metal keys, my knuckles white, heart thudding a relentless, erratic beat against my ribs. I have to find the groundskeeper. Right now.

Sarah’s breath came in quick, ragged hitches. The old orchard was a graveyard of stumps, but she sprinted straight to the top of the hill, her boots slipping on the dew-soaked grass. The apple tree her grandfather helped her plant was reduced to a flat, pale disk. She grabbed the edge of her sweater, twisting the fabric so tightly her fingers went numb. "No, no, no," she whispered, her eyes darting from the stump to the encroaching bulldozers at the property line. She paced around the severed trunk, counting her steps, then reversed direction and counted again. The smell of raw pine and diesel fuel made her stomach pitch. She pulled out her phone, dialing her sister's number with jerky, inaccurate taps, hanging up before it rang, then dialing again. The sun was rising, and the machines would start any minute.

The clearing is entirely wrong. I drop my duffel bag in the dirt, staring at the raw stump where my white pine used to anchor the yard. My throat closes up. I swallow hard, but the lump refuses to move. I walk to the edge of the porch, back to the car, and then to the porch again. Who was up here? Poachers? The utility company? I frantically scan the tree line, looking for tire tracks, dragging my shoes through the pine needles. My breathing feels shallow, like I can’t quite fill my lungs. I pat my pockets—keys, wallet, phone—checking them three times in rapid succession. I step onto the stump, the wood still oozing sap, and jump off immediately as if it burned me. Every snap of a twig in the woods makes me flinch and spin around.

David stared at the pile of mulch in his front yard. He tapped his left foot, one-two-three-four, exactly on the beat of his racing pulse. The HOA had actually done it. The willow he planted when he was ten was entirely erased. He rushed into the house, grabbing the stack of violation letters from the kitchen counter. He shuffled through them, dropping two on the floor, ignoring them to read the third one twice. His jaw clenched so hard his teeth squeaked. He looked out the window, then marched to the door, then stopped, his hand hovering over the brass knob. He wiped a sudden layer of sweat from his forehead with the back of his sleeve. If he confronted the president now, what would happen? He began tearing the letters into tiny, methodical squares, unable to stay still.

I bite the frayed skin around my thumbnail as I look over the back patio. The magnolia is just a stump. The new estate managers work fast. I speed-walk to the perimeter fence, my eyes darting across the manicured lawn. I left my jacket inside, and a chill raises goosebumps on my arms, but I can't stop to go back for it. Did they grind the roots too? I fall to my knees, clawing at the woodchips. Splinters slip under my fingernails, but I barely register the sting. I need to find a piece of it, just one branch or a leaf. I scramble up, peering into the nearby dumpster, my chest rising and falling in rapid, shallow bursts. I pull out my phone, hands shaking so much the screen blurs. I have to call the lawyer before they haul it away.

The highway traffic rushed past, rattling the windows of Maya’s parked sedan. She stood on the gravel shoulder, her arms wrapped tightly across her chest. The birch she had planted a decade ago was gone, a jagged stump left in its wake. She shifted her weight from left to right, left to right, her gaze locked on the wood. The DOT trucks were parked a quarter-mile down the road. She took a step toward them, then quickly stepped back, chewing her bottom lip until it bled. What if they cited her for trespassing? What if they threw the wood in the chipper already? She pulled her keys out, jingling them incessantly in her right hand. Every time a semi-truck roared by, she jolted, her shoulders hiking up toward her ears. She patted her chest, trying to regulate her erratic, thumping heartbeat.

The stained-glass windows reflect onto the freshly poured concrete where my dogwood used to be. I drag my hand through my hair, gripping the roots tight. Why concrete? I walk the perimeter of the new patio, my footsteps echoing too loudly. I check my watch: 4:12 PM. The pastor's office is open until five. I march toward the heavy wooden doors, my stomach twisting into a tight knot. I stop with my hand on the cold iron handle. What if they tell me I had no right to plant it anyway? I back away, pacing a tight circle on the pavement. My mouth is as dry as cotton. I pull my water bottle from my backpack, take a sip, and immediately spit it out onto the grass. The shadows are getting longer, stretching toward me like dark fingers.

Marcus read the small metal plaque mounted on the stump. 'Removed due to Dutch Elm Disease.' He read it again. Then a third time. His fingers drummed a frantic, arrhythmic beat against his thighs. He looked left down the garden path, then right, then left again. The rest of the trees were standing. Was it a mistake? Did they cut the wrong one? He pulled out his garden map, the paper crinkling noisily in his unsteady grip. He traced the path with his index finger, smudging the ink with his sweaty pads. He folded the map, unfolded it, and folded it again until the creases tore. He took out his phone, clicking the camera open, snapping ten blurry photos of the stump in rapid succession. The battery icon flashed red. He gasped, dropping the phone back into his pocket and sprinting toward the visitor center.

I grip the rusted railing of the fire escape, staring down into the courtyard. The fig tree I planted in middle school is a flat plate of pale wood. I rush down the metal stairs, my sneakers clanging violently, almost tripping twice. When I reach the bottom, I circle the stump, my eyes darting to the landlord’s window, then to the dumpsters. My breath comes out in sharp, high-pitched puffs. I tug at the collar of my shirt, suddenly feeling like the fabric is choking me. Did he leave any cuttings? Can I root a branch? I dive toward the trash bins, throwing open the plastic lids. The smell of rotting food hits me, but I dig through the black bags anyway, my hands moving in a frantic blur. If I don't find a branch today, it'll all go to the landfill tomorrow.

Dropping his suitcases in the driveway, Leo stared at the gap in the canopy. The cedar was gone. He rubbed the back of his neck, his fingers pressing hard into the tense muscles. He walked toward the fresh stump, stopping every two steps to look over his shoulder. The house was dark. He dialed his mother’s number, his thumb slipping twice on the screen before the call connected. It went straight to voicemail. He hung up and called again. "Pick up, pick up," he muttered, pacing back and forth across the front walk. The fresh scent of cedar sap filled his nose, making his stomach churn violently. He walked to his bags, picked them up, set them down again. He checked the time, calculated the time zones, and realized it was 3 AM. He couldn't knock on the door. He couldn't leave.

I stared at the crumpled orientation flyer, my thumb rubbing circles over the ink until it smudged. "Room 4B: Mr. Harrison." The hallway suddenly felt too warm, the fluorescent lights buzzing like a swarm of angry bees inside my skull. I swallowed hard, but my throat was completely dry. I tugged at my collar, remembering the sharp sting of chalk snapping against the blackboard, the way his booming voice used to make me shrink into my desk. "Are you okay, Mom?" Leo asked, pulling at my sleeve. I forced my mouth into a stiff, trembling line that barely resembled a smile. "Just fine, sweetie," I managed, my voice pitching a full octave higher than normal. I wiped my damp palms against my jeans, mentally calculating if it was too late to request a transfer to literally any other second-grade class.

David paced the linoleum hallway, his heavy boots squeaking with every sharp turn. He checked his watch for the fourth time in two minutes. Through the narrow glass pane of the classroom door, he saw the unmistakable floral cardigan of Mrs. Gable. His stomach performed a slow, sickening flip. He stopped pacing and leaned his forehead against the cool cinderblock wall, closing his eyes as a wave of heat rushed up his neck. He remembered the detention slips, the disappointed sighs, the way she looked at him over her wire-rimmed glasses. He aggressively chewed his thumbnail down to the quick, tasting copper. "Mr. Vance?" a voice called out from the doorway. David flinched, his shoulders hiking up to his ears, and he dropped his half-chewed nail. He wiped a bead of sweat from his temple, pasted on a grin, and stepped forward.

The glowing screen of my laptop blurred as I read the back-to-school welcome email. *Welcome to 5th grade! I am Ms. Albright.* I pushed my chair back so fast it tipped over with a loud clatter, but I didn't bother picking it up. I began pacing the small home office, my breath coming in short, shallow hitches. I grabbed my coffee mug, but my hands were shaking so badly that dark liquid sloshed over the rim, staining the carpet. Ms. Albright. The woman who had ripped up my science fair poster in front of the entire class. Now, she was going to be teaching my sensitive, quiet little Maya. I picked up my phone, dialed the principal's office, hung up before it rang, and dialed again. My foot tapped a frantic rhythm against the floorboards as I listened to the dial tone, chewing my bottom lip until it bled.

Elena squeezed her daughter’s hand a little too tightly as they crossed the threshold of Room 112. "Mom, you're hurting me," Chloe whined, pulling her fingers away. Elena didn't hear her. Her gaze was locked on the towering figure arranging textbooks at the front desk. Mr. Sterling hadn't aged a day, his severe posture identical to the ones that haunted Elena's middle school memories. Her breathing grew erratic, and she felt a sudden, desperate urge to sprint back to the parking lot. She adjusted the strap of her purse, switching it from one shoulder to the other, then back again. Her eyes darted toward the exit, calculating the distance. "Let's go say hi," Chloe chirped, skipping forward. Elena froze in place, her feet feeling as though they were encased in solid concrete, watching helplessly as her daughter approached the lion's den.

"Look what my new teacher gave me!" Toby yelled, slapping a syllabus onto the kitchen island. I flipped it over, and the bold, cursive header leaped off the page: *Madame Dubois*. My breath hitched, catching sharply in my throat. I pressed my palms flat against the cool marble countertop, trying to steady the sudden trembling in my knees. The scent of lavender and peppermint seemed to materialize out of thin air, dragging me back twenty years to a classroom where I was mocked for my terrible pronunciation. "She speaks fast, but she seems nice," Toby said, oblivious to the way I was repeatedly smoothing down the edges of the paper until the corners frayed. I tried to speak, to offer some encouraging word, but my chest felt incredibly tight, trapped in an invisible vice that refused to let me draw a full breath.

Marcus adjusted his tie in the rearview mirror three times before turning off the car. Walking into the high school gymnasium, the smell of floor wax and stale sweat hit him instantly. He scanned the bleachers, his leg bouncing with restless energy until his eyes landed on Coach Henderson. Marcus swallowed heavily, feeling a distinct lump form in his throat. He immediately shoved his hands deep into his pockets to hide their tremors. He remembered the relentless drills, the barking insults, the agonizing rope climbs. He walked toward the bleachers, his heart drumming a frantic, syncopated rhythm against his ribs. He bumped into a folding chair, apologizing profusely to the empty plastic seat. Every time Henderson blew his silver whistle, Marcus blinked rapidly, fighting the instinct to drop and give him twenty. He stood behind his teenage son, hovering closer than necessary.

I stared unblinking at the name tag pinned to the welcome packet. *Mrs. Calloway. History.* The kitchen clock ticked, each second echoing loudly in the silent room. I rubbed the back of my neck, feeling the cold clamminess of my own skin. I stood up, walked to the fridge, opened it, and closed it without looking inside. I did this three times. Mrs. Calloway had a reputation for breaking students down, and I had barely survived her barrage of pop quizzes. I picked up the packet, dropped it, and bent down to retrieve it, my fingers fumbling clumsily with the slick paper. My mind raced through a dozen fabricated excuses I could use to pull my son from the class. Allergies? A sudden interest in geography? I began pacing a tight circle around the dining table, my teeth grinding together so hard my jaw began to ache.

Sarah balanced the tower of tissue boxes and markers in her arms, struggling to navigate the bustling school corridor. She glanced at the room number on her sticky note—Room 204. Mr. Abernathy. The box of markers slipped from her grasp, scattering across the linoleum, but Sarah remained frozen, staring at the placard beside the door. Her pulse pounded furiously in her ears, drowning out the chatter of passing parents. She vividly recalled the way he used to publicly read the lowest test scores aloud. She dropped to her knees to gather the markers, her movements jerky and uncoordinated. She snapped three marker caps in her haste, her breathing shallow and rapid. "Need a hand?" a familiar, raspy voice asked from above. Sarah squeezed her eyes shut, a cold sweat breaking out across her forehead as she mentally braced for impact.

The colorful handprints covering the classroom door should have been welcoming, but they felt like a warning sign. I read the placard: *Art - Ms. Vance*. My stomach performed a series of violent somersaults. I twisted my wedding ring around my finger, spinning it faster and faster until the metal dug into my skin. She used to hold my paintings up as examples of what lacking effort looked like. I peeked through the small window, spotting her wiping down an easel. I took two steps back, bumping hard into the drinking fountain. I pressed the button, but the water splashed over my chin as I tried to swallow, my hands shaking too much to cup the stream. My daughter pulled at my purse strap, asking if we could go inside. I nodded, though my feet remained firmly rooted to the spot, unresponsive to my commands.

James sat in the miniature plastic chair, his knees awkwardly touching his chin. The kindergarten orientation was in full swing, but James wasn’t listening to the phonics curriculum. He was staring at Mrs. Higgins. He bounced his right leg so vigorously that the entire table of crayons vibrated, sending a red wax stick rolling onto the floor. He didn't pick it up. He picked at a loose thread on his cuff, unraveling it inch by inch until a long string dangled from his sleeve. He vividly remembered the time she had forced him to sit in the coat closet for spilling his milk. He rubbed his temples, feeling a dull ache forming behind his eyes. When she asked for parent volunteers, James instantly shrank down in his tiny chair, his gaze fixed intensely on the patterned rug, praying the floor would swallow him.

I hit play on the answering machine while unpacking groceries. "Hi, this is Mr. Gable, your son's new English teacher." The carton of eggs slipped through my fingers, shattering against the tile floor. Yolk seeped into the grout, but I just stared at the blinking red light of the machine, my heart hammering a wild beat against my sternum. I checked the locks on the front door, an illogical reaction, before retreating to the kitchen. My thoughts spun in dizzying circles, landing on every humiliating essay I had ever read aloud in his class. I grabbed a paper towel to clean the mess, but instead, I just shredded it into tiny, ragged pieces, letting them fall like snow over the broken shells. I needed to call him back. I picked up the receiver, dialed three numbers, slammed it back into the cradle, and squeezed my eyes shut.

At the back of the auditorium, Clara stood with her arms crossed tightly over her chest, digging her nails into her own biceps. The stage curtains parted to reveal Mr. Lancer, baton in hand, preparing the middle school orchestra. Clara’s breath caught, her chest feeling compressed beneath an invisible weight. She shifted her weight from left to right, unable to stand still for more than three seconds. She remembered the sharp rap of that very same baton against her music stand, his harsh critiques of her off-key violin playing echoing in her memory. Her palms grew uncomfortably damp, and she wiped them repeatedly on her silk skirt, ruining the fabric. When her son raised his flute to his lips, Clara instinctively held her breath, her jaw clenched so tightly her teeth ached, waiting for the inevitable crack of the baton.

I stared at the empty magnetic strip on the kitchen wall. Chef Rossi’s custom Damascus steel knives were gone. "He took the early train. Moved to the coast," the sous-chef muttered, not meeting my eyes. I gripped the edge of the stainless steel prep table until my knuckles turned stark white. My breath caught high in my chest, refusing to go deeper. The dinner rush was exactly three hours away. I picked up a whisk, but my fingers trembled so badly it clattered loudly against the aluminum mixing bowl. I quickly shoved my hands into my apron pockets, shifting my weight from my left foot to my right, then back again. My mind raced through the evening's menu—the soufflés, the complex demi-glace. Without his nod from the pass, how was I supposed to know if any of it was right?

Elias stopped dead in the hallway of the firm. The frosted glass door no longer bore the name "Arthur Pendelton, Senior Partner." A blank placard stared back at him. Elias loosened his silk tie, suddenly feeling as though the collar was strangling him. He paced three steps to the left, then three steps to the right, his dress shoes squeaking loudly against the polished marble. He pulled his phone from his pocket, opened his messages, typed "Are you coming in?", deleted it, typed "Did I do something?", and deleted that too. His thumb hovered over the call button, slick with sweat. He dragged a hand through his carefully styled hair, ruining the part. Tomorrow was the biggest merger negotiation of his career. He swallowed hard against a completely dry throat, his leg bouncing as he leaned heavily against the wall.

The roll-up door of the garage was already open when I arrived, but Old Man Miller’s dented red rolling tool chest was missing from bay three. I wiped my hands on my greasy rag, even though they were perfectly clean. "Miller packed up last night," the shop owner called out. "Said he's done." I nodded too fast, my teeth clamped down hard on my lower lip. I walked over to the half-rebuilt transmission we were supposed to finish today. I picked up a wrench, dropped it, and bent down to grab it, my heart hammering against my ribs like a misfiring piston. I checked my phone—no missed calls, no texts. I opened the manual, reading the same diagram five times without absorbing a single line. The rhythmic tapping of my steel-toed boot against the concrete echoed loudly in the quiet bay.

Elara climbed the spiraling stone stairs, her arms full of dried nightshade. She pushed open the heavy oak door of the Archmage’s sanctum, expecting the familiar scent of pipe weed. The room was stripped bare; the crystal foci, the ancient tomes, all vanished. Elara dropped the nightshade. The delicate leaves shattered on the floorboards. She took a short, sharp breath, pressing her palms against her temples. Sparks of purple magic crackled involuntarily from her fingertips, singeing the edges of her sleeves. She walked to the empty desk, her chest rising and falling in rapid, uneven jerks. The Council trials were in two days. She squeezed her eyes shut, her mind a swirl of half-remembered incantations and fizzling spells. She picked up a stray quill, snapping it in half in her trembling grip, leaving a splinter digging deep into her thumb.

I scrubbed my hands under the hot water until the skin burned pink. "Dr. Vance cleared out her locker last night. Permanent leave," the scrub nurse mentioned casually over the rush of the sink. The antibacterial soap suddenly felt like ice. I stared at my soapy hands, my breathing turning shallow and erratic behind my surgical mask. The water shut off automatically, but I stood there, rubbing my wrists raw. We had a triple bypass scheduled in twenty minutes. I was supposed to be the assist. I stepped back, knocking my hip hard against the sterile cart. I barely felt the bruise forming. My eyes darted toward the operating room doors. I swallowed repeatedly, trying to force moisture back into my parched mouth, mentally replaying the surgical steps so fast they blurred together into a chaotic, incomprehensible mess.

Julian sat in the first chair, staring at the conductor's podium. Maestro Vane’s customized rosewood baton was absent. Instead, a stranger with a generic fiberglass stick was arranging sheet music. Julian reached for his violin tuning pegs, twisting the A-string up, then down, then up again. A sharp snap echoed through the tuning hall as the string broke, lashing the back of his hand. He didn't wince. He quickly unzipped his case, fumbling with a replacement string, his fingers clumsy and stiff. He kept glancing toward the stage door, biting the inside of his cheek until he tasted copper. The symphony's debut was tonight. He pressed the instrument under his chin, his bow hovering over the strings, vibrating slightly in the air. His foot tapped a frantic, off-beat rhythm against the hardwood floor that completely ignored the metronome.

The door to the lab was unlocked, but Professor Aris’s desk was entirely devoid of the towering stacks of research papers. I opened my laptop, my fingers flying over the keyboard to refresh my email inbox. Once. Twice. Five times. Nothing. "Admin says he took early pension," a postdoc whispered from the centrifuge. I gripped the edge of my laptop screen, pressing my thumb into the plastic bezel until it creaked. My doctoral defense was scheduled for next week. I pushed back my rolling chair, stood up, sat back down, and immediately stood up again. I paced the narrow aisle between the chemical hoods, my breath whistling through my teeth. I grabbed my notes, but the printed words danced and scattered across the page. I pulled my hair back into a tight ponytail, immediately undid it, and pulled it back again.

The chalk dust in the gym usually smelled like home to Maya, but today it just made her stomach churn. Coach Dan’s corner chair was empty. His clipboard, usually laden with her Olympic trial routines, rested in the trash can. Maya plunged her hands into the chalk bucket, coating her palms. She rubbed them together. Then she reached in and coated them again. The friction burned, but she kept rubbing. She walked toward the uneven bars, her chest tight, pulling in air in tiny, desperate sips. She looked up at the high bar, her vision swimming. She wiped her hands on her leotard, leaving stark white handprints on the dark fabric. She bounced on her toes, a rapid, jerky movement, repeatedly scanning the empty bleachers. Without his voice shouting the timing from the floor, the bars looked a hundred feet tall.

I unlocked the atelier at precisely six in the morning, ready to begin the final fittings. Madame Rousseau’s velvet chair was empty. Her gold-handled shears and the worn leather measuring tape she never let out of her sight were missing. A note from the landlord lay on the cutting table: Lease transferred. I grabbed a bolt of silk, my hands shaking so violently the fabric rippled like water. I reached for my own shears, but I couldn't get my fingers through the metal loops. I squeezed my eyes shut, my heart thudding a frantic rhythm against my ribs. The runway show was in four days. I bit my thumbnail, tearing the edge off, not caring as it snagged. I walked around the dress form, my steps fast and uneven, unwilling to risk a single cut into the expensive fabric alone.

Sam’s eyes remained locked on his second monitor. The lead developer’s Slack icon was a hollow, gray circle. A system message in the general channel read: User deactivated. Sam clicked his mouse. He highlighted a block of code, un-highlighted it, and highlighted it again. His heel hammered a relentless staccato beat against the metal leg of his desk. He opened a terminal window, his fingers hovering over the keys, but he couldn't remember the deployment command. He wiped his sweating palms on his jeans. The production server was throwing sixty errors a minute. He reached for his water bottle, but knocked it over, sending water spilling across his notebook. He scrambled to wipe it up with his sleeve, his breath catching in his throat as the error count ticked up to seventy. He stared at the screen, his hands hovering over the keyboard, unable to type a single character.

Walking into the bullpen, I tossed my coat onto my chair and turned to toss my partner a donut. Detective Miller’s desk was stripped to the wood. No family photos, no brass lamp, no mug. The captain walked by and clapped my shoulder. "Miller turned in his badge last night. Enjoy the solo desk." I crushed the paper bag holding the donut. I threw it in the trash, pacing to the window and back. I picked up the thick homicide file we’d been working on for six months. The trial testimony was tomorrow. I flipped the folder open, my fingers slipping on the glossy crime scene photos. I rubbed the back of my neck, feeling a cold sweat breaking out at my hairline. I sat down, stood right back up, and began clicking my ballpoint pen over and over.

Leo walked into the sunlit studio, dropping his canvas bag. Master Julian’s easel was folded. His vast collection of sable brushes had vanished from the jars. The gallery owner was sweeping the floor. "He retired to Tuscany," she said without looking up. "You have to finish the commission." Leo felt the blood drain from his face. He grabbed a piece of charcoal, gripping it so tightly it snapped into three jagged pieces in his palm. He dusted his hands on his apron, leaving dark, smeared streaks. He walked up to the half-finished mural. His breathing grew loud in the quiet room. He picked up a brush, dipping it in oil paint, but his hand vibrated, sending a stray drop of crimson splashing onto the pristine white floorboards. He backed away from the wall, his eyes darting wildly across the canvas.

The glowing digits of the alarm clock blurred as I stared at them: 2:14 AM. The floorboards out in the hallway groaned softly, followed by the muffled, hushed tones of Mark's voice. I kept my breathing slow and even, gripping the edge of the duvet so tightly my knuckles ached. He had said he was just going for a glass of water. A water glass doesn't talk back. My chest felt tight, the thumping of my own pulse loud enough that I thought it would give me away. I played back the last three weeks in my mind, searching every smiled interaction and skipped dinner for a clue. The murmur stopped. Footsteps approached. I squeezed my eyes shut, my jaw locked so hard my teeth ground together, waiting for the bedroom door to creak open.

Elena scrubbed the same spot on the kitchen counter for the fifth time, her eyes darting repeatedly to the sleek black smartphone sitting face-down on the dining table. David had stepped out to start the car, but only after excusing himself to the patio twice during breakfast, speaking in a low murmur with a hand cupped over his mouth. The sponge in Elena's hand was practically shredded. Her breath caught in her throat every time the phone vibrated against the wood, emitting a dull humming sound. She wiped her clammy palms on her jeans, taking a half-step toward the table before jerking back. What if she looked? What if she didn't? Her stomach churned like she had swallowed a handful of stones, and she gnawed at her lower lip until the metallic taste of blood bloomed on her tongue.

I sat completely still on the sofa, the TV blaring some comedy special that I wasn't actually hearing. Across the room, Sarah stood by the window, her silhouette framed by the streetlights. She had her phone pressed to her ear, her voice dropping to an inaudible whisper whenever I shifted my weight on the cushions. My fingernails dug half-moons into the meat of my palms. I tried to swallow, but my throat was entirely dry. Every time she laughed—a soft, private sound that used to belong to me—a cold prickle crawled up the back of my neck. I rehearsed a dozen casual questions in my head: Who is that? Everything okay? Work stuff? But my mouth refused to open. I just sat there, bouncing my right knee up and down so fast it shook the entire coffee table.

The rhythmic hum of the tires usually put Julian at ease, but today the passenger seat felt like a cage. Next to him, Marcus suddenly silenced the car's Bluetooth, snatched his phone from the dashboard mount, and pressed it to his ear. "I can't talk right now," Marcus muttered, his eyes darting to Julian before he abruptly ended the call. Julian's left leg began to bounce, his heel striking the floor mat in a rapid, uncontrollable staccato. He stared out the window at the passing trees, though the green blur didn't register. His chest rose and fell in shallow, jagged gasps. He pressed two fingers against his neck, feeling a frantic pulse drumming against his skin. The silence in the cabin was suffocating, heavy with unspoken questions that piled up in Julian’s throat, making it impossible to draw a full breath.

I stood frozen in the cereal aisle, a box of oatmeal dangling limply from my hand. Down by the dairy section, Liam was pacing. He had slipped away while I was weighing apples, pulling his phone from his pocket with a swift, guarded motion. From my vantage point behind a display of granola bars, I watched his free hand run frantically through his hair. My stomach twisted into a tight, heavy knot. I dropped the oatmeal into the cart; the soft thud sounded deafening. I needed air. I pulled at the collar of my sweater, suddenly sweating despite the chill of the refrigerated section. My mind raced through our recent arguments, tabulating every unexplained late night. I squeezed the shopping cart handle, my eyes locked on his moving lips, desperately trying to read them from fifty feet away.

The candle on the bistro table flickered, casting long, dancing shadows across Maya’s untouched plate. Greg had excused himself to the restroom ten minutes ago, but Maya could see his reflection in the mirrored wall near the coat check. He was tucked into a quiet alcove, phone pressed tightly to his ear, his back turned to the dining room. Maya tore her paper napkin into tiny, jagged strips, piling them into a snowy mountain beside her fork. Her heart hammered against her ribs like a trapped bird. She took a sip of ice water, but the liquid did nothing to soothe the sandpaper dryness in her throat. She replayed the way he had quickly shielded his screen when a message popped up earlier. The pile of torn paper grew higher as she watched him end the call and take a deep breath.

The carpet muffled my footsteps as I carried two mugs of tea toward the study. The door was cracked open just an inch. "I told you, she doesn't know. Just wait until Friday," Chloe’s voice drifted through the gap, barely louder than a breath. I froze, the hot ceramic of the mugs scalding my fingers. I didn't flinch. I couldn't move. The air vanished from my lungs, leaving me hollowed out and lightheaded. A buzzing sound started deep inside my ears, drowning out the ambient hum of the refrigerator downstairs. Friday. What was happening on Friday? I stared at the sliver of light spilling onto the hallway floor, my knees trembling so violently I thought I might drop the tea. I backed away, inch by excruciating inch, until I reached the kitchen, where I leaned heavily against the cool tiles.

Autumn leaves crunched beneath Arthur’s boots, but the sound failed to cover the low muttering behind him. He stopped and turned, pretending to admire a towering oak. Thirty yards back down the trail, Ben was standing stationary, his phone plastered to his cheek, gesturing emphatically with his free hand. Arthur’s jaw locked. He shoved his hands deep into his coat pockets, balling them into fists until his fingernails bit into his own flesh. A cold sweat broke out across his forehead, chilling him in the brisk October wind. He began pacing a small circle in the dirt, repeatedly checking his watch. Every passing second felt like an hour. He tried to focus on the distant sound of a dog barking, but all his mind could process was the secret distance Ben had deliberately created between them on an otherwise empty path.

The hot shower sprayed against my back, but I was shivering. I had turned the water off three times already, straining to listen. Through the thin drywall separating the bathroom from the guest room, I could hear the cadence of Jason’s voice. Not the words, just the secretive, urgent rhythm of a conversation he thought was entirely private. I stood dripping on the bathmat, a towel clutched to my chest, my eyes wide and unblinking as I stared at the frosted glass of the window. My stomach roiled, pitching like a small boat in rough waters. I began to brush my teeth, brushing so hard and fast my gums stung, just to have something to do. When I spit the foam into the sink, my hands were shaking too much to properly turn the faucet off.

The overhead intercom announced a boarding delay for Flight 402, but Clara didn't hear a word. Her gaze was locked on the glass partition of the adjacent boarding area, where Thomas was pacing with his phone. He had told her he was going to buy a magazine. There was no newsstand over there. Clara gripped the armrests of her vinyl seat, her knuckles white. She tapped her right foot against her carry-on bag in a frantic, ceaseless rhythm. Her chest felt wrapped in tight iron bands. Was he canceling the trip? Was someone else waiting for him back home? She bit down on her thumbnail, tearing away a strip of cuticle. She didn’t notice the slight sting, entirely consumed by the sight of Thomas checking over his shoulder before speaking into the receiver again.

The bass of the party music thumped against the soles of my shoes, but the lively chatter around the kitchen island faded into white noise. Through the sliding glass doors, I watched Ryan standing alone on the dark balcony. The screen of his phone illuminated his face as he held it to his ear, his brow deeply furrowed. I brought my plastic cup to my lips but didn't drink. My throat had closed up entirely. I shifted my weight from leg to leg, rubbing the back of my neck where a sudden, prickly heat had erupted. A friend touched my shoulder to ask a question, and I jumped, splashing my drink onto the floor. I mumbled a hasty apology, my eyes darting right back to the balcony. Ryan was laughing now, a soft, intimate smile that made my chest cave in.

Cardboard boxes were stacked high in the living room, but the packing tape hung forgotten in Leo’s trembling hand. He stared down the hallway toward the closed door of the garage. Sam had been in there for twenty minutes. A few moments ago, Leo had gone to ask about the kitchen supplies, only to hear Sam speaking in a hushed, pleading tone. Leo had backed away instantly. Now, he sat on a taped-up box labeled 'Books,' pulling violently at a loose thread on his sweater until it began to unravel. His breaths came short and fast, barely filling the top of his lungs. He felt dizzy. They were signing the lease on the new place tomorrow. He squeezed his eyes shut, pressing the heels of his hands hard against his temples as if he could physically crush the swirling, chaotic thoughts inside his skull.

Maya stared at the glowing screen, the familiar bubble letters of her fifteen-year-old handwriting staring back from a viral Twitter thread. Her jaw tightened, and she pressed her palms flat against the cool mahogany desk, trying to steady the faint tremor in her fingers. The office around her blurred into white noise. A notification popped up in the corner of her monitor: a text from her older brother with a link and a question mark. She swallowed hard, tasting copper. Her leg began to bounce under the desk, the rhythmic tapping of her heel echoing loudly in her ears. She dragged her cursor to the upper right corner of the window, but her hand jerked, clicking empty space instead. The thread had ten thousand retweets. Ten thousand people reading about her obsession with the lead singer of a local grunge band.

My thumb hovered over the refresh button. I bit the inside of my cheek until I tasted blood, staring at the blog post. Someone had scanned every single page of my pink velvet journal and uploaded it. The barista called out a caramel macchiato, but the sound seemed to come from underwater. I tugged aggressively at the sleeves of my oversized sweater, pulling them down to cover my knuckles. The view counter at the bottom of the page ticked up by three. I closed my eyes, picturing my coworkers scrolling through my dramatic prose about the ninth-grade talent show. My chest felt tight, like someone had wrapped a heavy iron band around my ribs and was slowly pulling it taut. I pushed away my half-eaten muffin. The smell of roasted espresso beans suddenly made my stomach churn.

Julian paced the length of his living room rug, wearing a path into the faded Persian wool. Every few seconds, he stopped to check the tablet resting on the coffee table. The website was still there, his terrible poetry from 2004 displayed in a brutal, high-definition gallery. He dragged both hands through his hair, gripping the roots until his scalp stung. His phone buzzed on the sofa. He lunged toward it, knocking over a half-empty glass of water, watching the puddle spread across the wood floor. He didn't bother grabbing a towel. He stared at the Caller ID—his high school ex-girlfriend. Julian’s breath hitched. He backed away from the ringing device, his back hitting the cold plaster wall. He slid down until he was sitting on the floor, pulling his knees tightly against his chest while the ringtone looped.

The subway rattled through the dark tunnel, but I barely registered the swaying of the train. I kept rereading the URL my sister had texted me. TeenAngstArchive.com. My stomach flipped. I wrapped my fingers around the overhead metal bar, squeezing until my knuckles turned stark white. A teenager seated across from me giggled at her phone, and my head snapped up, convinced she was laughing at my entry about my imaginary romance with the chemistry teacher. I chewed my thumbnail down to the quick. The train halted at the next station, doors hissing open. I needed air. I shoved past a businessman in a gray suit, murmuring a breathless apology, and bolted up the concrete stairs to the street level, gulping down the smoggy city air as if I were surfacing from a deep dive.

Sarah’s reflection in the dark kitchen window looked pale. The laptop sat open on the island counter, brightly illuminating the digitized pages of her junior-year diary. She picked up a dish towel, wringing it between her hands over and over until the fabric was twisted into a tight knot. The kitchen clock ticked loudly, each second hammering into her skull. She checked her email inbox. Empty. She checked her Instagram mentions. Three new tags. She threw the dish towel onto the marble counter and squeezed her eyes shut. She began opening and closing the kitchen drawers, mindlessly rearranging the silverware. Forks with forks. Spoons with spoons. Her breath came in short, shallow hiccups. She imagined the PTA moms reading her furious teenage rants about her parents. She grabbed the edge of the counter, waiting for the floor to stop tilting.

I threw my phone onto the bed, but immediately picked it up again to check the forum. The thread titled "Check out this tragic 90s kid diary" was still active. I wiped my sweaty palms on my denim jeans. Why did I ever donate that lockbox to the thrift store? I walked to the window, pulled the blinds shut, and then checked the lock on my bedroom door. My heart pounded a rapid rhythm against my ribs, fast as a hummingbird's wings. I crawled under my duvet, pulling the heavy fabric over my head to create a dark, soundproof cave. Even in the gloom, I couldn't stop seeing the scanned image of my terrible adolescent handwriting. I squeezed my eyes shut and started counting backwards from one hundred by sevens, trying to drown out the noise in my own head.

David sat in the back corner of the university library, hidden behind a stack of reference books. He kept minimizing and maximizing the browser window. Someone had found his old spiral notebook and posted it on a message board. He tapped his pen against the desk in an erratic beat, stopping abruptly when a librarian shot him a warning glare. He swallowed repeatedly, but his mouth was dry as dust. He needed to study for his finals, but the words in his textbook scrambled into nonsense shapes. He pulled his baseball cap low over his eyes and hunched his shoulders inward, trying to make himself as small as possible. His phone vibrated in his pocket. He flinched, knocking his knee hard against the underside of the wooden desk. He ignored the throbbing pain, unable to face whoever was messaging him.

I was holding a jar of marinara sauce when the notification popped up. A Google Alert for my name. I clicked the link, and there it was—my middle school diary, complete with doodle-filled margins, featured on a popular nostalgia blog. The glass jar slipped from my clammy fingers, shattering on the linoleum floor. Red sauce splattered across my white sneakers. I didn't move. A store employee rushed over with a mop, asking if I was okay. I nodded vigorously, unable to form words. I abandoned my shopping cart right in the pasta aisle and power-walked toward the sliding glass exit doors. My breathing grew ragged. Every shopper I passed seemed to be looking at me, knowing the deeply guarded secrets I had penned when I was thirteen. I fumbled for my car keys, dropping them twice before finally unlocking the door.

Elena sat on the cold park bench, scrolling rapidly through the digital archives on her phone. The handwriting on the screen was undeniably hers. She bit her lower lip so hard she tasted copper. A pigeon landed near her feet, and she flinched, almost dropping her device into a puddle. She rubbed her forehead, where a dull ache was beginning to bloom into a heavy, throbbing migraine. She stood up, took two steps down the walking path, then immediately sat back down. She unlocked her screen again, staring at the number of comments under the post. Fifty-two. She couldn't bring herself to read them. She wrapped her arms around her waist, shivering despite the mild spring weather, and stared blankly at the ducks swimming in the pond, her mind trapped in a loop of worst-case scenarios.

The dentist’s waiting room was quiet, save for the hum of the aquarium filter. I kept scrolling down the webpage, my eyes scanning the uploaded pages of my diary from senior year. My leg bounced rapidly, vibrating the small table holding outdated magazines. The receptionist called my name. I jumped, my heart leaping into my throat. I stood up, but my knees felt like water. I cleared my throat, trying to find my voice. "Could I use the restroom first?" I asked, my voice cracking on the last word. I didn't wait for her answer. I locked myself in the tiny bathroom, splashed freezing water on my flushed face, and stared at the mirror. My pupils were blown wide. I imagined my boss, my friends, my landlord all laughing at my most guarded adolescent entries.

Marcus sat motionless on the weight bench, a heavy dumbbell forgotten at his feet. His thumb swiped down the screen of his smartphone, refreshing the social media page. His high school journal, the one he thought he threw away a decade ago, was the subject of a viral video. Sweat dripped down his temples, but not from the workout. He wiped his face with a towel, gripping the rough cotton until his knuckles ached. He looked around the crowded gym. The music pumping through the speakers felt deafeningly loud. A guy on the neighboring bench asked if he was done with the weights. Marcus just stared at him blankly, unable to process the question. He grabbed his gym bag, stuffed his belongings inside with haphazard, jerky movements, and practically sprinted toward the locker room, his chest heaving with quick, shallow breaths.

The clatter of silverware against porcelain faded into the background. I stared down at the brightly lit screen hidden under the dining table. A link from an anonymous email led directly to a blog displaying my sixteen-year-old diary. The mac and cheese on my plate suddenly looked like yellow paste. "Are you okay, sweetheart?" my mom asked. I jolted, nearly knocking over my glass of iced tea. "Fine," I squeaked out, the pitch of my voice artificially high. I shoved my hands under my thighs to stop them from trembling. I imagined my cousins, who were sitting right next to me, stumbling across the post. I started chewing on the inside of my cheek, tearing away small bits of skin. I mumbled an excuse about feeling unwell, pushed my chair back so forcefully it scraped loudly against the tile, and retreated upstairs.

Elias bought the crumbling copy of Great Expectations without bargaining, practically throwing the coins at the cashier. Once outside, he ducked into an alleyway, his thumb rubbing so hard against his jeans that the denim felt hot. The folded parchment protruded from page forty-two. He swallowed, a dry, clicking sound in his throat, and pulled it free. The wax seal matched the crest on the signet ring he had inherited from his grandfather. His pulse thrummed behind his eyes, blurring the edges of his vision. He traced the brittle edges of the paper, his chest rising and falling in rapid, shallow hitches. "Not here," he muttered, glancing over his shoulder at a pigeon that had landed too loudly. He shoved the book and the letter into his satchel, keeping his hand clamped over the buckle as he power-walked toward his apartment.

The yellowed envelope slipped from the spine of the secondhand cookbook, landing on my rug with a soft slap. I didn't touch it. I sat on the edge of the mattress, gnawing on my thumbnail until the metallic taste of copper bloomed on my tongue. The handwriting on the front—bold, slanting ink—was unmistakably my mother’s. But she had been dead for ten years, and this book was published yesterday. I stood up, took three steps toward the window, then turned back, my bare feet leaving damp imprints on the floorboards. I picked up my phone, dialed my brother’s number, hung up before the first ring. My stomach did a slow, sickening roll. I crouched down, hovering my fingers an inch over the paper. The ceiling fan clicked rhythmically overhead, matching the hammering in my chest. I couldn't open it. Not yet.

Clara’s spoon clattered against the porcelain saucer, sending a splash of hot chamomile tea over the rim. She ignored the puddle, her wide eyes locked on the folded note she had just extracted from the margins of a library copy of Dante's Inferno. The ink was fresh. I know what you did on the bridge, Clara. She scraped her chair backward, the wooden legs shrieking against the tile. Her gaze darted to the barista steaming milk, then to the old man reading a newspaper in the corner. Did he look up? Was he watching her? She snatched the note, crumpling it into a tight ball inside her clammy fist. The air in the cafe suddenly felt thick, unbreathable, smelling overwhelmingly of roasted beans and stale perfume. She grabbed her coat, not bothering to put her arms through the sleeves, and bolted for the glass doors.

My knee bounced so fast it rattled the empty plastic cup on the folding tray table. The commuter train swayed, but the tremor in my hands had nothing to do with the tracks. I smoothed out the receipt I’d found tucked inside the used sci-fi paperback. It wasn't a receipt. It was a list of dates, coordinates, and my exact legal name, printed in tiny, precise letters. I pressed the heels of my hands against my eyelids until fireworks exploded in the dark. Breathe in, count to four, breathe out. The mantra did nothing to slow the jackhammer against my ribs. The passenger across the aisle shifted, and I instantly shoved the paper deep into my jacket pocket, zipping it shut. I kept my fingers wrapped around the zipper pull, my eyes fixed on the blurring landscape outside, waiting for the train to stop.

The floorboards groaned under Julian’s weight as he sifted through the boxes of donated encyclopedias. When the thick, blue envelope tumbled out of volume four, he stopped breathing. Dust motes danced in the single shaft of sunlight piercing the attic window, but the air in Julian's lungs was trapped. The return address bore the crest of the university board. He wiped his palms on his trousers, leaving long, sweaty streaks down the corduroy. His tongue darted out to wet his cracked lips. He reached for the seal, pulled his hand back, and wiped his hands again. "It's just paper," he whispered to the empty room, but his voice cracked on the second syllable. He squeezed his eyes shut, his jaw muscles jumping as he finally pinched the edge of the flap, hesitating for five long seconds before tearing it open.

I shouldn't have bought the poetry anthology from that street vendor. The folded napkin slipped from between two sonnets and drifted onto my lap. Run. That was the only word written on it, scrawled in what looked like red lipstick. My throat closed up. I snapped the book shut with a loud crack, drawing a sharp glance from a mother pushing a stroller nearby. I forced a smile that felt like cracking plastic. The moment she passed, I tore the napkin into halves, then quarters, then eighths, until my fingernails were stained pink. I stuffed the confetti into the bottom of my coffee cup and pushed down the plastic lid. Every shadow stretching across the park grass seemed to point directly at my bench. I stood up, my knees locking, and began to walk briskly toward the subway, refusing to look behind me.

Professor Higgins stood at the chalkboard, droning on about the Industrial Revolution, but Maya couldn’t hear a word over the rushing sound in her own ears. The folded slip of notebook paper she had found tucked in her rented history textbook sat on her desk, demanding attention. Meet me after class. I found the drive. Maya’s pencil tap-tap-tapped a frantic rhythm against the wood. She checked the wall clock. Ten minutes left. Her stomach cramped, twisting into tight knots. She pressed her forearm against her abdomen and hunched forward, pretending to read the text. Her foot tapped the linoleum floor in double-time. She glanced around the lecture hall, studying the backs of fifty heads. Anyone in this room could have slipped it in there. She chewed the inside of her cheek until she tasted blood, watching the second hand sweep agonizingly slow.

The air in the shop smelled of old paper and dust, but all I could smell was the sharp tang of my own sweat. I had only pulled the leather-bound diary off the shelf to admire the gold foil. When the heavy, wax-sealed parchment fluttered out and landed on my boots, my muscles went rigid. The seal bore the emblem of the hospital—my hospital. The one I had fled three cities ago. I took a step backward, my heel clipping the edge of the mahogany bookshelf. The diary slipped from my slick fingers, hitting the floorboards with a thud that echoed like a gunshot through the silent store. I didn't reach down to retrieve it. I couldn't tear my eyes away from the red wax. My chest hitched, taking in half-breaths, as I slowly backed away until my shoulders hit the exit door.

Arthur filled his glass with tap water, drained it in three gulps, and filled it again. The pale pink envelope lay perfectly centered on his kitchen table, glaring at him from beside a dog-eared copy of To Kill a Mockingbird. He paced from the sink to the refrigerator, counting the tiles on the floor. Fourteen across, twelve down. He walked back to the table, reached out, and snatched his hand back as if the paper were hot coals. He ran his fingers through his thinning hair, tugging hard enough at the roots to sting. The handwritten name on the front was his wife’s, but the postmark was dated two days after her funeral. The refrigerator motor hummed, a low, vibrating growl that made his skin crawl. He grabbed a kitchen chair, gripped the wooden backrest until his knuckles turned stark white, and stared at the pink paper.

Rain pelted the bus shelter, but the chill sinking into my bones had nothing to do with the weather. I clutched the paperback thriller to my chest, the slick cover sliding against my wet jacket. Between chapters four and five, a Polaroid photograph with a message written in Sharpie on the white border was wedged tight. Look up. I squeezed my eyes shut, my teeth chattering in a staccato rhythm. I hugged my backpack closer, burying my chin into my collar. I didn't want to open my eyes. The headlights of passing cars sliced through the gloom, casting long, distorted shadows against the glass of the bus shelter. I dug my fingernails into my palms, leaving deep crescent moon indentations. "Just a prank," I whispered, the words barely audible over the drumming rain. I kept my head down, refusing to look up.

Marcus clicked his mouse fifty times a minute, not actually opening any files. The spreadsheet on his monitor blurred into a sea of meaningless green and white cells. He dragged his gaze back to the sticky note he had discovered inside the spine of the company’s ancient reference manual. They are auditing the 2019 files tomorrow. His throat felt like it was coated in sand. He swallowed hard, loosening his tie with erratic, jerky pulls. He looked over the partition of his cubicle. Janice was typing calmly. Dave was drinking coffee. Didn't they hear the roaring silence? Marcus slumped back in his chair, his leg bouncing violently enough to shake his desk lamp. He pulled open his bottom drawer, staring at the shredded documents stuffed in the black trash bag, his breathing growing so loud he thought the whole office would hear it.

The ocean breeze was supposed to be relaxing, but my skin felt prickly and too tight. I had bought the romance novel at a seaside thrift shop to distract myself. Instead, a folded sheet of hotel stationery fell out of the epilogue, landing on my beach towel. The handwriting detailed a flight number and a locker combination at the local airport. I grabbed a fistful of sand, squeezing it until the rough grains dug into my skin and fell away. I looked left down the shoreline, then right. A seagull squawked, and I jumped, my hand flying to my chest to cover the wild, thumping beat against my ribs. I scrambled to gather my things, shoving the book, the note, and my sunscreen into my canvas tote haphazardly. I left my umbrella pitched in the sand, half-jogging toward the boardwalk without shaking out my towel.

The dusty Polaroid slipped from my fingers, fluttering onto the attic floorboards. I stared at it, my heart hammering against my ribs like a trapped bird. The date stamped in the corner—August 1998—mocked everything I knew. Mom always swore Grandpa died in the winter of ’95, before I could walk. Yet, in the glossy square, a four-year-old me sat happily on the shoulders of a man with Grandpa’s unmistakable crooked nose and silver hair. I wiped my suddenly clammy palms on my jeans, listening to the creak of the house settling. Was that a footstep downstairs? I snatched the photo back up, my thumb tracing the impossible date. I pressed my back against the rough chimney brick, taking quick, shallow breaths. If he didn't die then, where did he go? And what else had they made up?

Clara’s knee bounced in a frantic, uneven rhythm against the desk drawer. She swallowed hard, her mouth tasting of pennies and dust, as she held up the sepia-toned photograph to the desk lamp. Her father had woven endless tales of their ancestors arriving penniless, scraping a living from the harsh coal mines. But the man in the picture—unmistakably her great-grandfather Elias—stood sharply dressed on the grand balcony of a sprawling, opulent estate, a diamond pin glinting on his lapel. The inscription on the back read, "Elias at his summer home, 1921." Clara chewed the inside of her cheek until she tasted copper. She glanced over her shoulder at the closed study door, her fingers white-knuckling the fragile paper. Every sound in the empty hallway seemed magnified tenfold. She needed to ask him, but her throat felt entirely swollen shut.

I must have checked the back of the photograph ten times, rubbing my thumb over the faded ink as if friction could change the numbers. June 4th, 1990. My parents’ wedding anniversary. But the man slipping the ring onto my mother’s finger in the sunlit garden wasn't my father. It was Uncle Richard. My stomach did a slow, nauseating flip, and a fine sheen of sweat broke out across my forehead. I dropped the picture into the shoebox as though it had burned me, immediately shoving the box under my bed. I paced the narrow length of my childhood bedroom, tugging at the collar of my shirt to let some air in. Downstairs, I could hear Mom humming as she set the table for dinner. The clinking of silverware sounded unnaturally loud. I clamped my hands over my ears, squeezing my eyes shut.

Marcus picked at the frayed edge of his thumbnail, a persistent habit that flared up whenever the room felt too small. The birth certificate locked in his safe at home clearly stated he was born in Seattle. But the Kodak print in his hand, found tucked inside an old encyclopedia, showed a newborn Marcus—identified by the unique birthmark on his chin—wrapped in a hospital blanket stamped "St. Jude’s, Dublin." A woman he didn't recognize was holding him, her face partially obscured by the camera flash. His chest tightened, making each breath feel like he was pulling air through a tiny straw. He darted a glance toward the library entrance, half-expecting someone to burst in and snatch the book away. He slipped the photo into his inner jacket pocket, patting it twice to make sure it was hidden, his pulse thrumming in his ears.

The attic air was stifling, but a sudden chill washed over me, raising goosebumps along my arms. I stared at the black-and-white print of my father. He was a teenager, smiling brightly, standing shoulder-to-shoulder with a boy who shared his exact face, down to the dimple on the left cheek. "My brother and I, 1976," the messy scrawl on the back read. Dad was an only child. He’d repeated that fact my entire life, usually when lamenting his lonely childhood. I began to tap my foot rapidly against the floorboards, my gaze darting between the photograph and the trapdoor leading back downstairs. I bit down on my lower lip, tasting the familiar metallic tang. Who was the other boy? I shoved the photo into my back pocket and hurried toward the ladder, my hands shaking so badly I almost missed the first rung.

Elena’s gaze remained locked on the glossy print, her breathing shallow and erratic. Her parents had testified under oath that they were miles away in a crowded theater on the night of the warehouse fire. They had framed the ticket stubs. Yet here they were, illuminated by the eerie orange glow of the burning building, standing mere feet from the caution tape. Her mother was holding a lighter. Elena’s hands trembled, causing the image to blur. She scrambled backward, hitting the edge of her bed, and pulled her knees tight against her chest. The ticking of her wall clock grew deafening, each click pounding against her temples. She flinched as a car door slammed out on the street. Peering through a tiny crack in the window blinds, she watched a dark sedan idle by the curb, her heart hammering against her ribs.

I practically tore the album page trying to slide the picture out. It was a recent snap from a family reunion last summer, one I hadn't attended. There, in the background, sat Cousin Maya. Around her neck gleamed the sapphire pendant. The very same pendant Grandma claimed was stolen by a burglar ten years ago, the reason we had filed police reports and installed barred windows. A cold sweat prickled at the base of my neck. I stood up, walked to the window, and pulled the curtains completely shut, double-checking the locks. I grabbed my phone, dialing Maya’s number, but canceled the call before it could even ring. My thumb hovered over the screen, trembling. If Grandma had lied about the burglary, what else was a fabrication? I paced the length of the rug, my teeth grinding together so hard my jaw ached.

The brass trunk smelled of mothballs and cedar, but Arthur barely noticed. He was entirely focused on the small, crinkled photograph resting in his damp palms. Uncle Henry was the family hero, a decorated soldier who supposedly fought valiantly against the regime. But the crisp, immaculate uniform Henry wore in the photo bore the undeniable insignia of the very enemy he claimed to have defeated. Arthur’s stomach churned violently. He closed the trunk with a soft click, checking the locked door of his study for the third time in ten minutes. He began pacing the Persian rug, wearing a path from the desk to the fireplace. He wiped his brow with the back of his sleeve, staring blankly at the dancing flames. If anyone else saw this, their reputation would be ruined. He held the photo toward the fire, pulling it back at the last second.

I gripped the edge of the kitchen counter until my knuckles turned white. The photo on my phone screen, sent by an urban explorer friend, showed the old farmhouse. My parents told me it burned to the ground when I was three, forcing us to move across the country with nothing but the clothes on our backs. But the house in the picture was perfectly intact, the paint peeling but structurally sound. Worse, my childhood swing set was still in the yard. My throat went completely dry. I poured a glass of water, but my hand jerked, spilling half of it onto the linoleum. I ignored the mess, dialing my mother’s number. It went to voicemail. I left a message, my voice cracking, demanding she call me back immediately. I walked to the front door, engaging the deadbolt, jumping at the sound of the ice maker.

Julian pulled at the collar of his sweater, suddenly finding the wool suffocatingly tight. The family photo album lay open on his lap, displaying a picture of him at age ten, hugging a golden retriever. The caption read, "Buster's First Day." But Julian distinctly remembered getting Buster when he was six. He flipped forward a few pages. Another picture showed Buster, but with a different family, dated three years before Julian supposedly got him. His foot tapped out a frantic staccato on the coffee table. He squeezed his eyes closed, pressing the heels of his hands against his eyelids until bursts of color exploded in the darkness. Had they stolen a dog? Adopted a runaway and lied to him? He jumped as his phone buzzed on the couch cushions, staring at the incoming call from his sister, unable to force his finger to swipe answer.

The envelope was buried beneath a pile of old tax returns. I slid out a stack of glossy prints from a middle school graduation. I froze, my breath catching in my throat. Standing next to my younger brother was a girl who looked exactly like Sarah. The sister who supposedly died of a heart defect when we were infants. She had the same distinct widow’s peak, the same crooked smile. I dropped the photos onto the desk, taking three rapid steps backward until my shoulders hit the bookshelf. I rubbed my hands vigorously up and down my arms, trying to dispel the freezing chill that had taken hold of me. The walls of the home office felt like they were pressing inward. I grabbed my keys, dropping them twice, before finally making it out the front door, desperate to get away from the filing cabinet.

Diana stared at the oversized novelty check in the photograph, her mouth completely dry. The family legend was that her father won the lottery in 1985, lifting them out of poverty. But the photograph showed her father shaking hands with a notorious local crime boss, the novelty check made out to his "shell corporation" rather than him personally. Diana bit her thumbnail, tearing the cuticle until a bead of blood welled up. She didn't notice the sting. Her heart hammered a frantic rhythm against her ribcage. She shoved the picture into her purse, immediately looking around the empty basement as if the shadows might detach and grab her. She bolted up the wooden stairs, taking them two at a time, and slammed the basement door shut behind her, leaning her entire weight against the wood while she struggled to pull air into her lungs.

Julian’s eyes darted between the glossy cover of the academic journal and the byline on page forty-two. Dr. Marcus Thorne. Not Julian Vance. The air in his tiny office suddenly felt too thick to breathe. He stood up, knocking his knee against the desk, and began pacing the narrow strip of carpet. His thumbs rubbed aggressively over his knuckles. If he confronted Thorne, his doctoral funding could vanish overnight. If he said nothing, months of grueling archival research were gone forever. He grabbed his phone, his thumb hovering over the department head’s number. A bead of sweat trickled down his ribcage. He locked the screen, then unlocked it again. He sat down. He stood back up. The walls of the room seemed to inch closer with every erratic thump of his chest against his ribs.

I refreshed the homepage three times. The headline was unchanged: "The Future of Urban Architecture," by Clara Evans. I dragged my teeth over my lower lip until I tasted copper. Clara was my editor; I was the freelancer who had spent three weeks interviewing planners. My leg bounced beneath the table, rattling my coffee mug. I opened a blank email, typed "Dear Clara," and jammed the backspace key until the cursor blinked mockingly. Would she blackball me if I demanded a correction? I rubbed my clammy palms against my jeans. Every notification ping from my laptop made my shoulders jump. I walked to the sink, splashed cold water on my face, and stared at my shaking hands, calculating the cost of burning this bridge.

The corporate newsletter glowed on Maya’s monitor. Her comprehensive market analysis—complete with the graphs she had color-coded at 2:00 AM—sat squarely beneath the beaming headshot of her regional manager, David. Maya’s breath hitched. She clicked away to her inbox, then immediately clicked back. Her fingers hovered stiffly over the keyboard. She chewed on the edge of her thumbnail, pulling a strip of cuticle until it stung. A colleague walked past her cubicle, and Maya flinched, swiftly minimizing the window. Her heart hammered a rapid rhythm against her breastbone. If she marched into Human Resources, David would know. He controlled her performance review next month. She picked up her pen, clicked it repeatedly, and watched the ink cartridge dart in and out. The clicking echoed too loudly in her ears. She dropped the pen and pressed her palms flat against her hot cheeks.

The advance copy of the medical journal felt impossibly heavy. I flipped to page eighty, staring at the bold print. Lead Author: Dr. Aris Thorne. My name was nowhere in the acknowledgments. I couldn't seem to draw a full breath; the oxygen just caught at the back of my throat. I began pacing the length of the empty laboratory, my rubber-soled shoes squeaking against the linoleum. My gaze darted to the heavy oak door of Thorne's office. Should I knock? What if he fired me on the spot? I pulled my phone from my lab coat pocket, dropping it onto the counter. It clattered loudly, making me jump. I wiped my sweaty palms on my trousers. I picked up a glass beaker, realized my grip was trembling dangerously, and set it right back down before it could shatter.

Leo stared at the Sunday edition of the Tribune. The front-page exposé on the local water crisis was word-for-word his submission, but the byline read 'Eleanor Vance, Senior Correspondent.' Leo swallowed hard, but his throat felt lined with sandpaper. He shifted his weight from his left foot to his right, unable to keep still in the middle of the crowded coffee shop. Someone dropped a mug nearby, and Leo nearly leaped out of his skin. He grabbed a paper napkin and began tearing it into tiny, jagged strips, piling them into a snowy mound on the table. He needed this publication credit for his Columbia application. Without it, his portfolio was painfully thin. He pulled his phone out, dialed his faculty advisor's number, let it ring half a time, and hung up, staring wide-eyed at the black screen.

The fashion zine was spread open on my lap. The feature on sustainable textiles—the one I spent months sourcing in Peru—was signed by the creative director. A high-pitched ringing filled my ears. I squeezed my eyes shut, but the letters seemed burned into the back of my eyelids. I stood up, walked to the window, and stared down at the traffic, tapping an erratic staccato against the glass with my fingernails. If I sent a polite email asking for clarification, would they twist it as insubordination? The thought made my stomach twist into hard, tight knots. I walked back to the sofa, sat down, and immediately stood up again. My breath came in short, shallow gasps. I picked up the magazine, rolled it into a tight tube, and squeezed it until my knuckles turned stark white.

In the quiet hush of the library, Sarah stared at the screen. The historical society's quarterly review had just gone live. Her painstaking translation of the 18th-century merchant diaries was published under Professor Higgins’ name. A cold prickle washed down her arms. She hurriedly scrolled to the bottom of the page, searching for a footnote, a co-author tag, anything. Nothing. She bit down hard on the inside of her cheek. Her knee began to bounce under the wooden desk, shaking the heavy oak table until the librarian shot her a warning glare. Sarah froze, her shoulders hiked up to her ears.
