She knocked over a stack of paper cups, the cardboard cylinders scattering across the tile floor. She didn't pick them up. Instead, she sank to the floor right there, wrapping her arms tightly around her knees and rocking back and forth.

The bright yellow 'Notice to Vacate or Purchase' flyer was taped right over the peephole. I peeled it off, the strong adhesive tearing away a long strip of paint. I dropped my heavy backpack onto the linoleum. My hands shook so badly I couldn't properly unfold the paper. I read the numbers—the exorbitant purchase price, the massive down payment requirements. The page blurred, swimming entirely out of focus. I rubbed my eyes fiercely until they physically ached. I have three final exams next week. I dragged my desk chair to the window and sat down, violently biting the inside of my lip. I pulled out my phone, typed "cheap apartments near campus" into the search bar, deleted it, and typed it again. My stomach rolled, sour and tight, as I rushed toward the bathroom.

Arthur spread the bank statements across the dining table, the crisp white envelope from the building's new management resting ominously at the center. His wife, Martha, poured tea, the china cup clattering noisily against the saucer as she set it down. Arthur ran a hand through his thinning hair, his foot tapping a rapid, erratic rhythm against the table leg. He added up the columns of numbers three times, and every time, the pencil lead snapped against the paper. He threw the pencil across the room. It bounced off the floral wallpaper with a sharp clatter. Martha sat beside him, twisting her wedding band around and around her finger, the gold digging deep into her skin. Neither of them touched their tea. The grandfather clock in the corner ticked loudly, each second sounding like a hammer strike.

"So, how do we know each other?" Leo asked, his brow furrowing as he took a sip of his latte. I felt the paper cup in my hand crumple slightly under my tightening grip. A cold prickle washed over the back of my neck. "We built the treehouse behind Elm Street," I stammered, my knee bouncing so fast under the table that it rattled the sugar packets. I searched his eyes, waiting for the spark of recognition, but there was only a polite, blank stare. My pulse drummed in my ears, drowning out the cafe chatter. I bit the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper, my mind racing to find the exact memory that would fix this. "The summer it rained every day," I pushed on, my voice climbing an octave. "You broke your wrist." Leo just offered an apologetic, empty smile.

Sarah smoothed the front of her dress for the fifth time in a minute, her fingers catching on the sequins. Across the gymnasium, Maya stood by the punch bowl. It had been fifteen years. Taking a breath that didn't quite fill her lungs, Sarah approached, her heels clicking too loudly against the polished floor. "Maya! It's me, Sarah." Maya turned, a polite, practiced smile on her face. "Hi! Did we have homeroom together?" The air seemed to rush out of the room. Sarah’s hands darted to her necklace, twisting the silver chain until it bit into her skin. "No, we... we rode bikes every single day. We buried the time capsule." Maya tilted her head, her gaze drifting toward the exit. "Oh, gosh. I'm terrible with faces." Sarah swallowed hard, her throat tight and dry, her eyes darting toward the floor as a heavy buzzing filled her head.

The train lurched, but my stomach had already plummeted minutes ago. He was sitting two rows down, older now, but definitely Julian. I spent four stops rehearsing my opening line, wiping my damp palms on my jeans over and over. When I finally stepped up to him, the words tumbled out in a rush. "Julian, hey, it's Mark! From the old neighborhood." He looked up from his tablet, squinting. "Sorry, do I know you?" My chest tightened as if wrapped in iron bands. I shifted my weight from my left foot to my right, suddenly hyper-aware of the people sitting nearby. "Mark? We shared a tent at Camp Kennebec. The raccoon incident?" I let out a jagged little laugh that sounded entirely wrong. Julian shook his head. "I think you have the wrong guy." I stood frozen in the aisle, my fingers trembling as I reached for the overhead rail.

The loading circle spun on the screen, matching the frantic churning in Elias’s gut. He tapped his front tooth with his thumbnail, a rapid click-click-click, until Chloe’s face appeared on the video call. "Hi! So nice of you to reach out," she said brightly. "Though I have to admit, I'm drawing a blank." Elias froze. The script he had written on the notepad beside his keyboard suddenly looked like a foreign language. "We... we were next-door neighbors in Portland," he managed to say, his foot jiggling the desk so hard his webcam vibrated. "We had the tin-can telephone." Chloe leaned closer to her camera, her brow wrinkling. "Portland? We moved when I was seven. I don't remember much before Denver." Elias rubbed the back of his neck, feeling a sheen of cold moisture there. His gaze darted around his room as his breathing grew shallow and rapid.

I dropped the hardcover, the thud echoing too loudly in the quiet aisle. "Sam?" I gasped. She turned away from the fantasy section, her eyes scanning me with mild curiosity. "Yes? Can I help you?" I stepped forward, then stopped, my hands hovering awkwardly in the space between us. "It's me. Jamie. We used to catch frogs in the creek behind your grandmother's house." The silence stretched out, thick and heavy. I could hear my own heartbeat thumping against my ribs. I began picking at the cuticle of my thumb, tearing it until it stung. "We promised we'd move to New York together," I blurted out, the words stumbling over one another. Sam offered a gentle, pitying look. "I'm so sorry, Jamie, is it? I really don't recall." The fluorescent lights above seemed to flicker, and I suddenly felt an overwhelming urge to bolt for the door.

Elena stared at the new transfer standing by the water cooler. It was definitely Tom. She approached him with stiff, jerky steps, her fingernails digging into the palm of her hand. "Tom? It's Elena. From Mrs. Gable's fifth-grade class." Tom turned, holding a paper cup. "Oh, hey. Nice to meet you. Elena, right?" He extended a hand. She stared at it, her mind stalling. She didn't take it. "We were best friends," she pushed out, her voice tight and breathy. "We built the volcano model that exploded on the principal." Tom laughed, a polite, empty sound. "Wow, sounds like a fun childhood. My memory before high school is basically a black hole." Elena’s jaw clenched so hard her teeth ached. She took a step back, her eyes darting to the clock, the hallway, anywhere but his face. "Right. Sure," she mumbled, quickly turning on her heel.

The clinical smell of the ward made my stomach pitch. I clutched the bouquet of daisies so tightly the stems snapped against my knuckles. Sitting by the bed, Arthur looked up from his magazine. "Can I help you?" he asked, his voice raspy. I forced a smile that felt like cracking plastic. "Artie, it’s Ben. I heard you were in town, I wanted to check in." He blinked slowly. "Ben?" My throat closed up. I shifted my chair closer, the metal legs screeching against the linoleum. "Benji. We had matching bicycles. We swore a blood oath behind the bleachers." Arthur looked at the nurse passing by, then back at me, his eyes guarded. "I think you’ve made a mistake, pal." The walls of the small room felt like they were inching closer. I swallowed repeatedly, trying to clear the sudden, suffocating lump in my airway.

David paced the length of the park bench, turning precisely on his heel each time he reached the end. When a man in a trench coat finally sat down, David stopped abruptly, his chest rising and falling in quick, uneven bursts. "Michael," David breathed out, sitting at the far edge of the wood slats. "I saw your post online. It's David. Dave." Michael looked over, offering a slight nod. "Hello. Thanks for reaching out, but do we know each other?" David felt a cold drop of sweat trace down his spine. He began aggressively peeling the paper off his coffee cup. "The treehouse. The summer of '98. We were inseparable." Michael frowned, a look of genuine confusion crossing his features. "I spent the summer of '98 in London with my aunt. Sorry, man." David’s hands began to shake, and he quickly shoved them deep into his coat pockets.

I held the battered cardboard box against my chest like a shield. Standing on the porch of the new house next door, I stared at the woman directing the movers. "Chloe?" I squeaked. She turned, wiping her forehead. "Yes? Are you the neighbor?" I nodded too fast, my neck cracking. "I'm Mia. We lived next door to each other in Ohio. We had the secret knock." Chloe gave a polite, strained laugh. "Ohio? Man, I haven't thought about that place in decades. Nice to meet you, Mia." She reached out to shake my hand. I stared at her outstretched palm, my vision blurring slightly at the edges. I shifted my weight back and forth, the cardboard box threatening to slip from my sweaty grip. "But... the knock," I whispered, my voice trembling. She had already turned back to the movers, leaving me rooted to the concrete steps.

Marcus gripped the stem of his wine glass, his knuckles turning stark white. Across the dining table, Clara was telling a story to the host. When there was a lull, Marcus leaned forward, almost knocking over the salt shaker. "Clara, it's incredible to see you. It's Marcus. From Maple Drive." Clara looked across the centerpiece, her polite smile never wavering. "Maple Drive? Oh, my family did live there briefly. Nice to meet you, Marcus." A high-pitched ringing started in Marcus's ears. He set his glass down before his trembling fingers could drop it. "We caught fireflies every night," he said, his words coming out in a rushed, breathless string. "We buried my goldfish, Captain." Clara exchanged a brief, puzzled glance with the host. "I'm so sorry, I don't remember that at all." Marcus pulled at his collar, suddenly feeling as though the room was a hundred degrees.

The gallery was dead quiet, which only amplified the roaring in my head. I stood in front of the abstract painting, but I was only looking at the artist. It was Finn. I approached him, my footsteps feeling heavy and uncoordinated. "Finn," I said, my voice cracking slightly. "It's me, Toby. The tree fort? The time we stole your dad's cigars?" Finn looked at me, his expression perfectly blank. "I'm sorry, I don't think we've met. I grew up an only child, didn't have many friends around then." I felt the blood drain from my face. I started tapping my thigh rapidly with my fingertips. "No, we were best friends. Every single day after school." Finn took a small step back, his eyes darting to the security guard near the entrance. My chest heaved, and I abruptly spun around, pushing through the glass doors into the cold street.

Nina stood by the dessert table, aggressively shredding a napkin into tiny, snowy piles. She had finally spotted Jenna. Gathering what little breath she could manage, she walked over, her legs feeling like lead pipes. "Jenna? It's Nina." Jenna turned from the buffet, a plate of hors d'oeuvres in hand. "Hi! Are you with the bride's family?" Nina’s stomach performed a violent flip. She reached up, twisting a strand of hair around her index finger so tightly it pulled at her scalp. "No, Jenna, it's Nina. We shared a locker in middle school. We painted our nails with white-out." Jenna’s smile faltered, replaced by a look of mild bewilderment. "Wow, I have absolutely no memory of that. Middle school is such a blur." Nina swallowed against the dry scratch in her throat, her eyes darting frantically toward the exit signs glowing red above the double doors.

I refreshed the browser three times, but the smiling headshot didn’t change. It was definitely him. Dr. Marcus Thorne, LMFT. The same Marcus who used to lock me in the gym lockers. My fingers hovered over the keyboard, trembling so much I accidentally clicked his 'Book a Session' button. A cold sweat broke out across the back of my neck. I slammed the laptop shut, pushing it away as if it might bite. My chest tightened, drawing in short, shallow breaths that did nothing to fill my lungs. I stood up, paced to the window, turned around, and paced back to the desk. Did he use that same soft, empathetic smile while he watched kids cry back then? I rubbed my palms against my jeans, trying to wipe away the sudden dampness, but my pulse kept hammering a rapid rhythm against my ribs.

Elena’s knee bounced in a rapid staccato, the heel of her boot clicking relentlessly against the linoleum. She clutched her intake forms, the paper wrinkling under her tight grip. The receptionist had cheerfully said, 'Dr. Hayes will be right with you.' Chloe Hayes. The girl who used to slip cruel notes into Elena’s backpack every single morning in middle school. Elena bit down on the inside of her cheek, tasting a faint metallic tang. She glanced at the exit door, measuring the distance. Five steps. She could just stand up and walk out. What if Chloe recognized her? What if she remembered the nickname she gave her? Elena swallowed hard, her throat painfully dry. The doorknob to the inner office turned. Elena stopped breathing entirely, her fingernails digging deep crescents into her palms as the hinges creaked open.

My thumb froze over the glowing screen of the therapy app. 'Matched Therapist: David Kessler. Specialty: Trauma.' The room suddenly felt ten degrees hotter. I loosened the collar of my shirt, gasping for a proper breath. David Kessler. I closed my eyes, but the image of him holding my head underwater at the community pool flashed behind my eyelids. I tossed the phone onto the couch cushion and backed away, wiping my clammy hands on my trousers. I walked to the kitchen, poured a glass of water, and spilled half of it on the counter because my hands wouldn't stop shaking. He was supposed to help me heal? The walls of my apartment felt like they were pressing inward. I grabbed the phone again, rapidly swiping to find the cancel button, my chest heaving with every ragged exhale.

"You should totally see him, Julian. He's amazing," Sarah said, sliding the business card across the cafe table. Julian stared at the elegant embossed lettering: Dr. Thomas Vance, Clinical Psychologist. Julian’s stomach plummeted like he’d just stepped off a ledge. He quickly tucked his hands under his thighs to hide their violent shaking. "Tommy Vance?" he asked, his voice coming out as a reedy squeak. He cleared his throat, trying to force his vocal cords to cooperate. "From Oak Creek High?" Sarah nodded happily. Julian looked at the exit, then at the half-empty latte in front of him, feeling a sudden wave of sour nausea roll through his gut. The boy who had humiliated him daily in the cafeteria was now holding the keys to people's mental well-being. Julian’s leg began to jiggle uncontrollably under the wooden table.

I flipped the page of the local wellness magazine and my coffee mug slipped, shattering onto the kitchen tiles. Hot liquid splashed my ankles, but I didn't move. 'Local Hero: Therapist Tanya Brooks Wins Empathy Award.' Tanya. The girl who spread the rumor that made me switch schools in tenth grade. My heart did a painful flutter, beating violently against my sternum. I bent down to pick up the ceramic shards, but my fingers felt numb and uncoordinated. I nicked my thumb, watching a drop of blood well up, entirely disconnected from the sting. I left the mess on the floor and backed into the hallway, pulling my knees to my chest as I sat on the bottom stair. My breath came in sharp, ragged hitches. Tanya Brooks, a beacon of empathy? The air in the house suddenly felt entirely too thick to breathe.

The radio commercial droned on about finding inner peace, ending with a soothing voice: "Schedule your consultation with Dr. Greg Miller today." Liam slammed his foot on the brake, the car jerking violently before he pulled over to the shoulder. He threw the vehicle into park and gripped the steering wheel until his knuckles turned entirely white. Greg Miller. The guy who used to shove Liam into the snowbanks and steal his winter coat. Liam rolled down the window, gulping the crisp autumn air, but his chest remained stubbornly tight. He wiped a sheen of sweat from his forehead. He checked the rearview mirror, then the side mirrors, half-expecting Greg’s teenage sneer to appear in the reflection. Liam’s foot tapped an erratic beat against the floor mat. He couldn't put the car back in drive. His hands simply refused to let go of the leather wheel.

I stopped dead on the sidewalk, ignoring the annoyed grumbles of pedestrians swerving around me. The brass plaque by the oak door gleamed in the afternoon sun: Victoria Vance, Psychoanalyst. My stomach executed a sickening roll. Victoria. The architect of my high school misery, the girl who recorded me crying and sent it to the whole district. My pulse hammered in my ears, drowning out the city traffic. I shoved my hands deep into my coat pockets to hide their violent trembling. I needed to keep walking, but my feet felt encased in concrete. I stared at the door, half-expecting it to swing open and reveal her pointing and laughing. A bead of sweat trickled down my temple despite the biting wind. I spun on my heel, nearly tripping over my own feet, and practically sprinted down the opposite direction of the street.

Maya tapped her pen against her chin, listening to the guest speaker on the mental health podcast. The voice was smooth, cultured, and horribly familiar. "Healing begins with vulnerability," the speaker said. Maya glanced at the show notes. Guest: Dr. Aaron Price. Her pen snapped in half. Ink smeared across her fingers, but she just stared at it, her breathing turning shallow and fast. Aaron Price. The boy who locked her in the basement during the seventh-grade Halloween party. Maya stood up so fast her desk chair rolled backward and hit the wall with a loud bang. She paced the length of her tiny home office, rubbing her temples. She rushed back to the computer, her cursor darting erratically across the screen until she managed to click the pause button. The ensuing silence left her entirely alone with the rapid thudding of her own heart.

The little loading circle spun on my screen as I waited for the telehealth room to open. I bit down on my thumbnail, tearing the cuticle until I tasted copper. 'Connecting to Dr. Derek Shaw.' Derek Shaw. I had only recognized the name after the confirmation email hit my inbox. The guy who used to trip me in the cafeteria and dump my lunch in the trash. My knee jackhammered against the underside of my desk. I dragged my cursor toward the red 'Leave Meeting' button, my palm slick with sweat against the mouse. The camera light flicked on green. I gasped, jerking my hand back as if the mouse had burned me. My heart raced like a trapped bird beating its wings against a cage. I squeezed my eyes shut, my jaw clenched so tight my teeth ached, unable to look at the monitor.

Oliver stared at the email from his insurance provider. 'Your new network provider is Rachel Higgins, LCSW.' The glowing pixels seemed to blur together as Oliver’s breathing hitched. He backed his chair away from the monitor, scraping the casters loudly against the hardwood floor. Rachel. The girl who had made it her life’s mission to torment him about his weight every day of sophomore year. Oliver wrapped his arms around his own torso, suddenly hyper-aware of how much space he took up in the room. He swallowed repeatedly, trying to clear the massive lump forming in his throat. He picked up his phone, dialed the insurance hotline, and hung up before it even rang. He dialed again. Hung up. His hands were clammy, slipping against the glass screen. He couldn't go to her. He just couldn't. His chest felt wrapped in tight, unforgiving iron bands.

I wandered into the self-help aisle, running my fingers over the glossy spines. My hand stopped on a book titled 'Overcoming Childhood Trauma.' The author’s photo on the back cover hit me like a physical blow. Bradley Hayes. His face was older, framed by wire-rimmed glasses, but it was the same Bradley who used to spit on my shoes on the bus. The book slipped from my suddenly numb fingers, hitting the carpeted floor with a dull thud. I stumbled backward, bumping into the opposite shelf. A stack of paperbacks tumbled down around my ankles. I couldn't bring myself to pick them up. I felt a cold prickle of sweat break out across my hairline. I looked left, then right, suddenly convinced he might step out from behind the endcap. I grabbed my purse, clutching it tight to my chest, and bolted for the glass exit doors.

The glossy brochure slid out of the envelope and onto the kitchen island. Pine Valley Counseling Center. Sofia picked it up, her eyes scanning the list of staff. She stopped at the third portrait. Dr. Melissa Vance. Sofia dropped the paper as if it were a live coal. Melissa. The girl who had made ninth grade such a living hell that Sofia had begged her parents to home-school her. Sofia began to pace the length of the kitchen island, her bare feet slapping rapidly against the tile. She rubbed her stomach, a sudden sour wave of nausea rising in her throat. She snatched the brochure back up, tore it cleanly in half, then into quarters, then into tiny confetti-sized pieces. She dumped them into the trash can, but her hands wouldn't stop shaking. She kept staring at the garbage, taking rapid, shallow gulps of air.

I stare at the email on my phone, the screen blurring as my thumb hovers over the words "Financial Insolvency." A drop of crimson acrylic drips from my brush onto my shoe, but I don't move to wipe it away. My heart hammers against my ribs like a trapped bird. Sixty credits. I have sixty credits tied up in this fine arts program. I bite down on my thumbnail, tearing the cuticle until a sharp sting grounds me. If the doors lock next month, will the state university take my portfolio? Will my loans instantly demand repayment? I refresh the inbox, hoping it’s a sick prank from the IT department, but a follow-up message from the Dean drops in. My breathing grows shallow and quick, the studio suddenly feeling like a closet shrinking around me.

Marcus sat in the hushed library, his right leg bouncing with such rapid intensity that his coffee sloshed over the rim of its paper cup. The bold red font of the university’s press release glared from his laptop screen: permanently ceasing operations. He pressed the heels of his hands against his eyes, rubbing until bursts of static light popped in his vision. Three years of nursing prerequisites, gone. He opened a new tab, rapidly typing in transfer requirements for the college two towns over, then closed it before the page could load. He picked up his pen, clicked it open, clicked it shut, clicked it open, the sharp metallic snaps drawing glares from a nearby study group. Marcus didn't notice them; he was too busy calculating how much debt he owed for a degree that no longer existed.

The crisp autumn air usually clears my head, but today it feels too thin to fill my lungs. I walk across the historic quad, my hands shoved deep into my jacket pockets, my fingers curled into tight, sweaty fists. The emergency town hall meeting just ended, and the echoes of "bankruptcy" still ring in my ears. I’m one semester away from graduating. Just one. I stop by the oak tree, pulling my phone out to call my mom, but my thumb freezes over her contact picture. My jaw aches from clenching it. What do I even say? "Hey Mom, the school is broke and my diploma is vapor." I slide the phone back into my pocket, take two quick, jagged breaths, and start pacing a tight circle into the fallen leaves.

Elena chewed the plastic cap of her highlighter until it splintered with a sharp crack, spitting the blue shards into her palm. The international student affairs office had a line stretching out the door and down the tiled hallway. She shifted her weight from her left foot to her right, repeatedly checking the expiration date on her F-1 visa. If the campus boarded its windows by December, her legal status evaporated with it. She unzipped her backpack, touched her passport to ensure it was still there, zipped it back up, and immediately unzipped it to check again. A girl ahead of her started crying, and Elena’s stomach performed a sickening flip. She wiped her clammy palms on her jeans, her gaze darting toward the closed office door, silently begging for it to open.

I read the letter pinned to the bulletin board three times, my foot tapping a relentless rhythm against the linoleum floor. Closing. The community college is actually closing. I look down at my sleeping daughter in her stroller, my chest tightening as if a heavy iron plate just dropped onto my ribs. I chose this campus because it was ten minutes from her daycare. I run a hand through my hair, gripping the roots tight. If I have to transfer to the state campus downtown, that’s an hour commute each way. How do I pick her up on time? Who watches her during evening labs? I pull out my planner, flipping through pages of meticulously scheduled routines that are now completely useless, the lines of my handwriting swimming as my pulse throbs in my temples.

David stood perfectly still in the center of his shoebox dorm room, the printed notice crumpled in his sweaty grip. He was the first person in his family to ever set foot on a college campus, let alone get a scholarship. His parents had thrown a block party when his acceptance letter arrived. He began to pace, three steps to the mini-fridge, three steps to the bed. Turn around, repeat. The silence in the room was deafening, save for his own ragged breathing. He smoothed the crumpled paper out on his desk, his hand trembling so violently he knocked over a stack of textbooks. They hit the floor with a heavy thud. He stared at the ceiling, swallowing hard against a thick lump forming in his throat, unable to blink away the burning sensation in his eyes.

Coach didn't even look us in the eye when he delivered the news. I’m sitting on the locker room bench, repeatedly re-lacing my left cleat. Pull tight, cross over, tie. Undo it. Pull tight, cross over, tie. The athletic department is being liquidated along with the rest of the university. My scholarship vanishes on the first of the month. I stand up, sit back down, and wipe a layer of cold sweat from my forehead with the back of my wrist. Without the free ride, I can't afford a single credit hour. I grab my phone, opening my highlight reel, my thumb hovering over the 'share' button. Do I email other recruiters right now? Is it too late in the season? My knee bounces rapidly, the metal bench rattling beneath me in the quiet room.

Sarah sat on the hood of her sedan in the commuter lot, her keys jingling incessantly as she passed them back and forth between her trembling hands. At forty-two, returning to school had been a monumental leap of faith. Now, an email casually announced the doors would lock forever at the end of the term. She tugged at the collar of her blouse, suddenly feeling like she couldn't get enough air. Starting over here had been hard enough; the thought of transferring, of walking into another admissions office with her scattered transcripts, made her stomach violently churn. She dropped her keys, the metal clattering loudly against the asphalt. Instead of picking them up, she pressed the heels of her hands against her closed eyes, her breathing coming in short, erratic hitches.

The spotlight above the stage cuts out, leaving us standing in the dim work lights as the theater director reads the bankruptcy memo. I peel the label off my water bottle, tearing it into tiny, microscopic strips until a pile of shredded plastic gathers at my feet. My senior showcase was supposed to be next week. The casting directors from New York had already booked their flights. I swallow dryly, my throat feeling like sandpaper. I look at my scene partner, but the words of our script have entirely vanished from my brain. I dig my fingernails deep into my palms, the half-moon indents turning white. If the school shutters before the showcase, four years of vocal training and scene study end in an empty auditorium. I start shredding a stray thread on my costume sleeve.

Leo stroked the golden retriever’s fur much faster than usual, his fingers snagging in the thick coat. The veterinary tech program was being completely dissolved by Friday. He bit the inside of his cheek, tasting a faint metallic tang of blood, and shifted his weight constantly from heel to toe. This was the only clinic within a two-hundred-mile radius that offered large animal certification. He grabbed a clipboard from the counter, checked the dog’s vitals, put the clipboard down, and immediately picked it up to check again. His heart hammered a rapid, irregular rhythm against his ribcage. He reached for his phone to look up out-of-state programs, but his hands were shaking so much he dropped it onto the linoleum floor. The screen cracked, a jagged web mirroring the sudden, sharp splintering of his entire five-year plan.

I literally just transferred here. I stare at the "Immediate Closure" subject line, clicking my pen repeatedly—click, click, click—until the spring mechanism jams. I moved across the country, signed a twelve-month lease on an off-campus apartment, and paid out-of-state tuition in full. I push my chair back from the desk, standing up only to sit right back down. My chest feels tight, like someone has wrapped a thick leather belt around my lungs and is pulling it notch by notch. Can I get a refund? What happens to my lease? I open my banking app, staring at a checking account balance that reads fourteen dollars, my vision blurring. I take a deep, shuddering breath, violently rubbing my temples as a sharp, pulsing headache begins to bloom behind my eyes.

Dr. Aris forwarded the memo without any text in the body, just the attached PDF declaring the institution’s immediate insolvency. Maya sat in the basement laboratory, her eyes darting between the email and the humming rows of refrigerated centrifuges. Three years. Three years of cell culture data. She stood up, knocking her knee hard against the desk, but didn’t rub the bruise. Instead, she began hastily opening drawers, pulling out flash drives and shoving them into her pockets. Where does the grant money go? Who owns the proprietary research if the university ceases to exist? She felt a cold prickle of sweat break out across the back of her neck. She grabbed an external hard drive, fumbling the cord twice before managing to plug it in, her eyes fixed on the agonizingly slow progress bar.

I stared at the crisp white paper taped to the glass door of Luigi’s Diner. "Closing permanently." My teeth sank into my lower lip, tasting faint copper. I read the words again, then a third time, as a heavy stone dropped into my gut. Where would I go on Tuesday mornings? The library cafe? Too loud. The chain down the street? The coffee always tastes burnt. I pulled my phone out, almost dropping it on the pavement, my thumbs fumbling over the screen to search maps, but my vision blurred. I shoved it back into my pocket, pulled it out again, and refreshed the browser. Nothing changed. My chest tightened, breath coming in short, shallow puffs that fogged the diner's window. I just stood there, shifting my weight from left foot to right, unable to step away, unable to walk inside.

The blue light of the phone screen illuminated Clara’s face in the dark bedroom. The post read: *Thank you for ten years. Sakura Sushi is closing.* Clara sat bolt upright. She threw the blankets off, her bare feet hitting the hardwood floor. She began pacing the narrow strip between the bed and the dresser. Three steps forward, pivot, three steps back. She tapped the call button on their profile, but it was 2:00 AM. She hung up, dialed again, and hung up before it rang. Her fingernails drummed a rapid rhythm against the hard plastic phone case. What if she couldn't get a final reservation? What if they were already fully booked? She sat on the edge of the mattress, rubbing her temples raw, her leg bouncing so violently the entire bed frame rattled in the silent room.

Marcus leaned over the espresso machine, wiping his hands on his stained apron. "Lease is up, mate. Sunday's our last day." I nodded, but my throat closed entirely around the words of sympathy I meant to offer. My fingers curled around my ceramic mug so hard my knuckles turned a bruised shade of white. I looked around the chaotic, comforting mess of the Book & Bean. The worn armchair in the corner. The wobbly table where I was writing my thesis. I took a sip of my latte, but it tasted like ash, and a sudden coughing fit left me gasping for air. I wiped my sweaty palms on my jeans, knocking my pen onto the floor. I bent down to retrieve it, my heart hammering a staccato, uneven beat against my ribs, unable to picture the coming Monday.

Elias folded the neighborhood gazette, smoothing the center crease with his thumb over and over until the dark ink smudged his skin. *Luigi's Pizzeria to Shutter.* He stared at the grey smudge on his thumb. Leo only ate pizza on Fridays. Specifically, Luigi's cheese pizza with the blistered crust. Elias stood up, walked to the kitchen counter, and began rearranging the fruit bowl. Apples on the left, bananas on the right. No, bananas in the back. He grabbed his keys from the dish, jingled them loudly, and dropped them back. He checked his watch. 4:15 PM. Leo would be home at 5:00. Elias gripped the edge of the marble island, taking a deep breath that hitched in his throat, his eyes darting toward the front door, bracing for the precise moment the yellow school bus would hiss to a stop.

The neon ‘Open’ sign flickered its familiar crimson glow, but the bartender slipped a small flyer under my coaster. *Closing Party Next Saturday.* I peeled the wet label off my beer bottle, stripping it away in tiny, jagged shreds until a pile of damp paper confetti blanketed the mahogany bar. I swallowed hard, but there was a knot in my throat that wouldn't budge. This stool was my anchor after every grueling hospital shift. I tapped my boots against the brass rail, faster and faster, a drumbeat echoing the thudding in my ears. I pulled out my wallet, checked my cash, put it away, then pulled it out again. I needed to ask for the recipe to their garlic fries, but my jaw remained clamped shut, my teeth grinding together so hard my temples throbbed with a dull ache.

When the waitress set down the plate of pork buns, she leaned in close. "Just so you know, the landlord sold the building. We're out by the end of the month." Julian blinked. He picked up his wooden chopsticks, dropped them onto the table, and picked them up again. He stabbed at a dumpling, tearing the delicate wrapper. Hot broth spilled across the ceramic plate. He wiped his forehead with a napkin, leaving a faint smear of soy sauce on his brow. "End of the month," he repeated, his voice cracking on the final syllable. He pulled out his pocket planner, flipping through pages with such force that May tore halfway down the seam. He began calculating rapidly, muttering under his breath about freezer capacity and dry ice, his foot tapping a relentless beat against the wrought-iron leg of the bistro table.

The email subject line caught my eye immediately: *Au Revoir from Le Petit Cochon.* I didn't even open it. I minimized the window, opened it again, and stared at the bold font. This was the exact place where Sarah and I had our first date, and where the velvet ring box was currently sitting in my pocket waiting for tomorrow night. I sprang up from my office chair, knocking my knee hard against the desk drawer. I barely felt the sting. I started pacing the short length of my cubicle, dragging my nails lightly down the fabric walls. I picked up my phone, dialed Sarah's number, hung up before the first ring, and started typing a text. *Delete. Delete. Delete.* The cursor blinked at me. My own pulse raced so fast my vision swam with tiny black dots.

Hector stood under the flickering streetlight, clutching a warm foil-wrapped burrito. The vendor, an old man with a thick mustache, was packing away the salsa bowls. "Retiring back to Jalisco, amigo. Tomorrow's my last stand." Hector froze. The silver foil crinkled loudly under his sudden, crushing grip. He looked down at the burrito, then up at the vendor, then up and down the desolate avenue. He shifted his weight, his left knee jiggling uncontrollably. He reached into his pocket, pulled out a handful of crumpled bills, and shoved them toward the metal cart. "Give me another. Make it three. Actually, five." The vendor chuckled, but Hector wasn't smiling. Sweat gathered at his hairline despite the crisp autumn breeze. He chewed the inside of his cheek, tasting copper, his eyes darting to the empty spot on the pavement.

I spotted the 'For Lease' sign planted right in the center of the community garden box outside The Green Spoon. I stopped dead on the busy sidewalk, a passing pedestrian bumping hard into my shoulder. I didn't apologize. My hands immediately dove into my heavy coat pockets, balling into tight fists. My sanctuary. The only place in the city that served the allergen-free muffins I could actually eat. I started walking again, my pace doubling, almost a jog. I reached the glass door and peered inside at the empty wooden tables. My breath hitched, a short, ragged gasp escaping my lips. I pulled out my phone, swiping aimlessly past screens of colorful apps, not really seeing any of them. I bit down on my thumbnail, tearing the edge off, my mind racing through a barren wasteland of lunch breaks.

The manager handed out the laminated menus with a solemn nod. "Enjoy it, folks. Corporate is shutting this location down on the 31st." Maya’s fingers slipped on the smooth plastic edge. The menu clattered to the linoleum floor. She dove under the table to grab it, bumping her head hard on the underside of the wood. When she surfaced, her face was flushed, and she was panting lightly. She smoothed the menu flat on the table, running her bare hands over the printed lists of pancakes and omelets over and over. "The 31st," she whispered. She grabbed her water glass, taking a large gulp, but the ice cubes tumbled forward, splashing freezing water down the front of her blouse. She didn't grab a napkin. She just stared at the wet stain, her chest rising and falling in rapid bursts.

The handwritten chalkboard out front, usually boasting the soup of the day, bore a different message today. *Closing our doors forever. Thanks for the memories.* I read the chalk dust words, feeling an icy prickle wash over my scalp. I stepped back, bumping into a metal trash can, and stood there completely paralyzed. Every Tuesday and Thursday for six years, I sat at the third booth. I touched my neck, my fingertips pressing against the rapid, fluttering pulse jumping beneath my skin. I began to rock slightly on my heels, muttering the names of the cross streets. Main and 4th. Elm and 5th. Nothing else was close enough to the clinic. I dug my fingernails into my palms, squeezing until crescent moons indented my flesh, my eyes locked in a wide, unblinking stare at the smudged white lettering.

Arthur sat at the polished mahogany bar of The Oak Room, nursing his usual scotch. The bartender polished a glass, actively avoiding eye contact. "Building's being demolished for condos, Mr. Pendelton. End of the month." Arthur’s hand shot out, knocking his heavy crystal glass over. The amber liquid seeped rapidly into the cardboard coaster. He didn't ask for a towel. He stared at the puddle, his jaw muscles clenching and unclenching in rapid succession. He unbuttoned his crisp white collar, suddenly feeling as though the dimly lit, spacious room had shrunk to the size of a tiny closet. He pulled out a silk handkerchief and wiped his brow, which had broken out in a cold sweat. He stood up, sat back down, then stood up again, his shiny leather brogues pacing a tight circle around his barstool.

I pressed my back against the cool plaster of the banquet hall pillar, clutching a flute of champagne until my knuckles turned stark white. Across the room, Sarah was laughing by the ice sculpture, her head thrown back in that familiar way. My chest tightened, drawing in short, sharp breaths that barely reached my lungs. I took a hurried gulp of the sparkling wine, nearly choking as it went down the wrong pipe. Should I walk over? If I walk over, what do I do with my hands? My palms were slick with sweat, slipping against the damp crystal of the glass. I pulled out my phone, staring blankly at a black screen, desperately hoping I looked entirely engrossed in a fake email while my pulse hammered a frantic, deafening rhythm against my eardrums.

Marcus stood in front of the gilded bathroom mirror, undoing and retying his bow tie for the seventh time. The silk fabric felt like a noose against his Adam’s apple. He kept checking his watch; it had only been three minutes since he retreated here. Through the heavy oak door, the muffled bass of the wedding band pulsed. David was out there, sitting at Table 9. Marcus was assigned to Table 8. The seating chart was a tactical error by the bride. Marcus ran a trembling hand through his hair, noting the faint sheen of perspiration on his forehead. He splashed cold water on his face, taking a deep, shuddering breath. "Hey, good to see you," he whispered to his pale reflection, the words catching in his dry throat. "Hey. It's been a while."

The silver salad fork slipped right through my clammy fingers and clattered onto the china plate, echoing like a gunshot during the best man’s speech. I squeezed my eyes shut. Two tables away, Mark slowly turned his head toward the noise. I instantly ducked behind the towering floral centerpiece, pretending to examine the underside of a white rose. My stomach churned, twisting into heavy knots. I began picking frantically at a loose thread on my velvet dress, unraveling it inch by inch as my knee bounced rapidly against the underside of the table. Every time the heavy mahogany doors swung open, my head snapped up, calculating the exact distance between my chair and the nearest emergency exit. I just needed to survive the cake cutting without making eye contact.

Elena ripped her paper cocktail napkin into tiny, jagged shreds, piling them into a snowy mound beside her empty martini glass. Over the lively chatter of the reception, she distinctly heard Liam’s booming laugh. Her spine went entirely rigid. She glued her eyes to the ice cubes melting in her glass, her jaw clamped so tight her back teeth ground together. The bartender asked if she wanted another, but Elena couldn't force her throat to swallow, let alone speak. She gave a quick, jerky nod. The fabric of her silk gown felt suddenly suffocating, trapping the heat radiating from her skin. She tapped her heel against the brass footrail in double-time, mentally mapping the path to the coat check. If she left before the entrees arrived, would the newlyweds even notice?

Standing in the buffet line should have been safe, but there she was, exactly three people ahead of me, hovering over the prime rib station. I immediately shoved my hands deep into my pockets to hide the slight tremor in my fingers. My breathing turned shallow, catching high in my chest. I stared intently at the shiny silver chafing dish lids, avoiding any reflective surfaces that might betray my location. If she turns around, I thought, I will simply pretend I am deeply fascinated by the dinner rolls. I shifted my weight from my left foot to my right, then back again, my collar suddenly feeling entirely too tight for my neck. I ran a hand over my mouth, wiping away a fresh bead of sweat from my upper lip.

Julian stood by the dimly lit patio bar, aggressively stirring a gin and tonic he had no intention of drinking. The ice clinked a frantic, erratic tempo against the glass. The moment he saw Arthur step out onto the terrace, Julian’s breath hitched. He instantly pulled out his phone, scrolling blindly through a year-old text thread, his thumbs slipping over the screen. He hunched his shoulders forward, trying to physically shrink his six-foot frame into the shadows of the creeping ivy. Arthur was walking toward the bar. Julian’s heart thudded violently against his ribs, a wild bird trapped in a cage. He chewed viciously on the inside of his cheek, tasting the faint metallic tang of copper, entirely unable to tear his gaze away from his glowing, meaningless phone screen.

The DJ dimmed the chandelier lights and announced a couples' dance. I immediately retreated to the dessert table, seizing a plate and blindly loading it with macarons. I didn't even like coconut. Across the dancefloor, Alex was walking in my direction. I stopped chewing. The half-eaten pastry felt like dry sawdust in my mouth. I tried to swallow, but my throat had completely closed up. I took a sudden, jerky step backward, my heel catching on the edge of the carpet. I grabbed the edge of the linen tablecloth to steady myself, my knuckles bone-white. I looked frantically at the kitchen doors, then at the restrooms, calculating which destination I could reach faster. My chest heaved, pulling in air that somehow wasn't enough, as Alex closed the distance by another ten feet.

Chloe sat completely frozen at the edge of her Chiavari chair. Ryan was standing at the bar, chatting amicably with the bride's cousin. Chloe’s right leg bounced uncontrollably, vibrating the table enough to make the water goblets chime. She pressed both palms flat against her thighs, trying to force her muscles to stop twitching. She checked the time on her watch. 8:14 PM. She checked it again ten seconds later. Still 8:14 PM. Her mouth was incredibly dry, parched as though she had been wandering a desert rather than sitting in an air-conditioned ballroom. She grabbed a nearby dinner roll and began tearing it into microscopic crumbs, her eyes darting between Ryan's broad shoulders and the swinging doors of the kitchen. She just needed a place to hide.

I approached the guestbook with a forced, plastic smile, taking the feathered pen from the usher. As I looked down at the blank page, the signature directly above mine jumped out, practically written in neon lights. Jonathan Miller. My stomach did a violent somersault. I gripped the pen so tightly the plastic cracked faintly under my thumb. I tried to write my own name, but my hand was shaking so badly that the first letter was an illegible, jagged scrawl. I could hear his distinctive voice floating over from the gift table. I dropped the pen entirely. It rolled off the table and bounced onto the polished hardwood floor. I didn't bend down to pick it up. I just turned and walked away at a brisk, almost running pace, leaving my greeting unfinished.

Standing by the grand floral arch, Maya caught sight of the familiar blue suit out of the corner of her eye. Her chest restricted instantly. She spun around, turning her back to the courtyard, and immediately began a highly animated, completely fake conversation with a potted fern. She crossed her arms tightly over her chest, digging her manicured nails into her own biceps. Every rustle of footsteps on the gravel path sent a sharp jolt of electricity up her spine. She squeezed her eyes shut, repeatedly whispering a silent countdown from ten to one under her breath. When a passing waiter accidentally brushed against her elbow, Maya jumped a full inch off the ground, letting out a sharp, breathless gasp before stammering out a rapid string of incoherent apologies to the confused staff member.

I retreated to the women’s lounge for the fourth time in an hour, popping open my gold makeup compact. I didn't need powder; I just needed to look at something that wasn't Greg. The hinge of the mirror squeaked as I snapped it open and shut, over and over, establishing a frantic rhythm. My reflection showed wide, unblinking eyes and a pale complexion. Through the thin walls, I heard him laugh. My grip on the metal compact slipped, my palms slick with sudden perspiration. I braced both hands flat against the cold marble vanity, locking my elbows as my knees threatened to buckle. I took a deep, shuddering gulp of air, squeezing my eyes tightly shut. "Just make it to the cake," I whispered into the empty, tiled room. "Just survive the cake."

The best man tapped his glass, and the room fell completely silent. From her seat at the edge of the room, Jenna realized with a sickening jolt that Leo had stopped walking right behind her chair. She sat bolt upright, her spine rigid against the wooden rungs. She could feel the faint heat of his presence at her back. Jenna clamped her teeth down hard on her lower lip, tasting salt. Her hands rested in her lap, fingers twisted together into a tight, pale knot. She stared unblinkingly at the center of the best man’s forehead, completely deaf to the speech. Every breath she took was shallow, silent, and deliberate, terrified that if she moved even a fraction of an inch, the chair would squeak and he would look down.

I stared at the empty patch of gravel where my Honda should have been. My pulse pounded in my ears, drowning out the ticking of the hallway clock. I picked up my phone, dialed the non-emergency number, and immediately hung up. What if it wasn't stolen? What if it was the HOA? I rubbed my sweaty palms against my jeans and paced from the kitchen to the living room. Seven steps there, seven steps back. The tire tracks in the driveway showed a heavy truck had been there. I chewed on my bottom lip until I tasted copper. If I didn't have my car, I couldn't get to the interview at noon. If I missed the interview, I couldn't make rent. My chest tightened as I stared at the phone screen, willing it to ring, my thumbs trembling over the keypad.

Elias pressed his forehead against the cold windowpane, his breath fogging the glass as the flashing amber lights of the tow truck bathed his living room in an erratic glow. He tapped his index finger against the sill—tap-tap-tap, tap-tap-tap. His stomach churned as the mechanical winch whined, lifting his sedan by the front wheels. He should go out there. He needed to go out there and show them the driveway was his property. Instead, he swallowed hard, his throat dry, and backed away into the shadows of the curtains. The truck lurched forward. Elias’s hands shook as he pulled his phone from his pocket, dropping it twice on the hardwood floor before finally dialing his landlord. "Hey, uh, they took it," he rasped, his breathing shallow and quick. "The car. It's gone. What do I do? What do I do now?"

The driveway was empty. I blinked, rubbed my eyes, and looked again. Just a rectangular dry spot on the damp concrete. My breath caught in my throat. I walked to the curb, looking left down Elm Street, then right, then left again. Nothing. My keys jingled wildly in my trembling hands. I walked a tight circle on the lawn, digging my nails into my palms. It was parked right here. I had paid the registration. Hadn't I? I yanked my wallet out, flipping through receipts with clumsy, stiff fingers. The paper slipped out and scattered in the wind. I dropped to my knees, scrambling to gather them, my heart hammering against my ribs like a trapped bird. Every passing car sounded like a siren. I squeezed my eyes shut, rocking slightly, trying to remember if I had moved it.

Clara sat on the edge of her porch, her knees pulled tight to her chest. She gnawed on the edge of her thumbnail, pulling until the cuticle bled. Down the street, the red taillights of the flatbed disappeared around the corner, taking her silver Corolla with it. She checked the time on her cracked phone screen. 8:14 AM. Her shift started at 8:30. She bounced her leg rapidly, the heel of her sneaker drumming a frantic rhythm against the wooden planks. How much was a tow fee? Three hundred? Four hundred? She opened her banking app, watching the loading circle spin. Her breath came in short, jagged gasps. $42.18 in checking. The screen blurred as she forgot to blink. She refreshed the app, hoping the number would magically change, her chest feeling as though a heavy iron block rested perfectly over her lungs.

I traced the fresh gouges in the asphalt with the toe of my shoe. They dragged it right out of my own carport. I pulled my jacket tight around my shoulders, shivering despite the mild morning sun. I need to call the police. Or the impound lot. Or maybe the bank? Did I miss a payment? I pulled up my email, typing 'auto loan' into the search bar, my thumb slipping and hitting the wrong letters twice. The little spinning wheel on the screen seemed to mock me. I paced the length of the driveway, counting my steps aloud. "One, two, three..." I stopped, losing track, and stared at the empty space. If it’s repossessed, my credit is ruined. If it’s stolen, I have to deal with insurance. I rubbed my temples, trying to massage away the high-pitched ringing echoing in my ears.

Marcus burst through his front door in just his socks and pajama pants, his footsteps echoing on the porch. "Wait!" he yelled, his voice cracking. The tow truck driver didn't hear him over the roar of the diesel engine. Marcus sprinted down the driveway, his socks soaking up the morning dew. He stopped short of the curb, chest heaving, gulping down air as if he were drowning. He patted his pockets—empty. He had left his phone and wallet inside. He looked from the departing truck to his open front door, shifting his weight from one foot to the other. He rubbed the back of his neck furiously, his skin hot to the touch. The quiet suburban street felt intensely loud, every rustling leaf sounding like an accusation. He stood frozen on the concrete, his hands clenching and unclenching at his sides.

"But it was in my driveway," I said into the receiver, my voice a full octave higher than normal. I paced a tight figure-eight on the bare pavement where my truck had sat for three years. "You can't just authorize a tow from private property!" I squeezed the phone so hard my knuckles turned white. On the other end, the HOA president droned on about bylaws and expired tags. I couldn't hear the words over the rush of blood in my ears. I squatted down, picking at a weed growing in the concrete crack, snapping it into tiny pieces. "Where did they take it?" I asked, my breath catching on the last word. I stood up too fast, black spots dancing in my vision. I began opening and closing my fists, desperate to grab the steering wheel that was miles away by now.

Jenna stared at the empty spot next to the porch, her backpack slipping slowly off her shoulder to hit the dirt with a soft thud. She clamped both hands over her mouth. The driveway was completely bare. She spun around, scanning the street, her eyes darting between the parked cars, looking for the familiar dented bumper of her sedan. She checked her watch—finals started in forty minutes. A cold sweat broke out across her forehead, making her bangs stick to her skin. She pulled out her phone to call an Uber, but her fingers shook violently, causing her to drop the device. It clattered against the asphalt. Jenna sank to her knees, staring at the cracked screen without making a move to pick it up. Her breathing became rapid and shallow, her chest rising and falling in quick, jerky motions.

The yellow lights flashed against the walls of my bedroom. I threw on a hoodie and ran outside. A massive truck was already hooked to the front axle of my minivan. I opened my mouth to yell, but my throat closed completely. The burly driver slammed the metal lever, and my van hoisted into the air with a screech. I took a step forward, then immediately took two steps back, retreating to the safety of my porch shadows. I chewed on the inside of my cheek until I tasted blood. The driver looked my way, and I instantly looked down at my slippers, shrinking against the doorframe. My heart hammered wildly against my ribs. I needed that van to pick up the kids. But the words wouldn't come out. I just stood there, shivering in the mild air, watching my only lifeline roll down the street.

"You gave them our address?" Liam’s voice wavered, breaking on the final syllable. He paced the length of the living room, dodging the coffee table. He checked the window for the fifth time in three minutes. The driveway remained completely empty. His roommate scratched the back of his head. "I told them the junk car was on the street, not the driveway." Liam pressed the heels of his hands into his eyes until bursts of color exploded in his vision. He grabbed his keys from the bowl, looked at them, and threw them back. They clattered loudly. He walked into the kitchen, opened the fridge, stared blankly at a jar of mustard, and slammed the door shut. He couldn't afford the impound fees. He didn't even know which company took it. His knee bounced frantically against the counter as he grabbed the kitchen phone.

I peeled the neon orange sticker off the front door. The adhesive clung stubbornly to the wood. Vehicle Removed. I stared at the bold black letters until they blurred together. I turned around to look at the driveway. Bare concrete. I read the sticker again. My hands felt clammy, and the slip of paper rattled as my fingers trembled. I looked down the street, hoping to see the tow truck turning around, but there was only empty asphalt. I pulled my phone from my pocket, unlocking and locking the screen five times without opening an app. A tight knot formed right beneath my sternum, making it impossible to take a full breath. I sat heavily on the porch step, resting my elbows on my knees and burying my face in my hands. The paper crumpled tightly in my grip.

Greg tapped the replay button on his phone screen again. The black-and-white security footage showed the flatbed truck backing into his private driveway, hooking up his SUV, and vanishing into the night. It was 3:00 AM. He swiped to dial the local precinct but canceled the call before the first ring. He wiped a layer of sweat from his upper lip with the back of his hand. He stood up from the kitchen table, walked to the back door, checked the deadbolt, and walked back. The silence of the house pressed against his eardrums. He hit replay. The truck backed in. The SUV disappeared. He rubbed his chest, exactly over his heart, trying to soothe the rapid, rhythmic thudding beneath his ribs. He drank a glass of water, choking slightly as he swallowed too fast, his eyes darting toward the front window.

I hit the refresh button on the patent database for the fifth time in three minutes. The coffee in my stomach churned, a sour acid rising in the back of my throat. My fingers hovered over the keyboard, slick with cold sweat, as the search results finally loaded. There it was. US Patent 1145982: Responsive Thermal Weave. The exact schematics I had spent three years building in my garage stared back at me, filed six months ago by a shell corporation. I rubbed my clammy palms against my jeans, leaving dark, damp streaks on the denim. The room suddenly felt suffocatingly small, the walls closing in on me. The prototype on my desk—my life’s savings—now looked like nothing but useless scraps of wire and cloth. My breathing turned shallow and erratic. What was I going to tell the investors at tomorrow’s meeting?

Elias stood before the glass display case, his pocket watch ticking wildly in his damp grip. Behind the polished brass stanchions sat the Mechanical Nightingale, winding its intricate gears to sing. It was the exact replica of the blueprints he had hidden under his floorboards. His jaw tightened so fiercely his teeth ground together. He darted a glance left, then right, convinced the exhibition guards were marching toward him to accuse him of theft. He pulled at his stiff collar, trying to draw a full breath into his constricting chest, but the air felt impossibly thin. He backed away, his boot catching on the carpet, stumbling clumsily. If the Royal Academy found his workshop, they would ruin him. He chewed rapidly on the inside of his cheek, tasting copper, as he hurried toward the heavy oak exit doors, glancing over his shoulder every few seconds.

The glossy pages of the KitchenCo catalog slipped through my trembling fingers. Page forty-two. The Auto-Julienne Pro. I blinked hard, rubbing my eyes until colorful spots danced in my vision, praying I had misread the glossy print. I hadn't. The blade housing, the ergonomic grip, the exact angle of the slicing mechanism—it was mine. My right knee began to bounce rapidly against the underside of the conference table, rattling my half-empty water glass. The executive across from me was still talking, his lips moving, but all I could hear was the rushing pulse drumming in my ears. I swallowed dryly, my tongue feeling like sandpaper. The briefcase holding my 3D-printed prototype suddenly felt like it weighed a hundred pounds. If I opened it now, I'd look like a cheap knock-off artist. I bit down on my thumbnail, tearing the edge to the quick.

Maya paced her dormitory, bare feet wearing a groove into the cheap carpet. She walked from the window to the door, turned, and repeated the path, her arms crossed tightly over her stomach. On her bed, her laptop screen glowed with the email from her university’s legal department. Prior art found. Patent US99281A. She stopped to stare at the screen, her heart hammering violently against her ribs. She picked up her phone, dialed her professor's number, then instantly ended the call before it could ring. She dropped the phone onto the mattress, burying both hands in her hair and pulling at the roots. Three years of clinical trials. The massive student loans. She began calculating numbers in her head, the figures blurring together in a chaotic swarm. She walked back to the window, chewing on her lower lip until a drop of copper welled up.

My thumb hovered over the publish button, shaking so badly I had to steady my right wrist with my left hand. Just one final check of the marketplace. I typed the core function into the search bar, expecting the usual irrelevant results. Instead, a sleek purple icon appeared. I clicked it, my breath catching in my throat. The interface, the proprietary algorithm, even the exact hex codes for the color scheme—all identical. Released two weeks ago by a tech giant. A sudden wave of ice poured over my scalp, trickling down my spine. I pushed my rolling chair back so violently it slammed into the wall, knocking a framed poster to the floor with a loud crack. I couldn't drag enough oxygen into my lungs. My investors had promised a blue-ocean market. I grabbed my phone, pacing tight circles around the shattered glass.

Arthur stood in the middle of the crowded exposition hall, completely frozen. He stared at the vibrant, drought-resistant corn stalks displayed at the mega-agri booth. Beside the exhibit, a glossy placard boasted "Patent Pending: Genetically Stabilized Arid-Corn." It was his crossbreed. The exact genetic markers he had isolated in his greenhouse over the last decade. He wiped a layer of slick sweat from his forehead with the back of a trembling hand. The chatter of the crowd morphed into a deafening roar in his ears. He shoved his hands deep into his overall pockets to hide their violent shaking. What if they sued him for growing his own seeds? He glanced at the corporate representatives in their tailored suits, convinced they were already watching him. He backed away into the aisle, bumping into a passerby without apologizing, his chest heaving as he hurried toward the exit.

The cease-and-desist letter trembled in my fingers, the crisp white paper crinkling under my grip. I read the legal jargon three times, my vision swimming. Someone had patented the radial acoustic bracing system. The exact carving technique I had developed for my custom cellos. A sharp, localized pain bloomed behind my left eye. I looked around my dusty workshop, at the half-finished instruments hanging from the ceiling. I walked over to the nearest workbench and aggressively swept a pile of wood shavings onto the floor, needing to move, to do something. My breath came in short, jagged gasps. I picked up a chisel, then immediately set it down, my hands lacking the steady control required to carve. I pulled my phone from my apron, opened my contacts, and scrolled to my lawyer’s name, my thumb hovering endlessly over the call icon without pressing down.

The commuter train rattled along the tracks, but Julian felt completely detached from the motion. He stared unblinking at the open page of Renewable Tech Monthly. The headline screamed about a revolutionary flexible solar mesh, patented last Tuesday by a firm in Berlin. He traced the schematic with a clammy index finger, noting the identical polymer layering he had kept secret on his encrypted hard drive. His knee jackhammered up and down, knocking against the folding table. He abruptly closed the magazine, shoving it into his leather satchel. He pulled it out ten seconds later, hastily flipping back to the page to verify the filing date. Tuesday. He unbuttoned the top two buttons of his dress shirt, feeling a sudden, suffocating heat radiating from his collar. He looked out the window, counting the passing streetlights, desperately trying to force his racing pulse to match their steady rhythm.

I stood in aisle four, the brightly colored toy box heavy in my hands. I traced the interlocking joints through the plastic packaging. I had spent two years carving these exact shapes out of wood for my son, refining the locking mechanism in our garage. I dropped the box back onto the shelf, my hands retreating to my pockets as if the cardboard had burned me. My heart thumped against my ribs like a trapped bird. I backed away, my eyes darting up to the security dome on the ceiling. Could the corporate lawyers trace my small online shop? I began calculating legal fees in my head, a dizzying swarm of zeros. I clutched my purse tightly against my chest, rushing past the cash registers and out into the parking lot without buying a single thing, desperate to fill my lungs with outside air.

Elena sat in the taxi, eyes glued to the towering digital billboard. The glowing letters flashed: "Miracle-Peptide 7." She pulled a glass vial from her purse, her fingers slick with cold perspiration. The advertised ingredient list scrolled past, matching her proprietary lab notes compound for compound. She tapped her nails aggressively against her phone screen, navigating to the patent registry. Registered to a multinational conglomerate. Her breath hitched, catching sharply in her throat. She gripped the leather handle on the car door until her knuckles turned stark white. She closed her eyes, but the chemical formulas kept flashing behind her eyelids. She needed water, but her throat felt completely swollen shut. She leaned forward, her voice cracking as she told the driver to turn around and take her back to the laboratory immediately.

I wiped grease from my hands with a shop rag, staring at the glossy brochure the dealership rep left on my counter. The cutaway diagram of the new engine featured a highly specific dual-injection valve. My valve. I shoved the rag into my back pocket, pacing the short length of my auto shop. I walked to the filing cabinet, ripping the drawer open so hard the metal tracks shrieked. I pulled out my folder of schematics. The date was stamped clearly, but it didn't matter. The automaker had filed their patent eight months ago. A cold sweat broke out along my hairline, dripping down and stinging my eyes. I kept swallowing, trying to clear a sharp metallic taste from my mouth. The steady hum of the air compressor suddenly sounded deafening, pressing against my eardrums until my head began to throb in rhythm with the machinery.

Standing barefoot on the boardwalk, Marcus watched the stranger walk toward the surf. Tucked under the man's arm was a board featuring the exact hydrodynamic fin setup Marcus had spent three winters perfecting in his shed. Marcus pulled his sunglasses down, blinking rapidly against the harsh morning sun. He pulled out his phone, his thumb slipping against the glass screen as he searched the international surf registry. Hydro-Glide Fin. Patented. The words blurred together. He began to bite the dead skin around his thumb, tearing at it until a sting of pain grounded him. His knees felt utterly hollow, like they might buckle into the sand at any moment. He looked back up, watching the surfer paddle out, tracing perfect cuts through the water. Marcus rubbed his chest, pressing his palm hard against his sternum to physically calm the wild, erratic thudding trapped beneath his ribs.

I double-checked the figure-eight knot on Leo’s harness, tugging the rope until my fingers burned. "Okay, dad, I got it," he muttered, brushing past me to the rock face. For fifteen years, this crag had been my sanctuary, but watching my ten-year-old scale the limestone filled my mouth with the taste of pennies. He reached for a crimp hold twenty feet up, and my breath hitched, trapping itself in my lungs. My hand hovered over the belay device, gripping the brake line so tight my knuckles glowed white. A small spray of chalk dust drifted down as his foot slipped half an inch. I swallowed hard, my heart hammering a frantic rhythm against my ribs. "Keep three points of contact!" I shouted, my voice cracking slightly. I didn't blink, convinced that if I looked away for a millisecond, gravity would somehow win.

Elias stood motionless by the door of his woodshop, his jaw clamped shut as the high-pitched whine of the lathe filled the air. His daughter, Maya, guided the gouge into the spinning mahogany block. Wood chips flew, pinging off her safety goggles. Elias took a half-step forward, his right hand twitching toward the red emergency stop button. He had spent decades at that very machine, yet seeing her small hands mere inches from the blur of the rotating wood made a cold sweat prickle along his hairline. He repeatedly shifted his weight from his left foot to his right, mentally rehearsing the quickest route to the first aid kit. When a deeper knot in the wood caused the tool to chatter loudly, Elias flinched, biting down on his lower lip until a sharp metallic taste blossomed in his mouth, his eyes wide and unblinking.

The familiar hum of the apiary usually lowered my blood pressure, but today, my pulse thudded directly behind my eyes. I pulled the mesh veil over my seven-year-old daughter’s head, zipping it shut. Then I unzipped it, checked the fabric for invisible tears, and zipped it again. "I'm fine, Mom," Chloe giggled, marching toward the hive with my old smoker in her gloved hands. I trailed exactly one step behind her, my hands hovering in the air like a referee ready to call a foul. The bees swarmed thick as she lifted the wooden lid. A stray worker buzzed past my ear, and my stomach plummeted into my shoes. I frantically scanned the cuffs of her jacket, patting down my own pockets to verify the location of the EpiPen for the fourth time in ten minutes, holding my breath until she replaced the lid.

The frigid tide washed over Marcus’s boots, but he didn't step back. He stood rigidly on the shoreline, the binoculars pressed so firmly against his face that the plastic dug into his skin. Out beyond the breakers, a small figure in a black wetsuit paddled furiously toward a massive swell. Marcus’s chest rose and fell in rapid, shallow bursts. He muttered quiet, fragmented instructions to the wind. "Dig deep, pop up, keep your center." As the wave pitched, his son stood, wobbling slightly on the fiberglass board. Marcus stopped breathing entirely, his hands trembling against the binoculars. The ocean roared, a mountain of white water collapsing right behind the boy. Marcus dropped the glasses, his heart slamming wildly against his sternum, waiting agonizing seconds for a dark head to breach the foamy surface.

We were deep in the Appalachian damp, surrounded by towering oaks. I had hunted wild mushrooms here since college, but watching twelve-year-old Sam sprint ahead made my throat tighten into a knot. "Wait up!" I called out, my pace quickening into a jog. He knelt beside a decaying log, reaching for a cluster of pale, bell-shaped caps. I closed the distance in three strides, grabbing his wrist with a clammy hand just before his fingers brushed the gills. "Let me see it first," I insisted, my voice louder than intended. I dropped to my knees, turning the specimen over with my pocketknife. I scrutinized the volva, checked the spore print color, and ran through my mental encyclopedia. My leg bounced rapidly against the wet earth. Destroying Angel or a harmless field mushroom? I wiped a bead of sweat from my brow, snatching the entire cluster away.

Sarah stood by the garage wall, aggressively chewing on her thumbnail. Underneath the suspended chassis of her prized 1968 Mustang, her teenage son, Toby, was wrestling with a rusted exhaust bolt. The hydraulic lift hissed softly. Sarah’s eyes darted to the locking pins on the lift columns, verifying their engagement for the sixth time. "You need a breaker bar for that," she called out, stepping forward, then forcing herself to step back. Toby grunted, applying his full body weight to the wrench. The heavy steel frame of the car creaked. Sarah’s stomach performed a violent flip. She crossed her arms tightly over her chest, tapping her steel-toed boot against the concrete floor in a staccato rhythm. Every time the wrench slipped with a loud clank, she flinched, her eyes widening, instantly mapping out the exact trajectory the heavy engine block would take if the supports failed.

The scent of kerosene usually brought me peace, but tonight, it made bile rise in my throat. I stood rigidly at the edge of the patio, a heavy, soaking-wet fire blanket clutched in my fists. In the center of the yard, my son ignited the Kevlar wicks of his staff. The twin flames roared to life. "Keep it away from your face," I shouted, my voice pitching up an octave. He began to spin, tracing fiery figure-eights in the air. I tracked every rotation with wide, unblinking eyes, my jaw locked so tight my teeth ached. A stray drop of fuel flew from the wick, landing on the dry grass, and I instantly lunged forward, stomping the tiny spark out with excessive force. My chest heaved, my grip on the damp blanket turning my knuckles bone-white as the flames danced inches from his shirt.

David hovered like a shadow behind his daughter, Elena, at the shooting line. For years, the rhythmic thwack of arrows hitting canvas targets had been his meditation. Now, watching her load a carbon-fiber arrow into his high-tension compound bow, his palms grew slick with sweat. He wiped them down his jeans, his eyes darting between the razor-sharp broadhead and her unprotected forearm. "Anchor point," he reminded her quickly, his words rushing together. Elena pulled the bowstring back, her arm shaking under the fifty-pound draw weight. David’s breathing stopped completely. He leaned in, his hands raised halfway, fingers twitching, ready to grab the bow if the string slipped. The taught cable hummed near her cheek. He counted the seconds in his head, shifting his weight from heel to toe, his heart pounding a frantic drumroll against his ribs until the arrow finally leaped from the rest.

I watched from the doorway, rubbing the back of my neck so hard the skin burned. My teenager, Liam, had the soldering iron in one hand and a magnifying glass in the other, leaning over a delicate motherboard I used to tinker with. A wisp of smoke curled into the air. I cleared my throat, stepping closer to inspect the tiny copper traces. "Don't hold it there too long," I instructed, my voice tight. He adjusted his grip, bringing the 400-degree tip millimeters from a fragile capacitor. I instinctively reached out, my fingers hovering an inch above his shoulder, ready to yank him back. My foot tapped a restless rhythm on the floorboards. I mentally calculated the cost of the parts, but mostly pictured the searing iron slipping onto his bare forearm. I swallowed hard, unable to look away from the glowing metal tip.

The wind howled across the bay, snapping the mainsail with a sound like a gunshot. Nora gripped the starboard rail, her knuckles completely drained of color. At the helm of the small sloop, her nine-year-old son wrestled with the tiller, his small frame leaning hard against the shifting gusts. Nora’s eyes darted rapidly from the heavy boom swinging overhead to the dark, churning water below. She chewed vigorously on the inside of her cheek until she tasted copper. "Watch the jibe!" she yelled over the wind, already taking two sudden strides toward the cockpit. She hovered right behind him, her hands trembling as she grabbed a spare line. Every time the boat tilted dramatically, her stomach dropped into a bottomless void, and she caught herself holding her breath for a minute at a time, calculating the exact distance to the bright orange life rings.

"Just a little closer to the edge, I need a better angle," my daughter muttered, dragging my heavy Dobsonian telescope across the flat roof of our apartment building. I swallowed the lump in my throat and darted in front of her, planting myself squarely between her and the low parapet. "That's far enough," I said, my tone sharper than I intended. The streetlights flickered four stories below us. I kept my knees slightly bent, constantly shifting my weight, my hands outstretched as if ready to catch a falling boulder. While she adjusted the eyepiece, looking for Saturn, I couldn't focus on the stars. My eyes stayed locked on her sneakers, measuring the inches between her rubber soles and the roof's edge. I rubbed my clammy palms against my jacket, jumping slightly when an unexpected gust of wind rattled the metal telescope mount.

Arthur paced the snow-packed platform at the top of the black diamond run, completely ignoring the majestic alpine view he usually loved. His son, barely waist-high, adjusted his goggles and shuffled his skis toward the steep drop-off. Arthur’s chest felt as tight as a coiled spring. He jabbed his poles into the ice, pulled them out, and jabbed them again. "Keep your weight forward!" Arthur shouted, his words swallowed by the frigid wind. The boy pushed off, disappearing over the precipice. Arthur lunged forward, his heart slamming violently in his ears. He skidded to the edge, his eyes frantically scanning the icy moguls below. When he momentarily lost sight of the bright red jacket behind a cluster of pines, Arthur’s breath hitched. He gripped his ski poles until his gloves creaked, chewing on his freezing bottom lip, waiting for the red jacket to emerge.

The ping from my phone was louder than the cafe's espresso machine. *HarperCollins.* I stared at the bolded subject line, my thumb hovering a millimeter above the glass. My breath caught somewhere behind my collarbone. *Thank you for your submission, but...* The coffee shop blurred. I gnawed on the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper. I had banked everything on this draft. Three years of early mornings, skipped lunches, ignored friends. If they didn't want it, who would?
