Evelyn’s knee began a rapid, involuntary bounce against the lower cabinets. She checked the locks on her front door twice, then a third time. The silence of the house felt deafening, amplified by the rushing blood in her ears. She poured a glass of water, but her hand shook violently, spilling half of it across the linoleum. She left the puddle, staring at the silver paper.

I tapped my spoon against my coffee cup—clink, clink, clink—until the barista shot me a glare. I dropped the spoon, but my foot took over, bouncing a frantic staccato under the tiny cafe table. Sitting right in front of me was a velvet jewelry box handed to me by Marcus, a kid I taught in juvenile detention ten years ago. He had just smiled, placed it down, and walked away before I could speak. My chest felt tight, the air in the bustling shop suddenly too thin to breathe. I wiped a sheen of cold sweat from my forehead. Is it stolen? Is it a threat? My thoughts spun, blurring the chatter of the cafe into a dull roar. I slid my phone out, my thumb hovering over 9-1-1, my pulse throbbing in my throat as I stared at the dark velvet.

Professor Higgins adjusted his glasses, took them off, cleaned them on his tie, and put them back on. The antique wooden duck sat on his blotter. Attached was a note: For the man who taught me everything. There was no signature. Higgins stood up, walking to the blinds and peering through the slats into the quad. He let them snap shut and began arranging his pens into a perfectly straight line. He realized his jaw was clamped so tight his teeth ached. He forced his mouth open, rubbing his temples where a sharp throb had begun to echo. Every time footsteps echoed in the corridor, he flinched, his eyes darting to the frosted glass of his office door. He picked up the phone receiver, listened to the dial tone, and hung up. His breath came in short, sharp hitches. Who left it here?

The auditorium was empty, the stage lights powered down. Only the glow of the exit sign illuminated the bouquet of black roses resting on my director’s chair. I froze in the aisle. My throat closed up, making it impossible to swallow. I tugged at the hem of my sweater, unraveling a loose thread until it snapped around my finger. Black roses. The last time I saw those, it was opening night of the disastrous play where Sarah had her accident. I took a step backward, my heel catching on the carpet. I grabbed the armrest of the nearest seat to steady myself, my chest rising and falling in quick, jagged movements. I scanned the dark rafters, the shadowy wings of the stage. The silence felt heavy, pressing down on my lungs. I backed toward the exit doors, unable to look away from the chair.

Mr. Vance found the wrapped package resting on the hood of his snow-covered sedan. He dropped his briefcase in the slush. His breath plumed in rapid, shallow bursts in the freezing air. The tag simply read, A blast from the past. He rubbed his gloved hands together, not from the cold, but from a sudden, creeping numbness in his fingers. He looked up and down the suburban street. Empty. The wind rustled the bare branches, and Vance jumped, whipping his head around. His stomach twisted into a tight, hard knot. He reached out, hesitated, and pulled his hand back, slipping it into his coat pocket. He paced a tight circle around the car, his boots crunching loudly. He chewed the inside of his cheek until he tasted copper. He just wanted to get inside, lock the deadbolt, and draw the curtains.

I stood by the tetherball pole, clutching the hand-painted mug tightly against my chest. Timmy had handed it to me through the chain-link fence during recess and bolted. Timmy, who had moved away in the middle of the night three years ago. My eyes darted across the street, scanning the parked cars, the rustling bushes, the shadowy alleys between the houses. My heart battered against my ribs, a wild and erratic rhythm. "Mrs. Gable?" a student asked, tugging my skirt. I jumped, nearly dropping the mug. "I'm fine, go play," I snapped, my voice cracking at an uncomfortably high pitch. I rubbed my clammy hands on my coat, my breathing shallow. Why was he back? Where were his parents? I squeezed the handle of the mug, my knuckles turning white, jumping at every loud shout from the playground.

Arthur stared at the unmarked thumb drive sitting next to his pigeonhole. Someone had attached a sticky note: You'll want to see this - Chloe. He swallowed dryly, his Adam's apple bobbing. He picked up the drive, the plastic feeling slick against his sweating fingers. The breakroom chatter faded into a buzzing static in his ears. He walked to the water cooler, filled a cup, and drank it in one gulp, but his throat remained parched. He began tapping the plastic drive against his thigh. Tap, tap, tap, tap. What did she record? Did she have his phone back then? He pulled out his chair to sit down, misjudged the distance, and landed heavily, his breath catching in a sharp gasp. He stared at his laptop screen, his chest tight, unable to insert the tiny device into the USB port.

The canvas was delivered by a courier at noon. I hadn’t touched my brushes since. I paced the length of my studio, stepping over discarded rags and paint tubes, my heart hammering a relentless beat against my sternum. It was a perfect recreation of my own ruined masterpiece, signed by Leo, my former protégé. I bit down on my thumbnail, tearing the cuticle until it bled. I barely noticed the sting. I wiped my brow, leaving a streak of cerulean blue across my sweating forehead. He knows, I thought, the phrase looping endlessly in my mind. He knows what I did. I backed into a stool, sending it clattering to the hardwood floor. I flinched violently at the noise, spinning around. The painted eyes on the canvas seemed to follow me. My breath hitched, thin and insufficient, as I backed toward the door.

The notification pinged loudly in the quiet room. Maria jumped in her ergonomic chair, her knee slamming hard into the underside of the desk. She winced, rubbing the sore spot, her eyes fixed on the screen. It was an e-gift card for a luxury resort from a username she recognized: Dropout_Danny99. Her pulse fluttered in the hollow of her throat. She closed the email tab. Then reopened it. She grabbed a paperclip from her organizer and unbent it, twisting the metal wire until it snapped in half. She threw the pieces down and immediately grabbed another. Her chest felt constricted, as if a heavy weight rested on her lungs. She clicked on Danny’s profile, her hand trembling so much the cursor danced wildly across the screen. Why a five-thousand-dollar gift? What did he expect in return? The screen blurred as her breathing grew ragged.

The marching band played the processional, but I couldn't hear the brass over the rushing blood in my ears. I squeezed the velvet box inside my robe pocket, the sharp corners pressing into my damp palm. Before the ceremony, Lily had shoved it into my hands with a manic, unblinking smile and whispered, "Open it when I cross the stage." I shifted my weight from foot to foot, my academic gown feeling like a stifling wool blanket. I pulled at my collar, gasping for a full breath that wouldn't come. I scanned the sea of blue caps, my stomach churning violently. As Lily’s name was called, my fingers fumbled with the tiny brass latch in my pocket. The clasp wouldn't give. My hands were shaking too badly. I ripped the box out of my pocket, tearing at the velvet, my eyes wide and unblinking.

The headlights illuminated the solitary apple resting on the hood of Mr. Harrison’s car. It wasn't red, but a dull, bruised black, skewered with a rusted silver hairpin. Harrison dropped his keys. They clattered on the asphalt, the sound echoing sharply in the empty lot. He scrambled to pick them up, his fingers slipping clumsily against the metal. He stood up fast, dizzy, and leaned against the driver’s door. He wiped a sheen of cold sweat from his upper lip. Only one student used to wear those antique silver hairpins. He swallowed hard, his throat tight, and looked over his shoulder into the deep shadows between the parked vehicles. His chest heaved in rapid, shallow jerks. Fumbling the key into the lock, he missed twice, scratching the paint. He threw himself into the driver’s seat, slamming the lock button down before pulling the door shut.

The bright pink paper taped to my door flutters in the drafty hallway, but I can’t force my fingers to unpeel it. My heartbeat thuds in my ears, a rapid, uneven rhythm that makes the narrow corridor spin. I unlock my door, stepping inside without touching the notice, but I know exactly what thirty-day countdown is written on it. The leaky faucet drips into the sink, and I pace from the kitchen counter to the window, rubbing my sweaty palms against my jeans. Where do I go? I pull up my bank app, staring at the double-digit balance until the screen blurs. "It's fine, just breathe," I mutter to the empty room, but my chest feels like it’s bound in iron wire. I sit on the edge of the mattress, bouncing my knee so fast the bed frame rattles against the wall.

Elias stared at the certified letter on the kitchen island, his jaw clamped so tight his teeth ground together. He picked up his coffee mug, but his hand shook, sending lukewarm sloshes over the ceramic rim and onto his knuckles. Thirty days. The words echoed loudly in his skull, drowning out the cartoons his daughter was watching in the next room. He walked to the living room archway, leaning heavily against the doorframe, mapping out the boxes he’d need, the deposits he didn't have, the conversations he couldn't bear to initiate. He pulled his phone from his pocket, opened his contacts, and closed them again. He chewed on his thumbnail until he tasted copper. "Daddy, look!" Maya cheered, pointing at the TV. Elias forced his mouth into a smile that didn't reach his eyes, his breathing shallow and quick as he nodded.

The landlord's envelope sits on my rusted radiator like a ticking bomb. I’ve walked past it six times in the last twenty minutes, my bare feet leaving damp prints on the hardwood. My throat is entirely dry, but every time I try to swallow a glass of water, my stomach threatens to rebel. I pull out a scratchpad, gripping the pen so hard my knuckles turn white, and begin writing numbers. Rent. Movers. Groceries. The math doesn't change, no matter how many times I scratch out the figures and rewrite them in the margins. I jump when the refrigerator compressor kicks on, dropping the pen. I scramble to pick it up, my breaths coming in short, greedy gasps. I have until the end of the month. I look at the calendar, watching the days shrink, feeling the walls of the tiny studio closing in.

Martha sat in the rocking chair, a crumpled piece of legal paper clutched to her chest. The chair creaked backward and forward in a rapid, ceaseless rhythm, completely out of sync with the quiet snowfall outside the cabin window. She smoothed the paper out on her apron, her wrinkled fingers tracing the bolded 'Notice to Vacate' at the top, then immediately balled it up again. She rose suddenly, knocking the chair backward, and began opening every cabinet in the kitchen. Cans of soup, bags of flour, a tin of loose tea. She pulled them out, stacked them on the counter, and then, realizing she had nowhere to take them, pushed them all back inside. Her chest heaved. She walked to the rotary phone, lifted the heavy receiver, listened to the dial tone, and slammed it back down before the operator could speak.

I slide down the door until I hit the linoleum floor, the yellow slip of paper resting in my lap. The silence of the basement is suffocating. I pull my knees to my chest, wrapping my arms around my legs, rocking slightly. I try to make a plan, but my brain feels like a television stuck on static. Every time I close my eyes, I see my belongings tossed out on the rainy sidewalk. I bite down on my lower lip, pressing until the pain cuts through the buzzing in my head. My phone buzzes in my pocket with a text from my roommate. Did you see the door? I type yes, delete it, type what do we do, and delete that too. I throw the phone onto the rug, dragging my hands through my hair, gripping the roots until my scalp burns.

David folded the eviction notice into perfect, tiny squares until it was small enough to hide in his palm. He walked the length of the hardwood floor—twelve steps to the window, turn, twelve steps to the kitchen. He did this for an hour, the floorboards groaning under his heavy, loud tread. His collar felt too tight, so he yanked at his tie, popping the top button off his work shirt. It rolled under the sofa, but he didn't stop to look for it. He needed to call his mother, or maybe a lawyer, but his throat had completely closed up. He paused by the window, peering out through the blinds at the streetlamps flickering to life. A passing police car made him flinch, pulling away from the glass as if he had already been caught trespassing in his own home.

The letter in the mail pile has my name, but the return address is the property management company. I don’t open it immediately. Instead, I sweep the entire kitchen, wash every dish in the sink, and scrub the stovetop until my arms ache. The envelope sits on the table, demanding attention. Finally, I tear it open. The bold print blurs. Thirty days to surrender the premises. I drop the letter. I need to pack. I run to my bedroom, pull my suitcase from the closet, and open it on the bed. I stare at my clothes. Shirts? Pants? I grab a handful of socks, drop them in, then take them out again. My lungs can't seem to draw in enough air. I sit on the edge of the mattress, bouncing both heels against the floorboards, counting the days on my fingers over and over.

Claire stared at the velvet-lined walls of the elevator, her fingers drumming an erratic beat against her leather purse. The doorman had handed her the envelope with a pitiful grimace. She didn't need to read the legal jargon to know what it meant; the missed payments had caught up. As the numbers above the elevator door ticked upward, she felt the air thinning. She stepped into her penthouse, kicking off her heels, and immediately poured a glass of wine, spilling a dark red stain across the marble counter. She ignored it, pacing the length of her floor-to-ceiling windows. The city sparkled below, oblivious to her. She picked up her phone to dial her ex-husband, stopped, and bit down on her cuticle until it bled. She checked her bank app again, hoping for a miracle that hadn't appeared the last twenty times she looked.

I trace the embossed lettering of the eviction notice with a trembling index finger. The coffee in my mug has gone completely cold, but I keep lifting it to my lips, forgetting not to drink, only to grimace at the bitter taste. I have finals next week. I open my laptop, staring at the blank Word document for my history essay, but all I see are moving boxes. I minimize the window, open the classifieds, and type 'cheap rooms' into the search bar. My foot taps against the desk leg—thud, thud, thud. "Hey, you okay?" my roommate calls from the hallway. I snap the laptop shut, nearly catching my fingers in the hinge. "Fine!" I squeak, my voice pitching up two octaves. I clear my throat, rubbing my clammy hands on my sweatpants. "Everything is totally fine." I reopen the laptop, my vision swimming.

The pink slip was stapled directly to the aluminum siding of Unit 44. Greg stood on the gravel driveway, his keys dangling from his frozen hand. The wind howled, but he didn't feel the cold. He stared at the staple, hyper-focused on the way it dug into the metal. His chest tightened, a heavy weight pressing down on his ribs. He unlocked the door, stepping inside the dark, cramped space, and immediately began checking the locks on the windows. He knew they couldn't force him out tonight, but he drew the curtains anyway, peering through the smallest crack at the landlord's truck parked down the street. He sat on the faded sofa, unlacing his work boots, then lacing them back up again. He couldn't take them off. He needed to be ready to move, ready to run, ready for whatever happened next.

The wax seal on the landlord’s envelope is broken, the jagged edge scratching my thumb. I stand in the center of the parlor, listening to the grandfather clock tick off the seconds. Each tock feels like a hammer against my skull. They’re selling the house. We have to be out by the 31st. I pick up a porcelain figurine from the mantle, turning it over and over in my slick hands until it almost slips and shatters. I place it down gently, backing away as if the furniture might attack me. I pull out my phone, opening up the map application, zooming out to see the neighboring towns. Rents are too high everywhere. I zoom out further, my thumb swiping rapidly across the screen, searching for a green patch, a cheap suburb, anywhere. My breathing hitches, short and raspy, echoing in the cavernous, empty room.

Sarah found the certified letter stuffed into her rusted mailbox, the sea breeze threatening to snatch it from her grasp. She read the first line and stopped, her eyes darting to the crashing waves, then back to the paper. She walked up the wooden stairs to her deck, her steps completely silent. She sat on the wicker chair, wrapping her thick cardigan tightly around her torso, though she was sweating. She picked up a pen and started making a list on the back of the envelope. Call Jim. Check savings. Sell car. She crossed out Sell car so violently the pen tore through the paper. She stood up, walked to the railing, and chewed the inside of her cheek. The rhythmic pounding of the surf, usually a comfort, now sounded like a countdown. She squeezed her eyes shut, digging her fingernails deep into the wooden bannister.

Marcus’s right heel struck the terminal floor in a rapid, relentless staccato. The red lettering on the departure board blurred as he stared at the word 'Delayed,' his fingers wearing a smooth groove into his phone’s screen case. In two hours, Elena would walk down the aisle. He had the wedding rings in his breast pocket. He pressed a hand over his chest, feeling the small velvet box, then checked his watch. 14:05. He checked it again ten seconds later. 14:05. The air in the gate area felt thick, suffocating. He approached the desk, his voice a tight rasp. "Is there any update? Even a rough estimate?" The agent shook her head. Marcus turned away, running both hands violently through his hair, his eyes darting toward the runway where planes sat motionless like heavy, flightless birds. He checked his watch again. 14:06.

I paced the length of Gate 4B twenty-two times, carefully avoiding the cracks in the linoleum. My throat felt like sandpaper, and no matter how much water I gulped from the overpriced bottle, the dryness remained. The final interview for the director role was supposed to start at three. It was now two-thirty, and our aircraft hadn't even arrived from Chicago. I ducked into the restroom, splashing cold water on my face and accidentally soaking the collar of my tailored shirt. Great. Now I looked exactly how I felt. I pulled out my notes, murmuring my opening pitch to the mirror, but the words scrambled together like alphabet soup. "I bring ten years of... ten years of..." I couldn't remember my own resume. My phone buzzed in my pocket. The recruitment team. My stomach dropped to the floor, my thumbs freezing over the screen.

Julian crushed the empty paper coffee cup in his fist, tossing it into a bin before immediately buying another one he didn't want. His wife’s last text—Water broke, heading to hospital now—was timestamped three hours ago. Outside the floor-to-ceiling windows, a blizzard buried the tarmac in unforgiving white. He stood right at the glass, pressing his forehead against the cold pane as if his sheer willpower could melt the ice on the wings. His phone vibrated, and he snatched it up so fast it nearly slipped from his sweaty palms. It was his mother-in-law. "Julian, she's fully dilated. Where are you?" Her voice crackled through the terrible airport reception. "I'm trapped in Denver," he choked out, his chest tightening as he watched another ground crew vehicle skid in the snow. "Put me on speaker. Don't let her push without me."

The black suit felt like a straightjacket. I tugged at my collar, loosening the dark tie for the fourth time in ten minutes. The departure screen flashed the updated boarding time: 4:00 PM. The eulogy I was supposed to deliver at 3:30 PM sat heavy in my breast pocket, the ink probably smudged from how many times my damp hands had clutched the folded paper. I sat down, stood back up, and walked over to the nearest charging station, plugging in my phone even though the battery was at ninety percent. Every time the overhead speaker chimed, my heart gave a violent jolt against my ribs, followed by a sinking crash when the announcement was for another city entirely. I couldn't miss saying goodbye to him. I squeezed my eyes shut, taking quick, shallow breaths, waiting for the PA system to finally call my name.

Sarah’s fingers drummed a rapid, silent sonata against her hard plastic suitcase. The gate agent had just announced another mechanical delay. She pulled up the photo her husband had sent thirty minutes ago: Lily in her purple tulle dress, waiting on the piano bench. 'She goes on in an hour,' the caption read. Sarah chewed on her thumbnail until she tasted copper. She stalked up to the counter, her voice pitched half an octave higher than normal. "Excuse me, are there any other airlines flying to Boston today? I don't care the cost." The agent offered a sympathetic, useless smile. Sarah retreated, her pulse hammering in her ears, her fingers returning to their relentless tapping on the luggage handle as she calculated driving times she knew were utterly impossible. She stared at Lily's smiling photo, a heavy lump forming in her throat.

My leg bounced so hard the entire row of connected airport chairs rattled, earning a glare from the woman sleeping next to me. I muttered a quick apology, but my knee resumed its rapid oscillation five seconds later. The screen overhead glared back at me in mocking neon orange: 'Flight 809 - Delayed due to weather.' My Biology 401 final, the only thing standing between me and a diploma, started in exactly forty-five minutes. I aggressively flipped through my flashcards, but the Krebs cycle diagrams looked like alien hieroglyphs. I couldn't process a single word. I grabbed my phone, opening my email app to draft yet another message to Professor Higgins. 'Please, I have proof of the delay.' I backspaced the entire thing. The terminal air conditioning was freezing, yet a bead of sweat rolled down the back of my neck, soaking into my collar.

David gripped the leather handle of his briefcase so tightly his knuckles blanched. Inside were the cashier's checks, meticulously gathered over the last ten years for the down payment on the Seattle property. The notary appointment was scheduled for noon. The clock above the gate read 11:15, and the boarding doors remained firmly, stubbornly shut. He dialed his realtor’s number for the sixth time, listening to the dial tone with his eyes squeezed shut. "Pick up, pick up, pick up," he whispered under his breath. It went straight to voicemail. David snapped his phone shut and resumed pacing the twenty-foot stretch of carpet between the garbage can and the drinking fountain. He imagined the sellers packing up their paperwork, shaking their heads, and calling the backup buyer. He stopped, leaned over his knees, and forced himself to take a long, unsteady breath.

I kept refreshing the flight status app, dragging my thumb down the screen until my joint ached. 'Status: Unknown.' I wrapped my cardigan tighter around my chest, shivering despite the stuffy terminal air. My brother’s last text was a single line: 'The doctor says you need to hurry.' I walked up to the priority desk, tears pricking the corners of my eyes before I even opened my mouth. "Please," I said, my voice cracking entirely. "Is there a seat on the connecting flight through Atlanta? I’ll sit in the jump seat. I’ll stand in the aisle." The agent typed at an agonizingly slow pace, shaking his head. I backed away, pressing my knuckles hard against my mouth to stifle a sound. I found a secluded corner, sank to the carpeted floor, and began rocking back and forth, staring blankly at the wall.

Chloe chewed aggressively on the end of her plastic pen until it snapped, leaving a bitter taste of ink on her tongue. The investor pitch was supposed to be the culmination of three years of sleepless nights, and her co-founder was currently standing in a Silicon Valley boardroom alone. The intercom crackled, announcing a further delay to flight 412 due to a missing flight attendant. Chloe’s stomach performed a violent somersault. She rushed to the airport lounge bathroom, locking herself in a stall just to have a moment of silence. She pulled out her laptop, balancing it on her knees, and tried to load the video conferencing software. The little loading wheel spun relentlessly on the screen. "Come on, come on," she muttered, tapping her heel against the tile floor in a rapid 4/4 time. The wheel kept spinning, mocking her.

I held the court documents tightly against my chest, the manila edges digging into my skin. Today, Maya was supposed to legally become my daughter at 9 AM. The terminal clock mocked me: 8:15 AM. The plane hadn't even arrived. I pulled out my phone to call the social worker, but my hands were shaking so badly I dropped it. I scrambled to pick it up, my breathing turning into short, shallow gasps. A woman asked if I needed water, but I couldn't form the words. I shook my head, resuming my relentless pacing along the window. If I missed the hearing, the judge could reschedule for next month. I squeezed my eyes shut, willing the airplane to appear on the empty runway. My watch ticked loudly, each second sounding like a hammer striking an anvil inside my mind.

Arthur paced behind the row of seating, muttering his opening monologue under his breath at triple speed. He checked the departure board again. Still glowing yellow: 'Delayed - Awaiting Crew.' The curtain for opening night of Macbeth rose in exactly three hours in London, and he was stuck in Paris. He rubbed his face, smudging the carefully applied base makeup he had put on in the airport lounge bathroom. His leg bounced involuntarily every time he paused. The understudy was good, but this was Arthur’s debut, his one shot at the West End. He walked over to the desk, gripping the edge of the counter until his fingertips turned stark white. "Is there any word from the crew? Are they in the building?" he demanded, his voice trembling slightly. The agent averted her eyes, and Arthur’s stomach plunged down to his shoes.

I unzipped my backpack, checked that my passport and visa application were still there, and zipped it back up. Three minutes later, I did the exact same thing. The overhead speaker chirped, announcing a further delay for the flight to Chicago due to mechanical issues. My immigration interview was at 1:00 PM. If I wasn't sitting in that government office, my legal status expired at midnight. I wiped a layer of clammy sweat from my forehead with the back of my sleeve. I felt incredibly dizzy, the bright fluorescent lights of the terminal seeming to flicker and hum loudly. I walked to the window, pressing my forehead against the cool glass, counting backward from ten in my native language. It didn't help. My heart thudded violently against my ribs like a trapped bird. I unzipped my backpack to check my passport one more time.

I sat on the edge of my old twin bed, tracing the faded glow-in-the-dark stars peeled halfway off the drywall. Downstairs, the muffled hum of the television meant Dad was watching the evening news. I checked the balance on my banking app for the fifth time since pulling into the driveway, staring at the two-digit number until the screen blurred. My suitcases sat by the door, completely zipped shut, as if opening them would make this permanent. I rubbed my thumb over my knuckles, pressing hard against the bone. If I went down to the kitchen for a glass of water, they would ask about my job search. They would ask about the lease I broke. I pulled my knees to my chest, squeezing my eyes shut and listening to the ceiling fan tick rhythmically overhead, my pulse matching its rapid, uneven pace.

Marcus pushed his peas around the floral ceramic plate, the metallic scrape of his fork unnaturally loud in the quiet dining room. His mother kept glancing at him over her reading glasses, offering him more pot roast, asking if the mattress in the guest room was firm enough. He swallowed hard, a lump forming in his throat that tasted like dry cardboard. His left leg bounced under the mahogany table, vibrating the floorboards. "It's a stepping stone," his father said heartily, clapping Marcus on the shoulder. Marcus gave a tight, close-lipped smile, his chest tightening as he calculated the weeks it would take to save up a deposit. He kept his eyes locked on his half-empty water glass, his fingernails digging crescent moons into the meat of his palms under the napkin on his lap. The ticking grandfather clock in the hallway sounded like a judge's gavel.

The cardboard flaps of the moving box refused to stay folded down. Every time I pressed them flat, they sprang back up, mocking my attempts to organize this tiny attic room. Mom had cleared out her sewing supplies to make space, leaving behind a faint smell of lavender and dust. I wiped my damp palms on my jeans and picked up a stack of my college textbooks. Where do they go? Where do I go? I paced the five steps from the dormer window to the closet, over and over, my breath coming fast and shallow. I picked up my phone, opened a blank text to my ex-roommate, stared at the blinking cursor, and deleted it. A floorboard creaked in the hall. I instantly dropped the books onto the bed and grabbed a shirt, aggressively pretending to fold it just in case someone walked in.

Elena stood perfectly still in the hallway, listening to the clinking of coffee mugs in the kitchen below. She checked her watch: 7:15 AM. If she went down now, she would interrupt her parents' morning crossword ritual. If she waited until 7:30, her dad would be leaving for work, and she’d have to perform the cheerful daughter routine while standing in her pajamas. Her stomach churned violently, acid rising in the back of her throat. She stepped back into her childhood bedroom, quietly pulling the door shut until it clicked softly. She sat on the floor with her back pressed against the wood, pulling a loose thread on her sweatpants until it unraveled an inch. She practiced her lines in a whisper to the empty room. "I have three interviews lined up." "The market is just tough right now." Her hands wouldn't stop shaking.

I kept the engine running in the driveway for twenty minutes. The headlights illuminated the closed garage door, casting harsh shadows on the siding of the house I grew up in. My hands gripped the leather steering wheel so tightly my knuckles ached. I could just put it in reverse. I could drive back to the city, sleep in my car, and figure it out tomorrow. The dashboard clock flipped to 11:42 PM. They were definitely asleep. I killed the ignition, the sudden silence rushing into the cabin and making my ears ring. As I crept up the front walk, my keys jingled in my pocket, sounding like wind chimes in a hurricane. I slid the key into the deadbolt, pausing, trying to control my ragged breathing before I turned the lock. The thought of facing the photo collages in the hallway made me feel entirely weightless.

David loaded his clothes into the ancient washing machine, flinching every time the metal drum clanked. His mother appeared in the doorway, holding a basket of folded towels. "You know, you can use the permanent press cycle for those dress shirts," she offered gently. David’s jaw clamped shut so hard his teeth ground together. "I know, Mom," he said, his voice a half-octave higher than normal. He shoved the remaining shirts into the machine, slamming the lid down faster than intended. The loud bang echoed off the concrete basement walls. He squeezed his eyes shut, his chest rising and falling in rapid, uneven jerks. He expected a lecture, or a question about his savings, or a remark about his failed startup. Instead, she just set the towels down and left. David leaned his forehead against the cold metal of the washer, violently chewing the inside of his cheek.

I splashed cold water on my face, watching the droplets run down the foggy bathroom mirror. It was the same mirror I used to practice my high school graduation speech in, back when I thought thirty meant a mortgage and a corner office. Now, it just reflected dark circles under my eyes and a forced, tight-lipped smile. I grabbed a towel, wringing the cotton fabric between my hands until my fingers cramped. Dad’s heavy footsteps thumped up the stairs, approaching the door. I immediately turned the faucet back on full blast, drowning out the silence. "You doing okay in there, kiddo?" his voice carried through the wood. I swallowed the thick, dry lump in my throat, forcing my breathing to steady. "Just fine!" I called back, my voice painfully bright. I stayed hovering over the sink, waiting until his footsteps retreated completely before letting out a breath.

Sarah sat completely rigid on the floral sofa, a ceramic teacup balanced precariously on her knee. Her parents sat across from her, excitedly outlining a six-month plan they had typed up and printed. "We think you could take some local courses," her father read from the crisp white paper. Sarah felt a cold sweat breaking out on the back of her neck. The room seemed to be shrinking, the walls pressing inward while the patterned wallpaper blurred into a dizzying swirl of roses. She nodded, a jerky, mechanical movement, while her thumbnail relentlessly picked at the skin around her index finger. A tiny drop of blood welled up. The clinking of her mother's spoon against a saucer sounded deafening. Sarah couldn't draw a full breath; her lungs felt encased in iron. She visually swept the room for the front door, mapping the exact distance to the exit.

Pushing the shopping cart down the cereal aisle, I kept two steps behind my mother. "Get whatever you like, sweetie. You're home now," she said, tossing a box of my favorite childhood brand into the basket. I stared at the cartoon leprechaun on the box, feeling a sudden, intense heat flush up my neck to my ears. I shifted my weight from foot to foot, avoiding eye contact with Mrs. Gable, a neighbor who was pushing her cart toward us. I ducked my head, intensely studying a display of granola bars. If she recognizes me, she’s going to ask why I’m not in Chicago anymore. She’ll ask about the wedding that isn't happening. My heart battered against my ribs like a trapped bird. I abandoned the cart, muttering something about forgetting the milk, and speed-walked toward the back of the store, my vision tunneling to a narrow point.

Arthur arranged his dual monitors on the rickety card table his father had hauled up from the basement. The ethernet cable trailed across the floral carpet, a bright blue tripwire in the middle of his parents' guest room. He booted up his laptop, his foot tapping out a relentless staccato rhythm against the metal table leg. His email inbox loaded, displaying zero new messages from the recruiters he had contacted last week. He immediately refreshed the page. Then he refreshed it again. He stood up, paced the length of the small room, and sat back down to refresh the page a third time. The house was utterly silent, save for the hum of the refrigerator two floors below. Arthur rubbed his temples, feeling the rapid pulse jumping beneath his skin. He opened a new browser tab, typed "hiring immediately," and hit enter, holding his breath as the results loaded.

I stood by the kitchen trash can, gripping the thick envelope from the collections agency. It had been forwarded to my parents' address, glaring at me in stark black ink. I shoved it deep under the coffee grounds and empty eggshells, pressing it down until my hands were covered in grime. I washed my hands aggressively at the sink, scrubbing the soap into my skin until it turned raw and pink. Behind me, the front door unlocked. Dad was home early. I grabbed a dish towel, scrubbing a completely clean countertop in rapid, tight circles. "Hey, you're back," I said, my voice completely devoid of its normal register. He dropped his keys in the ceramic bowl. I kept scrubbing, my eyes locked on the synthetic marble, refusing to look toward the trash can. My chest felt tight, and my legs felt entirely disconnected from the rest of my body.

Chloe sat on the rusted patio swing, letting it squeak back and forth in the damp evening air. Through the kitchen window, she watched her parents moving around the island, chopping vegetables together. They looked settled, complete. Her phone buzzed in her lap, illuminating her face in the dark. It was a text from a former coworker about a potential freelance gig. Chloe read it, her thumbs hovering over the keyboard. She typed a yes. Then she deleted it. She typed a no. She deleted that, too. Her breathing grew shallow and rapid, pulling the cold night air into her tightening throat. She locked the screen, shoved the phone into her jacket pocket, and wrapped her arms tight around her ribs. She rocked the swing faster, the squeaking metal growing louder and more erratic, drowning out the quiet, stable domesticity glowing just a few feet away through the glass.

The barista hands over my iced latte, her sleeve riding up to reveal a jagged, crying moon on her forearm. It’s my sketch. Not just a similar design, but the exact doodle I posted to my dormant art blog three years ago. The coins slip from my sweaty fingers, scattering across the polished counter with a deafening clatter. I drop to my knees to gather them, my chest tightening as if wrapped in iron bands. Does she know? Did she recognize my name on the cup? I fumble with the quarters, my heart drumming a frantic, syncopated beat against my ribs. I want to stand up and ask her about it, but my throat feels like it’s packed with dry cotton. Snatching the last dime, I grab the sweating plastic cup, refusing to make eye contact, and hurry out the door.

At the gallery opening, Julian spots a man studying his centerpiece. As the patron turns, the overhead spotlight catches the side of his neck, illuminating the intricate, geometric wolf Julian spent months perfecting. Julian’s breath immediately hitches. He wipes his clammy palms on the sides of his tailored slacks, taking a sudden, jerky step backward. He bumps into a waiter, sending a tray of champagne flutes dangerously wobbling. Apologizing in a rushed, breathless whisper, Julian retreats behind a marble sculpture. He presses two fingers against his pulse point, feeling it race like a trapped bird. The man points at the canvas, then taps his neck. Julian bites his thumbnail until it stings. If the man demands an explanation for the duplicated exclusivity, Julian has no idea what he’ll say.

Scrolling through my feed at two in the morning, a tagged photo makes me freeze. A guy in Brazil just won a local competition with his new back piece—a massive, exact replica of my charcoal portrait of Persephone. My foot starts tapping a frantic, ceaseless rhythm against my desk leg. I click on his profile, then back to the photo, refreshing the page three times as a cold sweat breaks out along my hairline. Did he credit me in the tiny, untranslated caption? I highlight the text, my cursor shaking so badly I miss the first few letters. Dropping the mouse, I begin to pace the length of my tiny bedroom, running a hand through my hair until the roots ache. My stomach churns with sour acid. Millions of people have liked the post, and I’m just a ghost behind the ink on a stranger's skin.

Hanging onto the subway rail, Maya glances at the woman seated directly below her. Right above the woman’s ankle is the crescent floral design Maya spent weeks illustrating for an indie magazine cover. Maya instantly stops breathing, shrinking deeper into the collar of her oversized coat. She turns her head away, staring intensely at the passing black tunnel outside the window, but her peripheral vision stays locked on the tattoo. Her leg begins to bounce, vibrating the entire bench seat. The woman shifts, adjusting her shopping bags, and Maya’s fingernails dig into her own palms until crescent moons, much like the drawing, are indented into her flesh. She silently counts the stops left until her destination, her chest rising and falling in shallow, rapid bursts. She prays the woman doesn't look up, doesn't try to strike up a casual conversation about local artists.

The guy in the lane next to mine pulls himself out of the community pool, water cascading down his pale back. Spanning across his ribs is my oil painting of the sinking galleon. I immediately sink lower into the heavily chlorinated water until it reaches my chin, my heart hammering violently against my sternum. I desperately want to leave, but my towel and keys are sitting right next to his duffel bag on the tiled edge. I chew ruthlessly on my lower lip, tasting a sudden, sharp hint of copper. He starts stretching, lingering by the edge of the pool. I paddle backward, putting as much distance between us as the floating lane dividers will allow. My breathing echoes loudly in my ears, drowning out the splash of the other swimmers. I squeeze my eyes shut, wishing I could dissolve into the deep end.

Elias wanders through the buzzing tattoo convention, stopping cold when he spots his own proprietary flash sheet taped to a rival artist's booth. Worse, the artist is actively buzzing his crying dagger design into a client’s thigh. A cold prickle erupts at the base of Elias’s skull. His knees lock rigidly in place, the loud hum of fifty tattoo machines suddenly sounding like a swarm of angry hornets inside his head. He shifts his weight from his left foot to his right, repeatedly clenching and unclenching his fists. A drop of sweat rolls down his spine. Should he interrupt? Demand they stop? He takes a hesitant half-step forward, but his throat closes up completely. The client laughs at a joke the artist makes, and Elias quickly spins around, speed-walking toward the emergency exit doors as he furiously rubs the back of his neck.

It’s a blind date, and things are going fine until he rolls up his sleeves to pour the Cabernet. Right there, wrapped around his forearm, is my linework of the entangled vipers. I grip the fragile stem of my wine glass so hard I expect the crystal to shatter into a hundred pieces. A single, icy bead of sweat travels down my temple. "Where did you get that?" I squeak, my voice pitching up two octaves higher than normal. He smiles, admiring the ink, entirely unaware that the floor is tilting beneath my chair. I press my knees tightly together under the table to stop them from shaking. My appetite completely vanishes, replaced by a heavy, leaden knot twisting in my gut. I frantically scan the dim restaurant, wondering how fast I can pay my half of the bill and escape into the cool night air.

Sitting on the boardwalk bench, Clara watches a skateboarder kickflip over a discarded soda can. As he lands, his calf is fully exposed, bearing a vibrant watercolor lotus. Her lotus. The exact piece she painted after her mother passed. Clara’s breath hitches loudly in her throat. She immediately dives into her canvas tote bag, her hands trembling so violently she drops her phone onto the concrete. She digs past her wallet and loose pens, desperately hunting for her sketchbook to verify the tiny, intentional flaws she hides in her work. Her pulse thuds loudly in her ears. The skateboarder does a U-turn and starts rolling back in her direction. Clara freezes, her hand still buried deep in the bag. She pulls her sunhat low over her face, holding her breath until her lungs burn, waiting for the clatter of polyurethane wheels to fade away.

I am halfway through my guest lecture when the student in the front row stretches. Her sleeve slips, revealing a dot-work etching of a ruined cathedral. My cathedral. I abruptly lose my place in my notes. The silence in the auditorium stretches for five agonizing seconds. I clear my throat, but my mouth is suddenly devoid of moisture, tasting like chalk dust. I shift my weight from my left foot to my right, gripping the edges of the wooden podium until my knuckles turn bloodless white. A sea of expectant faces stares up at me. I blink rapidly, trying to banish the dark spots dancing at the edges of my vision. I flip the page back and forth without reading a single word, my mind completely blank as a cold flush creeps up my neck, paralyzing my vocal cords.

The triage nurse wraps the cuff around Liam’s arm. Reaching for the stethoscope, she reveals the skull and rose etched into her bicep. It’s his signature piece, the one he refused to sell reproduction rights for. The cuff inflates, squeezing Liam’s arm tight. The heart rate monitor next to the bed suddenly beeps in a rapid, staccato rhythm. Liam stares fixedly at the acoustic ceiling tiles, counting them. Seven across, twelve down. He swallows hard, his Adam’s apple bobbing. The nurse frowns at the digital readout, then looks at him. Liam rigidly turns his head away, focusing on a crumpled medical poster on the wall. He picks at a loose thread on his jeans, pulling it until it threatens to unravel the entire seam, wishing the linoleum floor would open up and swallow him whole.

A stranger takes off his shirt in the gym locker room, and my abstract skyline spans his broad shoulder blades. I quickly pivot around to face my locker, fumbling with the combination dial. My hands are entirely clammy, slipping clumsily off the smooth metal of the lock. Thirty-two to the right, or was it left? The metal loudly clicks, refusing to open. The locker room benches creak behind me as the man sits down. I tug at my collar, feeling a sudden, stifling lack of oxygen in the humid room. My foot taps a frantic rhythm against the damp tile floor. If I just grab my towel, I can leave my duffel bag here and come back later. I pull my baseball cap down low over my eyes, shrinking into myself as I speed-walk toward the exit without showering, leaving all my belongings behind.

The cashier scans the cereal boxes, her hands flying across the scanner. Splashed across the back of her left hand is the sprawling, geometric mandala Sophie drew during her darkest, most vulnerable month. Sophie’s stomach immediately does a violent, sickening flip. She frantically pats down the pockets of her jacket, her hands trembling as she searches for her wallet. When she pulls out a twenty-dollar bill, her fingers shake so badly the crisp paper flutters in the air. She shoves the money across the counter, refusing to look at the cashier’s face. The cashier tries to hand her the change, but Sophie is already grabbing her unbagged groceries, clutching them tightly to her chest. She practically sprints toward the sliding automatic doors, her breathing coming in short, shallow gasps until the cool parking lot air hits her burning face.

Elias froze near the espresso machine, his fingers slipping off his paper cup. Above the barista station hung three familiar ink portraits. His portraits. The ones he kept locked in the bottom drawer of his desk. His chest tightened, his lungs suddenly forgetting how to pull in air. He rubbed his damp palms against his jeans, his gaze darting between the chatting customers and the framed artwork. Had his roommate taken them? Were people pointing at the messy crosshatching? A woman raised her latte, squinting at the centerpiece. Elias swallowed hard, tasting copper. His foot began a rapid, involuntary staccato tap against the floorboards. If he walked out now, maybe no one would connect him to the initials in the corner. He backed toward the door, bumping into a chair, muttering a hasty apology as blood rushed deafeningly in his ears.

The projector screen flared to life, illuminating the boardroom in harsh white light. I stopped breathing. Right there, on slide four of the quarterly review, was my midnight concept art. The raw, messy render I had left on the shared server by mistake. My fingers clamped onto the edge of the mahogany table, my knuckles turning white. The CEO adjusted his glasses, praising the innovative new direction. My stomach twisted into a tight, heavy knot. I bit the inside of my cheek until I tasted blood, keeping my eyes fixed firmly on the patterned carpet. What if they zoomed in on the flawed shading? What if they asked who made it? A bead of sweat trickled down the back of my neck. I needed a glass of water. I needed the floor to open up and swallow me whole before slide five appeared.

Maya’s teeth clicked together as she chewed the ragged edge of her thumbnail. The student gallery was packed, but all she could see was the clay figure resting on a velvet pedestal in the center of the room. It was her private piece, the one modeled after her late sister, left in the kiln room to dry. How did it get out here? She paced a tight circle behind a large marble pillar, peeking out every few seconds. Two critics hovered near her piece, whispering. Maya’s pulse hammered a frantic rhythm against her ribs. She tugged at the collar of her sweater, suddenly feeling suffocated by the thick wool. She tried to step forward, to grab the sculpture and run, but her knees felt like water. She just stood there in the shadows, her breath coming in short, shallow hitches as a critic reached out a finger.

I kept my hood pulled low, hands shoved deep into my pockets, my fingernails digging into my palms. There it was, right in the boutique’s illuminated display window. The canvas I had spray-painted behind the abandoned textile factory, the one with my real name accidentally bleeding through the layers of neon pink. My jaw ached from clenching it so hard. Shoppers stopped on the sidewalk, pointing at the dripping spray paint. I shifted my weight from left to right, my eyes darting up and down the street. Did the boutique owner see me painting it? Are the police going to show up? My throat felt like it was coated in sandpaper. I took a step back, then another, my heart slamming against my sternum like a trapped bird. Every time the shop bell rang, I flinched, convinced someone was coming out to point me out.

Leo stopped dead in the middle of the hallway. Pasted to the cinderblock wall was a massive poster for the spring play. The background was his. The swirling, chaotic margins he doodled during math class when his mind was spinning. The sketchbook had gone missing on Tuesday. Now, hundreds of students were walking past it. His throat closed up. He pressed his back against a row of lockers, staring wide-eyed at the blue-ink monsters blown up to poster size. A group of seniors stopped to point at the intricate lines. Leo’s hands shook as he fumbled for his phone, dropping it twice before it clattered onto the linoleum. He didn't pick it up. He couldn't drag his gaze away from the poster. His legs bounced restlessly, ready to sprint toward the nearest exit, counting the seconds until the bell would ring and clear the hall.

The local library's display case gleamed under the fluorescent lights. I stood frozen in the nonfiction aisle, staring through the gap in the books. Sitting on a clear plastic stand was my leather-bound journal, opened to the page with my most personal calligraphy poem. The lock was broken. My chest heaved as I struggled to pull in enough oxygen. I wiped my sweaty palms on my skirt over and over. The librarian walked past the case, adjusting her glasses. Did she read it? Did she recognize my handwriting? I pressed my fingers against my temples, a dull ache throbbing behind my eyes. I wanted to smash the glass, grab the journal, and sprint out the double doors. Instead, I stood pinned behind the biographies, gnawing on my lower lip, jumping out of my skin every time a book was scanned at the front desk.

Dinner chatter faded into a dull buzz as Clara walked into the dining room. Hanging right above the mantle was the canvas she had thrown in the basement trash. A dark, chaotic smear of acrylics she had painted during her darkest month. Her grandmother beamed from the head of the table, tapping her fork against her glass. Clara’s stomach plummeted. The room suddenly felt ten degrees hotter. She wrapped her arms tightly around her waist, digging her fingertips into her ribs. Her uncle squinted at the abstract shapes, tilting his head. Clara’s breathing grew loud in her own ears. She shifted her weight from foot to foot, her gaze darting to the front door, then to the kitchen, then back to the painting. She felt lightheaded, the edges of her vision blurring as her grandmother cleared her throat to make an announcement.

The notification badge glowed red on my monitor. I clicked the link and the room started spinning. My private character designs—the ones I had only ever emailed to Sarah—were sitting at the top of the largest fan forum on the internet. With over ten thousand likes. I pushed my rolling chair away from the desk so fast it slammed into the wall. I paced the length of my bedroom, running my hands through my hair and tugging at the roots. My pulse thudded in my neck. I refreshed the page. Fifteen thousand likes. The comments were dissecting every line, every flaw. My mouth went completely dry. I sat back down, my hands trembling violently as I hovered my mouse over the keyboard, trying to type out a message to the admins. I hit backspace ten times, unable to string the letters together.

Julian froze holding his coffee mug, the hot liquid sloshing over the brim and scalding his knuckles. He didn't feel the burn. Pinned to the marketing department's corkboard was a photograph of his childhood home. He had never shown it to anyone at the agency. A sticky note reading draft one was slapped across the center. His lungs hitched. He quickly placed the mug on the nearest desk, his hands shaking so much it rattled against the wood. He grabbed the hem of his shirt, twisting the fabric into a tight coil. Coworkers strolled past, oblivious to the buzzing static filling his head. He darted his eyes toward the manager's office, biting the inside of his cheek. Should he rip it down? What if someone saw him? He backed against a filing cabinet, his heart hammering against his ribs in a chaotic, uneven rhythm.

The summer heat was already suffocating, but seeing my painting leaning against the vendor’s folding table made me feel like I was drowning. It was the unfinished oil landscape I had reported stolen from my car last week. A price tag dangled from the canvas frame. My knees went weak, and I had to lean against a nearby lamppost to keep from collapsing. I couldn't tear my eyes away. A couple stopped to admire it, the man pointing at my signature in the bottom corner. My chest tightened painfully. I scratched frantically at the back of my neck, leaving red marks. I needed to confront the vendor, to scream that it was mine, but my vocal cords felt paralyzed. Every time the vendor looked in my direction, I flinched, shrinking back into the crowd, my breath coming in rapid, shallow gasps.

Nina stopped wiping the steel counter. The owner was handing out the newly printed summer menus to the waitstaff. On the cover of each one was a delicate watercolor illustration of a fig. Nina’s illustration. The one she painted on the inside cover of her private recipe diary. Her stomach dropped like a lead weight. She gripped the damp rag until her knuckles turned stark white, the coarse fabric biting into her palms. The kitchen noises—the clattering pans, the shouting line cooks—faded into a distant, underwater hum. She touched her throat, feeling the rapid, fluttery pulse beating there. She darted a look toward her locker. The padlock must have been left open. A waiter walked by, flipping the menu open and admiring the art. Nina quickly ducked into the walk-in freezer, squeezing her eyes shut and wrapping her arms around her shivering shoulders.

I walked into the town hall meeting and immediately stopped in my tracks. Sitting on the main presentation table was a cardboard model. My model. The wood replica of the pavilion I had built on my dining table, never meant for public eyes. I retreated to the back row, sinking into a folding chair. My hands were slick with cold sweat. I rubbed them aggressively against my corduroy pants. The mayor pointed directly at the intricate lattice roof—my roof—praising the anonymous donor. My jaw locked tight. I chewed my thumbnail down to the quick, tasting salt. The room felt entirely too small, the air thick and unbreathable. What if they called for the creator to step forward? I kept my head down, staring fixedly at the scuff marks on the floor, my legs jiggling in an endless, rhythmic tremor.

I scan the paper taped to the locker room door for the fifth time, my finger trembling as it traces the alphabetical list. A skips straight to C. My name isn't there. The hallway chatter around me fades into a high-pitched ringing. I press my sweaty palms against my jeans, wiping them over and over. How am I supposed to walk into the kitchen and look my dad in the eye? He bought me those new cleats just for this season. My chest feels tight, like a heavy stone is resting right on my sternum. I pull my phone out, open his contact, type "I didn't make the cut," and immediately backspace. I bite the inside of my lip, tasting copper. The bell rings for first period, but my feet feel glued to the linoleum tiles. If I walk into calculus, everyone will know.

Marcus sat in the driver's seat of his parked Honda, the engine off but the keys still clutched in his vise-like grip. The coach's voicemail had ended ten minutes ago, but Marcus’s right leg was still bouncing relentlessly against the steering column. "We're going with a taller lineup," the voice echoed in his ears. He stared blankly through the windshield at his dark driveway. Tomorrow, he would have to walk down the main corridor at school. The guys would ask. The girls would whisper. He rubbed the back of his neck, feeling a cold sweat prickling his skin despite the chilly autumn air. His breathing came in shallow, rapid hitches. He picked up his phone, stared at the black screen, dropped it in the cupholder, and then picked it up again five seconds later. The digital clock mocked him with how much night was left.

I sit on the edge of my bed, endlessly wrapping and unwrapping the athletic tape around my wrists. The crisp sound of the adhesive unspooling is the only noise in my bedroom. 3:14 AM blares from the digital clock. I squeeze my eyes shut, but all I see is my slight wobble on the balance beam during the final trials. It was half a second, barely a deduction, yet the elite squad list emailed tonight didn't have my name. My heart thumps a frantic, erratic beat against my ribs. I stand up and pace the length of my rug—eight steps to the door, eight steps to the window. If I’m not on the elite squad, the university scouts won't even look at me. I rub my clammy hands over my face, taking a breath that stops shallowly at the top of my lungs.

Chloe stood by the edge of the lap pool, the humid, chlorine-scented air suddenly suffocating. The A-team relay roster was pinned to the bulletin board across the deck. She didn’t need to walk over to know her name was missing; the pitying glances from the varsity girls had told her enough. She began picking violently at her cuticles, her thumbs slick with pool water and a tiny bead of blood. Her stomach twisted into tight, burning knots. The silence of her impending ride home with her older brother—the star butterfly swimmer—loomed like a physical wall. She shifted her weight from left to right, her toes curling into the wet tiles. Every time a door opened, her head snapped up, eyes darting around the cavernous natatorium, calculating exactly how long she could hide in the bathroom before someone forced her to speak.

The smooth leather of the baseball slips in my clammy hands as I toss it up and catch it, over and over. I’m the only one left in the dugout. The varsity roster is pinned to the chain-link fence, fluttering in the wind, a glaring reminder of my failure to secure the closing pitcher spot. My knee jiggles uncontrollably, vibrating the aluminum bench. I keep swallowing, trying to force down the dry, scratchy lump blocking my throat. Tomorrow's practice is going to be unbearable. Coach will want me on the JV squad again. I can already hear the upperclassmen snickering. I dig my fingernails into the seams of the baseball until they ache. I need to text my mom to pick me up, but my fingers are shaking too much to type out the words. The screen blurs as I stare at it.

Elena sat on the hard locker room bench, her unlaced skates heavy on her feet. She swiped down on her phone screen to refresh her email. Nothing new. The rejection from the pairs academy had arrived at 8:00 AM, but she had refreshed her inbox forty-seven times since then, as if the text might magically rearrange itself. She chewed the skin around her thumbnail, her foot tapping a rapid staccato against the rubber matting. When the rink doors swung open, she flinched, dropping the phone onto her lap. It was just the Zamboni driver. She exhaled a shaky, uneven breath and pressed the heels of her hands against her eyes. The junior championships were next month. Without an academy sponsor, her ice time would be cut in half. She picked up the phone. Swipe down. Loading circle. Still rejected.

I tap my pencil eraser against the edge of my desk in AP History. Tap-tap-tap-tap. The rhythm matches the frantic fluttering in my chest. Mr. Harrison is talking about the Cold War, but his voice sounds like he’s underwater. Yesterday, Coach pulled me aside and said my sprint times just weren't enough for the state traveling team. I glance at the clock. 10:14. In exactly forty-six minutes, lunchtime starts. The track team always sits at the round tables by the windows. Where do I sit now? If I sit with them, I’m the interloper who didn't make the cut. If I sit somewhere else, I’m the bitter loser. Sweat prickles under my arms, and I wipe my damp palms on my jeans. Tap-tap-tap-tap. My jaw aches from how hard I’ve been grinding my teeth since second period.

Liam stared blankly at the wall of his dorm room, his goalie mask resting uselessly on his knees. The draft for the starting lineup had concluded an hour ago. He wasn’t picked. He stood up, walked to the window, and immediately walked back to his bed. He repeated the loop. Window, bed, window, bed. His chest rose and fell in quick, shallow hitches. His phone buzzed on the nightstand, lighting up with a text from the backup center. Liam flinched at the noise and backed away from the device as if it were on fire. The local sports reporter was coming to interview the team at 4:00 PM. Liam grabbed the edge of his mattress, his knuckles turning stark white, his pulse thrumming loudly in his ears. He swallowed hard, trying to wet a throat that felt like it was coated in sand.

The ceiling fan spins in circles, and I trace its path with my eyes, unable to blink. The JV assignment letter is crumpled into a tight ball in my right fist. I keep squeezing it, the crinkling paper the loudest sound in my quiet bedroom. I sit up, lie back down, and sit up again. I can’t get enough air into my lungs. Tomorrow, I have to walk into the gym and put on the white practice jersey instead of the blue one. The blue one means varsity. I press my hands against my churning stomach. What will Mia and Sarah say? We promised we’d play varsity together this year. I reach for my phone, hovering my thumb over their group chat. My hand is trembling so noticeably that I drop the phone onto my duvet. I pull my knees to my chest and rock slightly.

David paced the length of the turf, long after the stadium lights had shut off. The darkness was complete, but he didn't need to see to know he was walking back and forth across the fifty-yard line. The head coach had given the starting quarterback spot to the new transfer student. David rubbed his forehead aggressively, leaving red streaks across his skin. His breath plumed in the cold air in short, rapid puffs. He stopped, stared at the dark bleachers, and his right leg immediately began to bounce. College scouts were coming on Friday. If he was on the bench, his scholarship chances vanished. He tugged at the collar of his jacket, suddenly feeling like it was strangling him. He pulled out his keys, jingled them incessantly, walked to the thirty-yard line, and then turned right back around.

I press the strings of my tennis racket into my palm, pressing harder and harder until deep red grid lines are stamped into my skin. The elite academy roster is posted on the clubhouse window, and my name is nowhere to be found. The sun is beating down on my neck, making me sweat profusely, but I feel entirely cold. My heart is beating so fast it feels like a hummingbird trapped behind my ribs. I need to walk back to the parking lot where my dad is waiting with the engine running. I take a step forward, but my knees feel like they are filled with water. I bite down on my lower lip until I taste salt. If I walk back to that car without the academy patch, the silent drive home is going to crush me. I just keep staring at the grid lines on my hand.

Sarah sat perfectly still on the stationary erg machine, though the rest of the boathouse was bustling with the top-boat crew loading the shells. She wasn’t in the boat. The coach had chosen a heavier girl for the starboard seat. Sarah’s fingers gripped the plastic handle of the machine so tightly her joints ached. She stared unblinking at the blank digital monitor. Her left foot tapped a furious, unbroken rhythm against the floorboards, a vibration that rattled the empty water bottle beside her. She felt a cold prickle of sweat trace its way down her spine. The regional qualifiers were entirely out of her hands now. Whenever one of the varsity girls walked past, Sarah rigidly locked her jaw and shifted her gaze to the ceiling, her chest constricting as she fought for a deep breath that simply wouldn't come.

Coach tapped my shoulder and pointed toward left field. My jaw tightened. I’ve pitched since I was seven, toeing the rubber, controlling the game’s heartbeat. Out there, the grass stretches endlessly. I chewed the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper, adjusting my glove three times before stepping onto the turf. Every fly ball in practice suddenly played on a loop in my head—the misjudged arcs, the sun blinding me, the ball dropping onto the grass. I wiped my palms on my pants, leaving dark sweat stains on the gray fabric. "Just track it," Coach had said. My chest felt tight, each breath shallower than the last. I kicked the dirt, staring up at the stadium lights, waiting for a crack of the bat that felt like an impending execution.

Maya stared at the oversized goalkeeper gloves resting on the bench. For three seasons, she had been the team's leading striker, living for the thrill of outrunning defenders. Now, the starting keeper was injured, and Coach needed her in the box. Maya’s leg bounced rapidly up and down. She swallowed hard, finding her mouth bone-dry. The net behind her looked massive, an impossible expanse to defend. As the referee blew the whistle to start the second half, Maya paced back and forth along the goal line, picking at the velcro straps on her wrists. The opposing team advanced the ball, their cleats tearing into the muddy pitch. Maya’s heart slammed against her ribs like a trapped bird. She bounced on the balls of her feet, her eyes darting constantly between the approaching forwards.

"Bring the ball up, Marcus." The words rang in my ears as I stood at the baseline. I’m a center. My domain is the paint, boxing out and catching rebounds. Now I was supposed to be the floor general? I dribbled the ball, but my fingers felt like stiff sausages. I swallowed loudly, my Adam’s apple bobbing. The opposing point guard dropped into a low stance, slapping the hardwood, his eyes locked on my waist. My stomach twisted into a cold knot. I looked left, then right, the play design entirely scrambled in my head. Wait, is it horns or baseline cut? I wiped my forehead, stinging sweat dripping into my left eye. I took a stuttering step forward, the ball suddenly feeling heavier than lead, my breathing turning into short, jagged gasps.

The rotation shifted, and Coach pushed Leo toward the outside hitter position. Leo, a career libero accustomed to digging spikes from the back row, looked up at the towering net. It seemed to grow taller by the second. He rubbed his hands together, his fingertips ice-cold despite the suffocating heat of the gymnasium. When the setter called his number, Leo’s stomach did a violent flip. He took his approach, stuttering on the second step. His mind raced—left, right-left, swing, don't hit the tape. He jumped, his arms swinging out of sync, feeling exposed without the comfort of the backcourt line. When his feet hit the floor again, he immediately checked the coach’s expression, his nails digging into the meat of his palms as he waited for the whistle to signal the next serve.

They handed me the red pinnie to switch to defense. Cornerback. I’ve spent my entire life running routes, catching passes, being the one chased. Now I had to do the chasing. I strapped my helmet back on, pulling the chinstrap so tight it pinched my jaw. Across the line of scrimmage, the receiver settled into his stance, adjusting his gloves. My knees felt weak, like the joints had been replaced with water. I backpedaled a few steps before the snap, my cleats catching awkwardly in the turf. Watch the hips, not the feet, I repeated mentally, over and over, until the words lost their meaning. The quarterback shouted the cadence. My breath caught in my throat. I shifted my weight from left to right, entirely guessing which way the world was about to tilt.

Sarah tapped her stick against the ice, creating a rapid, erratic rhythm. Coach had just moved her from defense to the wing, demanding more offensive pressure. She stared at the opposing netminder at the far end of the rink. The distance seemed unbridgeable. As the referee prepared to drop the puck for the face-off, Sarah shifted her weight aggressively from skate to skate. She tugged at her jersey collar, suddenly feeling suffocated by the heavy fabric. Her jaw clenched tight enough to make her teeth ache. Get open, find the lane, shoot, she chanted inwardly, but the instructions felt like a foreign language. The whistle shrieked, and she leaped forward, her heart thumping against her chest protector in a rapid, irregular beat, her eyes wide as she tried to anticipate a play she had never practiced.

"You're running the first leg today," Coach said, tossing me the baton. I stared at the smooth aluminum cylinder in my hand. I'm the anchor. I finish the race; I don't start it. I walked to the starting blocks, my stomach churning violently. The silence of the stadium before the gun is deafening. I knelt down, placing my fingers behind the white chalk line. They were trembling. I pressed them harder into the synthetic track to make them stop. On your marks. I raised my hips. My breath hitched, caught somewhere between my lungs and my throat. What if I false start? What if I slip on the drive phase? My eyes darted to the runners beside me, all perfectly still. I closed my eyes, a bead of sweat tracing the curve of my spine.

David treaded water in the center of the pool, his legs kicking in tight, hurried circles. He was a driver, built for speed on the perimeter, but today he was ordered to play center defender. The opposing center forward, a mountain of a man with broad shoulders, backed into him. David’s pulse hammered in his ears, drowning out the splashing water. He grabbed the man’s suit, his knuckles turning white under the water. The referee paced the deck above. David swallowed pool water, coughing violently, but didn't dare take his eyes off the ball moving around the perimeter. He kept checking his positioning, shifting left, then right, his mind racing through the wrestling moves he barely knew. Every splash in his peripheral vision made him flinch, his chest rising and falling in rapid, shallow bursts.

"Switch to stroke seat," the coxswain barked. I froze, the oar handle slipping slightly in my sweaty grip. Bow seat is easy—you just follow the rhythm of the boat. Stroke seat sets the pace for everyone. I carefully stepped over the riggers and slid into the front seat. The empty stretch of water ahead suddenly looked overwhelmingly vast. I rubbed my hands on my thighs, trying to dry them, but my palms instantly grew slick again. The eight faces behind me were waiting for my cue. My leg muscles twitched involuntarily against the foot stretchers. I gripped the oar, my jaw rigid, staring at the coxswain's unblinking eyes. Catch, drive, finish, recover. I recited the sequence endlessly. I took a short, jagged breath, my heart fluttering against my ribs like a trapped moth.

Liam stood at the edge of the scrum, pulling at the collar of his thick jersey. For years, he had been a winger, sprinting down the sidelines in open space. Today, injuries forced him into the flanker position, right into the brutal, grinding heart of the pack. The two forward lines crashed together with a sickening thud. Liam hesitated for a fraction of a second, his feet rooted to the mud. He chewed on his mouthguard continuously. He approached the tangle of bodies, his breath coming in quick, shallow puffs. He wiped his hands on his shorts over and over. When the ball popped out of the ruck, he lunged forward, but his eyes were squeezed half-shut, his shoulders rigid, every muscle coiled defensively as he anticipated the crushing impact of the opposing forwards.

"You're taking her spot on the beam," Coach whispered. The arena noise faded into a dull roar. I’m a floor specialist; the ground is solid, wide, forgiving. The balance beam is four inches of unforgiving suede. I dipped my hands in the chalk bowl, squeezing the white blocks until they crumbled into dust, coating my shaking fingers. I walked to the stairs, my legs feeling like they were made of lead. I wiped my hands on my leotard, then immediately chalked them again. My stomach rolled over itself. I mounted the beam, the leather cold against my bare feet. Standing up, the floor seemed twenty feet away. My breathing grew ragged. I stared at the end of the beam, trying to visualize the flight series, but all I saw was empty air waiting to swallow me.

Raj adjusted the unfamiliar helmet, the metal grille obscuring his vision. He had spent his entire career in the outfield, chasing down boundaries. Now, with the primary wicketkeeper out with a fractured finger, Raj crouched behind the stumps. The heavy padded gloves felt clumsy on his hands. He tapped them together, a restless, hollow sound echoing in his ears. The fast bowler started his run-up. Raj’s knees trembled slightly in his deep squat. He licked his chapped lips, tasting dust. The red leather ball hurtled down the pitch at ninety miles an hour. Raj held his breath, his eyes wide behind the grille, his body turning into a rigid block. He kept second-guessing his hand position, shifting his weight constantly as the batsman swung, completely unprepared for the vicious spin of the ball.

The glossy prospectus sitting on the communal printer had the words "Acquisition by Apex Global" stamped across the top. I read the headline three times, though the letters seemed to swim across the page. My knee bounced under the desk, a steady staccato rhythm against the metal frame. I pulled up my banking app, staring at the mortgage balance. Three hundred thousand left. If I lose the quarterly bonus... if my department is restructured... I swallowed hard, but my mouth felt like it was full of cotton. I picked up my phone, typed a message to my wife, deleted it, and set the phone face-down. Then I picked it up again. The cursor blinked rhythmically on my empty spreadsheet, matching the rapid thumping against my ribs. I needed to go to the bathroom, but my legs felt glued to the chair.

Through the thin glass walls of the conference room, Marcus watched the founders shaking hands with the men in tailored suits. He had caught fragments of their conversation by the coffee machine earlier—"synergy," "buyout," "streamlining overlapping departments." Marcus pressed his thumbnail into the edge of his desk until the plastic cracked. He glanced around the open-plan office; the junior developers were laughing over a ping-pong game, completely oblivious. Marcus grabbed his pen and chewed on the cap, the plastic splintering against his teeth. He had just signed the lease on a two-bedroom apartment. He opened up a new browser tab and typed in his LinkedIn password, his fingers slipping twice on the keyboard. A bead of cold moisture trickled down the back of his neck. He deleted the password, closed the tab, and immediately opened it again.

The moment Mrs. Higgins walked in with the man holding a clipboard, I knew. They stood by the display case, pointing at the ovens and murmuring about "franchise potential." My hands shook as I tried to fold the croissant dough, tearing the delicate layers I’d spent all morning laminating. Flour dusted the floor as I accidentally knocked over the measuring cup. The metal hit the tiles with a deafening clatter. "Everything alright back there?" Mrs. Higgins called out. "Perfectly fine!" I chirped, my voice an octave higher than usual. I gripped the edge of the stainless steel counter, pressing my fingertips into the cold metal to stop the trembling. My breathing came in short, shallow gasps. I’ve worked at this bakery for six years. I don’t have a college degree. Where else would I go? I stared at the ruined dough, unable to blink.

The official memo was pinned right next to the safety guidelines. Effective immediately, Titan Industries will assume all operational control. Sarah stood in the breakroom, her lukewarm soup completely forgotten on the table behind her. She read the final paragraph outlining "expected transitional redundancies," feeling a sudden heaviness in her chest. She rubbed her sternum, stepping away from the board, then immediately turning back to read it again. Maybe she had misread it. No, the words were exactly the same. She began to pace the length of the small linoleum floor, heel-to-toe, counting her steps. Twelve steps to the vending machine, twelve steps back. Her shift didn't end for another four hours. How was she supposed to operate the heavy press machinery now? Her palms left clammy imprints on her jeans as she wiped them down over and over again.

The "Company Update" email landed in our inboxes at 11:03 AM. By 11:05, the newsroom was dead silent. A hedge fund. We were being acquired by a hedge fund known for gutting local papers.
