Elena touched her fingertips to her collarbone, feeling the rapid, bird-like flutter of her heartbeat under her skin. She closed her eyes, but the brightly lit words seemed burned into the back of her eyelids.

"I should have told you years ago," Mom whispers, staring into her teacup. "You have a brother." My fork slips from my grasp, hitting the porcelain plate with a sharp crack. The noise echoes in the quiet dining room. I stare at her, my mouth slightly open, trying to force air into my lungs. The room feels suddenly too warm, the collar of my sweater itching terribly against my neck. I reach for my water glass, but my hand is shaking so much the ice clinks against the sides, threatening to spill. I pull my hand back and trap it under my thigh to force it still. A brother. My mind races through a slideshow of every lonely summer, every solitary birthday. I bite down on my lower lip, tasting salt, completely unable to form a single question out of the thousands colliding in my head.

Thomas sat on the green slatted bench, tearing a paper coffee cup into increasingly smaller pieces. The park path was mostly empty, save for a few dog walkers. Every time gravel crunched under approaching footsteps, Thomas snapped his head up, his shoulders drawing up to his ears, only to deflate when a stranger passed by. He looked at his watch. 2:14 PM. They had agreed on 2:15. He stood up, dusted non-existent crumbs from his slacks, and sat back down. His leg bounced in a rapid staccato, matching the racing rhythm in his chest. He pulled his phone out, checked his reflection in the dark screen, and shoved it back into his pocket. He was about to meet a piece of his mother he never knew existed. A woman in a yellow scarf rounded the corner, slowing her pace as she saw him. Thomas forgot how to exhale.

The three grey dots bubble up on my screen, disappearing, then reappearing. He’s typing. I throw the phone onto the couch cushion and pace a tight circle around the coffee table. My fingers tangle in my hair, pulling at the roots just hard enough to ground me. We share a dad. I pause my pacing to stare down at the illuminated screen. The dots are gone. No message. I let out a jagged breath and grab the phone again, almost dropping it. Should I say something else? Was my opening text too weird? I chew on the inside of my cheek until it stings. I sit on the edge of the sofa, leaning forward with my elbows on my knees, staring unblinking at the empty chat log. My heart hammers against my ribs, a relentless, painful thudding. Suddenly, the screen lights up with a block of text.

The mahogany clock in the corner of the lawyer's office ticked with agonizing precision. Mr. Henderson adjusted his glasses and slid the thick manila folder across the polished desk. "Your mother left a portion of the estate to a man named Arthur Pendelton. Your half-brother." Clara gripped the leather armrests of her chair, her knuckles turning stark white. The ticking of the clock seemed to grow louder, drowning out the lawyer's continued explanations. A ringing started in her ears. She pressed her lips together into a thin, bloodless line, refusing to let her jaw tremble. She crossed her legs, then uncrossed them, unable to find a position that didn't feel unnatural. She stared at the closed folder, imagining a stranger’s face leaping out from the pages. Her throat tightened, feeling as though she had swallowed a stone, as she reached out a remarkably unsteady hand toward the documents.

I stopped dead on the cracked driveway, my chest tightening as if wrapped in heavy iron bands. There, sitting between a rusty toaster and a stack of faded paperbacks, was Barnaby. The mismatched button eyes stared back at me, unmistakable. I wiped my damp palms on my jeans, swallowing the thick lump in my throat. My foot tapped a frantic rhythm against the pavement. What if the seller remembered my mother donating him? What if they asked questions? I pulled a crumpled five-dollar bill from my pocket, my fingers trembling so badly I dropped it twice. "How much?" I rasped, the words catching. Every second the woman took to look up from her phone felt like an hour, my pulse hammering against my ribs while I waited for her to decide the stuffed bear's fate.

Elena’s fingernails dug crescent moons into her palms. The plush bear sat on the folding table, its missing blue ribbon a glaring confirmation of its identity. She stepped forward, then backward, her breathing shallow and rapid. The buzzing of a lawnmower next door sounded like a jet engine roaring in her ears. She kept darting her eyes toward the old man running the cashbox, then back to the stuffed animal. If she reached for it, would he snatch it away? She chewed on her bottom lip until a metallic taste blossomed on her tongue. The sun beat down on her neck, making her skin prickle with cold sweat. She took a stuttering breath, willing her locked knees to bend, certain that at any moment a stranger’s hand would swoop down and take away the only piece of her childhood that mattered.

The cardboard box labeled "50 Cents" held a familiar patch of matted brown fur. I froze, my stomach doing a violent flip. I rubbed my clammy hands together, my gaze darting between the teddy bear and the busy sidewalk. "Is this..." I muttered, my voice barely a squeak. I shoved my hands into my pockets, pulling out a handful of lint and coins, dropping a quarter that rolled into the gutter. My chest heaved with quick, sharp intakes of air. I needed to pick the bear up, to check the faded tag for my initials, but my arms felt like lead. A woman pushed past me, her purse brushing the table. I flinched, my heart leaping into my throat. I threw three dimes and a nickel into the empty tray, snatching the toy and speed-walking away before anyone could say a word.

David paced behind the neighbor's hedge, wiping his forehead with the back of a trembling wrist. He peeked through the leaves again. The yellow teddy bear with the stitched-on smile was still there, perched atop a pile of old VHS tapes. He checked his watch—9:02 AM. He checked it again—9:03 AM. A knot twisted in his gut, pulling tighter with every passing second. A little girl in a pink sundress pointed at the table. David’s breath hitched, and he squeezed his eyes shut, his jaw clamped so tight his teeth ached. He practically sprinted out from behind the bushes, his boots scuffing loudly against the concrete. "Excuse me, wait, please don't," he blurted out, his words tripping over each other as he wedged himself between the child and the table, throwing a crumpled ten-dollar bill at the stunned seller.

I stared at the threadbare paws resting on the plaid blanket, my pulse thudding a frantic tempo in my ears. It was him. Captain Fluff. I shifted my weight from my left foot to my right, back and forth, unable to stand still. I opened my mouth to speak, but my throat was entirely dry. What if I was wrong? What if I picked him up and it wasn't him? I rubbed the back of my neck, feeling the cold sweat clinging to my hairline. The teenager running the garage sale gave me a weird look. I forced a laugh that sounded more like a choke. My fingers twitched, desperate to grab the bear, but I kept them glued to my sides. The world seemed to tilt slightly, the chatter of bargain hunters fading into a loud, persistent ringing in my head.

Sweat pooled at the base of Sarah’s spine. She stood rigid in front of the folding table, staring at the purple stuffed bear with the burnt paw. Her breathing came in short, jagged gasps. She glanced left, then right, convinced the actual owner of the house would step out and recognize her from twenty years ago. Her right leg bounced uncontrollably. She unzipped her purse, the metal zipper catching halfway. She yanked at it, tearing the fabric, oblivious to everything except getting the money out. A dog barked two houses down, and Sarah jumped, nearly knocking over a crystal vase. She clutched the purple bear to her chest, the matted fur scratching her chin. "Keep the change," she squeaked, shoving a twenty into the surprised vendor’s hand, her eyes wide and unblinking as she backed away toward her parked car.

The instant I recognized the green corduroy overalls on the stuffed bear, a cold wave washed over me. I chewed the inside of my cheek until it bled. My eyes flicked constantly to the older couple inspecting a lamp nearby, certain they would suddenly pivot and claim the toy. I squeezed my eyes shut, taking a ragged breath, then opened them. He was still there. I patted my pockets—empty. I patted my jacket—wallet! My fingers fumbled clumsily with the leather clasp, dropping two credit cards onto the grass. I dropped to my knees, scraping my hands against the dirt, my chest tight as if I were underwater. I scooped up the plastic cards, my heart hammering a relentless rhythm against my ribs. I practically threw a dollar coin onto the table, snatching the bear by its faded overalls.

Julian’s mouth went bone dry. The teddy bear, missing its left glass eye just like his childhood companion, sat cheerfully on a lawn chair. He rubbed his palms against his khaki shorts, leaving dark, damp streaks. His mind raced through a dozen chaotic thoughts—how did it get from his mother’s attic in Seattle to a driveway in Ohio? Was it a trick? He shifted his weight relentlessly, unable to anchor his feet to the ground. When the homeowner approached, Julian recoiled, his shoulders hiking up to his ears. "Just looking," he stammered, his voice cracking on the second syllable. He bit his thumbnail, tearing at the cuticle, his gaze locked onto the stuffed animal. He wanted to run, to escape the crushing pressure in his chest, but his shaking hands were already reaching out, desperate to grab the plush fabric.

I stood at the edge of the cul-de-sac, staring past a rack of vintage coats to the blue teddy bear resting on a cardboard box. My stomach churned, tossing breakfast back up to the back of my throat. I swallowed hard, grimacing. My left foot tapped a frantic, irregular beat against the asphalt. I kept checking over my shoulder, though I had come alone. I pulled my phone out, opened the camera, closed it, and shoved it back into my pocket without taking a picture. The air felt incredibly thin. I took a step forward, then hesitated, my muscles rigid. "Is anyone buying that?" I called out, my words rushed and slurring together. The seller shook his head. I practically jogged over, my chest heaving, throwing a fistful of crumpled bills onto the table before grabbing the stuffed animal and bolting.

Maya stood completely frozen by the bargain bin, her knuckles white as she gripped the handle of her tote bag. At the bottom of the pile lay a faded corduroy bear, the same one her father had sewn a red patch onto when she was six. Her breathing turned shallow, coming in rapid little puffs. She stared intently at the red patch, her eyes darting to the people browsing the clothing rack right next to it. Any second, one of them would dig through the bin. She bit her lip so hard she tasted copper. The afternoon sun was warm, but Maya shivered violently, goosebumps erupting on her arms. She forced her stiff, trembling hand to reach into the pile of discarded toys, her pulse roaring in her ears like a rushing river. She snatched the bear and spun around immediately.

The yard sale was crowded, but my vision tunneled straight to the tattered white bear propped against a lawnmower. I recognized the ink stain on its foot from a broken pen in the third grade. My breathing hitched, and my hands immediately went clammy. I paced a tight circle by the entrance, unable to commit to walking up the driveway. Every time someone walked past the bear, my heart skipped a frantic beat. I pulled at the collar of my shirt, suddenly feeling like the fabric was choking me. "Excuse me," I mumbled to a passing neighbor, my voice trembling and weak. I rubbed my eyes, checking again to make sure the bear was real. My legs felt like jelly as I finally pushed through the crowd, my mind racing with a dozen disastrous scenarios where I wouldn't reach it in time.

Marcus stared at the velvet snout of the teddy bear resting on the picnic table. His chest felt compressed, as if invisible weights were stacked upon his ribs. He uncrossed and recrossed his arms, shifting his gaze rapidly from the stuffed animal to the driveway entrance. What if the person who bought his childhood home was here? He took a sip from his water bottle, but the liquid caught in his dry throat, sending him into a coughing fit. His face flushed hot, and he wiped away the tears forming in the corners of his eyes. A teenager picked up a video game next to the bear. Marcus gasped quietly, taking a sudden, jerky step forward. His fingers flexed and curled into tight fists. He pulled his wallet out, fumbling with the zipper, dropping all his coins onto the concrete.

Oliver stared at the glaring projection at the front of the admissions workshop. His leg bounced so fast the heavy wooden table vibrated, earning a sharp glare from the girl beside him. He couldn’t stop staring at the second paragraph on the screen—the deeply personal anecdote about his mother’s illness. He swallowed hard, but his throat felt coated in sand. His fingers dug into his kneecaps as the speaker dissected his concluding sentence, calling it raw. Every time a student in the crowded auditorium took a note, Oliver’s stomach performed a tight, painful flip. He slouched down in his plastic chair, pulling the collar of his sweater over his chin, desperately trying to shrink into a microscopic speck before anyone recognized the fiercely guarded secret he had just paid forty dollars to see broadcast to a room of two hundred strangers.

The iced latte sat untouched, condensation pooling on the faux-wood table. My thumb hovered over the glowing screen of my phone, trembling just enough to make the text blur. There it was, right on the university’s official admissions page: my essay about the broken toaster. I chewed the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper. Did I sign a release form? What if they linked my name? I furiously tapped the back button, then reopened the page, hoping it was a cached error. The coffee shop’s jazz music felt suddenly deafening, a chaotic mess of saxophones that mirrored the buzzing in my ears. I squeezed my eyes shut, pressing the cool glass of the phone against my forehead, mentally replaying every form I had clicked agree on over the last six months, waiting for the ground to swallow me whole.

Maya ripped the staple out of the packet Mr. Harrison had just distributed to the senior class. Her heart hammered against her ribs like a trapped bird. The title was slightly altered, but the words were unmistakably hers. She pressed her palms flat against her desk, leaving damp silhouettes on the laminate surface. "This piece demonstrates excellent vulnerability," Mr. Harrison announced, pacing the aisles. Maya’s breathing grew shallow, restricted to the top two inches of her lungs. She darted her eyes around the room. Liam was highlighting her second paragraph. Chloe was frowning at her metaphor about the ocean. What if they realized the anonymous author was the girl sitting in the third row? She gripped the edge of her seat, her knuckles turning bone-white, waiting for the inevitable moment someone would turn around and connect the deeply personal story to her face.

"Hey, isn't this your story about the treehouse?" My little brother shoved his laptop inches from my nose. I blinked at the glare, reading the opening line featured on a prominent college prep blog. A cold drop of sweat trickled down my spine. I snatched the laptop from him, my fingers fumbling awkwardly over the trackpad as I scrolled to the bottom, searching frantically for an author attribution. My chest tightened with every passing second. "Where did you find this?" I demanded, my voice an octave higher than normal. "Just on Reddit," he shrugged. Reddit. The word echoed in my skull, accompanied by a sudden wave of nausea. I started opening new tabs, typing my own phrases into the search bar with shaking hands, wondering how many thousands of internet strangers were currently picking apart the darkest moment of my childhood.

David paced the narrow strip of carpet between their twin beds, leaving a trail of crushed fabric. His roommate, entirely unaware of the impending crisis, kept reading the stellar example essay aloud from the admissions pamphlet. Every syllable felt like a physical blow. David rubbed the back of his neck, his skin flushed and burning. He abruptly stopped pacing and pretended to organize his desk, shuffling the same three textbooks over and over again. "It’s so weird, right?" his roommate chuckled. "Who writes about stealing a stop sign?" David forced a laugh, but it sounded more like a choke. He began to bite his fingernails, working on a jagged edge on his thumb until it bled. He stared intensely at the peeling paint on the wall, calculating exactly how long it would take to pack his bags and transfer to a school in another time zone.

Mrs. Gable beamed at me, sliding a glossy brochure across her mahogany desk. "Look what the state university sent as their gold standard!" I looked down, and the air instantly left the room. It was my piece on my grandfather’s watch. I grabbed the arms of the leather guest chair, my fingertips digging into the upholstery. I couldn't pull enough oxygen into my lungs. "Do... do other schools have this?" I stammered, my knee bouncing a rapid staccato rhythm that rattled the loose pens on her desk. I didn't wait for her answer. I was already picturing my overly critical aunt finding it in the mail, or the kids from my debate team reading it during study hall. I wiped my clammy palms on my jeans, staring unblinking at the brochure as if it were a live grenade sitting innocuously next to a stapler.

The notification pinged loudly in the silent library. Then another. And another. Elena glanced at her locked screen to see the group chat erupting with screenshots of a prominent admissions prep website. She opened the image, and the blood drained from her face. It was her essay. Her secret, agonizingly drafted essay. She shoved her phone face-down on the table, treating it like it might bite her. She stood up, sat back down, and then stood up again, her chair screeching against the floor tiles. Gathering her backpack, her hands shook so badly she dropped her water bottle. It clattered loudly, drawing irritated shushes from the surrounding tables. She practically ran toward the exit, her pulse roaring in her ears, repeatedly whispering "no, no, no" under her breath as she frantically brainstormed ways to delete the entire internet before Monday morning.

I stood frozen by the wall of metal mailboxes, staring at the glossy alumni magazine in my hands. Page fourteen. "The Essays That Got Them Here." My vision tunneled until nothing existed except my own words printed in crisp, black Garamond font. A sudden wave of heat radiated across my chest and up into my cheeks. I crumpled the magazine, stuffing it deep into my backpack. I power-walked out of the mailroom, checking over my shoulder every few seconds. Were people looking at me differently? That guy in the hoodie—was he smirking? I ducked into an empty bathroom stall, locking the door and pressing my back against the cool metal. I pulled out my phone, my thumb slipping on the screen from the sweat, dialing the admissions office number I had memorized months ago, my teeth chattering lightly despite the sweltering September heat.

Julian sat at the head of the tutoring table, meant to be guiding the juniors through their college apps. Instead, he was staring at the handout provided by the director. "Sample A" was his own submission from last year. He tapped his pen against his notebook—tap, tap, tap, tap—the rhythm frantic and uneven. A junior raised her hand, pointing to his third paragraph. "I feel like this part is a little contrived, don't you?" Julian swallowed thickly. His mouth felt like it was stuffed with cotton. "Uh," he rasped, clearing his throat violently. "Maybe." He pulled at the collar of his shirt, suddenly feeling suffocated. He kept checking the clock on the wall, the second hand moving at a glacial pace. He bounced both heels on the floor, mapping out the quickest, most inconspicuous path to the exit the second the bell rang.

The subject line read: *Learn from the Best!* I absentmindedly clicked the link while brushing my teeth, only for my toothbrush to slip and clatter into the porcelain sink. Staring back at me from the screen was the deeply humiliating story of my middle school spelling bee failure, now immortalized on a national prep forum. My heart launched into a frenzied gallop against my ribs. I grabbed a towel, wiping the toothpaste from my mouth with jerky, erratic motions. I paced the short length of my bathroom, my mind racing through a rolodex of every person I had ever met who might subscribe to this newsletter. I tried to take a deep breath, but my chest felt banded in iron. I immediately opened a draft email to the website's webmaster, my fingers hitting the backspace key just as often as the letters.

The representative from the university adjusted her microphone, projecting a slide onto the gymnasium wall. Sam’s stomach performed a violent, dizzying somersault. There, blown up to ten feet tall, were his exact words about the summer he worked at the cemetery. He sank so low in the bleachers his knees brushed his chin. He pulled his baseball cap down, shielding his eyes, but he could still hear her reading his deepest thoughts out loud to the entire junior class. His hands felt clammy and freezing cold at the same time. He kept shifting his weight, entirely incapable of sitting still, picking furiously at a loose thread on his jeans until a large hole formed. When the girl sitting next to him squinted at the screen and muttered, "I wonder who wrote this," Sam squeezed his eyes shut and stopped breathing altogether, praying for a fire drill.

I was just supposed to be picking up my sister from the open house. But as I passed the bulletin board outside the guidance office, my feet glued themselves to the linoleum. Pinned under a bold heading titled "What Success Looks Like" was my essay. The one about my parents' divorce. A dull roar filled my ears, drowning out the chatter of milling parents. I checked my pulse against my wrist; it was racing so fast I couldn't count the beats. I kept glancing around the hallway, expecting a spotlight to suddenly drop on my head. I reached out, my hand hovering over the thumbtack, debating if I could rip the paper down before anyone noticed. Every time a teacher walked past, I flinched, snapping my arms to my sides, my mind spinning violently with the undeniable reality that my deepest wounds were public property.

Leo’s thumb traced the jagged handwriting on the crumpled blue stationary he pulled from his father's cedar chest. *Skydiving in the Alps. Learn to tango. See the Northern Lights.* The paper fluttered in his vibrating hands. He dropped it onto the floorboards, wiping his suddenly clammy palms on his jeans. He checked his watch, then the door, then his watch again. The air in the attic felt too thick to breathe. How was he supposed to do this? He had a mortgage, a bad knee, and he got dizzy standing on a stepstool. His chest tightened as he stared at the list. He pressed his knuckles against his lips, gnawing on a loose piece of skin, imagining the sheer drop out of an airplane, the endless ice, the heavy ticking of a clock that had already run out for his dad.

The coffee is cold, but I drink it anyway, my heel bouncing a relentless rhythm against the linoleum. Mom’s neat cursive stares back at me from an old grocery receipt. *Swim with sharks. Publish the poems.* I tap my pen against the table, a staccato beat matching the thumping behind my ribs. I don't know the first thing about publishing, and I can't even swim in the deep end without my lungs seizing. I stand up, pace to the sink, turn the faucet on, turn it off. I sit back down. The receipt looks heavier now. I chew on the end of the pen until the plastic cracks. She left this here for me to find, didn't she? I swallow hard, my throat feeling like sandpaper, as the walls of the dim kitchen seem to inch just a little closer together.

Maya rubbed her temples, pushing away the dusty ledgers. Beneath them lay a bright red notebook. Flipping it open, she recognized her mother's looping script outlining twenty unfulfilled dreams. *Hike the Appalachian trail. Apologize to Sarah.* Maya dropped the book as if the leather had burned her. She stumbled back, hitting the edge of the desk, knocking a stack of pens to the carpet. She crouched to pick them up, but her fingers fumbled, unable to grasp the smooth plastic. Her breath came in short, jagged gasps. Sarah was the sister who hadn't spoken to them in a decade. Maya squeezed her eyes shut, pressing the heels of her hands against her eyelids until colors exploded in the darkness. She imagined the phone ringing, the heavy silence on the other end. She grabbed her keys, jangling them loudly, needing to be anywhere else.

I scrape the grease off dad's workbench, my rag snagging on a laminated card tucked under a rusty wrench. *Things to do before the curtain falls,* it reads. I wipe my brow, leaving a streak of oil. *Build a boat. See Rome.* My stomach plummets. I’m a math teacher who can barely assemble flat-pack furniture. I stare at the words, feeling a cold bead of sweat slide down my neck. I start organizing the screwdrivers by size, then by color, then by size again, my hands clumsy and cold. If I don't build the boat, did I fail him? I look at the pile of rotting lumber in the corner. My chest compresses, my pulse drumming a frantic rhythm in my ears as the heavy silence of the empty garage stretches out infinitely around me.

The slip of paper fluttered out of the worn copy of *Pride and Prejudice*. Elias caught it before it hit the rug. His mother’s handwriting listed five destinations: *Tokyo, Paris, Cairo, Buenos Aires, Sydney.* Elias shoved the paper into his pocket, his jaw locking. He checked his phone. No messages. He pulled the paper out, read the words, and folded it into a tiny, precise square. Then he unfolded it. Then he folded it again. He walked to the window, peering out at the street below, his shoe tapping a frantic rhythm on the floorboards. His bank account was currently overdrawn by twelve dollars. He tugged at his collar, suddenly feeling as though the room’s thermostat had been cranked to a stifling heat. The foreign cities on the page felt like a looming shadow creeping up the back of his neck.

I pop the glovebox of dad’s Buick looking for the registration, but find a folded napkin instead. *Ride a bull. Eat fugu. Tell Mark I forgive him.* The engine idles in the driveway, rumbling beneath me. I grip the steering wheel until my knuckles turn a stark, bloodless white. Mark is my uncle. They haven't spoken since 1998. I roll the window down, desperate for a breeze, but the stagnant summer air offers nothing. I roll it back up. My breaths come in short, reedy hitches. I reach for the gear shift, but my hand is shaking so badly I miss it, knocking my wrist against the console. I stare at the napkin, the ink slightly blurred by a coffee stain. I press my forehead against the cool glass of the window, squeezing my eyes shut, listening to the rushing roar of blood in my ears.

Clara clicked the file labeled "Before I Go.docx" on her mother's laptop. The screen flared bright white, illuminating her widened eyes. The list contained fifty elaborate tasks, from funding a scholarship to climbing Mount Kilimanjaro. Clara’s teeth clamped down on her lower lip, tasting copper. She scrolled down, then rapidly scrolled back to the top. The cursor blinked. Blinked. Blinked. Clara hovered her trembling finger over the delete key. She pressed it. The list vanished into the digital trash. Instantly, she hit 'undo', her breath catching in her throat as the words reappeared. She pushed her chair away from the desk, her knees bouncing violently. She picked up her phone, dialed half a number, and hung up. The glowing screen felt like an interrogation spotlight. She crossed her arms tightly over her chest, shivering despite the heavy wool sweater she wore.

Buried beneath mom’s tangled pearl necklaces is a tightly rolled piece of parchment tied with a brittle ribbon. The ribbon snaps as I pull it. *Paint a mural. Rescue a greyhound.* I stare at the words, my stomach churning like a washing machine off-balance. I don’t own a paintbrush. I’m severely allergic to dogs. I carefully place the paper on the dresser, smoothing the curled edges down, but they spring back up. I press them down again, holding my palms flat against the wood. When I lift my hands, the paper curls instantly. A sour taste rises in the back of my throat. I pace the length of the bedroom, counting my steps. One, two, three, turn. One, two, three, turn. My fingers twist the pieces of the broken ribbon into knots, pulling them so tight the rough fabric slices into my skin.

The fluorescent lights of the bank vault hummed a high, piercing note. Arthur unfolded the yellowed legal pad he found beneath his father's will. *Skydive. Forgive myself.* Arthur swallowed, his Adam’s apple bobbing sharply. He loosened his silk tie, suddenly hyper-aware of the thick concrete walls pressing in on him from all sides. He slid the legal pad back into the metal box, then quickly yanked it back out, staring at the phrase *Forgive myself*. His pulse thudded against his temples. He closed his eyes and began to hum under his breath, a tuneless sound, trying to drown out the buzzing lights. He dropped the paper on the small viewing table and backed away until his shoulders hit the cold wall of the vault. He rubbed his hands together vigorously, as if trying to generate heat in the sterile, airless room.

I slide the refrigerator away from the wall to sweep, and a faded index card flutters to the tile. Mom’s handwriting. *See the Grand Canyon. Learn French.* The broom slips from my grasp, clattering in the empty house. My knees feel like water. I sink onto the dusty floorboards, pulling my knees to my chest. I rock forward, just an inch, then back. I can’t even remember how to pay my own electric bill on time. I pick at a loose thread on my jeans, pulling it until the denim seam begins to tear. The moving truck comes tomorrow. I look at the card, then at the towering stacks of cardboard boxes surrounding me. My chest heaves with quick, shallow intakes of air. I squeeze my eyes shut, listening to the blood rushing in my ears, but the shadows of the boxes only seem to multiply.

Julian brushed the damp soil from the mason jar he’d unearthed beneath the rhododendron. Inside, a rolled piece of lined paper read: *Climb Everest. Ride a motorcycle across the country.* Julian’s grip tightened on his trowel until his knuckles ached. He stood up abruptly, nearly tripping over his boots. He walked to the garden gate, touched the iron latch, and walked back. He read the note again. Everest. His father had died in a hospital bed, never leaving the state. Julian’s mouth went completely dry. He tried to swallow, but couldn't. He looked up at the sky, the vast expanse of blue suddenly feeling overwhelmingly heavy. He crouched back down, throwing a handful of dirt over the jar, then frantically digging it back out. His breaths came fast, harsh scrapes against his throat, as he stared at the muddy paper in his trembling, soil-stained hands.

I pull dad's cracked leather wallet from the hospital bag. Tucked behind my baby photo is a folded square of paper. *Sing on a stage. See an eclipse. Fall in love again.* The living room lights flicker. I drop the wallet onto the coffee table and vigorously rub my slick, sweaty palms against my thighs. Fall in love again? He never dated after mom died. I walk into the kitchen, open the fridge, stare at a jar of mustard, and shut it. I return to the living room. The tiny paper looks like a bomb waiting to detonate. I pick it up, my fingers clumsy and rigid. My vision blurs, the neat handwriting swimming on the page. I press my knuckles hard against my teeth, biting down to ground myself against the sudden, violent spinning of the room.

Elias pressed his face against the grimy glass of the pawn shop window, his breath fogging the pane. There it was. The sapphire teardrop surrounded by tarnished silver leaves—Nana’s ring. His pulse drummed against his temples, a rapid, relentless beat. He checked his phone screen again; his bank app showed exactly forty-two dollars. He chewed the inside of his cheek until he tasted copper, his eyes darting between the price tag and the heavy-set man behind the counter. "How much to hold it?" Elias’s voice cracked, and he cleared his throat, wiping his clammy palms on his jeans. If his uncle had pawned this, what else was missing? He bounced on his heels, recounting the crumpled bills in his wallet, his chest tightening with every second that a stranger lingered near the display case.

The bell above the door chimed, and I flinched, nearly dropping the silver candelabra I was inspecting. My eyes locked onto the velvet tray the owner was pulling from the safe. The gold band with the distinct chip in the emerald. Gram's ring. My lungs decided to stop working. I took a short, jagged breath, my fingers drumming a rapid rhythm on the edge of the glass counter. "Where did you get that?" I asked, the words rushing out in a high-pitched blur. The clerk looked up slowly, taking his sweet time. I shifted my weight from my left foot to my right, then back again, my nails digging half-moons into my palms. I needed to call my mother, but my hands were shaking too much to unlock my phone. Someone had been in her house, and the thought made my stomach twist into a cold knot.

Rain hammered the tin roof of "Gold & Guns," but Sarah couldn't hear it over the rushing sound in her own ears. She stared at the delicate pearl setting resting under the fluorescent light. It was her grandmother's. It had to be. Sarah swallowed hard, her mouth suddenly feeling like it was packed with cotton. She reached into her purse, hurriedly digging through receipts and loose change, her breathing shallow and fast. She had to buy it back before her sister found out. What if the clerk realized its true worth? What if someone else bought it while she ran to the ATM? She kept her hand clamped over the glass right above the ring, her leg bouncing so hard it rattled the display case. "I need this one," she blurted out, her eyes wide, staring intensely at the clerk’s slow-moving hands.

I walked past the window three times before I finally forced myself to stop. Nestled between a replica watch and a tarnished compass was the unmistakable ruby cluster of Abuela's engagement ring. A cold sweat broke out across the back of my neck. I pushed the heavy door open, the stale air hitting me like a wall. "Can I see the ruby?" I asked, cringing at the slight tremor in my voice. As the man handed it over, I almost dropped it. My heart beat so fast it felt like a trapped bird battering against my ribs. How did it get here? Was it taken during the move? I checked my watch, then glanced over my shoulder at the door, then back at the ring. Every shadow moving past the shop window made my breath hitch. I didn't have enough cash, and they closed in ten minutes.

Marcus gnawed on his thumbnail until it tore, his gaze fixed on the platinum band resting on the faded velvet cushion. The engraved initials inside the band confirmed the impossible. It was his grandmother's engagement ring, missing since the funeral last month. His right foot tapped a relentless staccato against the wooden floorboards. He pulled his wallet out, then shoved it back into his pocket, then pulled it out again. "Is there a layaway plan?" he asked, his words tumbling over each other. The old woman behind the register squinted at him over her spectacles. Marcus wiped a bead of sweat from his forehead with the back of his sleeve. He couldn't leave it here, not with strangers coming in and out. He imagined someone else buying it, slipping it onto an unfamiliar finger. His chest seized, and he began to count the loose coins in his pocket.

The glaring neon lights of the exchange shop made my eyes water, but I couldn't blink. There, sitting quietly under the glass, was Oma’s opal ring. My stomach did a violent flip. I grabbed the edge of the counter, my knuckles turning stark white. "Hey! Excuse me! The opal!" I shouted louder than intended, making the two other customers turn and stare. I ignored them, my gaze locked on the shimmering stone. My mind raced through the events of the past week, trying to piece together how the family heirloom had vanished from the locked safe. Did I leave it open? Was it my fault? I took a quick, sharp breath, feeling a bead of sweat trickle down my spine. The clerk took a step toward me, and I instantly reached for my credit card, fumbling it twice before it clattered onto the glass top.

Julian stood paralyzed in front of the pawn shop window, his reflection ghostly pale against the glass. The vintage amethyst ring sitting in the corner of the display was identical to the one he had sworn he placed in his grandmother's casket ten years ago. His throat constricted. He rubbed his temples with trembling fingers, trying to squeeze out the impossible thoughts flooding his mind. He took one step toward the door, hesitated, and stepped back. His heart hammered against his sternum, a rapid, echoing thud. He pulled his phone from his pocket, dialing his brother’s number, only to hang up before the first ring. He couldn't speak. He paced the length of the storefront, pulling his collar away from his neck. The air felt thick, suffocating. He stopped abruptly, staring at the ring again, his breathing ragged as a stranger walked into the shop.

I couldn't stop bouncing my knee. It was driving the guy next to me crazy, but I didn’t care. I leaned closer to the scratched display case, my breath clouding the glass directly above the diamond solitaire. It had the same tiny imperfection on the band, the one Nonna always rubbed with her thumb. I swallowed, but my mouth was completely dry. "How much for the diamond?" I asked. My voice sounded thin, almost squeaky. The guy behind the counter went to answer the phone instead. "Wait, please, just tell me the price!" I interrupted, gripping the edge of the counter. I glanced at the clock on the wall. A quarter to five. The bank closed at five. I ran a hand through my hair, tugging at the roots. If he sold it to someone else, I’d never see it again. "Sir, please," I urged, my heart doing double-time.

The cold wind howling outside the pawn shop was nothing compared to the chill spreading through David’s veins. Sitting under a cheap spotlight was his late grandmother's turquoise ring. He patted his pockets—wallet, phone, keys—in a rapid, repetitive loop. He stepped up to the counter, his teeth chattering, though the shop was overly heated. "Can I see that?" he asked, pointing a shaky finger at the display. As the clerk retrieved it, David’s eyes darted toward the security camera, then to the man loitering by the guitars, then back to the ring. The silver was still unpolished, exactly as it had been when his cousin 'borrowed' it. David squeezed his eyes shut, taking a quick, shallow gulp of air. He had to confront his cousin, but first, he had to secure the ring. His fingers slipped twice on his phone screen as he tried to open his banking app.

The ceiling fan chopped through the thick, humid air of the shop, but it did nothing to cool me down. I wiped my sweaty palms on my shorts for the fifth time in a minute. Right there, nestled next to a pile of cheap watches, was the gold filigree ring. Grandma's ring. The one that was supposed to be safe in my jewelry box. I bit my lower lip, tasting salt and copper. My mind spun like a broken compass. Did my roommate take it? Did I drop it? I tapped the glass rapidly with my index finger. "Miss? The gold one. Please," I called out, the words catching in my throat. I shifted my weight back and forth, feeling a tight band of pressure wrapping around my chest. I couldn't look away from the ring, convinced it might vanish into thin air if I blinked.

Under the buzzing fluorescent lights, Lena’s face drained of color. The sapphire ring in the center of the display was her grandmother’s, unmistakable due to the slight warping on the left prong. Lena wrapped her arms tightly across her chest, her fingernails digging into her own sleeves. She looked over her shoulder at the dark street outside, then back at the ring. The pawn broker was busy haggling with a customer over a television. Lena paced a tight circle, her boots clicking sharply against the linoleum. She checked the time on her phone, then immediately checked it again, having not registered the numbers. She needed fifty dollars. She reached into her bag, dumping its contents onto a nearby chair, feverishly sifting through lipstick tubes and crumpled tissues to find her emergency cash, her breath coming in quick, shallow gasps.

I pressed my forehead against the cool glass of the display case. It was the only thing keeping me grounded. Babushka's ruby ring was right there, tagged with a bright yellow sticker that read '$150'. My heart fluttered like a moth trapped in a jar. I rubbed the back of my neck, where the hair was standing on end. I pulled out my phone to call Dad, but my thumb hovered over his name, trembling violently. If I told him, he would know the apartment had been broken into. I squeezed my phone so hard my joints popped. "I'll take the ruby," I croaked to the attendant, instantly clearing my throat. "I mean, I want to buy it. Right now." I pulled every bill from my wallet, my hands moving so fast I dropped a twenty onto the dusty floor. I snatched it up, my eyes darting wildly toward the door.

The air in the attic was thick with dust, but it was the yellowed piece of paper in my hand that made it hard to breathe. "I, Thomas Miller, tender my resignation..." It was dated 1993. The year I was born. My thumb traced the faded ink, my pulse drumming a chaotic beat against my temples. Did Dad almost throw away the pension that paid for my college? My mind raced through a dozen alternate timelines, each bleaker than the last. I dropped the box of files, the loud thud echoing in the cramped space, and rubbed my clammy palms against my jeans. If he had submitted this, we would have lost the house. I paced the short length of the floorboards, biting the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper, unable to put the fragile sheet down.

Elena’s knee bounced in a rapid, unyielding rhythm against the underside of the mahogany desk. Staring at the draft resignation letter she’d pulled from her mother’s vintage leather briefcase, she aggressively chewed a jagged edge into her thumbnail. The stationary bore the logo of a company her mother still led thirty years later. "I cannot continue under these conditions," the feminine script read. Elena’s chest tightened as she read the words over and over, her breathing growing shallow. She grabbed her phone, unlocked it, locked it, and set it down again without looking at the screen. Her mother had always been the pillar of stability, the immovable rock of their family. If that foundation was built on a moment’s hesitation, what else was fragile? A cold sweat prickled at her hairline as she stared blindly at the forgotten document.

I needed the recipe for Mom’s pound cake, but flipping through the stained cookbook, a folded napkin tumbled onto the linoleum. I recognized Dad’s blocky handwriting immediately. "Effective immediately, I am stepping down." The kitchen suddenly felt ten degrees hotter. I pressed two fingers to my neck, feeling my pulse hammer a rapid tattoo against my skin. Dad loved that hardware store. Why would he write this in 1988? I started tapping my foot, a rapid staccato that rattled the loose tile near the fridge. Was it about the debts he never mentioned? Was he being forced out? I read the three sentences six times, my eyes darting across the faded blue ink until the letters blurred together. I swallowed hard, but my throat was entirely dry. I reached for a glass of water, my hand shaking so much the ice clinked violently against the rim.

Marcus shoved another empty cardboard box across the living room carpet, his jaw locked tight. As he emptied his father’s desk drawer, a crumpled piece of legal paper slipped from a ledger. "Resignation," the heading read, dated forty years prior. Marcus stopped breathing for a long second, then took a sharp, jagged inhale. He stood up abruptly, nearly knocking over a floor lamp. He walked to the window, pulled the curtains back, let them drop, and turned back to the desk. He rubbed the back of his neck, his fingers slick with sweat. His father had always preached company loyalty, demanding Marcus stay at his own dead-end accounting job. Had it all been a hypocritical act? Marcus squeezed the paper, uncrumpling and re-crumpling the edges. He needed to ask him, but his stomach tied itself into rigid knots at the thought of confronting the old man.

Rummaging through the fireproof safe for my passport, I dragged out a stack of manila folders. A piece of hotel stationery fluttered to the rug. "I am leaving the firm," my mother had written in 1999. I sat back on my heels, wrapping my arms tightly around my knees. The air in the bedroom felt impossibly thin. 1999 was the year my parents divorced. I began picking at the frayed edge of the carpet, pulling a long string of nylon free. Did she want to leave her career too? Was I the reason she felt trapped? A heavy pressure settled squarely on my ribs. I picked up the paper, set it down, and stood up to pace the length of the bed. My mind spun like a broken compass, re-evaluating every childhood memory, every tired smile she had ever given me over breakfast.

The harsh fluorescent lights of the garage cast long shadows over the workbench. Sarah dug through the bottom drawer of the rusted red toolbox, her fingers brushing against a grease-stained envelope. Inside was a draft resignation letter her father had written to the shop owner, dated 1982. Sarah swallowed repeatedly, trying to rid herself of a sudden metallic taste in her mouth. She wiped her oil-slicked hands on a rag, twisting the fabric until her knuckles turned stark white. Her eyes darted from the letter to the hydraulic lift her father had ultimately died repairing. If he had handed this envelope in, he wouldn’t have been under that car. She began pacing a tight circle around a stack of tires, her chest rising and falling in quick, shallow jerks. She tugged at her collar, feeling as though the vast garage was shrinking around her.

I slid the Beatles album out of its cardboard sleeve, blinking rapidly when a folded sheet of lined notebook paper drifted to the floor. It was a letter in Mom’s elegant cursive, detailing her immediate resignation from the philharmonic orchestra in 1976. My fingers immediately went to my lips, gnawing on a piece of chapped skin. She always told me playing the cello was her greatest joy. Why would she draft this? I looked at the grandfather clock, watching the pendulum swing with punishing slowness. I tapped my fingers against the vinyl record, a rapid, erratic rhythm. The silence in the living room was deafening, pressing against my eardrums. I checked my phone, screen blank, before tossing it onto the sofa. Everything I knew about her past felt like a carefully constructed facade, ready to shatter. I pressed the heels of my hands against my eyes, willing my heart to slow down.

Prying up the damaged floorboards in the study, David uncovered a pristine, sealed envelope tucked between the joists. He tore it open, pulling out his father’s draft resignation from the city council, dated twenty-five years ago. David’s breath hitched. He dropped his crowbar; it hit the subfloor with a loud clang that made him flinch violently. He stared at the handwritten manifesto detailing rampant corruption, his jaw clamped so tightly his teeth ached. He started walking toward the door, stopped, and pivoted back to the window, peeking out through the blinds at the quiet suburban street. His father had been murdered in a "random mugging" two days after this date. David’s hands shook uncontrollably as he tried to slide the paper back into the envelope, missing the opening twice. He felt a cold bead of sweat slide slowly down the back of his neck.

I plunged my hands into the pockets of Mom’s old houndstooth coat, intending to take it to the dry cleaners. My fingers closed around a stiff, folded paper. It was a letter to the hospital board. "I can no longer ethically serve as Chief of Surgery." The date was exactly a month before her stroke. My stomach performed a violent flip, dropping into my shoes. I collapsed onto the edge of the mattress, my leg immediately springing into a rapid, unyielding bounce. I read the words until they lost all meaning, my eyes darting haphazardly across the stationary. What did she know? I stood up, walked to the closet, closed the door, and opened it again. My chest felt tight, bound by invisible iron bands. I grabbed the edge of the dresser, grounding myself against the wood, as a rush of dizzying heat flooded my ears.

The heavy leather Bible had sat untouched on the mantel for a decade. When Arthur opened it to seek some quiet solace, a typed letter slipped from the book of Psalms. It was a draft from his father, resigning from the ministry in 1968. Arthur’s eyes widened, locking onto the faded typewriter ink. He slammed the heavy book shut, sending a cloud of dust into the air, before immediately reopening it. He dragged a trembling hand through his thinning hair, his eyes darting toward the hallway to ensure he was still alone. He began to read aloud, his voice catching and stuttering over the syllables. "I have... I have lost my faith." Arthur's knees felt suddenly entirely hollow, incapable of bearing his weight. He gripped the edge of the mantelpiece until his knuckles turned white, his breath whistling sharply through his teeth in the silent room.

I was carefully sliding the 1995 vacation photos out of the sticky magnetic album when a piece of looseleaf caught my eye, hidden behind a picture of Dad at the Grand Canyon. "Please accept my resignation from the CIA." I stopped breathing. The air in the room suddenly felt entirely still and suffocatingly heavy. I looked at the picture of the smiling man in the polo shirt, then back to the paper. I swallowed a lump in my throat that felt the size of a golf ball. I started to pace the small living room, my bare feet slapping softly against the hardwood. I checked the deadbolt on the front door, turning the latch back and forth three times just to be sure it was locked. My mind raced through a thousand forgotten childhood memories, searching wildly for clues hidden in plain sight.

Chloe dug through the tangled mass of thread in her mother’s wooden sewing box, searching for a safety pin. Instead, she pulled out a heavily folded piece of parchment. It was a draft resignation letter directed to the textile mill, citing the dangerous chemical exposure, dated 1974. Chloe’s heart slammed against her ribs like a trapped bird. Her mother had worked there until the day the factory closed, eventually dying of lung disease. Chloe dropped the letter onto the table, taking two quick steps backward, her hands flying to cover her mouth. She began to chew aggressively on the inside of her lip, tasting blood. She wrapped her arms around her own torso, shivering despite the mid-July heat radiating through the kitchen window. The ticking of the wall clock seemed to grow louder with every passing second, echoing the heavy, erratic thumping in her own chest.

My pulse thudded in my ears as I stared at the blue ink on the crumpled napkin. *Climb Kilimanjaro. Move to Paris. Sail the Mediterranean alone.* Alone. That word blurred as my grip tightened on the paper, crumpling the edges. I wiped my damp palms on my jeans, taking short, shallow breaths. Clara had never mentioned Paris. She’d never mentioned the ocean. I glanced at the packed suitcase sitting by the door, ostensibly for her weekend business trip. My leg started bouncing rapidly against the coffee table. I read the list again, my eyes darting between the handwritten lines and the brass handle of her luggage. Were we just a layover? I chewed on the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper, listening to the ticking of the hallway clock, waiting for the sound of her key turning in the lock.

Marcus smoothed out the piece of parchment he’d found tucked inside David’s sock drawer. His chest tightened like a coiled spring. *1. Skydive over Dubai. 2. Cave diving in Mexico. 3. Base jumping.* Marcus’s breath hitched. He pressed two fingers to his neck, feeling his pulse hammer against his skin. David was an accountant. David got motion sickness on ferries. Marcus paced the length of the bedroom, his slippers shuffling rapidly against the hardwood floor. He kept looking at the closed bathroom door, hearing the shower running inside. He picked up his phone, dialed half of his brother’s number, then deleted it, his thumb shaking. Why would David want to jump off a mountain? What changed? Marcus rubbed his forehead, pacing faster now, entirely unable to sit down until the water turned off and he could demand an explanation.

The moleskine journal fell open when I accidentally knocked it off the nightstand. The heading, penned in Julian's neat cursive, read *Before I Go*. I stopped breathing. The air in the room suddenly felt too thick, too heavy. I read the items—*See the Northern Lights, Write letters to the kids, Visit the old cabin*—and my stomach plummeted into a cold, dark abyss. I sank onto the edge of the mattress, my knees giving out entirely. My teeth chattered, though it was the middle of July. Julian's recent doctor appointments flashed through my mind in rapid succession. *Just routine bloodwork,* he had said. My fingernails dug half-moons into my palms. I stared at the bathroom door, listening to him humming while shaving. I squeezed my eyes shut, trying to swallow the giant, painful lump lodged firmly in my throat.

Sarah’s foot tapped a rapid staccato against the linoleum. She stared at the computer screen, the glow illuminating the sweat beading on her upper lip. Tom had left his email open. The drafted message was titled *My Bucket List* and sent to a luxury concierge service. *Purchase a Tuscan vineyard. Buy a vintage Aston Martin. Rent a private island.* Sarah pulled at her collar, gasping for air that wouldn’t quite fill her lungs. They were three months behind on the mortgage. She clicked on the sent folder, her index finger trembling on the mouse. *Deposit wired,* read the latest reply. The room spun slightly. She braced both hands on the edge of the desk, knuckles turning stark white. The front door creaked open downstairs, followed by Tom’s cheerful whistling. Sarah couldn’t form a sound, her throat entirely paralyzed.

I stared at the corkboard in the garage. Hidden behind a pile of old winter coats was a pristine vision board labeled *The Real Dream*. It featured pictures of a rustic off-grid cabin, alpaca farming, and a crossed-out photo of a city skyline. My chest squeezed. I tugged at the neck of my t-shirt. I had just signed a ten-year lease for my downtown bakery. My leg began to bounce, shaking the stepstool I was standing on. Did Maya hate our life here? I bit my thumbnail, tearing the edge until it bled. I scanned the board, my eyes darting from corner to corner, looking for any picture of me, any hint that I belonged in this pastoral fantasy. There was nothing. Just sheep and mountains. The garage suddenly felt entirely devoid of oxygen. I clutched my chest, listening to my own rapid, shallow breathing.

Liam’s eyes darted back and forth across the crumpled receipt. Written on the back in Chloe’s pink glitter pen were five life goals. The first four were innocuous: learn Italian, run a marathon, bake a perfect soufflé. The fifth made the blood drain entirely from Liam’s face. *Find out what happened to James.* Liam dropped the paper as if it were a burning coal. He began to pace the kitchen, his sneakers squeaking sharply on the tiles. He rubbed his clammy hands together, his heart beating a relentless drum solo against his ribs. James was the college boyfriend, the one who broke her heart a decade ago. Liam opened the fridge, stared blindly at the milk, and slammed it shut. He checked his watch. She would be home in five minutes. He picked up the paper, smoothed it out, and dropped it again.

The leather-bound diary was wedged behind the spare towels. I didn't mean to pry, but it fell open to a page titled *Things To Do Before I Die*. The words blurred together as a ringing sound filled my ears. *Tell the truth about the accident. Find the family in Seattle. Confess.* My knees turned to water, and I slid down the bathroom wall, the cold tiles biting through my shirt. I swallowed hard, but my mouth was completely devoid of moisture. Who was the family in Seattle? What accident? My fingers shook so violently that the diary slipped from my grasp, landing with a heavy thud. I pulled my knees to my chest and wrapped my arms around them, rocking slightly. I heard the garage door opening downstairs, signaling his return. I clamped a hand over my mouth to quiet my ragged breathing.

Elena stared at the digital document left open on the tablet. *To Complete By My 30th Birthday.* That was exactly two weeks away. She scrolled down the list, her heart thumping against her sternum like a trapped bird. *Quit my job. Empty the savings. Disappear for a year.* Elena wiped her damp palms on her skirt. She checked the bank account app on her phone; the balance was zero. Her breath caught in her throat, coming out in a sharp, involuntary wheeze. She dialed his number, tapping her foot at a rapid pace, but it went straight to voicemail. The apartment was entirely quiet, save for the ticking of the wall clock. She looked at the empty closet on his side of the room. A cold sweat broke out across her forehead as she rapidly tore open every drawer in the dresser.

I found the pink envelope tucked inside a cookbook. *My Life's Dreams.* I smiled at first, expecting recipes or travel destinations. But as I read the bullet points, my stomach tied itself into a tight, hard knot. *Have a baby by thirty-two. Foster three children. Buy a minivan.* I couldn't seem to draw a full breath. I backed away from the kitchen counter until my spine hit the refrigerator. I squeezed my eyes shut, my pulse pounding a relentless rhythm in my temples. We had agreed on a childfree life. We had sworn to it. I dragged trembling fingers through my hair, tugging at the roots. I looked at the clock, then out the window at the driveway. Any second now, she would walk through that door. I shoved the paper back into the cookbook, pacing circles around the kitchen island, unable to sit.

Arthur found the spiral notebook under the couch cushions. The page was titled *My Legacy*. He adjusted his glasses, tracing the words with a shaking finger. *Donate the house to the charity. Give all investments to the shelter. Leave with only the clothes on my back.* Arthur’s jaw dropped. A cold chill cascaded down his spine, settling in the pit of his stomach. He rubbed the back of his neck, which was slick with sweat. Evelyn was a generous woman, but this was absolute destitution. He began to pace the living room, his breathing shallow and rapid. He picked up his tea, but his hand trembled so fiercely that hot liquid splashed onto the rug. He didn't even notice. He just stared at the front window, chewing relentlessly on his lower lip until he tasted blood, waiting for Evelyn to return from the market.

The printout was sitting right on the printer tray. *My Final Chapter,* the header read. I picked it up, expecting a novel outline. Instead, my chest tightened until my ribs ached. *Join the frontline medics in the war zone. Sell all assets to fund the mission. Never look back.* My vision swam. I clutched the edge of the desk, swaying on my feet as a high-pitched ringing pierced my ears. My throat went completely dry. I tried to swallow, but I couldn't. I looked at the framed photo of us on the desk, then back to the paper. My hands were shaking so badly the paper rustled loudly in the quiet study. I bolted to the bathroom and splashed ice-cold water onto my face, bracing my hands against the porcelain sink while I stared at my pale, wide-eyed reflection, struggling to draw air.

Jenna stared at the sticky note attached to Robert’s bathroom mirror. It was titled *The Ascension List*. She leaned closer, her breath fogging the glass. *Sever earthly attachments. Transfer funds to the Brethren. Prepare for the Comet.* Jenna’s stomach plummeted. Her pulse hammered a wild rhythm in her neck. She backed out of the bathroom, her eyes darting around their shared bedroom as if seeing it for the first time. She pulled her phone from her pocket, her thumbs slipping on the screen as she fumbled to unlock it. She needed to call her sister, but her fingers refused to coordinate. She heard the crunch of gravel in the driveway. Robert's car. Jenna spun around, her breathing turning into short, ragged gasps. She shoved her phone back into her pocket and stood frozen in the center of the room, her heart racing wildly.

I hit refresh on the literary blog, my thumbnail caught between my teeth. The headline hasn't changed: *E.R. Vance Exposed.* The side-by-side text comparisons blur together as my foot taps a rapid, uneven rhythm against the desk leg. Vance’s *The Obsidian Sea*, the book that got me through college, matches a forgotten nineties serial word for word. I press my palms flat against the cold surface of my desk, trying to steady the faint tremor in my fingers. If Vance didn't write those words, who did I write all those fan letters to? Who have I been emulating? I chew the rough edge of my cuticle until I taste copper. My own unfinished manuscript sits in the open window behind the browser. I drag my cursor over my first chapter, my pulse thrumming in my ears, wondering if every word I’ve ever written is just a lie.

Marcus adjusted his glasses, wiped them on his sweater, and put them back on. The article on his phone remained the same. *Bestseller Plagiarism Scandal.* He stood in the crowded bookstore aisle, clutching a pristine hardback of *The Autumn Sovereign*. His chest felt uncomfortably tight, like the air had been sucked through the vents. He stared at the towering cardboard display of his hero's works, then down at his own self-published debut in his satchel, heavily inspired by the same prose. He shifted his weight from left to right, repeatedly pressing the book's spine into his palm until it left a red crease. "Did you need help finding anything?" a clerk asked. Marcus flinched, dropping the hardback. It hit the linoleum with a loud smack. He stammered a fragmented apology, backed away, and bolted for the exit without picking it up.

The tea kettle whistles, but I can't force my hands to let go of the edge of the kitchen island. Thirty minutes until the book club arrives. Thirty minutes until I have to explain why I made them buy copies of a stolen masterpiece. The exposé broke this morning. I keep rubbing my thumb over the author's headshot on the dust jacket, the glossy paper squeaking under the friction. My breathing is shallow, catching in my throat every time a car drives past the front window. What if they think I knew? I forced copies on my coworkers. I named my cat after the protagonist. I pace from the stove to the sink, turning the kettle off, then rearranging the teacups. They don't look right. The spacing is wrong. I shove them into a tight circle, my heart hammering a chaotic beat.

Professor Higgins stood before the whiteboard, the dry-erase marker squeaking as he wrote *Originality in Modernism*. He capped the marker, uncapped it, and capped it again, the plastic clicking loudly in the silent lecture hall. His phone sat on the podium, face-up, displaying the damning email from his department head. His entire syllabus revolved around Clara Bellmont’s essays. Essays that, as of midnight, were proven to be translated verbatim from obscure French journals. He tugged at his collar, finding the fabric suddenly abrasive. The students would arrive in ten minutes. He opened his briefcase, shuffled his meticulously typed lecture notes, and shoved them back inside, only to pull them out again. His mouth tasted like ash. He stared at the door, shifting his weight, mentally discarding five different opening sentences, his fingers drumming a relentless staccato on the wood of the podium.

The buzzing needle pauses. "You okay? You're twitching," the artist says, wiping ink from my forearm. I nod quickly, keeping my eyes glued to the ceiling tiles. I can't look down at my phone. The notification is still sitting on the lock screen: *Fantasy Icon Admits to Ghostwriter Theft.* The quote from chapter four—the very quote currently being etched permanently into my skin—isn't his. I swallow hard, my throat completely dry. "Just… take a second," I croak. I grip the armrests of the chair, my knuckles turning stark white. The smell of green soap and antiseptic is suddenly cloying, making my stomach pitch and roll. I flex my fingers, trying to stop the localized shaking, but the tremor travels up to my elbow. I have a thief's words bleeding into my epidermis. "Actually, can we take a break?" I ask, my voice cracking.

Sarah sat in the microfilm room, the harsh fluorescent lights humming above her. She wound the spool of the seventies literary magazine forward, backward, then forward again. The words on the illuminated screen were identical to the opening paragraph of last year’s Pulitzer winner. Her idol. Her mentor. She swallowed, but her throat felt coated in dust. She pulled out her notebook, dropping her pen twice before her trembling fingers could maintain a proper grip. She copied a sentence, struck it out, and rubbed her temples. The quiet of the library pressed in on her ears, amplifying the rushing sound of her own blood. If she published her discovery, she would destroy a legend. If she stayed quiet, she was complicit. She chewed the inside of her cheek until she tasted iron, her leg bouncing with enough force to make the table vibrate.

I stare at the cardboard box labeled *Favorites*. The packing tape is half torn, my box cutter resting frozen in my hand. The podcast playing in the background drones on about the mounting evidence: side-by-side comparisons of my favorite sci-fi series and obscure Soviet-era short stories. I run my free hand through my hair, gripping the roots tight enough to sting. I have twenty books by him. First editions. Signed copies. I spent thousands. My breathing hitches, short and rapid, as I look around my half-empty apartment. The walls seem to inch closer. I drop the box cutter and pick up the top book, flipping the pages rapidly without reading a single word. The paper cuts my index finger. I don’t even look at the blood. I just keep flipping pages, the loud rustle drowning out the calm voice of the podcast host.

The convention hall buzzed with thousands of fans, but Liam stood completely rigid near the entrance of Panel Room B. He held his VIP pass in a white-knuckled grip, the plastic digging into his palm. A murmur swept through the crowd, people huddled over their glowing screens. The news had just broken. The entire universe of the *Starfall* series was lifted from a dormant fan-fiction forum. Liam checked his phone, locked it, and checked it again. The battery icon blinked red. He looked at the line forming for the autograph session, his stomach doing a sudden, violent flip. He backed up, bumping into a woman dressed in cosplay. "Sorry," he muttered, his eyes darting toward the exit doors, then back to the panel room. He pulled at the neck of his t-shirt, gasping for a full breath that wouldn't come, paralyzed between the crowd and the exits.

The red light on my microphone is glowing, but I’ve been staring at the wall for ten minutes. I clear my throat, take a sip of lukewarm water, and set the glass down so hard it chips. I just read the exposé on my second monitor. The author I’ve championed on this channel for three years stole his entire memoir from a deceased journalist's private diaries. I rub my palms against my jeans, trying to wipe away the clammy sweat. My subscribers are expecting my review of his newest release at noon. I look at the clock. 11:15. I spin my chair in a half-circle, push off the desk, and stand up, only to immediately sit back down. I type a tweet, delete it, type an apology, delete that too. The cursor blinks rhythmically. I press my hands over my eyes until bursts of color explode.

Elena’s office felt ten degrees hotter than it had a minute ago. The manuscript pages of *The Glass Monarch* lay scattered across her mahogany desk. On her monitor was a link an intern had just sent her: a direct text match to an out-of-print novella from the eighties. Elena was the one who acquired this book. She was the one who pushed a massive marketing budget. She picked up her red pen, clicked the top repeatedly—*click-clack, click-clack*—until the plastic casing cracked. She threw it in the trash and stood up, pacing the short distance from her desk to the window. Five steps there, five steps back. She pulled her phone from her pocket, dialed the publisher’s number, and hung up before it could ring. Her breath came in short, jagged gasps. She leaned against the filing cabinet, sliding down until she was sitting on the carpet.

The train rattles into the tunnel, plunging the carriage into intermittent darkness, but the screen of my tablet remains glaringly bright. *Plagiarism Claims Confirmed.* I read the headline for the fourth time. The author whose poetry I recited at my wedding is a fraud. I cross my arms tightly over my chest, pulling my jacket closed even though the subway car is stiflingly hot. The fluorescent lights hum, making my teeth ache. I glance around the crowded car. Does anyone else know? The man across from me is reading a newspaper; the woman beside him is asleep. I tap my foot against the sticky floor, the rhythm relentless and uneven. I pull up my wedding video on my phone, watching myself standing at the altar, speaking those stolen words. I shut my eyes tight, digging my nails into my forearms.

The ice in Arthur’s lemonade melted, watering down the drink he hadn't touched. He sat on the porch swing, the chain creaking as he pushed off the floorboards over and over, driving a relentless, unceasing momentum. A crumpled printout of an investigative article sat on the table beside him. The detective novels he had read to his late wife, the ones she had loved in her final days, were carbon copies of translated Spanish procedurals. He rubbed his face with both hands, dragging his fingertips hard across his cheekbones. He reached for his glass, but his hand was shaking so badly that the liquid sloshed over the rim, spilling onto his trousers. He didn't bother to wipe it up. He just stared at the wet stain, his chest rising and falling in rapid, shallow bursts, listening to the cicadas buzz.

The notification chime cut through the cafe chatter. I unlocked my screen, my thumb hovering over the glass. Friend Request: Marcus Thorne. The half-eaten croissant on my plate suddenly looked like cardboard, and a cold stone settled in the pit of my stomach. My pulse thumped against my eardrums, a fast, erratic rhythm. Why now? It had been fifteen years since the locker room incidents. Did he want to apologize, or was this a new game? I rubbed my sweaty palms against my denim jeans, staring at the little profile picture of a smiling man with a golden retriever. My breathing turned shallow. I locked the phone, flipped it face down on the table, and pushed it as far away from my coffee cup as possible, but the black rectangle still felt like a ticking bomb waiting to detonate.

Elena’s cursor froze on the screen. The small red notification badge glared back at her in the dim glow of her office monitor. Chloe Davis wants to connect. Elena’s jaw clenched so tight her teeth ached, and she instinctively pulled her cardigan tighter around her shoulders, despite the stifling heat of the room. The rhythmic tapping of her foot against the carpet grew faster, mimicking the frantic flutter in her chest. She remembered the whispered taunts in the cafeteria, the spilled milk, the laughter that used to echo off the tiled walls. Her finger hovered over the mouse clicker. A drop of sweat traced its way down her spine. If she ignored it, Chloe might reach out somewhere else. If she accepted it, the door was open. Elena shoved her chair back so violently the wheels shrieked against the plastic floor mat.

The onions were sizzling perfectly in the pan when my phone lit up on the counter. I wiped my hands on my apron and leaned over. New request: Trent Higgins. The wooden spoon slipped from my grip, clattering against the stovetop and splattering oil. My breath caught in my throat, refusing to go down. I squeezed my eyes shut, but I could still see the muddy puddle behind the middle school bleachers. I backed away from the counter until my shoulders hit the refrigerator door. My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird. I needed to turn down the heat on the stove, but my legs felt rooted to the linoleum. The onions began to burn, filling the kitchen with acrid smoke, while I just stood there, staring blindly at the dark silhouette on my screen.

Julian dropped the dumbbell with a loud clang, ignoring the annoyed glare from the man on the adjacent bench. He had just checked his notifications during his rest period, and the name Seth Cutler was staring back at him. Julian immediately started chewing on his lower lip, tearing at a small piece of loose skin until he tasted copper. He wiped his face with a towel, though the sudden chill spreading through his limbs had nothing to do with the air conditioning. Seth. The guy who used to shove him into lockers. Why was Seth looking for him on a professional networking site? Julian paced a tight circle around the weight bench. His breaths came in short, jagged gasps. He imagined Seth looking at his current job title, finding a way to ruin this, too. Julian grabbed his gym bag and bolted for the exit.

I was doing my usual midnight doom-scrolling when the pop-up appeared. Friend Request: Sarah Jenkins. The glow of the tablet suddenly felt blindingly bright. I tossed the device onto the duvet like it was burning hot. My throat went completely dry, and I reached for my water glass, my hand trembling so badly the ice cubes rattled against the glass sides. Sarah. Just reading the name brought back the scent of cheap vanilla perfume and the harsh sting of being cornered in the girls' bathroom. I pulled my knees up to my chest and wrapped my arms around them, rocking slightly. The silence of my bedroom was deafening, save for the rush of blood pulsing in my ears. I kept glancing at the tablet, expecting it to buzz again, half-convinced she was somehow standing right outside my apartment door, waiting to knock.

Arthur sat on the park bench, enjoying the autumn breeze, until his tablet chimed with a notification. A social media request from Reginald Vance. Arthur’s fingers instantly curled into fists, crumpling the edge of his paper coffee cup until the hot liquid spilled over his knuckles. He barely felt the burn. Reginald. It had been forty years since high school, yet the name sent a violent shudder down Arthur's spine. He rapidly tapped his cane against the pavement, a frantic staccato beat that chased away a nearby flock of pigeons. He stared at the blue sky, but his vision blurred, replaced by memories of torn textbooks and mocking laughter. Arthur swallowed hard, trying to dislodge the heavy lump in his throat. He fumbled to turn off the tablet, pressing the power button with a shaking thumb, desperate to make the screen go black.

The subway rattled along the dark tunnel as I absentmindedly sorted through my notifications. Then I saw it. Friend Request: Derek Vance. The air in the crowded train car instantly felt ten degrees hotter and completely devoid of oxygen. I tugged at the collar of my shirt, gasping for a proper breath. The overhead lights flickered, and for a split second, the reflection in the window wasn’t a grown man in a suit, but a small teenager pinned against a chain-link fence. My thumbs hovered over the keypad, paralyzed. Did I block him? Did I delete the request? If I blocked him, he’d know I saw it. My knee began to bounce rapidly against the seat in front of me. The train pulled into the next station with a screech of brakes, and I practically shoved my way out the doors, desperate for open air.

Maya was surrounded by towering stacks of library books when her phone lit up. The name Brittany Hall flashed across the locked screen. Maya immediately slammed her textbook shut, the loud thwack echoing through the quiet reading room. Several students shushed her, but she didn’t notice. She stared at the phone, her breathing growing shallow and fast. She wrapped her arms around her stomach, leaning forward over the desk as a wave of nausea washed over her. Brittany’s smiling face in the tiny circular icon felt like a threat. Maya bit down hard on her thumbnail, tearing the edge away. She glanced over her shoulder, an irrational urge telling her Brittany was creeping up behind her in the library aisles. Packing her backpack with frantic, jerky movements, Maya left her notes behind, needing to get to the safety of her dorm room immediately.

The music was thumping through the floorboards at the party, but all the sound seemed to drain from the room the moment I glanced at my screen. Leo Carmichael has sent you a friend request. The plastic red cup crinkled in my tightening grip. "You okay, man?" my friend Josh asked, his voice sounding like it was underwater. I couldn't respond. I just nodded mechanically, my eyes glued to Leo's name. A cold sweat broke out across my forehead, and my stomach did a violent flip. I excused myself, pushing through the dancing crowd with my head down, rushing toward the bathroom. I locked the door behind me, leaned over the sink, and splashed cold water on my face. My reflection in the mirror was pale, wide-eyed. Leo was back. The walls of the tiny bathroom felt like they were inching closer together.

Clara was slicing crusts off a peanut butter sandwich when her smartwatch vibrated against her wrist. She glanced down. Request pending: Veronica Shields. The knife slipped, leaving a deep gash in the wooden cutting board. Clara froze, her heart instantly shifting into a galloping, chaotic rhythm. She gripped the edge of the kitchen counter so tightly her knuckles turned white. Veronica. The name tasted like dirt and humiliation. Clara squeezed her eyes shut, trying to block out the memory of her middle school art project being stomped into pieces.
