She began to pace the length of the kitchen island, her bare feet slapping against the tiles. She stopped, looked at her smartwatch, and aggressively swiped the notification away. But the damage was done. Her hands were shaking too badly to finish making the sandwich, and the silence of the empty house suddenly felt suffocating.

I sat at the departure gate, waiting for my flight to board, and popped open my laptop to kill time. A banner notification instantly slid down from the top right corner. Gavin Reece sent you a connection request. The loud chatter of the airport terminal faded into a dull, rushing static in my ears. I slammed the laptop shut so hard the hinge cracked. The businessman sitting next to me jumped, giving me a weird look, but I couldn't bring myself to apologize. I rubbed my hands briskly up and down my thighs, trying to wipe away the sudden clamminess in my palms. Why was Gavin looking for me? How did he find my professional profile? I stood up, grabbing my carry-on bag, and started walking aimlessly up and down the concourse, checking over my shoulder every few steps, unable to stay in one place.

Sitting in the idling car at the school pickup line, Marcus idly scrolled through his phone. A little red bubble popped up. Friend Request: Toby Baxter. Marcus instantly dropped the phone into the cupholder as if it had given him an electric shock. His chest tightened, a heavy weight pressing down on his lungs, making it impossible to draw a full breath. He cranked the car's air conditioning to the maximum setting, though the autumn air outside was cool. Toby. The guy who used to wait for him by the bike racks. Marcus constantly checked his rearview mirror, his leg bouncing up and down, making his keys jingle against the steering column. He picked up his phone, his thumb hovering over the word 'Delete', trembling so intensely he was certain he might accidentally tap 'Accept' instead.

I stare at the brown cardboard box on the porch, my pulse drumming against my ribs. The label clearly says "Arthur Pendelton," the guy who lived here before me. I step back inside, locking the deadbolt and clicking the chain into place. What if Arthur comes back for it? My hands tremble as I peer through the peephole. A white van is idling at the end of the cul-de-sac. Have they been watching? I chew on my thumbnail until I taste copper. I can't leave the package out there, but bringing it inside feels like tampering with federal mail. Prison time. Fines. I pace the hallway, rubbing my damp palms against my jeans. Every rustle of the wind against the siding makes me jump. I need a glass of water, but I can't tear my eyes away from the front window.

Clara stared at the heavy wooden crate resting on her welcome mat, addressed to "E. Thorne." Her foot tapped out a relentless, erratic rhythm against the hardwood floor. She bit her lower lip, pressing her back flat against the closed door. Thorne had moved out months ago, but the landlord mentioned he had a habit of keeping spare keys. Clara rushed to the kitchen, grabbed a heavy frying pan, and set it on the counter near the entryway. She dialed the post office, her finger slipping twice on the keypad. The line rang endlessly. She paced from the window to the door and back again, checking the locks three times. The crate hummed slightly—or was that just the refrigerator? She held her breath, pressing her ear to the wood, her chest tight. If someone knocked right now, she was sure her knees would give out.

The mail carrier dropped a padded envelope in my mailbox and sped off down the dirt road. I jogged out, expecting my seeds, but the name read *J. Miller*. Miller vanished three years ago. I drop the envelope on the gravel like it burns. My stomach twists into a tight, hard knot. I look at the tree line, scanning the deep pines. The shadows seem longer today. I pick it up by the very corner, rushing back inside and throwing the deadbolt. I draw all the blinds, plunging the cabin into twilight. My breath comes in short, shallow hitches. Why is he getting mail now? Who sent this? I push a heavy oak chair under the front doorknob. The envelope sits on the table, mocking me. I grab my phone, but there’s no signal. I tap my foot, staring at the locked door.

Marcus picked up the small, square parcel outside room 4B. *To: Greg H.* Greg was expelled last semester. Marcus dropped the box onto his desk, immediately rubbing the back of his neck. His leg bounced up and down, rattling his chair. Greg was known for bad debts and shady friends. What if the people who sent this came looking for it? Marcus walked to the window, peering down at the campus quad. Every guy in a hoodie looked like someone coming to collect. He went back to the door, checking the latch, then returned to his desk. He pushed the box into the furthest corner of his bottom drawer and buried it under his winter sweaters. He swallowed hard, his throat dry. A loud knock echoed down the hall, and Marcus flinched, dropping his pen and knocking his coffee mug onto the carpet.

I hold the thick envelope meant for *Ms. Alana Vance*. I don't know her, but the return address is the Department of Corrections. My chest constricts, making it hard to draw a full breath. I slide the envelope under a stack of magazines on the glass coffee table, then immediately pull it back out. Leaving it there feels like a ticking bomb. I pace the length of the living room, picking at the loose thread on my sweater until it unravels completely. I check the digital peephole camera again. The hallway is empty, but my heart races like I’ve just sprinted up ten flights of stairs. What if she’s looking for me to forward it? What if the sender comes to my door looking for her? I grab my keys, then drop them. I can't leave. I have to stay and guard the door.

The heavy rectangular package sat on the porch bench. Sarah read the name: *V. Petrov*. She stepped backward, wiping her suddenly clammy hands on her skirt. The landlord had warned her Petrov was "complicated." She locked the front door and peered through the blinds, her fingers gripping the plastic slats so hard her knuckles turned white. A dark sedan slowly rolled past the house, pausing for a fraction of a second before accelerating. Sarah gasped, dropping the blinds. She rushed to the kitchen to ensure the back door was locked, then checked the front door again. Her stomach churned. She grabbed her phone, typing out a message to her brother, deleting it, and typing it again. The letters blurred together. The ticking of the wall clock sounded like a hammer against an anvil. She squeezed her eyes shut, wishing the box would just disappear.

"Evelyn Reed," I whisper to the empty room, reading the label on the enormous box blocking my front door. The previous owner. I chew on the inside of my cheek until it bleeds. I can't step over it, and I can't leave it outside. It’s too big. I drag it into the foyer, my breath catching at every scrape of cardboard on tile. I run to the window, peeking out from behind the curtain. Did the delivery guy leave? Is he coming back? I sit on the bottom stair, pulling my knees to my chest. My mind races through a dozen scenarios, each worse than the last. Evelyn could sue me for holding her mail. Or maybe it’s something illegal. I jump up, grab a roll of packing tape, and reinforce the already sealed edges, just in case. My hands won't stop shaking.

The courier handed David a cold, styrofoam cooler. The label read *Dr. Harrison*, the marine biologist who rented the place last summer. David closed the door, his breathing shallow and rapid. He placed the cooler on the granite island and took three steps back. There was a faint sloshing sound inside. David rubbed his forehead, leaving a streak of sweat. He grabbed a kitchen towel to wipe his hands, but dropped it on the floor. What if it was organic matter? What if it needed refrigeration right now? He didn't want to open it, but leaving it might ruin whatever was inside. He picked up his phone, dialed the property manager, and hung up before it rang. He paced around the kitchen island, his eyes darting toward the cooler every few seconds. He couldn't sit down. He just kept walking in circles.

The pink padded mailer is crammed into my tiny mailbox. *To: Trixie L.* Trixie hasn't lived in lot 42 for a year. I hold the package by the edges, my pulse throbbing in my ears. The return address says 'Final Notice Collections'. I sprint the ten yards back to my door, slamming it shut and clicking the deadbolt. I peer out the grimy window. A stray dog is sniffing the dirt, but to me, it looks like a scout. I toss the mailer onto the worn sofa, then grab it again, shoving it into the microwave and slamming the door. No, that's stupid. I pull it out and hide it beneath the sink. My stomach is doing backflips. I sit at the tiny table, bouncing my leg so fast the entire floor shakes. If someone knocks, I’m not answering. Not today. Not ever.

Maya stared at the ornate, wax-sealed wooden box left in the vestibule. It bore the name *Eleanor Vance*, the woman who had died in the very apartment Maya now rented. Maya’s breath hitched. She backed away until her shoulders hit the wall. Her hands fluttered near her chest, unsure what to do. The hallway felt suddenly freezing. She wanted to call the super, but her phone was upstairs. She couldn't bring herself to walk past the box to reach the stairs. Maya bit her nails, tasting chipped polish. The shadows in the stairwell seemed to stretch toward her. She squeezed her eyes shut and counted to ten, but when she opened them, the box was still there, sitting innocently on the tile. A floorboard creaked above her, and Maya let out a sharp squeak, pressing herself harder against the cold plaster wall.

A courier shoves a sleek silver briefcase into my arms, mutters "For Mr. Sterling," and bolts. I stand in the doorway, staring at the handle. Sterling was the jeweler who got raided last year. I drag the briefcase inside, locking all three deadbolts. My shirt clings to my damp back. I set it on the kitchen table and back away. Is there a tracker inside? I rush to the window, peering down at the busy street. Everyone looks suspicious. The guy in the trench coat. The woman on her phone. They’re all looking up at my window. I pull the blinds down and retreat to the bathroom, sitting on the edge of the tub. My teeth chatter despite the summer heat. I splash cold water on my face, but I still feel lightheaded. I shouldn’t have signed for it. I shouldn't have opened the door.

The Amazon box sat on the welcome mat, addressed to a *Leo Finch*. Julian stared at the name, his throat tightening. He quickly dragged the box inside and locked the door. He began to pace the length of his small room. Seven steps forward, turn, seven steps back. His hands were stuffed deeply into his pockets, fingers curled into tight fists. He stopped to check the window latch, rattling it to make sure it wouldn't budge. He stared at the cardboard, his mind spinning. Returning it meant talking to the post office clerk. Keeping it meant federal mail theft. He ran a hand through his hair, tugging at the roots. A sudden dog bark from the street made him jump, knocking his knee against the coffee table. He barely felt the pain, his eyes locked on the front door, waiting for a knock.

The familiar handwriting on the pale blue envelope sat like a live explosive on the kitchen counter. Maya paced from the sink to the stove, her slippers slapping against the linoleum. Seven years. Why now? She picked up her coffee mug, but her hands shook so badly the dark liquid slopped over the rim, burning her knuckles. She didn’t feel the heat. Setting the mug down with a sharp clatter, she wiped her palms on her jeans. She stared at the letter, her chest rising and falling in quick, shallow hitches. "I'm sorry," the opening line peeked through the thin paper. She backed away until her spine hit the refrigerator door, the hum of the motor vibrating against her stiff shoulders. She chewed the inside of her cheek until she tasted copper, unable to look away from the small piece of paper.

The key nearly snapped in the mailbox lock, my fingers trembling too violently to care. I had already pulled the thick parchment out, staring at the return address. Eight years had passed since the trial. My breath caught high in my throat, refusing to go down to my lungs. I walked up the driveway, the gravel crunching under my boots, but the sound felt muffled by the rushing blood roaring in my ears. I sat on the porch step, dropping the envelope, then snatching it up again. "I owe you an apology," the visible script read through the backlight of the sun. I rubbed my thumb over the ink, my knee bouncing in a rapid, uncontrollable rhythm. I needed a glass of water. I needed to run back to my car. Instead, I sat there, picking at my cuticles until they stung.

Arthur stared at the email sitting at the top of his inbox. The subject line read simply, Apology - from David. His ergonomic chair suddenly felt like it was made of jagged rocks. He swallowed hard, his throat dry as sandpaper, and clicked away to another tab, but immediately clicked back. Ten years of silence, broken on a random Tuesday morning. He tapped his pen against the desk—tap, tap, tap, tap—until the plastic barrel cracked under his grip. His leg jogged up and down beneath the mahogany desk, knocking against the drawer. He reached for his mouse, his index finger hovering a millimeter above the left button. A cold sweat broke out across the back of his neck, sticking his collar to his skin. If he opened it, it was real. If he didn't, it would sit there, glowing on his monitor forever.

I ordered a black tea, but when the barista handed it to me, my grip slipped and the cup almost plummeted to the floor. I rushed to the corner booth, the wrinkled envelope burning a hole in my coat pocket. Five years ago, she ruined my life. I pulled the letter out and placed it face down on the table. My heart drummed a wild, erratic beat against my ribs. I kept checking the window, convinced she might be standing on the pavement watching me, though the postmark was from three states away. I tore a paper napkin into tiny, jagged shreds, piling them into a snowy mountain on my saucer. "Please forgive me," the first line had said. I pressed my palms against my eyes, trying to block out the harsh overhead lights, but my eyelids wouldn't stop their rapid fluttering.

The letter lay on the floral bedspread, innocent and white. Clara stood by the bedroom door, refusing to cross the threshold. Her chest felt tight, as if invisible bands were ratcheting around her ribs. She had found it tucked into an old textbook from college, a delayed apology note hidden for over a decade. She took one step forward, then aborted the movement, pivoting to pace the length of the hallway. Her breathing grew shallow and loud in the quiet apartment. She grabbed a hair tie from her wrist, twisting it around her fingers until the tips turned purple, then snapped it back against her skin. The sting grounded her for only a second before the racing pulse in her neck resumed its relentless thumping. She couldn't read it. She couldn't throw it away. She was trapped in the hallway, staring at the white rectangle.

I sat on the cold slatted bench, watching the pigeons peck at scattered breadcrumbs. The folded piece of notebook paper in my hand felt heavy, like a brick resting in my palm. It had been slipped under my door this morning, a confession and apology for a lie told twelve years ago. I smoothed out the creases, my fingers leaving sweaty prints on the blue lines. I read the first sentence, then immediately folded it back up, shoving it into my pocket. Two seconds later, I pulled it out again. My teeth ground together so fiercely my jaw ached. I tapped my right foot to the tempo of a song I couldn't hear. What if the rest of the page changed everything I thought I knew? I squeezed my eyes shut, drawing in a jagged breath that snagged on the lump in my throat.

Elias held the postcard up to the peephole's light. It was a picture of the Grand Canyon, but the back was filled with crammed, microscopic handwriting begging for forgiveness after fifteen years. He wiped a bead of sweat from his temple. The hallway felt suddenly devoid of oxygen. He unlocked his apartment door, locked it behind him, checked the deadbolt twice, and backed away. He dropped the postcard onto the entry table as if it were coated in acid. His stomach churned in sharp, unhappy circles. He walked into the kitchen, opened the fridge, stared at the mustard jar, and closed it again without seeing anything inside. The silence of the apartment was deafening, amplifying the rush of blood in his ears. He looked back down the hall at the entryway. The postcard sat there, a tiny paper ghost demanding his immediate attention.

The commuter train rattled over the tracks, but the vibrations couldn't mask the violent shaking of my knees. I stared down at my lap where the heavy cream envelope rested. The wax seal was broken. I had torn it open at the station but hadn't possessed the courage to unfold the letter. Nine years of radio silence, and now this. I chewed viciously on my bottom lip, tasting salt. The woman next to me shifted, and I jumped, my elbow slamming into the window. I mumbled an apology, my voice cracking entirely. I stared at the letterhead peeking out, my vision blurring as my pupils dilated. I wanted to pull the emergency brake. I wanted the train doors to slide open right now so I could sprint into the rain. Instead, I sat trapped in my seat, hyperventilating quietly into my scarf.

Margaret knelt in the dirt, her trowel digging savagely into the soil. She ripped out a weed, tossing it over her shoulder. The crumpled letter was stuffed into her gardening apron, crinkling loudly with every movement. He was sorry. After twenty years, he was sorry. She dug another hole, much too deep for the petunia bulb sitting beside her knee. Her breath came in short, raspy gasps, and dirt caked beneath her fingernails. She suddenly dropped the trowel and wiped her soiled hands on her thighs, leaving muddy streaks down the denim. She reached for the letter, her hand hovering just over the pocket, but her fingers twitched violently, refusing to grasp the paper. She stood up, dizzy, the bright afternoon sun blinding her. She began pacing the length of the garden bed, her heart hammering an inescapable rhythm against her breastbone.

The engine idled in the empty parking lot, the heater blasting, but I was shivering uncontrollably. The letter rested on the passenger seat. I gripped the steering wheel so tightly my knuckles turned stark white. It had arrived in today's mail, an apology for the crash that happened nearly a decade ago. I rolled down the window to let the freezing air hit my face, but my lungs still felt compressed, trapped in a vice. I looked at the envelope, then quickly darted my eyes to the rearview mirror, checking for a threat that wasn't there. I turned the radio on, immediately turned it off, and then drummed my thumbs against the leather wheel. A sudden loud honk from a distant highway made me flinch so hard I banged my knee against the steering column. I pressed my head against the cold glass, gasping for air.

Dust motes danced in the shaft of light cutting through the attic window. Julian knelt beside the open cedar trunk, a yellowed letter resting lightly in his trembling hand. It was dated 1998, a desperate apology from his father that had been lost in the move. Julian swallowed repeatedly, his throat making a thick clicking sound. He shifted his weight, his knee joints popping in the quiet space. He read the first three words and abruptly stood up, his head narrowly missing a low beam. He walked to the tiny window, stared out at the street, and then marched back to the trunk. He picked up the letter, dropped it, and wiped his clammy palms on his corduroys. His pulse beat a hammering tattoo at his temples. He felt a sudden, desperate urge to climb down the ladder and seal the attic hatch forever.

I slid the book out from the return drop, and a folded piece of parchment fluttered to the carpet. I picked it up. It had my name on it, written in handwriting I hadn't seen since the fallout six years ago. I sank into the nearest reading chair. The quiet hush of the library felt suffocating, pressing in on my eardrums. I unfolded the paper, but my eyes couldn't focus on the words; the letters scrambled and swam like insects on the page. My leg began to bounce, the heel of my shoe tapping a rapid, erratic code against the floorboards. I bit down on my thumbnail, tearing the edge until a sharp jolt of pain radiated down my finger. I shoved the letter into my bag, zipped it shut, and then instantly unzipped it to check if it was still there.

The thick, cream-colored envelope felt unusually heavy in my hands. I ran my thumb over the silver embossed letters spelling out "Class of 2014," and a sudden tightness gripped my chest. My coffee went cold on the counter as I stared at the RSVP date, my mind racing through a rolodex of faces I hadn't seen in a decade. I looked down at my worn sweatpants and the stack of past-due bills beside the microwave. A fine layer of sweat formed on my palms. Could I lose fifteen pounds in three months? Could I invent a promotion? I paced the length of my tiny kitchen, breathing in shallow, rapid hitches. The glossy card stared back at me, demanding an answer I wasn't ready to give. I buried it at the bottom of the recycling bin, but I could still feel it sitting there.

Marcus clicked the email open, and the colorful banner of the Westridge High mascot filled his monitor. His jaw clamped shut automatically. He pushed his office chair back so violently it slammed into the filing cabinet. Getting up, he began to pace the length of his cubicle, his fingernails digging small crescents into his palms. The reunion was in six weeks. Six weeks to somehow undo the last ten years of middle management mediocrity. He swallowed hard, trying to push down the metallic taste of nausea rising in the back of his throat. He clicked over to his LinkedIn profile, scrutinizing his lackluster job history, then opened a new tab to check the price of tailored suits. His knee bounced rapidly under the desk as he sat back down, reading the invitation's cheerful greeting over and over until the words blurred together.

I sat in the driver's seat with the engine off, staring at the glossy postcard resting on my steering wheel. The golden bulldog logo of Crestview High gleamed in the afternoon sun. My teeth caught my lower lip, gnawing at the dry skin there until I tasted copper. I checked the rearview mirror, tracing the new fine lines around my eyes and the thinning patches near my temples. Ten years. My breathing grew shallow, my chest rising and falling in quick, uneven jerks. I turned the ignition on, then immediately off again. If I didn't go, they would whisper about what a failure I'd become. If I did go, they would see it for themselves. I tapped my fingers frantically against the dashboard in a chaotic rhythm, my stomach churning violently like I was strapped into a roller coaster ascending the steepest drop.

"Hey, looks like a blast from the past," David said, tossing the sleek black envelope onto the coffee table. Sarah’s eyes locked onto the gold-foil lettering of Oakwood Academy, and her fingers instantly went cold. She pulled her knees up to her chest, wrapping her arms tightly around her shins. "Are you going to open it?" David asked, but his voice sounded muffled, like he was speaking underwater. Sarah’s heart thudded violently against her ribs. She could already hear the echoing acoustics of the gymnasium, feel the burning gaze of the popular crowd judging her mismatched thrift-store clothes. She swallowed dryly. Her right foot began a frantic, rhythmic tapping against the cushion. "Maybe later," she squeaked, her eyes darting toward the hallway, desperately wanting to retreat into the dark quiet of their bedroom.

The notification popped up on my screen just as I brought the cappuccino to my lips. 'Lincoln High Class of 2015 - 10 Year Bash!' My hand jerked, sending hot foam spilling over the ceramic rim and onto my fingers. I didn't even feel the burn. My chest tightened like a heavy iron band was being ratcheted closed around my ribs. I stared at the RSVP list. Going: 142. Michael Reynolds, Jessica Thorne, David Vance. The names jumped off the screen, each one a sharp jab to my lungs. I started chewing furiously on my thumbnail, stripping away the polish in jagged flakes. Could I afford a flight? What if nobody recognized me? What if they did? I shoved my phone into my bag and stood up so quickly my chair screeched against the cafe floor, my breathing ragged as I practically sprinted for the exit.

Elena stood frozen before the full-length mirror, the crumpled beige invitation clutched tightly in her fist. Her eyes darted from the silver embossed letters to her reflection, analyzing every perceived flaw with ruthless precision. She pinched the fabric of her blouse, pulling it away from her waist, then smoothed her hair down, only to aggressively ruffle it again seconds later. A cold bead of sweat trickled down the back of her neck. The room felt suddenly stifling, the air too thick to draw into her lungs. She dropped the invitation onto the dresser as if it burned her skin, taking three rapid steps backward. Her pulse hammered a frantic rhythm in her ears. Twenty days. She had exactly twenty days to transform into someone successful, someone unbothered, someone who didn't feel like a fraud. She pressed her palms against her eyes, breathing in quick, shallow gasps.

"This came to our address for you," my mother said, sliding the heavy cardstock across the dining table. I saw the familiar royal blue crest of St. Jude's, and my appetite vanished entirely. The piece of roast chicken in my mouth turned to ash, impossible to swallow. I pushed my plate away, my leg bouncing so vigorously under the table that the silverware rattled against the porcelain. "A ten-year reunion!" my dad chimed in. I wiped my clammy palms on my jeans, my mind flashing to the empty seat beside me. They would all be married. They would all have toddlers and mortgages. I gripped the edge of the table until my knuckles turned white, my heart performing frantic acrobatics in my chest. "Yeah," I whispered, my voice trembling. I excused myself to the bathroom, desperate to splash cold water on my flushed face.

Julian sat on the wooden bench in the locker room, his towel draped over his shoulders. His phone buzzed with a text from an old number. Bro! You going to the 20-year next month? Julian stared at the glowing screen, the ambient noise of showers and slamming lockers fading into a high-pitched ringing in his ears. He swallowed hard. His fingers hovered over the keyboard, shaking so badly he couldn't hit the right letters. He deleted a string of gibberish, his breath catching in his throat. He looked down at his expanding waistline and the fading tattoo on his arm, a sudden wave of nausea rolling through his stomach. He locked the screen and tossed the phone into his duffel bag, but the device felt like a ticking bomb. He sat there shivering despite the humid air, his jaw clenched tight enough to crack a tooth.

Mrs. Gable from next door handed me the envelope over the chain-link fence. "Accidentally came to my box," she smiled. I thanked her, but seeing the return address—Riverside High Alumni Association—made my fingers stiffen. Buster tugged his leash, but I stood rooted to the pavement. The summer heat suddenly felt suffocating, pressing down on my chest like a physical weight. My vision blurred. I could hear phantom lockers slamming and cruel laughter echoing down the hallway. I folded the thick paper once, twice, three times, creasing it so fiercely my thumbnail split. I needed to lock the door. I practically dragged Buster up the driveway, my heart beating a frantic staccato against my ribs as I fumbled wildly with my house keys.

Chloe sorted the mail with practiced efficiency. Bill, junk, catalog, bill. Then her hand stopped mid-air. The crimson envelope bore the seal of Montgomery Prep. The breath she had just taken stuck in her throat, refusing to go down or come back up. She dropped the letter onto the marble counter as if it were a live scorpion. Her hands moved to her neck, rubbing the back of it in fast, erratic strokes. She began pacing around the kitchen island, her bare feet slapping sharply against the hardwood. Twenty laps. Thirty. She stopped and peeked at the envelope from across the room, her stomach twisting into painful, tight knots. She grabbed a stack of magazines and threw them over the crimson paper, burying it entirely. She backed away, her chest heaving, refusing to look away until her shoulders hit the hallway wall.

"Oh, your mom gave me this to pass along," Greg said, pulling a slightly crushed envelope from his jacket over the noise of the crowded bar. I took it, recognizing the Central High font instantly. The thumping bass of the music seemed to drop away, replaced by a rushing sound in my ears. I set my pint glass down so hard the amber liquid sloshed over the rim, pooling on the sticky table. "You okay?" Greg mouthed. I nodded vigorously, forcing a rigid, unblinking smile. Beneath the table, my knees were bouncing fast enough to vibrate the floorboards. I shoved the envelope into my back pocket, but it felt like a burning coal against my skin. I began peeling the wet label off my beer bottle, stripping it down to the bare glass in tiny, obsessive shreds while my lungs struggled to pull in enough oxygen.

The line of cars inched forward outside the elementary school. Waiting for her daughter, Maya absentmindedly refreshed her inbox. An email titled "Franklin High 15-Year Gala" sat at the top. Maya slammed on the brakes a second too early, jolting the SUV to a harsh stop. A cold sweat broke out across her forehead, sticking her bangs to her skin. She stared at the subject line, her jaw tight, her teeth grinding together. Her thumb hovered over the delete button, trembling violently. Could she face Chloe and the old varsity squad? Could she explain her incomplete degree and the minivan? The car behind her honked loudly. Maya flinched, dropping her phone into the passenger footwell. She gripped the leather steering wheel with both hands, squeezing until her knuckles lost all their color, her breath coming in quick, shallow gasps as the school bell finally rang.

The heavy knock on the apartment door made Maya drop her coffee mug. It shattered, but she ignored the mess, creeping barefoot toward the peephole. No one. Just a dozen red lilies resting on the welcome mat. She cracked the door open, snatched the bouquet, and slammed the deadbolt shut, her chest heaving as her fingers fumbled with the chain lock. She tore through the plastic wrapping, shaking the stems until petals rained down on the hardwood. Nothing. No note. No signature. She peered through the blinds, her gaze darting to the parked cars below. Her phone buzzed on the counter, and she jumped, pressing her knuckles hard against her lips. Who knew she lived here now? She hadn't even given her own mother the new address yet.

The delivery guy practically shoved the arrangement of white roses onto my desk before vanishing. "Secret admirer?" Sarah chirped from the next cubicle. I forced a laugh, but my throat felt tight and dry. I dug through the thorny stems, my thumb catching on a sharp edge. A drop of blood welled up, but I barely felt it. There was no card. My stomach dropped like a stone. I immediately opened my sent emails, staring at the spreadsheet I had accidentally forwarded to our main competitor yesterday. Did they know? Was this a twisted corporate warning? My knee began bouncing a rapid staccato rhythm against the underside of my desk. I pulled my collar away from my neck, suddenly suffocating in the air-conditioned room. Every time the elevator dinged, I squeezed my eyes shut.

Arthur stared at the massive bouquet of orchids sitting on the kitchen island. He checked the floor, flipped the wrapping paper over, and ran his hands through the damp moss at the base. Zero documentation. His pulse drummed heavily in his ears. He picked up his wife’s unlocked phone from the counter, his thumb hovering over her messaging app. He wiped a sudden layer of sweat from his forehead with the back of his sleeve. Who sends orchids on a random Tuesday? He paced the length of the kitchen, biting down on his thumbnail until the cuticle throbbed. He paused to glance out the window, studying the empty driveway. When the garage door motor suddenly rumbled to life, Arthur flinched, hastily shoving the phone back into its exact original position and wiping his damp palms on his jeans.

The nurse placed the yellow daisies on my bedside table with a sympathetic smile, leaving before I could ask who dropped them off. I rifled through the leaves. Blank. Empty. My breath hitched, catching somewhere in the middle of my chest. Why would someone send flowers today, of all days? The biopsy results weren't supposed to come back until tomorrow. Did Dr. Evans call my family first? I reached for the plastic cup of water, but my hand was trembling so badly it splashed over the rim and soaked my paper gown. I chewed the inside of my cheek, tasting copper. Every time a footstep echoed in the sterile hallway, I grabbed the thin blanket and pulled it up to my chin. They were pity flowers. I just knew it. I couldn't tear my eyes away from the bright, mocking petals.

Ten minutes to curtain, and the stage manager deposited a sprawling arrangement of black dahlias on Elias's vanity. "Just arrived at the stage door," she said, hurrying out. Elias tore through the dark blooms. No envelope. His stomach clamped into a tight knot. Black dahlias were Julian Thorne’s signature—the ruthless theater critic who had utterly destroyed Elias’s career three years ago in London. He rushed to the doorway, peering out at the chaotic backstage wings, his breathing turning shallow and erratic. He pressed two fingers against his neck, feeling his pulse hammer violently against his skin. Thorne was out there. He had to be. Elias looked at his reflection in the bulb-lit mirror, watching his pale, clammy complexion beneath the heavy stage makeup. He squeezed his hands into fists to stop the shaking, but the tremor had already moved into his knees.

I was hauling the last box of kitchenware inside when I saw them—a bundle of dead, dried baby’s breath resting on the porch swing. I dropped the cardboard box. Plates clattered and broke inside, but I didn't care. I kicked the pile of dead flowers away, frantically searching the porch planks for a note. Nothing. I backed up against the front door, my chest rising and falling in quick, jagged gasps. The wind chimes clanged loudly, making me jump and smack my head against the doorframe. I fumbled for my keys, dropping them twice on the welcome mat before finally jamming the right one into the lock. Once inside, I slid the deadbolt home, then pushed the heavy oak console table directly against the door. I sat on the floor, pulling my knees tight against my chest, listening to the wind.

The bouquet of wilting carnations was left on the bridal suite's vanity. Chloe ripped the cellophane apart, tossing the stems onto the floor to search for a tag. None. These weren't the hydrangeas she had meticulously ordered. Her hands fluttered to her hair, accidentally pulling a curl loose from her intricate updo. She grabbed her phone, dialing Liam’s number for the fifth time in ten minutes. Straight to voicemail. She began to pace the small room, the heavy silk of her gown swishing aggressively with each sharp turn. She chewed her lower lip so hard it stung. Why was his phone off? Why were these cheap flowers here? She rushed to the window, scanning the courtyard below for his car. Her breathing came in short, rapid puffs, fogging up the glass as she gripped the windowsill with white-knuckled intensity.

The bell above the café door jingled, and a man in a trench coat walked straight to the counter, dropped a bundle of thorny purple thistles by the register, and left without ordering. I stared at the door as it swung shut. I grabbed a pair of tongs to flip the flowers over, searching for a tag. Just green stems. A cold sweat broke out across my shoulder blades. I ducked below the counter, pulling my phone from my apron pocket. My fingers were slick, slipping on the screen as I typed a message to my manager. I peeked over the espresso machine, my eyes darting toward the street window. A figure was standing across the street, staring right at the shop. I scrambled back down to the floor, my heart thudding against my ribs like a trapped bird.

Marcus stared at the extravagant bouquet of tulips resting on his desk. He sifted through the green foliage twice. No card. He pulled up his digital calendar, his eyes darting frantically across the grid of dates. It was Tuesday the 14th. He opened his desk drawer, tossing aside paperclips and pens to check his physical planner. His chest felt unusually tight, and a thin film of sweat prickled at his hairline. Was it their anniversary? No, that was October. Her birthday? May. He bit down on his knuckle, mentally scrolling through every conversation they had over the past week. Did she get a promotion? Did someone die? He picked up the receiver of his office phone, dialing his wife's number, then slammed it back down before it could ring. If he asked, and he was supposed to know, he was a dead man.

A single blue hydrangea was taped to my windshield when I left the precinct. I didn’t touch it. I just stood in the empty parking garage, the silence ringing loudly in my ears. I leaned in close, inspecting the stem. No note. My stomach twisted into a heavy knot. The serial killer we were hunting always left a blue hydrangea with the bodies. I slowly reached for my service weapon, unsnapping the holster with a quiet click. I spun around, scanning the concrete pillars and the shadows pooling between parked cars. Every distant drip of water sounded like a footstep. I backed up slowly, pressing my spine against the cold metal of my car door. I reached into my pocket for my radio, but my hand was shaking so violently I dropped it onto the asphalt. The clatter echoed endlessly.

The delivery boy vanished before Beatrice could even grab her cane. Left behind on the porch was a lavish arrangement of pink peonies. She hobbled out, turning the heavy ceramic vase around. No card. She quickly dragged the vase inside and locked the door, engaging the chain and the deadbolt. She peeked through the floral curtains, her heart fluttering uncomfortably fast in her chest. Her son had warned her about this. Scammers, he had said. They leave packages to see if the house is empty, or to coax you into opening the door. She moved to the telephone on the wall, her frail fingers struggling to press the buttons. The line rang and rang. She held the receiver tightly to her ear, glancing repeatedly between the peonies on the table and the locked front door, her breath coming in shallow little wheezes.

There was a single red rose shoved through the vents of my locker. I pulled it out, immediately checking the floor for a dropped note. Nothing. I clutched my binder tight against my chest, my eyes darting down the crowded high school hallway. A group of varsity guys was laughing by the water fountain. Were they looking at me? I quickly shoved the rose into my backpack and zipped it shut, my face burning. My palms felt clammy, sticking to the plastic cover of my binder. This was exactly what happened to Chloe last month before the whole school got that group text making fun of her. I ducked my head, walking as fast as I could toward the girls' bathroom. I locked myself in a stall, sitting on the closed lid of the toilet, waiting for the warning bell to ring.

I roll the window down, then up, then down again, unable to find a comfortable temperature. Across the street, the yellow treads of the excavator idle with a low, rumbling hum that vibrates right into my molars. That’s my bedroom window up there. The one with the chipped blue paint. I check my watch—8:55 AM. Five minutes until the crew starts. I tap my thumbs against the steering wheel to a frantic, erratic beat, chewing the inside of my cheek until I taste copper. A worker in a hard hat walks up to the porch, clipboard in hand, and I instinctively duck a little in the driver's seat. My chest feels tight, wrapped in iron bands. I need to leave, but my hands are locked in a death grip around the leather wheel, paralyzed as the heavy diesel engine suddenly revs.

Elias paced the length of the empty living room, his footsteps echoing too loudly off the bare hardwood. Three steps to the fireplace, turn, three steps to the hallway, turn. He checked his phone. No new messages. The demolition crew was late, or maybe they were early—he couldn't remember what time they had agreed on. He knelt to adjust the flaps of the single cardboard box left by the door, resealing the tape three times just to give his trembling fingers something to do. Through the bay window, a heavy truck hissed its air brakes down the street, and Elias jolted, knocking his knee hard against the doorframe. He rubbed his face, his breaths coming in short, shallow hitches. The floral wallpaper of his youth seemed to mock him, peeling at the edges, waiting for the wrecking ball that he knew was lumbering ever closer.

I keep pulling up weeds, even though the whole garden will be dust by noon. Dirt is caked under my fingernails, and my knees ache from kneeling on the flagstones. Why am I doing this? The contract is signed. The city approved the rezoning. Yet, my heart is a trapped bird battering against my ribs. I stand up, wiping my palms on my jeans, leaving dark, sweaty streaks. The old oak tree with my tire swing stands tall against the grey morning sky. I hear the crunch of gravel in the driveway and freeze. The demolition foreman is getting out of his truck. I bite my thumbnail down to the quick, tasting dirt. I want to yell at him to stop, to tell him there’s been a mistake, but my throat is completely sealed shut. I just stand there, shivering despite the heavy summer heat.

The coffee in Clara’s cup rippled, betraying the relentless bouncing of her knee under the café table. She kept her eyes glued to the window, watching the chain-link fence surrounding her childhood home. A wrecking ball dangled from the crane parked in the driveway. She picked up a sugar packet, tearing the edge, pouring it out, then immediately tore another, spilling white crystals over the saucer in her haste. "Are you going to drink that?" the waitress asked. Clara jolted, spilling hot liquid onto her wrist. "Just waiting," she muttered quickly, wiping the table with three napkins. She couldn't tear her gaze away from the front porch where she used to wait for the school bus. Her stomach churned like a washing machine on the spin cycle, and she repeatedly checked the lock screen of her silenced phone, bracing for the inevitable crash.

“Are they there yet?” my sister asks over the phone. I pace the length of the motel room, winding the phone cord around my index finger so tightly the tip turns purple. “No, not yet,” I manage to say, my voice pitching an octave higher than normal. I unwrap my finger and start picking at a loose thread on my sweater. Every passing siren or loud truck outside the window sends a jolt of electricity straight down my spine. The developers said they’d start the demolition of our old farmhouse at dawn. It’s now seven in the morning. I sit on the edge of the mattress, then immediately stand up again, unable to bear the stillness. “Call me when it starts,” she says. I nod, forgetting she can’t see me, and hang up. I press my cold palms against my burning cheeks, struggling to catch my breath.

The grandfather clock in the hallway had already been sold, leaving a pale rectangular ghost on the faded floral wallpaper. Marcus stood in the empty space, rubbing his thumb obsessively over his knuckles until the skin was raw and red. Outside, the hydraulic whine of heavy machinery pierced the quiet suburban morning. The crew was positioning the excavator. Marcus swallowed hard, but his mouth was completely dry, feeling like a mouthful of sawdust. He walked to the front window, then backed away, then walked to it again. He could hear the foreman shouting instructions. Marcus pulled his keys from his pocket, tossing them up and catching them, over and over, the sharp metallic clinks failing to drown out the roar of the diesel engines. He squeezed his eyes shut, his chest rising and falling in rapid, shallow bursts, bracing for the first sickening crunch of timber.

I hold the camera up to my eye, but the viewfinder keeps blurring. My hands are shaking too much to keep the frame steady. Through the lens, the little yellow house looks so small, dwarfed by the massive green bulldozer idling at the edge of the lawn. I lower the camera, wipe my sweaty palms on my jacket, and take a deep, shuddering breath that gets stuck halfway down my throat. The foreman waves his arm. I raise the camera again. I need to capture the porch where Dad taught me to play guitar. The shutter clicks, but my finger slips, taking three rapid-fire shots of the dirt. My heart beats a frantic tattoo against my ribs, echoing in my ears. I want to run, but my boots feel like they are cemented to the sidewalk. I just stare, biting my lower lip until it bleeds.

Lying in his childhood bed for the very last time, Leo stared at the glow-in-the-dark stars stuck to the ceiling. The demolition was scheduled for eight in the morning. It was currently three in the morning. He flipped onto his left side, kicked the blanket off, then immediately pulled it back over his shoulders. The silence of the empty house was deafening, amplified by the frantic thumping in his own ears. He traced the familiar crack in the plaster wall with a trembling index finger. What if he had left something in the attic? What if the safety deposit box key was still under the floorboards? He threw the covers back and swung his legs out of bed, his bare feet hitting the cold wood. He paced the small perimeter of the room, breathing rapidly through his nose, opening and closing his empty fists in the dark.

The yellow caution tape snaps violently in the wind, a bright plastic barrier between me and the place I grew up. I stand on the sidewalk, shifting my weight from my left foot to my right, back and forth, unable to stand still. Over by the azalea bushes, now crushed under the treads of a backhoe, I spot a glint of blue. It’s my old toy truck. I step toward the tape, my chest tightening. Should I grab it? The engine of the bulldozer coughs to life with a deafening roar. I flinch, stepping back so quickly I almost trip over the curb. My breathing turns jagged. I clutch the collar of my coat, pulling it tight against my neck. The operator in the cab pulls a lever. I squeeze my eyes shut and press my hands firmly over my ears, waiting for the impact.

Sarah handed the signed clearance papers to the developer, her hand vibrating so intensely that the paper rustled. She immediately crossed her arms, tucking her hands tightly under her armpits to hide the tremor. They stood in the center of the kitchen, stripped of its appliances, leaving only scuffed linoleum. "We bring the house down in twenty minutes," the developer said smoothly. Sarah nodded, unable to force a single word past the tight knot in her throat. She darted her eyes toward the doorway, then to the ceiling, then to the floor. Every sudden noise—a creaking floorboard, the wind rattling the loose windowpane—made her shoulders flinch toward her ears. She shifted from heel to toe, her stomach doing somersaults. She needed a glass of water, she needed air, she needed to be anywhere but standing inside this hollow shell before it was ripped apart.

I put the car in drive, but my foot refuses to press the gas pedal. In the rearview mirror, the wrecking crew is unspooling thick steel cables across the overgrown lawn of my childhood home. My knuckles are bone-white on the steering wheel. I glance at the mirror, look away, then immediately check it again. The heavy machinery lets out a sharp, pneumatic hiss. I gasp, my shoulders jumping instantly. I turn the radio on, blasting the volume to drown out the sounds of the crew, but immediately switch it off again because the noise makes my skin crawl. Sweat beads at my hairline despite the air conditioning blasting my face. I have to leave. I have to drive away before they swing the boom, but my foot just hovers over the pedal, shaking violently as I stare at the mirror, trapped in the driver's seat.

From the safety of the neighbor's porch, Julian watched the men in high-vis vests swarm his old family property. He chewed frantically on the plastic cap of a pen, mangling the tip until it cracked between his teeth. The enormous metal jaws of the excavator hovered just above the roof of the sunroom where his mother used to paint. He tapped his left foot in a rapid, ceaseless rhythm against the concrete steps. "It'll be over soon," Mrs. Gable said gently, placing a hand on his shoulder. Julian jerked slightly at her touch. He offered a tight, forced smile that didn't reach his wide, unblinking eyes. He swallowed hard, his throat clicking audibly, and wiped a clammy hand down the front of his jeans. As the excavator’s arm finally lurched downward, Julian sucked in a sharp breath and held it, unable to look away.

Maya’s thumb rubbed a rapid rhythm over her index knuckle as she stared at the refrigerator. Nailed beneath a plastic magnet was Lily’s latest masterpiece. A house, a sun, and a hulking, asymmetrical creature with three mismatched horns. Barnaby. Maya swallowed hard, the dry click in her throat sounding louder than the cartoon blaring in the living room. She hadn't thought about Barnaby in twenty years. She stepped closer, her chest tight, breath catching in her upper lungs. How could a four-year-old draw the exact jagged teeth and plaid vest of a companion Maya had entirely invented? She glanced quickly toward the hallway, half-expecting to see a shadow stretching across the floorboards. Her fingers trembled as she reached out to touch the waxy crayon marks, quickly pulling her hand back as if the paper itself might burn her. She needed a glass of water.

I wiped my palms flat against my denim jeans, leaving damp streaks on the fabric. "And who is this, Sophie?" I asked, struggling to keep my voice steady. My foot tapped an incessant beat against the hardwood floor. Sophie pointed a sticky finger at the stick figure with an antenna and wheels instead of legs. "That’s Mr. Beep. He lives in the closet." The air in the room suddenly felt entirely too thin. I took a short, shallow breath, my eyes darting toward the half-open closet door behind her. Mr. Beep. I used to whisper all my secrets to Mr. Beep when the thunderstorms rolled in. I stood up quickly, nearly knocking over the small wooden chair, and took three brisk steps toward the window. "Let's close that closet door, okay?" I muttered, not waiting for her answer before pushing the white wooden panel shut until the latch clicked.

Elena gnawed on the inside of her cheek until she tasted copper. The digital canvas on her niece’s tablet glowed brightly in the dim living room, displaying a crude sketch of a woman with spider legs and a weeping willow for hair. Sylvia. Elena’s pulse thrummed a chaotic tempo against her temples. She pressed her fingernails into the meat of her palms, forcing herself to breathe in, out, in, out, but the air felt like sludge. She dropped the tablet onto the sofa cushion and stood, pacing the short distance between the coffee table and the window blinds. She peered through the slats into the dark yard, her eyes scanning the shadows beneath the oak tree where Sylvia used to sit. Elena rushed to the front door, her hands fumbling awkwardly with the deadbolt, sliding it home with a sharp, metallic clack. Only then did she dare look back at the sofa.

My hands wouldn't stop shaking. I dropped the spiral notebook onto the kitchen island, staring at the graphite smudges. Chloe had drawn him perfectly: the tall man with no eyes and a top hat, holding a bunch of black balloons. I backed away, my hip colliding hard with the edge of the counter, but I hardly felt the bruise forming. The whistling man. I rubbed the back of my neck, feeling the cold clamminess of my own skin. The silence in the kitchen was deafening, pressing against my eardrums until I swore I could hear a faint, reedy tune drifting down from the upstairs vents. I grabbed my car keys from the bowl, the metal jingling wildly in my unsteady grip. I needed to leave the house before Chloe came home from school. I just needed to be somewhere else, anywhere else, surrounded by a crowd of real, breathing people.

Marcus peeled a strip of skin from his cuticle with his teeth, wincing at the sharp sting. Beside him, little Emma hummed a nursery rhyme, a blue marker squeaking across her construction paper. Marcus stared fixedly at the shape emerging on the page. A dog with bat wings and a coiled spring for a tail. He shifted his weight from leg to leg, the floorboards creaking under his boots. "Where... where did you see that, Emma?" His voice was a thin, reedy whisper. He cleared his throat loudly and tried again, but the tightness in his chest wouldn't loosen. Emma didn't look up, just grabbed a green marker. "Rufus told me to draw him." Marcus stood up so fast his vision swam with black dots. He wrapped his arms tightly across his chest, his gaze locked on the empty corner of the room, waiting for a shadow to detach itself from the wall.

The steering wheel leather squeaked under my tight grip. I stared straight ahead through the windshield, my heart fluttering against my ribs like a trapped bird beating its wings against a cage. In the backseat, my niece Mia hummed happily, her art class project resting on her lap. It was a watercolor of a striped elephant with three trunks—Pip. I kept checking the rearview mirror, my eyes darting to the empty seat beside Mia every five seconds. A cold drop of sweat slid down my spine, tracing the line of my vertebrae. I pressed the accelerator down a fraction more, eager to pull into the bright, sunlit driveway of my brother's house. Every time a car passed us, I flinched, my shoulders jumping toward my ears. Pip used to tell me he was waiting for me in the dark. I swallowed the lump in my throat, turning up the radio volume.

Sarah froze halfway down the driveway, her grip tightening on the handles of the grocery bags until the plastic cut deep red grooves into her fingers. There, rendered in vibrant pink and yellow sidewalk chalk, was a snake with a human face and a top hat. Sir Hiss. A harsh, shallow breath tore through her lips. She spun around, scanning the empty suburban street, her eyes wide and unblinking. The wind rustled the dry autumn leaves, making a sound exactly like the slithering whispers she remembered from the crawlspace of her childhood home. She took a slow step backward, her pulse hammering in her ears, drowning out the distant hum of traffic. Dropping the groceries—letting oranges roll wildly into the gutter—she retreated to the porch. She fumbled violently with her key ring, jamming the brass into the lock and twisting, desperate to get the heavy oak door open.

I tugged at the collar of my shirt, suddenly finding the cotton fabric unbearably restrictive. A pile of loose printer paper lay scattered across my niece’s floral rug. Every single page featured the same towering figure entirely composed of jagged triangles. I used to call him the Glass Man. My jaw clamped shut so tightly my teeth ached, and I began to pace the narrow strip of floor between the bed and the dresser. I rubbed my temples, pressing hard against the throbbing ache building behind my eyes. I walked to the window, pulled the curtains shut, then immediately ripped them open again, unable to decide if the daylight made it better or worse. I knelt down, hastily sweeping the papers into a messy stack, my movements jerky and uncoordinated. I shoved them deep into the bottom of the trash can, covering them with crumpled tissues, hiding the jagged lines from view.

David’s right knee bounced in a rapid, uncontrollable staccato as he sat on the folding chair in the elementary school gymnasium. The walls were plastered with finger paintings. Directly across from him was his niece’s contribution: a sprawling black mass devouring a yellow circle. The Gloom. A cold slick of sweat coated David’s palms. He wiped them vigorously on his corduroy trousers, but the dampness returned instantly. "It's... it's very creative," he muttered to his sister, his words stumbling over each other. His gaze darted frantically toward the glowing red EXIT sign above the double doors. The air in the gym felt thick, suffocating, smelling of floor wax and stale juice boxes. He stood abruptly, the metal chair screeching loudly against the linoleum. "Excuse me. Bathroom," he clipped out, power-walking down the corridor without waiting for her reply, his eyes refusing to look at the shadows stretching beneath the lockers.

I twisted the silver ring on my index finger round and round, the metal biting into my skin until it left a red, angry mark. Zoe had proudly handed me a scrap of cardboard ripped from a moving box, decorated with a sharpie. The drawing depicted a little girl holding hands with a floating, empty suit of armor. I held my breath, the silence in the half-empty living room pressing heavily against my ears. I slowly lowered the cardboard, my gaze sweeping the corners of the room where the evening shadows were beginning to gather and pool. My stomach churned like a washing machine on spin cycle. I cleared my throat, forcing a high-pitched, unnatural laugh that echoed awkwardly off the bare walls. "Hey, Zoe," I squeaked, "how about we go get some ice cream right now? Let's go. Right this second." I practically sprinted to the entryway to grab my shoes.

Clara watched the wooden stick drag through the damp sand, her breath coming in quick, shallow hitches. Seven-year-old Lily was intently carving out a shape in the playground sandbox: a figure with long, weeping branches for arms and two hollow holes for eyes. Clara wrapped her arms around herself, digging her fingers into her own biceps. She began to pace a tight circle around the edge of the sandbox, her boots kicking up small clouds of dust. She pulled nervously at a loose strand of her hair, wrapping it so tightly around her index finger that the tip turned purple. She kept glancing at the line of trees bordering the park, half-convinced the rustling leaves were whispering her name in that familiar, papery voice. "Okay, Lily, time to go!" Clara blurted out, lunging forward to grab the little girl’s hand, dragging her toward the car before she could even drop the stick.

My thumb hammered the plunger of my ballpoint pen—click-click-click-click-click—as I stared at the computer monitor. It was just a digital photo my sister had uploaded to the family album, capturing her daughter holding up a crayon drawing. But the drawing was unmistakably of the grinning, multi-eyed cat I had hallucinated under my bed every night when I was nine. I shoved my rolling chair back so violently it crashed into the office bookshelf. I stood up, my chest heaving as if I’d just sprinted up a flight of stairs. I walked to the light switch, flicking it on to flood the room with harsh fluorescent light, even though it was the middle of the afternoon. I couldn't tear my eyes away from the screen, yet my feet refused to step closer to the desk. I grabbed a throw pillow from the armchair and hugged it tightly to my chest, squeezing my eyes shut.

I must have checked my watch forty times in the last ten minutes. The heavy oak door to Mr. Sterling’s office remained shut. On the other side, Mark was making his case for the Regional Director spot. I wiped my palms on my slacks, realizing too late I’d left damp streaks across the dark fabric. My right leg bounced rhythmically against the desk leg, a rapid thump-thump-thump that I couldn't seem to stop. I took a sip of my lukewarm coffee, but it tasted like ash. Had I emphasized my Q3 sales numbers enough in my own interview? Maybe I should have brought the physical portfolio instead of just the flash drive. The door handle clicked, and my heart slammed against my ribs. Mark walked out, flashing a wide, easy grin. I swallowed hard, my throat suddenly like sandpaper, and stood up on shaky legs.

Elias rearranged the ceramic display for the fifth time, ensuring the handles of the mugs all faced precisely forty-five degrees. The district manager was due any second to announce the new store manager. Across the aisle, Chloe casually chatted with a customer, her laughter floating over the racks. Elias’s jaw ached from grinding his teeth. He picked at a loose thread on his uniform vest, winding it around his finger until the tip turned purple. Every time the electronic chime above the entrance sounded, his breath hitched, and his eyes darted to the glass doors. He picked up a dust cloth, rubbing vigorously at a nonexistent smudge on the shelf. He needed to look busy. He needed to look indispensable. His stomach executed a slow, painful somersault as a dark corporate sedan finally pulled into the parking lot.

The rhythmic chopping of my knife against the wooden board sounded way too loud in the cramped kitchen. Julian was working the station next to mine, humming a light French tune while he prepped his station for the lunch rush. Chef had said he would make his decision on the new Sous Chef before service started. I stared intently at the mound of parsley, chopping it finer and finer until it was practically green dust. My chef's coat felt two sizes too small, the collar digging into my neck and making it hard to draw a full breath. I accidentally knocked over a small container of kosher salt, sending white crystals scattering across the stainless steel prep table. "You good over there?" Julian asked, raising an eyebrow. "Fine," I clipped, my voice cracking slightly. I hastily swept the salt into my hand, my fingers trembling slightly.

Clara’s cursor blinked steadily at the end of line 42. She hadn't typed a single character in twenty minutes. On her secondary monitor, the Slack application remained open, her eyes locked onto the green dot next to the CTO’s name. He and David were in the glass-walled conference room across the floor, discussing the Lead Developer role. Clara chewed on the inside of her cheek until she tasted the faint, metallic tang of blood. She grabbed her water bottle and took a gulp, only to nearly choke when David suddenly stood up in the conference room. She coughed into her elbow, her pulse drumming a frantic beat behind her ears. She forced her eyes back to her code, placing her fingers firmly on the home row of her keyboard. Her hands were clammy, slipping slightly against the plastic keys as she waited for her own inevitable summons.

I tapped the end of my ballpoint pen against the mahogany conference table. Click. Click. Click. "Keep it down," Sarah hissed from the chair beside me. I shoved the pen into my pocket, but my fingers immediately started peeling the paper label off my water bottle instead. The creative director was reviewing our final campaign pitches for the Senior Art Director spot. He slowly flipped through my storyboards, his expression completely unreadable. Did he pause too long on the third slide? I should have used the bolder typography. The muted tones looked entirely washed out under these harsh fluorescent lights. I shifted my weight, the leather chair squeaking loudly in the silent room. Sarah sat perfectly still, her posture impeccably straight, a serene smile resting on her face. I wiped a bead of sweat from my temple and took a short, shallow breath, waiting for him to speak.

Marcus paced the length of the breakroom, counting the off-white linoleum tiles. Fifteen steps from the refrigerator to the door. Turn around. Fifteen steps back. The nursing supervisor was updating the duty roster for next month, which would officially reveal the new Charge Nurse. Beside the coffee maker, Lewis was quietly doing a crossword puzzle, occasionally tapping his pen against his chin. Marcus stopped pacing and checked his phone. No new emails. He locked the screen, slid it into his scrubs pocket, and then immediately pulled it out to check again. His stomach felt like a tight, twisted washcloth. He walked over to the sink and washed his hands for the third time in ten minutes, scrubbing the soap into his knuckles until the skin turned a blotchy, irritated red. The heavy sound of the supervisor's sensible clogs echoing down the hallway made him freeze in place.

The elevator ride up to the fiftieth floor had never felt so suffocating. I stared at the digital numbers climbing higher, my reflection in the polished brass doors looking incredibly pale. Today was the day the partners decided who would make Senior Associate: me or Peterson. I straightened my tie, then loosened it slightly, then tightened it again. Was the knot completely centered? I patted the folder containing my closing arguments for the Miller case. Peterson stepped into the elevator at the fortieth floor, holding two coffees and whistling a cheerful melody. "Morning!" he chimed, holding out a cup to me. I reached for it, cursing the slight tremor in my fingers that caused a drop of hot liquid to spill onto my thumb. I swallowed the thick lump in my throat, offering a stiff, silent nod as the doors finally dinged open to the main lobby.

The faculty lounge was painfully quiet. Dr. Aris sat at the corner table, violently erasing a completely legible equation from his notepad. The tenure-track committee was meeting next door. Either he or Dr. Vance would secure the permanent position in the physics department. Vance was casually flipping through a scientific journal, his legs crossed at the ankle. Aris brushed the eraser shavings off the table with quick, sweeping motions of his hand. He took a deep breath, but the air caught halfway down his windpipe. He stood up, walked to the window, and stared blankly at the campus quad. He tapped his index finger rapidly against the glass pane, reviewing the publication list he had submitted. Should he have included the minor paper from last spring? The doorknob of the committee room rattled, and Aris whipped around, his shoulders instantly hiking up to his ears.

I hovered my mouse over the refresh button on the CRM dashboard. Click. The sales leaderboard remained entirely unchanged. I was tied with Jessica, and the branch manager had promised the Team Lead promotion to whoever closed the week on top. It was 4:55 PM on Friday. I bit down on my thumbnail, tearing away a tiny sliver of cuticle. Across the aisle, Jessica was on a call, her voice dripping with practiced, persuasive charm. I grabbed my headset, then put it back down. I picked it up again. Who else could I possibly call? I had already dialed every promising lead in my pipeline. I bounced my heel against the carpeted floor, creating a rapid vibration that visibly rattled my dual desk monitors. My mouth tasted like stale coffee and copper as the digital clock in the corner of my screen slowly flipped to 4:56.

Maya adjusted the collar of her blouse, pulling the fabric away from her neck. The newsroom buzzed with the usual afternoon chaos, but all she could hear was the rushing sound in her own ears. The Editor-in-Chief was stepping down, and he had narrowed the replacements down to Maya and Thomas. Thomas was currently laughing loudly by the water cooler, tossing a crumpled paper cup perfectly into the bin. Maya’s eyes darted back to her blank monitor. She picked up a stack of press releases, tapped them against the desk to align their edges, and set them down. She picked them up and tapped them again. Her breathing was short, trapped entirely in the upper part of her chest. When the intercom buzzed and the editor finally requested her presence in his office, Maya jerked violently, knocking her pencil cup completely off the desk and scattering pens everywhere.

"So, we'll find out today," Liam said, leaning against the doorframe of my cubicle. He looked relaxed, his sleeves rolled up to reveal a casual confidence I deeply envied. We were the last two up for the Senior Forensics Analyst position. "Yeah. Guess so," I muttered, forcing the corners of my mouth upward into a stiff, unnatural curve. I shoved my hands deeply into my pockets so he wouldn't see the way my fingers were twitching. My stomach churned, feeling as though I had swallowed a handful of heavy stones. As soon as Liam sauntered back to his desk, I collapsed into my chair and aggressively rubbed my face with both hands. I pulled up the internal HR portal, staring blindly at the company logo. I needed this raise. I couldn't afford to be passed over again. My foot began its frantic tapping against the modesty panel.

The morning fog hung thick over the construction site as Foreman Davies walked toward the main trailer. Greg stood near the heavy machinery, kicking repeatedly at a clump of dried mud clinging to his steel-toed boots. He and Martinez were the final candidates for the Site Supervisor vacancy. Martinez was busy organizing the blueprints, humming quietly under his breath. Greg rubbed the back of his neck, his rough calluses scraping against his skin. He took off his hardhat, wiped a sheen of cold sweat from his forehead with the back of his forearm, and jammed the helmet back down onto his skull. His chest felt impossibly tight, constricted by an invisible steel band. When Davies finally emerged from the trailer, holding a clipboard and looking directly at him, Greg forgot how to exhale, locking his knees and bracing himself against the side of the nearby bulldozer.

I’ve counted the perforated holes in the metal ceiling panel thirteen times. Seven hundred and forty-two. Beside me, Greg from Accounting is humming a soft jazz tune, practically asleep on the handrail. My thumb rubs circles over the cracked screen of my phone. No signal. Still zero bars. I swallow hard, feeling the collar of my shirt closing in like a tightening fist. The air feels heavy, recycled, thick with the smell of old coffee and lingering cologne. "Do you think the cables are rated for this kind of static weight?" I ask, my voice pitching up slightly. Greg opens one eye, shrugging. I press my palm flat against the cool metal door, feeling for the slightest vibration. The silence stretches out, ringing in my ears, and I forcefully remind my lungs to take in another breath.

The digital display had been stuck on the number '14' since lunchtime. Elena marched three steps forward, spun on her heel, and marched three steps back. The rhythmic clicking of her heels echoed in the cramped space. Marcus sat cross-legged on the floor, sorting through his inbox offline. Elena chewed viciously on her thumbnail, tasting copper as she broke the skin. She reached out and hammered the red emergency button for the seventh time, waiting for the crackle of the intercom that never came. "We are going to miss the quarterly review," she muttered, her eyes darting between the closed doors and the emergency hatch in the ceiling. "They’ll start without us. They’ll reallocate our budget." She dragged her clammy palms down the sides of her wool skirt. The temperature in the box seemed to climb with every tick of her wristwatch.

"Did you hear that?" I ask, freezing mid-stride. Susan shakes her head, flipping a page of her magazine. "Hear what?" I press my ear against the brushed steel wall. A distant creak echoes down the shaft. My chest tightens. The space between the four walls feels visibly smaller than it did when we got in at 1:00 PM. I loosen my tie, unbuttoning the top two buttons, but the invisible band around my ribs refuses to yield. My foot taps a frantic, irregular rhythm against the linoleum. "The oxygen," I say, my breath coming out in short, shallow puffs. "There’s only so much cubic volume in here. We’ve been breathing it for hours." Susan looks up, her brow furrowing. I squeeze my eyes shut, pressing two fingers to the rapid pulse fluttering at the base of my throat, waiting for a rescue that feels lightyears away.

For two hours and forty-five minutes, David had been reorganizing the contents of his briefcase. First by size, then by color, and now by alphabetical order. His hands shook slightly as he dropped a yellow highlighter, the plastic clattering loudly against the elevator floor. Next to him, Sarah was silently doing a crossword puzzle on her tablet. David hastily grabbed the marker, his breathing audible and ragged. He wiped a sheen of sweat from his forehead with the back of his sleeve. "Do you think the maintenance guys go home at five?" he asked, his voice cracking. He didn't wait for her answer, instantly dropping to his knees to pry at the rubber seal between the doors with his bare fingers. The rigid plastic refused to yield, and David swallowed down the metallic taste of bile rising in the back of his throat.

Every five minutes, I illuminate my phone screen. 3:45. 3:50. 3:55. My battery is bleeding out at twelve percent. Over by the mirrored wall, Julian is stretching his calves. I stare at the seam where the two doors meet, imagining the dark, cavernous void of the shaft just inches away. What if the brakes give out? I read an article once about counterweight failures. My knee bounces up and down like a jackhammer. "Stop that," Julian says gently. I force my leg still, but the tremors just migrate to my hands. I shove them deep into my pockets, curling them into tight fists until my fingernails dig into my palms. The dim emergency lights flicker once, twice, and I let out a sharp, involuntary gasp, my heart hammering violently against my sternum as I brace for a sudden, plunging drop.

Arthur’s words tumbled out in a relentless, overlapping torrent. "Because if the fire department comes, they have to use the Jaws of Life, right? But the hydraulic fluid can leak, and what if we’re stuck between floors and have to climb out? I have bad knees. I can't jump." Beside him, Chloe casually peeled a tangerine, offering him a slice. Arthur recoiled, waving it away frantically. He wiped his damp palms on his khakis, leaving dark streaks on the fabric. He paced the exact diagonal length of the cab—four steps corner to corner—dodging Chloe's outstretched hand every time. His eyes were wide, the pupils blown dark in the dim emergency lighting. "The maintenance log on the wall says it was last inspected in 2019," Arthur rambled on, peeling the faded sticker off the panel with a trembling fingernail. "That's five years ago, Chloe. Five."

I have a flight to catch at seven. It’s four-thirty. It takes an hour to get to the airport, plus security. Beside me, Mark is leaning against the handrail, softly snoring. I stare at him, baffled by his stillness. My own heart is racing a marathon. I check my watch. Four-thirty-one. I pull up my flight itinerary, swiping down to refresh, even though I know there’s no service. The loading icon spins and spins. I tap my phone against my chin, a rapid staccato beat. If I miss this flight, I miss the merger meeting. If I miss the merger, the account falls through. I grab the red emergency phone again, slamming the receiver against my ear. Dead air. I drop the plastic handset and let it dangle by its metal cord, squeezing my eyes shut as a cold sweat breaks out across my brow.

The air conditioning had failed halfway through hour two. Maya peeled her suit jacket off, draping it over the brass railing, but the dampness under her arms remained. She pressed her cheek against the cool mirror at the back of the car, squeezing her eyes shut. Tom was sitting quietly in the corner, reviewing a stack of printed memos. Maya’s gaze darted to the digital floor indicator, permanently stuck between 32 and 33. She tugged at the collar of her silk blouse, gasping quietly as the fabric clung to her skin. Her legs felt weak, like overcooked noodles, yet she couldn't bring herself to sit down. Every unexpected groan of the building's infrastructure sent a violent shudder down her spine. She began counting backward from a thousand in her head, but lost her place at nine hundred and eighty, her mind spinning into a blank, buzzing void.

"There's a scraping sound," I whisper, pressing my palms against the stainless steel doors. Tanya looks up from her cuticles. "I don't hear anything." I press harder, trying to wedge my fingers into the microscopic gap between the rubber seals. "It's a metallic grind. Like a frayed cable." My voice pitches an octave higher than normal. Tanya sighs and goes back to her nails. I wipe the slick sheen of sweat from my upper lip with the back of my hand. The walls seem to be vibrating, or maybe that’s just my own trembling. I pace a tight circle around Tanya, my dress shoes squeaking loudly against the vinyl floor. The tiny vent in the ceiling is blowing a meager trickle of dusty air. I stand directly under it, craning my neck upward, taking rapid, shallow gulps of the recycled breeze like a fish out of water.

"We need to inventory our liquids," Kevin announced, his voice tight and reedy. He snatched the half-empty water bottle from his messenger bag, holding it up to the dim emergency light. Across the elevator, Rita slowly blinked at him over the rim of her reading glasses. Kevin began emptying his pockets onto the floor: two crumpled receipts, a pack of mints, and a ballpoint pen. His hands hovered over the items, fingers twitching. "If we ration the mints, we might stave off dehydration. It’s been three hours. The human body can only go three days without water." Rita didn't answer. Kevin stood up, wiped his clammy hands on his thighs, and immediately knelt back down to recount the mints. "Twelve," he muttered, swallowing dryly. "Six for me, six for you." He dragged his collar away from his neck, leaving a red blotch on his skin.

The bronze plaque above the door reads 'Maximum Capacity: 15 Persons or 2500 lbs'. I've read it so many times the letters have lost all meaning. Next to me, big Steve from logistics is mindlessly tossing a tennis ball against the wall. Thwack. Catch. Thwack. Catch. Every impact sends a jolt through my teeth. I pull out my phone calculator. I weigh one-sixty. Steve is easily two-fifty. Four hundred and ten pounds. Well under the limit. But what if the limit was calculated fifty years ago? Metal degrades. Thwack. Catch. "Can you please stop doing that?" I snap. Steve pauses, the ball resting in his massive palm. The sudden silence is somehow worse. I shift my weight from my left foot to my right, constantly adjusting, as if standing too still will somehow trigger a mechanical failure that sends us hurtling down twenty-eight stories.

The fluorescent panel above them hummed a constant, flat B-minor note. Liam kept his head firmly tucked between his knees, staring at the scuff marks on his leather oxfords.
