Beside him, Brenda was doing lunges, entirely unbothered by the three hours that had passed in the suspended steel box. Liam squeezed his eyes shut, but the humming bored directly into his skull. He grabbed the fabric of his trousers, twisting the gray wool until his knuckles turned entirely white. "Brenda," he croaked, the word barely escaping his dry throat. "Your jumping. The vibrations." Brenda paused mid-lunge. Liam kept his head down, unable to look up at the shifting walls. He focused entirely on drawing air in through his nose, counting one, two, three, and letting it out through his mouth, desperate to stop the floor from tilting in his mind.

I stared at the faded "Camp Wawanosh" logo on Mark’s coffee mug, my pulse suddenly drumming against my eardrums. My fingers tightened around my own paper cup until the hot liquid threatened to spill over the rim. Did he recognize me? Did he remember the talent show? I swallowed hard, the breakroom air suddenly feeling impossibly thick and heavy. I took a quick step backward toward the doorway, my eyes darting from his oblivious smile to the exit. "Oh, Wawanosh," I managed to squeak out, my voice sounding unnaturally high. "I went there in '08." Mark turned, his eyes widening with recognition, and I immediately began picking at the cuticle of my thumb, a cold sweat breaking out across my neck as I waited for the inevitable memory to drop.

Elena’s foot tapped a frantic, erratic rhythm against the elevator floor. Beside her, David casually hummed the unmistakably jaunty tune of the Camp Whispering Pines morning anthem. Elena’s stomach plummeted past her shoes. She pressed her back flat against the cool metal wall, her hands clammy. If David realized she was the notorious "Cabin 4 phantom" who had accidentally burned down the arts pavilion, she’d never live it down in the accounting department. She stared fixedly at the floor numbers lighting up—four, five, six—willing the elevator to move faster. Her breathing grew shallow. "Catchy song," she said, wincing at the slight tremor in her voice. David smiled brightly. "Whispering Pines, class of '15." Elena squeezed her eyes shut, her fingernails digging half-moons into her palms as the doors finally chimed open.

The pixelated background on Sarah’s screen shifted, revealing a framed photo of the unmistakable Lake Minnetonka canoe dock. My breath caught in my throat. I muted my microphone just in case my hyperventilating was audible. She was there. She knows about the incident with the camp director's golf cart. I quickly minimized the video window, but my leg bounced so hard under the desk that my monitor shook. I dragged my cursor over the 'Leave Meeting' button, hovering there, my heart hammering a frantic rhythm against my ribs. "Hey, is that Camp Minnetonka?" Dave from marketing asked on the call. I wiped my profusely sweating palms on my jeans. If Sarah said yes and mentioned the summer of 2012, I’d have to fake a power outage and move to another state.

Julian couldn't tear his eyes away from the woven friendship bracelet poking out from beneath his new manager's cuff. It was the intricate double-chevron pattern unique to Camp Silverleaf. He swallowed a lump the size of a golf ball. His collar felt suddenly two sizes too small, and he tugged at it, leaving a damp smear of perspiration on the fabric. If Arthur was at Silverleaf in '99, he definitely knew who sabotaged the rival color-war team. Julian shifted his weight from left to right, his gaze darting toward the exits of the conference hall. "Nice bracelet," Julian mumbled, his mouth completely dry. Arthur beamed. "Silverleaf! Did you go?" Julian’s pulse roared in his ears, drowning out the ambient chatter as he desperately racked his brain for an excuse to bolt for the restrooms.

When the company newsletter announced that the new IT guy, Greg, was a proud alumnus of Camp Kicking Horse, I instantly spilled my water bottle all over my keyboard. I didn't even grab a towel. I just sat there, my chest rising and falling in rapid, jerky motions. Kicking Horse. 2005. The year I sleepwalked into the mess hall and destroyed the banquet preparations. I bit down on my lower lip so hard I tasted copper. Footsteps approached my cubicle, and I aggressively swiveled my chair away, pretending to be utterly engrossed in the blank, dripping monitor. "Hey, I hear you're a Kicking Horse grad too!" Greg's booming voice echoed behind me. A cold prickle raced down my spine, and my hands shook violently as I slowly turned around to face my doom.

The silence in the car was shattered when the radio played an old acoustic song, and Marcus casually mentioned he learned it by the fire pits at Camp Ockanickon. Chloe’s knuckles turned bone-white on the steering wheel. Her eyes darted rapidly between the rearview mirror and the road. She abruptly rolled down her window, desperately needing the freezing December air to cool her suddenly flushed, burning cheeks. She had been the head counselor who accidentally stranded his younger brother's cabin on the island overnight. Her foot hovered erratically over the brake pedal. "Ockanickon?" she repeated, her voice cracking halfway through the word. She began to gnaw fiercely on the inside of her cheek. Every mile closer to the office felt like driving toward an execution, her stomach twisting into tighter and tighter knots.

I stared blankly at the potato salad on my paper plate, my appetite entirely vanished. Across the picnic table, Linda was regaling the team with a story about a miserable summer at Camp Arrowhead. My knee jackhammered against the underside of the wooden table, rattling the plastic cutlery. I kept my head down, letting my hair fall forward to shield my face. Don't look up. Don't make eye contact. She’ll recognize the scar on your chin. I pressed my thumb into my opposite palm, rubbing the skin raw. I was the one who threw the rogue horseshoe. "There was this one kid who totally ruined the tournament," Linda laughed. The air left my lungs in a sudden rush. I stood up so fast my plastic chair tipped backward into the grass, mumbling incoherently about needing more napkins.

"Sun Valley Rangers?" Liam asked, pointing to the faded sticker on Maya's laptop. Maya froze, the tiny paper cup crumpling completely in her fist. Water splashed down her blouse, but she didn’t seem to notice. Her chest felt as though invisible iron bands were tightening around it. Liam was the camp director's son. The same director Maya had accidentally pushed into the mud pit during the closing ceremonies. She took a tiny, shallow breath, her eyes locked on Liam’s perfectly oblivious smile. She took half a step backward, bumping hard into the water cooler jug. "Yeah," she whispered, the sound barely escaping her parched throat. She crossed her arms tightly over her chest, digging her fingers into her own biceps, calculating exactly how long it would take to pack up her desk and resign.

We were supposed to share a fun childhood fact for the icebreaker. When Toby announced he spent six summers at Camp Blackbird, the fluorescent lights above me suddenly seemed blindingly bright. My ears started ringing with a high-pitched whine. I dropped my pen, but my fingers were too stiff to properly grasp it from the carpet, so I just left it there, staring at my empty notepad. I had faked a contagious rash to get sent home early from Blackbird, shutting down the entire camp for three days. Toby was next to me. It was my turn to speak. I opened my mouth, but no sound came out. I wiped a layer of slick moisture from my upper lip, my heart thudding so violently against my ribcage I was certain the entire room could hear it.

As they walked toward the boardroom, Rachel noticed the distinctive wooden bear pendant hanging from the new executive's keychain. Camp Timberwolf. Her breath hitched. She abruptly stopped walking, causing a junior analyst to bump into her shoulder. Rachel didn't apologize; she just stared at the little carved bear, her stomach doing a series of violent flips. If he realized she was the legendary "kitchen raider" who had eaten all the s'mores rations, her professional reputation would be entirely decimated. She began twisting her silver ring around her finger, faster and faster, until the skin beneath it grew red and irritated. "Everything okay, Rachel?" the executive asked, turning back. She forced a rigid, closed-mouth smile, her eyes wide and unblinking. "Fine," she choked out, her feet feeling like they were encased in concrete blocks.

I held my champagne flute with both hands to stop the glass from vibrating against my teeth. Opposite me, Brian was enthusiastically describing the obstacle course at Camp Blue Lake. I took tiny, rapid sips, my eyes darting toward the coat check. Blue Lake. 2018. The year I accidentally launched his favorite counselor's kayak into the rapids. My face felt completely flushed, a localized heatwave radiating from my cheeks. I shifted from my left foot to my right, then back again, unable to find a comfortable stance. "Did you ever go to Blue Lake?" Brian asked, leaning in. I swallowed heavily, the champagne tasting like ash. I backed up slowly, bumping into a potted ficus. "I, uh, I have to go to the bathroom," I stammered, turning and speed-walking away before he could get another word out.

Nina’s fork scraped loudly against her plate, moving the same pile of peas back and forth for the fifth time. Sitting across from her, Ken was wearing a faded "Camp Lone Pine" t-shirt for casual Friday. Nina’s pulse drummed incessantly at her temples. She chewed relentlessly on the edge of her thumbnail, her eyes fixated on the cafeteria clock. She had been the one who accidentally released the camp director’s prized pigs. If Ken recognized her, she was doomed. She tried to take a deep breath, but her chest refused to expand fully. Ken glanced up, catching her stare. "You like the shirt?" he asked. Nina flinched, her knee jerking upward and smashing into the table. "Yep," she squeaked, grabbing her unbitten sandwich and hastily shoving it into her bag, eager to flee the room entirely.

I bounce my knee rapidly against the underside of the glass table, making the lobby magazines vibrate. Next to me, Liam casually scrolls through his phone, completely still. We’re both wearing the same shade of navy blue suit for the junior developer role, but my collar feels three sizes too tight. I press my thumb against my index finger, picking at the cuticle until a tiny bead of red blooms. "Did you review the sorting algorithm questions?" I ask, my voice a half-octave higher than normal. Liam nods, not looking up. I swallow hard, feeling my pulse hammer at the base of my throat. Every time the elevator dings, my stomach drops to the floor. I check my watch again. Two minutes have passed since I last checked. I wipe my damp palms on my slacks.

Maya’s eyes darted between the glowing screen of her laptop and Chloe, who was currently sipping a matcha latte with infuriating slowness. They had clicked ‘Submit’ on the senior illustrator application simultaneously. Maya chewed the inside of her cheek, tasting copper, and refreshed her inbox. Nothing. She refreshed it again. "You know it takes at least a week to process portfolios, right?" Chloe laughed. Maya offered a tight, closed-mouth smile. Her leg jiggled under the café table, shaking their ceramic mugs. She pulled up Chloe's online portfolio, scrutinizing the flawless color palettes, then quickly flipped back to her own, suddenly convinced her typography was entirely amateur. Maya closed her laptop with a sharp snap, only to open it exactly ten seconds later to check her spam folder.

The notification chime from my phone sounds like a fire alarm in the quiet of the library. Across the oak table, Sarah’s phone chimes the exact same tone. The fellowship results. I stare at the locked screen, my breathing suddenly shallow and rapid. My fingertips hover over the glass, trembling slightly, but I can't bring myself to swipe. Sarah leans forward, her eyes bright. "Open it!" she whispers loudly. I rub the back of my neck, feeling the cold sweat gathering there. "You go first," I say, my words rushing out in a single breath. If she gets it, I don't. That’s the reality of the single vacancy. I grip the edge of the wooden table so hard my knuckles turn stark white, squeezing my eyes shut and waiting for her reaction to dictate the trajectory of my entire year.

From the hallway, David could hear Marcus practicing his sales pitch, the confident baritone easily piercing the thin drywall of their shared apartment. David sat on the edge of his bed, tangling and untangling the cord of his headphones. He had the same virtual interview in forty-five minutes. He cleared his throat, but it felt coated in sand. He reached for his water glass, fumbling the grip, and spilled half of it down his dress shirt. "Dammit," he hissed through clenched teeth, grabbing a towel and dabbing frantically at the spreading dark stain. His heart hammered against his ribs like a trapped bird. He stared at his reflection in the webcam preview, noting the pale sheen on his forehead. Marcus laughed heartily at a joke on his call. David gripped the edges of his desk, entirely forgetting his opening line.

"They absolutely loved my signature cocktail idea," Jenna says, taking another sip of her IPA. I nod, offering a rapid string of "Yeah, that's great, totally." I peel the damp label off my beer bottle in microscopic shreds. We had both auditioned for the head mixologist spot three hours ago. I replay my own interview on a loop in my head. Did I shake the martini too long? Did the manager notice my hands shaking when I poured the vermouth? I bite down hard on my lower lip. "You okay?" Jenna asks. "Fine," I snap, a bit too quickly. I immediately backtrack. "I just... I forgot to mention the infusion technique. I should have mentioned it." I pull my phone out, contemplating emailing the owner, before shoving it back into my pocket, tapping my foot against the brass bar rail.

Arthur stared blankly at the spreadsheet, entirely incapable of processing the numbers. Three desks down, Ben was chatting amicably with the Director of Finance. They had both applied for the regional manager promotion yesterday. Arthur’s right eyelid developed a rhythmic twitch. He clicked his ballpoint pen: click-clack, click-clack, click-clack. A coworker glared at him, and he dropped the pen, letting it clatter loudly. He rubbed his clammy palms against his thighs. He knew Ben had led the Q3 merger, but Arthur had secured the overseas accounts. Was that enough? Arthur checked his reflection in his dark monitor, adjusting his tie for the fifth time in an hour. He watched Ben shake the director's hand, feeling a sudden, heavy knot pull tight in his stomach. He reached for his coffee, but his fingers trembled so much he left the mug on the desk.

I stare at the confirmation screen on my laptop, the bold text reading Application Received. Next to me on the sofa, Mark shuts his laptop with a satisfied sigh. "Thanks for sending me the link to this editorial gig," he says. I force a stiff nod, unable to meet his eyes. My stomach churns like a washing machine. Why did I tell him? He has a master's degree in literature; I only have a bachelor's. I grab a throw pillow and pull it tightly against my chest, wrapping my arms around it. I mentally review every typo I might have missed in my cover letter. Did I use an em dash correctly in the second paragraph? I pull up my sent folder on my phone, scanning the attached PDF. My breathing hitches. I read the first sentence five times, unable to comprehend the words.

The heavy velvet curtains closed behind them, plunging the backstage wings into dim shadows. Julian exhaled a long, shaky breath, immediately reaching into his pocket to retrieve his lucky silver coin. He flipped it over and over, the metal slick against his damp thumbs. Beside him, Mateo was practically glowing, humming the melody of the solo they had just performed for the director. "I think they liked the high note," Mateo whispered. Julian swallowed, feeling a lump in his throat the size of a golf ball. "Yeah. Probably." Julian paced a tight circle in the dust, his eyes darting toward the casting board even though the results wouldn't be posted for days. He replayed his own high note in his head. Was it flat? He squeezed his eyes shut, pressing the heels of his hands into his forehead. He couldn't stop pacing.

The walls in our shared workspace are paper thin. I can hear every word of Clara’s phone interview for the lead copywriter contract. I sit frozen in my ergonomic chair, entirely ignoring my own deadline. I bite my thumbnail down to the quick, spitting the small fragment into the wastebasket. She sounds so articulate. She just used the phrase "synergistic brand voice" without stumbling once. I rub my temples, feeling a dull ache building behind my eyes. I had my call with the same client yesterday, and I completely blanked when they asked about my past campaign metrics. I pull up Clara’s LinkedIn profile, scrolling through her endorsements, my chest tightening with every glowing recommendation. I stand up, pace to the window, sit back down, and immediately stand up again, unable to find a comfortable position.

Elias sat in the driver's seat of his sedan, the engine idling in the parking garage of the law firm. He tapped the steering wheel in a rapid, erratic rhythm. His roommate, Thomas, was upstairs interviewing for the exact same associate position Elias had interviewed for that morning. Elias checked the rearview mirror, wiping a bead of sweat from his upper lip. It was sixty degrees outside, but the collar of his dress shirt felt suffocating. He unbuttoned the top button, then immediately buttoned it again. He grabbed his phone, opening his email, swiping down to refresh. Nothing. He opened a mobile game, but closed it after ten seconds. What if Thomas remembered the recent Supreme Court precedent Elias had entirely forgotten to mention? Elias squeezed the steering wheel until his knuckles ached, his eyes glued to the elevator doors.

I sit in the dim light of my bedroom, refreshing the browser window for the twentieth time. The notification icon remains stubbornly gray. I know for a fact the hiring manager viewed Sam’s profile an hour ago; Sam texted a screenshot of it to our group chat. They both applied for the same digital marketing role I did. I chew on the inside of my cheek until I taste copper. I open a new tab, type in the company's website, close the tab, and open it again. My leg bounces under the desk, creating a rhythmic thumping noise against the floorboards. "Did you optimize your keywords?" Sam’s text from yesterday echoes in my head. I dive into my own profile, wildly rearranging my skills section, my pulse hammering in my ears as I try to guess what the algorithms want.

The fluorescent lights of the diner buzzed overhead. Leo stared into his black coffee, watching the dark liquid ripple. Across the sticky booth, Greg was eagerly devouring a plate of fries. They had just left the garage where they both tested for the master mechanic slot. "So, what are you gonna do if I get it?" Greg asked around a mouthful of potato. Leo’s stomach performed a violent flip. He dropped his fork, which clattered sharply against the porcelain plate. "I don't know," Leo muttered, his voice tight. He picked up a paper napkin and began tearing it into tiny, meticulous strips, piling them into a snowy mountain on the formica table. He couldn't afford to miss this pay bump. He rubbed the back of his neck, feeling the rigid tension in his muscles, and checked his phone screen again, despite it being completely black.

Marcus stared at the two glossy invitations sitting on his kitchen counter, the bold "Saturday at 8 PM" mocking him from both. He picked up his phone, opened a maps app, and calculated the travel time between Liam’s downtown loft and Sarah’s suburban backyard. Forty-two minutes. He chewed the inside of his cheek until it tasted like copper. If he stayed at Liam's for exactly forty-five minutes, slipped out during the toast, and caught the 9:15 train, he could make Sarah's cake-cutting. But what if the train was delayed? What if Liam noticed him edging toward the door? Marcus rubbed his damp palms on his jeans, pulling up the train schedule for the fifth time in ten minutes, his leg bouncing in a relentless, frantic rhythm against the kitchen barstool.

I have three tabs open on my browser: a transit map, an Uber fare estimator, and a weather tracker. Maya’s beach bonfire starts at sunset, exactly when Chloe’s rooftop cocktail hour begins. My fingers hover over the keyboard, typing "I might be a little late" into Chloe’s chat, before furiously backspacing. I switch to Maya’s chat. "Can't wait!" I type, but my thumb hovers over the send button, trembling slightly. The pulse in my neck is beating an erratic drum solo. If I wear the sundress, I'll freeze on the roof. If I wear the jumpsuit, I'll roast by the fire. I pace from the window to the door, gnawing on my thumbnail until the cuticle stings. The clock ticks loudly, each second shaving away my narrow window to figure out a physical impossibility.

Elena laid out the silk evening gown for David’s gala on the bed, right next to the distressed jeans for Maria’s dive-bar bash. Both events started precisely at seven. She walked into the bathroom, gripped the edges of the porcelain sink, and stared into the mirror. Her breathing was shallow, barely lifting her chest. "I can do both," she whispered to her reflection, though her voice hitched. She mentally mapped out the route, factoring in the weekend traffic and the endless red lights on 4th Avenue. She picked up a hairbrush, then immediately set it down to recheck the calendar app on her phone. The screen blurred as she swiped back and forth between the two unyielding blocks of time. She pressed the heels of her hands against her closed eyes, willing her racing heartbeat to slow down.

The silver gift bag is for Jake; the blue one is for Sam. I sit in my car with the engine idling, the air conditioning blasting directly into my face, yet there’s a persistent sheen of sweat on my forehead. My phone buzzes in the cup holder. "Where are you?" Jake texts. Two seconds later, "Party is starting!" from Sam. My stomach performs a violent somersault. I shift the car into drive, then immediately slam it back into park. If I go to Jake's first, Sam will see the time stamp on my inevitable Instagram tag and know he was second place. I drum my fingers against the steering wheel, a rapid-fire staccato, staring blindly at the intersection ahead. The green light turns yellow, then red, and I just sit there, trapped between turning left and turning right.

Arthur sat at the corner table of the crowded pizzeria, tapping his foot so hard the water in his glass rippled. To his left, three blocks away, was Ben’s surprise party. To his right, just across the bridge, was Clara’s masquerade. He checked his watch. 7:45. He checked it again. 7:46. He reached for a slice of pepperoni, but his throat felt as tight as a clenched fist; the thought of swallowing anything made him nauseous. He pulled out a crumpled piece of napkin where he had written a minute-by-minute itinerary. The ink was smudged from his sweaty fingers. If he ran the three blocks, he could show his face, hand over the gift, and fake a stomach ache. Arthur wiped his brow with the back of his sleeve, his eyes darting frantically between the two exits.

I stand in the middle of my closet, entirely paralyzed. A pile of discarded clothes rises around my ankles. Greg wants a formal dinner at eight; Leo is hosting a neon rave at exactly the same time. I zip up a black dress, then frantically claw at the zipper to take it off again. My chest feels like someone strapped a tight leather belt around my ribs. I grab my phone to check the group chats, my heart hammering against my sternum as I see photos of people already arriving at both places. "Where is our favorite girl?" Greg posts. I drop the phone onto the bed like it burned me. Taking a deep, shuddering breath, I stare at the ceiling, my mind spinning through a dizzying carousel of elaborate excuses, fake illnesses, and fabricated family emergencies.

Sitting in the dimly lit booth at Charlie’s celebration, Julian kept his phone hidden under his thigh. Every time it vibrated with a message from Oliver’s barbecue across town, Julian jolted, his shoulders hiking up toward his ears. "Having fun?" Charlie asked, passing a tray of shots. Julian forced a wide, brittle smile, nodding enthusiastically while his left leg bounced violently under the table. He threw the shot back, the alcohol burning all the way down, but it did nothing to loosen the tight knot in his stomach. He discreetly pulled up his sleeve to look at his watch. 9:15. Oliver would be slicing the brisket right now. Julian rubbed the back of his neck, picking at a loose thread on his collar, desperately trying to formulate a departure speech that wouldn't sound like a betrayal.

The subway car rattles, and I grip the overhead bar so tightly my knuckles are entirely white. I’m currently halfway between Zoe’s roller-skating party and Dan’s acoustic gig. I already spent thirty minutes at Zoe’s, smiling so hard my face ached, constantly looking over my shoulder at the clock on the rink wall. Now, I’m rushing to Dan’s, but the train is stalling between stations. The overhead speaker crackles with an unintelligible announcement. I let out a sharp, breathless exhale and begin pacing the length of the empty train car. I pull out my phone; no signal underground. I bite down hard on my lower lip, tasting salt, my mind flashing to the image of Dan looking out into the small crowd, searching for my face and only seeing an empty chair.

Fiona arranged the two identical cupcakes on her kitchen counter, one with a blue candle and one with a pink. It was a dry run. She checked the stopwatch on her phone, resetting it for the fourth time. "Happy birthday to you," she sang to the empty room, her voice shaking. She needed to perfect the timing. She had to drop off the blue cupcake at Derek’s apartment by noon, then drive across the county line to deliver the pink one to Hannah by twelve-thirty. She looked out the window at the thickening gray clouds. Rain meant traffic. Traffic meant delays. Fiona began tearing her cuticles with her teeth, a bad habit she thought she had outgrown in high school. She fumbled to pick up her keys, dropping them twice before hurrying out the door.

I lock myself in a bathroom stall at Party A. The bass from the living room rattles the thin door, but it’s nothing compared to the rapid thudding in my own ears. I turn on the sink faucet to drown out the noise, splashing ice-cold water onto my flushed cheeks. I pull up the Uber app. Surge pricing is at triple the normal rate, and the wait is twenty minutes. Party B is waiting. I grip the edges of the porcelain sink, my reflection staring back with wide, hyper-alert eyes. "I’m so sorry, I had a flat tire," I whisper to the mirror. No, too easily disprovable. "Food poisoning," I try, though my voice cracks on the syllables. I dry my hands on my jeans, taking rapid, shallow breaths before reaching for the doorknob with a trembling hand.

Standing on the sidewalk, Hector held a wrapped book in his left hand and a bottle of wine in his right. He looked left toward the neon sign of the karaoke bar where Pete was celebrating, then right toward the quiet townhouse where June was hosting her dinner. His feet remained glued to the concrete. Pedestrians bumped into his shoulders, but he barely registered the impacts. He pulled his collar away from his neck, suddenly feeling as though the evening air had turned oppressively humid. He mentally calculated the consequences of choosing left over right, the potential arguments, the hurt feelings, the silent treatments. A bead of sweat traced a slow line down his temple. He shoved both gifts into his messenger bag, pulling the strap tightly across his chest, unable to take a single step in either direction.

The revolving doors of the grand hotel deposit me into the lobby, where my nightmare becomes reality. The digital directory reads: "Sapphire Room: Mia's 25th" and "Ruby Room: Tom's 25th." They are right next to each other. I duck behind a large potted fern, my breath catching in my throat. I peek through the fronds. Mia’s friends are lingering near the coat check, while Tom’s brother is standing by the elevators. I shrink back, wrapping my arms tightly around my torso. If I step out, both groups will see me simultaneously. I pull my phone from my pocket, my thumbs slipping on the glass screen as I try to text my roommate for an emergency extraction. The walls of the expansive lobby suddenly feel like they are shrinking, pressing in on me from all sides as I crouch lower.

My thumbnail was bleeding again. I pressed it against my jeans, ignoring the sting as Leo laughed across the table. "Man, the look on your face when that dog chased us into the lake," he said, taking a sip of his latte. My breath hitched, catching somewhere near my collarbone. I traced the condensation on my glass, moving in the same circle over and over. "The lake?" I asked, my voice pitching up half an octave. "Leo, we hid in the old barn. The one with the rusted tractor." Leo frowned, shaking his head. "No way. We swam across Miller's Pond." A loud ringing started in my ears. If he was right about the lake, what else was I wrong about? I pressed my thumb harder into the denim, feeling my pulse throb in my fingertips. I needed to leave, right now.

Maya’s foot tapped a rapid staccato against the hardwood floor. She tore another piece of packing tape, the sharp rip making her flinch. "I just don't get why you're insisting the sky was green," she said, her eyes darting between the open cardboard box and Sarah. "It was the northern lights, Maya," Sarah replied patiently, folding a sweater. "We were freezing on the hood of your dad's car." Maya’s stomach did a slow, heavy roll. She rubbed her palms against her thighs, wiping away the sudden dampness. They hadn't been in her dad's car; they had been on the roof of the middle school, and the sky had been an angry, unnatural purple before the storm hit. She swallowed hard, tasting bile. Why was her chest so tight? If Sarah remembered the car, who had Maya been on the roof with?

The white lines on the highway blurred into a continuous streak. I gripped the steering wheel until my knuckles turned the color of bone, my chest rising and falling in shallow, rapid hitches. "You're crazy," Sam chuckled from the passenger seat, oblivious to the way I kept checking the rearview mirror. "The diner waitress definitely gave us her number. She wrote it on the back of the receipt." I bit the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper. "She told us to get out, Sam. She said they were calling the cops." I didn't look at him, keeping my eyes locked on the endless asphalt. He laughed again, a careless, booming sound that made the ringing in my ears louder. I checked the mirror again. There were no flashing lights yet, but the sour taste in my throat wouldn't go away.

David adjusted his tie for the fifth time in three minutes, the silk feeling like a noose against his adam's apple. He shifted his weight from his left foot to his right, staring at the punch bowl. Beside him, Greg was grinning. "Best night of senior year," Greg proclaimed loudly. "The night we broke into the pool and you did a backflip off the diving board." David’s mouth went completely dry. He hadn't been at the pool. He had been in the hospital with a broken collarbone. He looked around the crowded gymnasium, suddenly hyper-aware of the heat, the booming bass of the music, the closing walls. He reached up to loosen his collar, his fingers trembling slightly. "I didn't do a backflip," David whispered, though Greg was already turning away to greet someone else. David couldn't pull enough air into his lungs.

I kept folding and unfolding the edge of the quilt, watching the worn threads threaten to snap. "Mom threw out the comic books because of the water damage from the leak," Chris said casually from the beanbag chair, tossing a tennis ball in the air. "What?" I croaked, the word barely making it past the lump in my throat. I stood up, paced to the window, and paced back to the bed. "No, she gave them away. To the neighbor's kid. I watched her hand the box over." Chris caught the ball and frowned. "Dude, the pipe burst in '09. They were ruined." I pressed the heels of my hands against my closed eyes. The room felt ten degrees hotter. If it was a leak, why did I vividly remember the neighbor boy's gloating smile? My heart battered against my ribs like a trapped bird.

The fire crackled, sending orange embers spiraling into the dark sky, but Elena couldn't feel the warmth. She sat with her knees pulled tightly to her chest, her arms wrapped around them like a shield. "So the bear just walks right into our campsite," Mark was telling the others, waving a marshmallow stick. "And Elena starts screaming!" Elena’s jaw clenched. She stared into the flames, her breathing shallow. There hadn't been a bear. It was a man. A man in a heavy coat who stood at the edge of the trees for twenty minutes, just watching them. She chewed on her bottom lip, her eyes darting toward the pitch-black tree line beyond the fire's glow. Every snap of a twig made her shoulders jerk toward her ears. Mark was laughing, everyone was laughing, and Elena couldn't stop looking at the shadows.

My phone screen lit up with the time: 8:14 PM. I checked it again at 8:15. Beside me, Clara admired the abstract painting. "I still can't believe you bought this piece the day we met in Paris," she sighed happily. I dropped my phone back into my pocket, my fingers finding a loose thread in the lining to twist and pull. "We didn't meet in Paris, Clara," I said, trying to keep my voice steady despite the flutter in my stomach. "We met in London. At the train station." Clara turned to me, her brow furrowed in genuine confusion. "No, it was the Louvre. It was raining." The gallery walls seemed to inch closer together. I swallowed hard, the ambient chatter of the crowd suddenly deafening. I checked my phone again. 8:16 PM. If she remembered Paris, who had I been with in London?

Julian’s knee bounced, sending a tiny vibration through the plastic subway seat. He clasped his hands together, his thumbs circling each other at a dizzying speed. "I'm telling you, the guy left a briefcase," Arthur said, holding onto the overhead rail as the train swayed. Julian shook his head rapidly, his eyes fixed on the scuffed floor. "It wasn't a briefcase. It was a shoebox, Arthur. A taped-up shoebox." Arthur chuckled, "Nah, black leather briefcase. You have a terrible memory." Julian's chest constricted. He remembered the duct tape, the strange metallic smell, the way the man had sprinted off just before the doors closed. The train screeched around a curve, and Julian flinched, gripping the edge of his seat. He kept scanning the floor of their current car, looking under the boots of passengers, unable to take a full breath until the doors finally opened.

I systematically ripped my paper napkin into tiny squares, arranging them in a grid on the breakroom table. "The merger meeting was a disaster," Tom groaned across from me. "The CEO literally yelled at us for thirty minutes." I stopped tearing the napkin. My fingers felt like ice. "Tom," I whispered, checking the doorway. "The CEO wasn't there. It was just the HR director, and she was crying." Tom stopped chewing, staring at me as if I had grown a second head. "What are you talking about? He slammed his fist on the desk." A cold sweat broke out along my hairline. I swept the paper squares into the trash, my chair scraping loudly as I stood. I couldn't look at him. I just needed to reach the bathroom sink, to splash freezing water on my face.

Dust motes danced in the shaft of sunlight piercing the attic window, but Liam couldn't stop coughing. He wiped his clammy palms on his jeans. "Found the old Ouija board," Kevin announced from a dusty corner. "Remember when we asked it who lived in the house, and it spelled out your name?" Liam took a step backward, his back hitting a stack of boxes. "It didn't spell my name," Liam said, his voice cracking. "It spelled L-E-A-V-E." Kevin laughed, wiping a cobweb from his face. "Dude, no it didn't. It spelled L-I-A-M." Liam’s pulse hammered against his eardrums. He looked at the wooden board in Kevin's hands, then at the dark, shadowed eaves of the attic. The air felt incredibly thin, as if the oxygen had been sucked out of the room. He edged toward the trapdoor stairs, his eyes darting to every darkened corner.

I picked at the chipped green paint on the bench, wedging the flakes under my fingernails until they ached. "She wore a red dress," Chloe sighed nostalgically, watching the pigeons peck at scattered breadcrumbs. "The night she disappeared, it was a bright crimson dress." I swallowed the sudden, metallic lump in my throat. I squeezed my eyes shut, but the image remained seared behind my eyelids. "It was yellow, Chloe," I said, my voice barely a rustle of wind. "A yellow sundress with white daisies." Chloe shook her head firmly. "Nope. Red." My stomach dropped as if I were on a plunging elevator. I gripped the edge of the bench, my knuckles whitening. If Chloe told the police the dress was red, they would be looking for the wrong girl. I stood up abruptly, my legs feeling like lead, the sound of the pigeons' cooing suddenly unbearable.

Nora’s thumb mercilessly worked the cap of her pen, clicking it down and up, down and up. The sterile smell of bleach in the waiting room made her lightheaded. "He tripped on the stairs," her sister whispered, handing her a plastic cup of water. "I saw him tumble right down the oak staircase." Nora stopped clicking the pen. She stared at the water rippling in the cup. "He didn't trip," Nora said, her voice hollow and thin. "Someone pushed him from the balcony. I saw the hands." Her sister gave her a pitying look. "Nora, you're exhausted. We were standing by the stairs." Nora’s breathing quickened into short, sharp gasps. She dropped the pen, the plastic clattering loudly against the linoleum tiles. She looked at the swinging doors of the emergency room, her heart racing so fast her chest ached. She crossed her arms tightly, shivering violently.

My fingers froze over the keyboard. Across the glass table, Julian turned his laptop screen toward me, his face glowing in the harsh fluorescent light. It was the same interface. The same machine learning algorithm. Six months of my late nights, countless energy drinks, and missed family dinners were staring back at me from his screen. My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird. I swallowed hard, the sudden dryness in my throat making it difficult to breathe. "You... you coded the predictive module using Python?" I stammered, my knee bouncing violently against the underside of the desk. He nodded. I pulled at the collar of my shirt, suddenly feeling like the room was ten degrees hotter. If the boss saw this, one of us was out. I stared at the blinking cursor on my own identical screen, my hands trembling so much I had to tuck them under my thighs.

Elias clutched his conference folder to his chest, the cardboard bending under the force of his grip. Dr. Vance was already at the podium, projecting the very translated Sumerian texts Elias had spent the last two years deciphering in the basement archives. Elias shifted his weight from his left foot to his right, then back again. He chewed on the inside of his cheek until he tasted copper. His presentation was next. The exact same findings, right down to the grammatical nuances of the third tablet. He pulled his phone from his pocket, checked the blank screen, shoved it back, and immediately pulled it out again. His breathing grew shallow and rapid. If he walked out now, maybe nobody would notice. He picked at the edge of his name badge, peeling the laminate back millimeter by millimeter as Dr. Vance clicked to the next identical slide.

The clay slipped from my fingers, hitting the linoleum floor with a damp thud. I didn't bend down to pick it up. I couldn't stop staring at Maya’s workbench. She was smoothing out the wings of a fallen Icarus, the figure kneeling with its left arm outstretched toward an unseen sun. It was the exact pose of the sculpture under my damp tarp. I wiped my palms on my denim apron, but they instantly grew clammy again. How did she know? Did she look into my locker? My chest tightened, drawing in air in quick, inadequate gasps. The critique was in twenty minutes. I paced three steps to the sink, turned the water on, let it run, and turned it off without washing my hands. I approached my pedestal, my pulse thudding behind my eyes, and gripped the sculpting wire, wondering if I had time to chop off the wings and pretend it was someone else entirely.

Chef Marcel stood frozen at the pass, his plating tweezers suspended in mid-air. Beside him, sous-chef Leo was garnishing the VIP’s special: a pan-seared scallop over a bed of smoked parsnip purée, drizzled with blackberry reduction. It was the exact off-menu dish Marcel had been secretly perfecting all week to impress the Michelin inspector sitting at table four. Marcel’s jaw clenched so tight a dull ache radiated up to his temples. He dropped the tweezers; they clattered loudly against the stainless steel counter. He began wiping down his pristine cutting board, rubbing the towel over the same spotless patch of metal again and again. His eyes darted to the clock, then to the dining room doors, then back to Leo's identical dish. Marcel took a sudden step back, running a hand through his hair, his chest rising and falling in erratic, jerky movements as the waiter arrived to take the plate away.

The words blurred on the printed page in my hands. Claire was reading her opening chapter aloud to the critique circle, and her protagonist was a blind clockmaker who discovered time-travel through gears. My blind clockmaker. My time-traveling gears. A high-pitched ringing started in my ears, drowning out the murmur of the coffee shop. I crossed my legs, uncrossed them, and tapped my pen against my notebook in a rapid, staccato rhythm. I felt a bead of sweat trickle down my spine. Had I talked about this over drinks? Had she seen my blog? I pressed the heels of my hands against my eyes until bursts of color exploded in the darkness. When I opened them, the identical manuscript lay on the table. My mouth felt like it was stuffed with cotton. I reached for my iced coffee, but my fingers shook so badly I pulled back before I could knock it over.

Sarah’s drafting pencil snapped under the sudden pressure. She stared across the wide expanse of the firm’s layout table. Mark was pinning up the final renderings for the harbor redevelopment. The sloping glass roof, the integrated solar pathways, the cantilevered observation deck—it was a carbon copy of the blueprints rolled out in Sarah’s own portfolio. She swallowed heavily, her throat clicking in the silent room. She began to rapidly reorganize the markers on her desk, lining them up by color, then immediately scrambling them to do it again. She pressed two fingers to her neck, feeling the frantic, galloping rhythm of her pulse beneath her skin. The senior partners would be here in ten minutes to decide who led the project. Sarah walked to the window, hugged her arms tightly across her chest, and bit down on her thumbnail, tearing the edge right down to the quick.

I hung the last price tag on my display of hand-poured soy candles set inside vintage teacups. As I stepped back, I bumped into the folding table of the neighboring stall. I turned to apologize, but the words died in my throat. Row after row of vintage teacups, filled with soy wax, complete with the exact same dried lavender sprigs sprinkled on top. I patted my pockets frantically, looking for my car keys, though I had no intention of driving anywhere. My breathing hitched, shallow and erratic. I started rearranging my display, moving a floral cup to the left, then back to the right, unable to leave it alone. The fair gates were opening in five minutes. Shoppers would see us side-by-side. I tugged at the hem of my sweater, unraveling a loose thread, twisting it around my index finger until the tip turned purple, my eyes darting desperately toward the exit.

Detective Russo stared at the corkboard in the 9th precinct. Red yarn connected a pawn shop ticket to a blue Honda. It was the exact web he had built in his own basement office across town. He realized Captain Miller was explaining the very theory Russo had drafted at 3 A.M. Russo’s knee started a jackhammer rhythm against the edge of the briefing table. He clicked his ballpoint pen. Click-click. Click-click. The sound echoed too loudly in his own head. He stopped, shoved the pen into his pocket, and immediately started grinding his teeth. Three months of unauthorized undercover work, all leading to the exact same suspect the 9th had just casually pinned to a board. Russo wiped a sudden sheen of sweat from his upper lip. If he spoke up, he’d face a suspension for working outside his jurisdiction. He shifted his weight, his eyes wide and fixed on the red yarn.

I checked the torque on the servo motor for the fifth time, though I knew it was perfect. The gymnasium buzzed with the chatter of the regional science fair, but I only heard the whir of the robotics project at the next table. I peeked over the partition. It was my aquatic drone. The same dual-propeller system, the same waterproof casing salvaged from a cooler. My stomach did a violent flip, sour and heavy. I grabbed a microfiber cloth and polished my display board, scrubbing fiercely at an invisible smudge until the cardboard began to pill. The judges were two aisles down. I couldn't catch my breath, the air in the gym feeling incredibly thick. I opened my project notebook, flipped all the way to the back, closed it, and opened it again. "Nice drone," the kid next door said. I offered a tight, closed-mouth smile, my hands balled into tight fists inside my pockets.

Elena knelt in the soil of the east garden, her trowel digging into the earth. She looked up and froze. Three yards away, Thomas was unspooling the irrigation line in the exact spiral pattern she had spent the entire winter designing for the estate's centennial. Elena stood up so fast she felt dizzy. She wiped her dirt-caked hands on her trousers, over and over, leaving dark streaks down her thighs. She began pacing the short length of the rosebed, exactly four steps forward, four steps back. The estate manager had only approved one budget. She picked up her watering can, realized it was empty, and set it down heavily. Her chest felt compressed, as though an invisible band was tightening around her ribs. She looked at Thomas, then at her own half-planted spiral, her fingernails digging deep into the soft, fleshy palms of her hands.

The bass kicked through the studio monitors, rattling my ribs. I hit the spacebar, killing the track instantly. From the adjacent booth, muffled through the soundproof glass, the exact same beat continued to thump. Same tempo, same chopped vocal sample, same hi-hat roll. My mouth went bone dry. I spun my mixing chair around, facing the door, then spun back to the console. I reached for my water bottle, but my hand jerked, knocking it against the keyboard. Water pooled around the keys, but I just stared at it, the blood rushing in my ears drowning out the bass. We were pitching to the same label executive this afternoon. I aggressively scrubbed my hands over my face, tugging at my hair until the roots stung. I hit play again, stopped it after one second, and began tapping my foot at double the speed of the beat, my eyes fixed on the blinking interface.

Chloe’s tablet nearly slipped from her sweaty grasp as she stared at the ballroom setup. Winter Wonderland. Ice sculptures of swans, silver sequin tablecloths, and blue uplighting. It was spectacular. It was also exactly what the rival planning agency had just started setting up in the adjoining hall for the exact same corporate client. Chloe’s chest heaved. She tapped the screen of her tablet furiously, swiping through vendor invoices without seeing a single number. She bit down on her lower lip, tasting the metallic tang of blood. The CEO was arriving for a walkthrough in less than half an hour. Chloe walked briskly toward the catering doors, stopped abruptly, and turned back around. She smoothed the front of her blazer with trembling hands. "Pull the blue lights," she snapped at a technician, her voice cracking halfway through the sentence. She grabbed a walkie-talkie, gripping the plastic so tightly her knuckles shone stark white.

I watched Mark scroll through the rescue shelter’s website, the bright screen reflecting in his eyes. My knee bounced under the table, rattling my half-empty coffee mug. "Look at this pitbull mix," he said, turning the laptop towards me. I swallowed hard, tracing the rim of my cup with a trembling thumb. What about the deposit? What if it barks all night and Mrs. Higgins downstairs complains? I could already see the eviction notice taped to our door. I scratched at my wrist, my mind racing through calculations of vet bills and emergency surgeries we absolutely could not afford. "He's cute," I managed to say, my voice tight and unusually high-pitched. I stood up, needing to move, pacing the narrow stretch between the kitchen island and the sofa. "But who walks him when you work late? I can't. You know I can't."

Chloe tugged at the fraying threads of her sweater sleeve as Sarah enthusiastically outlined her plan to adopt a Bengal kitten. Sarah’s hands flew through the air, painting a picture of cozy evenings, but Chloe was busy taking short, shallow breaths. She imagined the litter box stench permeating the tiny apartment, settling into the fabric of her vintage armchair. Her chest felt tight. She pressed two fingers to her collarbone, feeling her pulse thudding like a trapped bird. "Cats are so independent," Sarah chirped. Chloe forced a stiff nod, her eyes darting toward the pristine beige rug they had just paid off. She cleared her throat twice before speaking. "Are you sure? I mean, the claws. And the hair. It gets everywhere, Sarah. In the air vents, in our food." She wiped her suddenly clammy palms on her jeans, unable to stop her leg from bouncing.

"A python?" I repeated, the words tasting like ash in my suddenly dry mouth. Greg grinned, completely oblivious to the cold sweat prickling at my hairline. I took a step back, pressing my shoulders flat against the hallway wall as if distancing myself from the empty glass terrarium he had just lugged into the living room. My fingernails dug into my palms. I kept glancing at the glass, visualizing the locking mechanism failing, the heavy lid sliding open in the dead of night. "They barely eat," Greg argued, dropping onto the couch. I rubbed my temples, squeezing my eyes shut to block out the image of a serpent slithering across my bare foot. "No, Greg. No." My voice was shaking, and I couldn't stop shifting my weight from foot to foot. "The landlord won't allow it. It's dangerous. Please, take that tank back right now."

Marcus systematically clicked his pen—in, out, in, out—while Julian described the macaw he’d seen at the pet store. The rhythmic clicking matched the rapid flutter in Marcus’s stomach. A macaw. A bird that could live for fifty years and scream loud enough to shatter glass. Marcus stared fixedly at the stack of law textbooks on his desk, his sanctuary of quiet study. He imagined feathers dusting his notes, the piercing squawks interrupting his focus during finals. He dragged a hand down his face, feeling the sudden heat in his cheeks. "Julian," Marcus started, stopping to clear his throat when the word squeaked. "We study in here. Birds are... they are loud. Very loud." He dropped the pen and immediately started twisting the silver ring on his index finger, pulling it up to the knuckle and pushing it back down in a relentless, frantic loop.

I chewed the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper, staring at the leash draped casually over the kitchen counter. Maya hadn't even brought the puppy home yet, but the mere sight of that nylon strap made my chest constrict. I walked over to my bookshelf, instinctively moving my rare first editions to a higher tier. My hands felt clumsy, dropping a paperback and making me jump at the thud. "I'll train him, I promise," Maya called from the bedroom. I didn't answer. I was too busy calculating the height of the coffee table, wondering if a beagle could reach my laptop cords. I knelt down, frantically wrapping the loose wires into tight bundles, my breath coming in short, uneven hitches. The apartment suddenly felt impossibly small, a delicate glass house waiting to be shattered by muddy paws and needle-sharp teeth.

Elena walked a tight circle around the kitchen island, her bare feet slapping quietly against the linoleum. "It's just a hamster," Jenna laughed, leaning against the fridge. Elena stopped, gripping the edge of the counter so hard her knuckles turned white. She looked at the tiny plastic tubes Jenna had brought home. Rodents. They chewed through walls. They carried things. Elena’s eyes darted toward the baseboards, searching for imaginary gaps. "They escape, Jenna," Elena said rapidly, her words tumbling over each other. "Remember my cousin’s gerbil? It got into the walls. It died in the drywall. The smell." She rubbed the back of her neck, shivering despite the heating being on full blast. "What if it gets into my room while I’m sleeping? I can't sleep with my door closed, it gets too stuffy." She began pacing again, her eyes wide and unblinking.

"We are barely keeping the houseplants alive," I mumbled, frantically wiping down the spotless dining table for the third time in ten minutes. Liam sighed, holding up a glossy brochure for a local animal rescue. My heart hammered against my ribs like a frantic drum. I scrubbed harder, the lemon scent of the cleaner doing nothing to settle my churning stomach. Between my double shifts at the hospital and his touring schedule, the apartment was empty for days. Who would be here? What if the dog choked on something? What if it got sick and I missed the signs? A drop of sweat rolled down my temple. I threw the rag into the sink with a wet slap. "I can't be responsible for another heartbeat, Liam. I just can't," I choked out, wrapping my arms around my torso tightly, trying to physically hold myself together.

David practically vibrated in his armchair as Sam unrolled the blueprints for a multi-level ferret enclosure. David’s thumbnail found its way between his teeth, and he bit down hard on the cuticle. Ferrets. Weasels. Fast, slinky predators that hid shiny objects and smelled like musky dampness. He swallowed, feeling a thick lump in his throat. Sam rambled enthusiastically about hammocks and tunnels, completely missing how David’s eyes were fixed, glassy and wide, on the open window. "They nip," David blurted out, his voice a full octave higher than normal. He immediately pulled his knees up to his chest, wrapping his arms around them in a tight, defensive ball. "They get under the furniture. You step on them. They bite your toes." He rocked slightly, just a millimeter back and forth, unable to shake the phantom sensation of tiny claws scurrying across the floorboards.

The text message glowed on my screen: Found the perfect Great Dane! Coming over tonight! I must have read it twenty times. My chest felt like someone had parked a car on it. I stood in the middle of our cramped, 500-square-foot living room, spinning slowly. A Great Dane. It was the size of a miniature horse. Where would it sleep? It would knock over the TV. It would smash the antique vase my grandmother gave me. I grabbed the vase, cradling it against my chest, taking quick, gulping breaths of air. I walked to my bedroom, set the vase on the highest shelf, then walked back out. I checked the lock on the front door. Twice. Three times. I sat on the edge of the sofa, my foot tapping a frantic, irregular rhythm on the floorboards, waiting for the inevitable knock.

Nadia’s stomach performed a complex series of flips as Farah gleefully unpacked a towering, carpeted cat tree. Nadia rubbed her palms against her thighs, leaving sweaty handprints on her slacks. She loved this apartment. She loved their pristine velvet sofa and the sheer, un-torn curtains. "She’s a rescue, completely house-trained," Farah promised, wrestling with a sisal-wrapped post. Nadia gave a jerky, unconvincing smile. Her mind flashed with images of shredded upholstery and knocked-over water glasses. She could feel a headache blooming at the base of her skull, a tight band of pressure wrapping around her forehead. "Cats... they climb," Nadia whispered, her eyes darting from the cat tree to the floating shelves adorned with fragile ceramics. She took a step backward, bumping into the wall, her fingers immediately seeking the reassuring, smooth fabric of the curtains, twisting the hem tightly.

"It stays in the box," Ben said, tapping the plastic enclosure. I didn't move. I couldn't. My feet felt cemented to the living room rug. Inside that box was a furry, eight-legged shadow the size of my fist. The hair on my arms stood straight up, and a cold shiver violently racked my spine. "Ben," I rasped, my vocal cords tight and unyielding. "Get it out." He rolled his eyes, explaining how low-maintenance tarantulas were, but his voice sounded muffled, like I was underwater. All my focus was locked on the creature. I watched it lift one thick leg, and my breath hitched, trapping the air in my lungs. My vision narrowed to a tunnel. "If that lid opens," I whispered, my jaw trembling so badly I could barely form the words, "I am moving out tonight. I'm not joking. Take it away."

Oliver’s pen scratched furiously across the back of an envelope. Rent. Groceries. Utilities. His breathing grew shallower with every number he jotted down. Across the room, Lucas was cooing over a picture of a hedgehog. "They need special heat lamps, Lucas," Oliver said, his voice clipped and breathless. He aggressively crossed out a number, the paper tearing slightly. "And exotic vets. Do you know what an exotic vet costs?" He stood up, knocking his chair back with a loud clatter. He began pacing the length of the kitchen, his hands buried deep in his pockets, his shoulders hunched up by his ears. "What if it gets sick on a Sunday? The emergency fee alone will drain our emergency fund." Lucas sighed, but Oliver didn't hear him. He was already opening his banking app again, his thumbs flying clumsily over the screen, eyes wide and unblinking.

My knee bounced in a rapid, uncontrollable rhythm against the underside of Mr. Henderson’s mahogany desk. Beside me, Leo sat perfectly still, casually flipping through the leather-bound document that granted him the sprawling coastal estate. I stared at the single, unadorned sheet of paper sitting in front of me. It was a photocopy of a handwritten note from our father, leaving me nothing but a set of coordinates and a sequence of numbers. My palms left damp smudges on the glass table top. I wiped them on my jeans, swallowed against the sandpaper dryness in my throat, and tried to regulate my shallow breaths. What did those numbers mean? If Leo noticed my trembling fingers as I folded the paper, he didn't say a word. I kept my eyes locked on the floor, my heart hammering a frantic, deafening beat against my ribs.

Clara chewed the inside of her cheek until she tasted copper. The attic was suffocatingly hot, but she pulled her cardigan tighter around her shoulders. In her left hand, she held the official notarized will leaving the family business equally to her and her brother, Thomas. In her right hand, she clutched a crumpled, tear-stained letter she had just pried from behind a loose baseboard. This letter, dated three days before their mother’s passing, signed the entire enterprise over to Thomas alone, claiming Clara could not be trusted. Her pulse throbbed in her temples. She paced the length of the dusty floorboards, five steps forward, five steps back. Thomas was downstairs making tea. She glanced at the trapdoor, her breathing turning rapid and shallow. She folded the secret letter, unfolded it, then folded it again, unable to make her hands stop moving.

The metallic click of the safety deposit box echoing through the quiet bank vault made me flinch. The teller stepped out, leaving Evelyn and me alone with the metal tray. Evelyn reached in first, pulling out a thick manila envelope. "Stock certificates," she murmured, a bright smile breaking across her face. "Mom really did hold onto them." I reached for the second envelope, my stomach twisting into tight, heavy knots. The paper felt unnaturally heavy. Inside was a ledger, its pages filled with red ink detailing millions in offshore debts—all in my name. A cold sweat broke out across the back of my neck. I clamped my teeth together to keep my jaw from shivering. Evelyn was already calculating her dividends, oblivious to the high-pitched ringing filling my ears. I squeezed the ledger tight, my knuckles turning stark white, unable to draw a full breath.

Marcus tapped his pen against the coffee mug—tap, tap, tap—until the ceramic chipped. He didn't notice. His eyes darted between the two laptops resting on the kitchen island. On the left screen, his sister Maya was successfully logging into their late father’s cryptocurrency wallet, watching the balances populate with dizzying strings of zeros. On the right screen, Marcus’s designated digital inheritance was rapidly auto-deleting. The screen flashed with encrypted warning prompts he couldn't decipher. He dragged a hand through his hair, tugging at the roots. His foot began a restless jiggle against the barstool. "Maya, it’s deleting," he managed to say, his voice cracking an octave higher than usual. He typed frantically, hitting the escape key over and over. His chest felt compressed under an invisible weight, and a cold prickling sensation crawled up his arms as the progress bar hit ninety-nine percent.

Dirt caked under my fingernails as I dug furiously at the base of the old oak tree. Julian stood behind me, holding the deed to the farmhouse that the lawyers had just handed him. "Are you sure about this?" he asked. I didn't answer. I couldn't. My heart was trapped in my throat, beating like a trapped bird. My shovel hit metal. I dropped the tool, falling to my knees to claw the rest of the soil away with shaking hands. It was a rusted tin box. I popped the latch, expecting the gold coins Dad had always promised me. Instead, there was a stack of faded photographs of people I didn't recognize, and a birth certificate with my name, but different parents. My vision tunneled. I gasped for air, clutching the rough bark of the tree, the world spinning in a nauseating blur.

The grandfather clock in the study ticked with agonizing slowness. Sarah sat on the edge of the velvet armchair, her posture rigid, repeatedly clicking the top of her ballpoint pen. Across the room, her brother David was celebrating, holding up the genuine velvet-lined box containing their grandmother’s legendary sapphire necklace. Sarah looked down at the box resting in her own lap. It was identical in every way, except the stones nestled inside were made of dull, cloudy glass. The appraisal note beneath them read: For the daughter who always loved pretending. Sarah swallowed hard, her mouth entirely devoid of moisture. She rubbed her damp palms against her slacks. David turned toward her, grinning widely. Sarah forced the corners of her mouth upward, but her lower lip trembled. She quickly snapped her box shut, her heart racing so fast it made her dizzy.

I peeled at the cuticle of my thumb until a bright bead of red welled up, but I barely registered the sting. The executor’s email sat open on my phone, illuminating the dark living room. My sister, Chloe, had been forwarded a pristine portfolio of intellectual property rights, guaranteeing her income for life. My attachment was a singular PDF titled The Truth. I hovered my finger over the screen. It was shaking so badly I almost dropped the phone. What did he leave me? I squeezed my eyes shut, taking three rapid, stuttering breaths. Every muscle in my back was pulled taut, aching with tension. The silence of the apartment felt deafening, pressing in on my eardrums. I wiped my sweaty brow with the back of my hand, finally tapping the icon. The file began to load, and I felt utterly sick to my stomach.

Arthur’s foot tapped out a frenetic rhythm against the hardwood floor. He stood in the dimly lit library, staring at the two leather-bound journals resting on the desk. His sister, Beatrice, had already claimed the red one, discovering a detailed map to offshore accounts and properties. Arthur slowly opened the black journal left for him. The pages were filled with their father's erratic scrawl, detailing a list of enemies who would soon come collecting. Arthur's stomach plummeted into his shoes. He traced the binding, the pulse visibly jumping in the hollow of his neck. He looked toward the heavy oak door, suddenly certain he could hear footsteps approaching in the hallway. He swallowed, but his throat was bone dry. He quickly shoved the book under his jacket, his eyes darting frantically to the windows, jumping at the sudden sound of a branch scraping the glass.

My teeth ground together as the lawyer handed over the final two envelopes. "To be opened privately," he instructed. Out in the hallway, my brother ripped his open with a laugh. "Keys to the Porsche!" he cheered, dangling the silver keychain. I looked at my envelope. It felt incredibly light. My fingers felt numb as I tore the seal. Inside was a single, silver bullet and a handwritten note that simply read: They know. The hallway spun. I leaned back against the cool plaster wall to keep my balance. My chest tightened, making every breath a shallow gasp. "What did you get?" my brother asked, turning toward me. I quickly crushed the note in my sweaty fist and shoved it into my pocket, unable to look him in the eye. "Nothing," I squeaked, my voice wavering. I couldn't stop bouncing on the balls of my feet.

The projector hummed loudly in the darkened living room. On the screen, their father’s recorded message concluded with a warm farewell to his eldest son, bequeathing him the family’s lucrative shipping company. The screen flickered, and the old man’s tone grew icy. "And to Elena," the recording said, "I leave the burden of the vault." The video abruptly ended. Elena remained frozen on the sofa. She picked at the frayed hem of her skirt, unraveling a long thread. Her breathing grew audible, hitching in her throat. She knew what was in the vault beneath the house. She had spent her entire childhood pretending it didn't exist. Her brother patted her shoulder, but Elena flinched violently at his touch. She stood up abruptly, knocking over her water glass. It shattered, but she ignored the mess, backing away toward the door with wide, unblinking eyes.

I stood in the center of the overgrown greenhouse, my teeth chattering despite the oppressive summer heat. Liam was entirely focused on the heirloom rosebushes, reading the meticulous cultivation diary our mother had left solely to him. I looked down at my own inheritance: a rusted watering can and a brass key wrapped in a map of the local cemetery. My stomach churned, acid bubbling up my throat. I squeezed the handle of the watering can until my knuckles ached. Why the cemetery? I shifted my weight from foot to foot, unable to find a comfortable stance. I kept checking my watch, though I had nowhere to be. The glass panes of the greenhouse seemed to bow inward, trapping the humid air. I wiped my slick palms on my shorts, staring at the brass key as if it were a live grenade waiting to detonate.

Oliver’s eyes darted furiously across the text message from the family lawyer. His sister, standing across the kitchen, held a certified check for two million dollars, crying tears of relief. Oliver looked back at his phone. His message contained no funds, only a legal summons and a transfer of liability for a collapsed mining venture. He began to pace the length of the kitchen island, his footsteps heavy and rapid. He ran a trembling hand over his face, feeling the cold clamminess of his own skin. "Oliver? What is it?" his sister asked. He tried to speak, but his vocal cords felt paralyzed. He shook his head, backing away until his spine hit the refrigerator door. The buzzing of the appliance vibrated against his back, matching the frantic fluttering in his chest. He shoved the phone into his pocket, constantly checking to see if it was still there.

I tap my thumb against my index finger, counting to four, then start again. The living room is a labyrinth of cardboard towers, each one leaning at a slightly different angle. "We should start with the attic," my brother, Leo, says casually. He tosses me a roll of packing tape. I fumble it, the heavy roll crashing onto the hardwood floor. My heart hammers against my ribs like a trapped bird. "Right," I say, my voice tight and thin. "The attic." I look up at the pull-down ceiling stairs. The wood is splintered, the springs rusted. What if the floorboards are rotten? What if we find the unpaid tax notices Mom always hinted at? I wipe my clammy palms on my jeans and swallow hard, unable to take a step forward. My breathing is too shallow, catching right at the top of my throat.

Clara’s leg bounced under the heavy mahogany dining table, her heel striking the rug in a rapid, relentless rhythm. Beside her, Thomas flipped through the stack of property deeds with infuriating slowness. Clara picked at the skin around her thumbnail until a tiny bead of blood welled up. She pressed it into a tissue, her eyes darting from the cracked plaster on the ceiling to the water stain creeping down the floral wallpaper. "It needs a lot of work before listing," the contractor had said yesterday. How much work? Ten thousand? Fifty thousand? She squeezed her eyes shut, but that only made the numbers spin faster in the darkness behind her eyelids. "You okay to sign this, Clara?" Thomas asked, extending a pen. Her hand hovered in the air, trembling so badly she had to grip her own wrist to steady it before taking the silver barrel.

I must have paced the length of the master bedroom twenty times before Maya finally pried the floorboard loose. Beneath it sat a small, steel lockbox. "Got it," she grinned, brushing dust from her knees. I didn't smile back. My stomach churned, a heavy, cold rock dropping into my intestines. I backed away, pressing my shoulders against the floral wallpaper, wishing I could sink right through it. "Open it," Maya urged, sliding the box toward me. I shook my head, my jaw locked tight. If Gran kept it hidden, there was a reason. Unpaid debts? A second will? Evidence of the feud that tore our dad away? I rubbed my temples, trying to slow the rush of blood thumping against my eardrums. "We don't have to," I whispered, the words coming out faster than intended. "We could just throw it in the dumpster. Let it go."

Every creak of the old Victorian house sent a jolt of electricity down Elias’s spine. He lay rigid on the lumpy guest bed, the duvet pulled tight under his chin despite the sweltering July heat. Down the hall, his sister snored softly, entirely oblivious to the heavy, suffocating silence of the rural property. Elias stared at the ceiling, cataloging the shadows. He mentally checked the deadbolts again. Front door, back door, basement hatch. Did he turn the stove off after making tea? He threw the covers back, his bare feet hitting the cold floorboards. He marched down the stairs, his breath catching every time a floorboard groaned. He checked the knobs on the gas range. All off. He checked the lock. Secured. Back in bed, he closed his eyes, but his heart continued its erratic sprint, anticipating the next phantom noise from the dark hallway.

The pruning shears slip in my sweaty grip, nicking the thick stem of Gran’s prized rosebush instead of cutting it. "Careful!" my sister Sarah calls from the porch, sipping her lemonade. I bite my lip, tasting copper. I can't look at her. I stare at the thorny tangle of vines choking the trellis. It’s too much. The weeds are waist-high, the fence is listing, and the roof is missing shingles. We’re supposed to fix this by ourselves? I drop the shears and wipe my forehead with the back of my dirt-caked glove. My chest feels constricted, as if someone has pulled a leather belt tight around my ribs. I take a ragged breath, but the air stops in my throat. I start pulling at the weeds with my bare hands, ripping them out in rapid, jerky motions, ignoring the thorns tearing into my skin.

Penny chewed the inside of her cheek as her brother unloaded the third box of photo albums onto the coffee table. She crossed her arms tightly over her chest, rocking slightly on her heels. "Look at this one," Mark laughed, holding up a faded Polaroid. Penny didn't look. She kept her gaze fixed on the grandfather clock in the corner. The pendulum swung back and forth, slicing the silence into sharp, rhythmic ticks. It was 2:15 PM. They had to leave by four to beat traffic. If they didn't leave by four, they'd miss the appointment with the appraiser. If they missed the appraiser, they couldn't list the house this month. "Mark, please," she interrupted, her voice cracking. "Can we just pack them? We're running out of time." She began shoving the albums haphazardly back into the cardboard box, her movements rushed and uncoordinated.

I shine the flashlight into the damp, smelling basement corner, and the beam shakes wildly. "It's just a little water damage," my brother calls down from the top of the stairs. "Nothing a patch can't fix." I swallow the bile rising in the back of my throat. The black spots blooming across the drywall aren't just water damage. The beam illuminates a sprawling web of dark fuzz eating away at the support beams. I take a step back, my boot squelching in a hidden puddle. My lungs feel too small. We signed the papers. We own this now. The inspector completely missed it. I drop the flashlight. It rolls across the concrete, casting erratic shadows before settling against the infected wall. I clutch my hair with both hands, pulling hard enough to sting, trying to ground myself against the dizzying spin of the room.

Mrs. Higgins leaned over the picket fence, her eyes scanning the overgrown lawn. "So sad about your dear grandmother," she drawled. "Are you two moving in, or selling?" Julian stood frozen, the heavy trash bag dangling from his grip. He felt a bead of sweat trace a cold path down his spine. His sister, standing by the porch, waved politely, but Julian couldn't form a response. His tongue felt like sandpaper. He envisioned the neighborhood association descending upon them, fining them for the peeling paint, the tall grass, the cracked driveway. His grip on the plastic bag tightened until his knuckles turned white. "We... we haven't," he stammered, his eyes darting to the ground. "Excuse me." He turned abruptly, practically sprinting back to the safety of the heavy oak front door, locking it with a loud click the second he was inside.

I hold the porcelain teacup with both hands, but they tremble so violently the matching saucer rattles in a discordant symphony. "Just put it in the bubble wrap," my sister sighs, casually tossing a silver spoon into a crate. I carefully lower the cup onto the dining table, snatching my hands back as if the ceramic is burning hot. I wipe my damp palms on my thighs. What if I drop it? It’s a Meissen original. It’s worth more than my car. The entire room is a minefield of delicate, irreplaceable artifacts, and I feel like an elephant crashing through the space. Every step I take makes the floorboards groan, sending vibrations into the china cabinets. I retreat to the corner of the room, pressing my back flat against the wall, refusing to touch anything else until she hands me a padded box.

The sky turned a bruised, ugly purple as the first rumble of thunder rattled the windowpanes of the old farmhouse. Chloe immediately stopped sorting the linens. She walked to the window, her fingernails biting into her palms. The old oak tree in the front yard swayed violently, its heavy branches scraping against the gutters. She checked the weather app on her phone for the fifth time in ten minutes. Severe thunderstorm warning. High winds. The roof was already missing shingles. Beside her, her brother hummed to the radio, oblivious to the dropping barometric pressure. Chloe began pacing the length of the hallway, her steps short and rapid. "We should move the boxes away from the windows," she said rapidly, already dragging a heavy carton of books across the carpet. "The glass is old. The frames are rotting. They're going to shatter."

"I want the piano," my sister announces, running her hand over the dusty keys. I stare at the massive, upright instrument. My chest tightens, the air growing thick and heavy. How are we going to move a piano? We don't have the money for professional movers. If we try to lift it, we'll gouge the hardwood floors. If we ruin the floors, the property value tanks. I rub the back of my neck, feeling a cold sweat prickle my skin. "It won't fit in your apartment," I say, my voice an octave higher than usual. "We'll figure it out," she dismisses. I begin to walk in tight circles around the living room, my gaze fixed on the sheer size of the wooden beast. The walls feel like they are inching closer together. I pull my collar away from my throat, gasping for a proper breath.

The house was completely empty, yet Liam’s chest felt as though a cinderblock rested squarely upon his ribs. He stood in the bare foyer, his keys digging painful crescents into his palm. His brother waited outside in the running car. Liam checked the thermostat again. Set to fifty-five. He checked the lock on the basement door. Secured. He walked to the kitchen and pressed his hand flat against the stove burners. Cold. He walked back to the front door, put his hand on the knob, but stopped. Did he lock the back patio door? He had checked it three times, but the memory was blurry. He jogged back through the hollow rooms, his boots echoing loudly off the bare walls. He yanked on the patio handle. Locked. He returned to the front door, his breath coming in shallow, ragged bursts, still unable to turn the deadbolt.

I tapped my toe against the linoleum, counting the floor tiles to keep my breathing even. Seven across. Fourteen down. The pharmacy line wasn't moving. My prescription for Lumisitol was written on a slip of paper I had folded and unfolded until the edges were soft like felt. It is a one-in-a-million defect, my doctor had said. I swallowed dryly, my heart fluttering against my ribs like a trapped moth. The woman in front of me finally reached the counter. "Picking up for Vance," she said. "Lumisitol."
