I froze, my nails digging half-moons into my palms. I stared at the back of her neck. Did she have the sudden dizzy spells too? Did she wake up gasping for air at 3 AM? My chest tightened. I wanted to ask her, to grab her shoulder, but my mouth tasted like copper and my throat simply locked shut.

Elias bounced his knee under the small cafe table, making his half-empty espresso cup rattle against the saucer. He checked his watch for the fourth time in two minutes. The forum had said look for the red scarf. When a man wearing one slid into the booth opposite him, Elias felt a cold prickle of sweat trace down his spine. The man reached for a napkin, and Elias watched the distinctive, rhythmic tremor in his left ring finger—the exact same involuntary twitch that Elias spent hours hiding in his pockets. He wiped his damp palms on his denim jeans, his breathing turning shallow. "You have the Felson's marker?" Elias asked, his voice cracking on the final syllable. The stranger nodded slowly. Elias gripped the edge of the table so hard his knuckles turned white, unable to tear his eyes away from that twitching finger.

I kept my eyes glued to the illuminated fasten seatbelt sign, my teeth grinding together as the turbulence tossed the cabin. It wasn't the flying that made my stomach churn; it was the sudden, sharp pop from the seat beside me. I whipped my head around. The passenger next to me was twisting her shoulder back into its socket with a sickening crunch. I subconsciously reached up to grip my own collarbone. "Ehlers-Danlos, type four?" I whispered, my pulse thudding loudly in my ears. She looked up, startled, and nodded. My breath hitched, catching somewhere behind my sternum. Type four. The vascular kind. The one with the ticking clock. I stared at the emergency exit door, my foot tapping a frantic, erratic rhythm against the carpeted floor. I squeezed my eyes shut, but all I could see were my own frayed blood vessels waiting to snap.

Clara picked at a loose thread on her sweater until it unraveled entirely, leaving a small hole in the wool. The waiting room of the geneticist's office was suffocatingly quiet. Across from her sat a young man reading a pamphlet titled Living with Alstrom Syndrome. Clara felt the blood drain from her face. She pulled her own identical pamphlet from her purse, her fingers trembling so badly she dropped it onto the carpet. The man looked up, his gaze dropping to the glossy paper at her feet. He met her eyes. Clara’s chest rose and fell in rapid, jerky motions. She wanted to bolt for the heavy glass doors, to escape the physical proof that her diagnosis was real and sitting right in front of her. Instead, she sat frozen, swallowing compulsively, her hands clamped together in her lap to stop their violent shaking.

I laid my pill organizer on the sticky diner table, my fingers blindly tracing the raised letters for Tuesday. I popped the compartment open, staring at the distinct, hexagonal blue pill. Just looking at it made my skin crawl with cold sweat. The waitress approached, pouring coffee into my mug. She stopped, the pot hovering mid-air. "Is that... Coralan?" she asked, her voice dropping to a whisper. I jerked back, bumping my knee painfully against the table leg. "Yes," I croaked, my heart suddenly hammering a frantic beat against my ribs. She reached into her apron pocket and pulled out a small amber bottle, shaking it slightly. The same hexagonal blue pills rattled inside. I stared at them, my breath coming in short, tight gasps. I looked at her pale face, frantically searching her eyes to see if she knew how much time we had left.

Marcus paced the length of the park bench, his boots leaving deep impressions in the wet grass. He chewed the inside of his cheek until he tasted iron. A woman sat on the other end, adjusting a very specific, bulky cervical collar. Marcus stopped dead, his eyes darting to the medical device. He wore the exact same custom mold beneath his winter coat. His breathing quickened, a tight knot forming in his stomach. "C5-C6 ossification?" he blurted out, the words tumbling past his lips. She looked up, her eyes wide, and nodded. Marcus slumped onto the bench, burying his damp face in his hands. His knee began to bounce violently. Seeing someone else trapped in the same rigid armor made the walls of his own life feel instantly, suffocatingly close. He rubbed his temples, squeezing his eyes shut as the ground seemed to tilt beneath him.

The elevator doors slid shut, sealing me inside the small metal box. I pressed the button for the fourteenth floor, my finger lingering on the glowing plastic. Only one specialist operated on the fourteenth floor. The only other person in the car, a tall man in a tailored suit, watched the floor numbers tick upward. "Dr. Aris?" he asked. I flinched, my grip tightening on my briefcase handle until my knuckles ached. "Yeah," I managed to say, my voice tight. "Me too. Bilateral vestibular failure," he added softly. The floor dropped out from under me. I pressed my back against the mirrored wall, desperately trying to ground myself as the familiar spinning sensation threatened to pull me under. I squeezed my eyes shut, my chest heaving. It was one thing to read the diagnosis on paper; it was another to be trapped in a rising box with it.

Sarah practically shredded the edge of her donor questionnaire, leaving a pile of tiny paper scraps on her lap. The clinic nurse was speaking to the man in the booth next to hers. "I am sorry," the nurse said gently, "but with a confirmed diagnosis of factor V Leiden, you can never donate." Sarah’s breath hitched. She dropped her pen. It clattered loudly onto the tile floor, but she could not bring herself to pick it up. She stared at her own form, where she had just checked the exact same box. Her heart sprinted, a loud thumping in her ears drowning out the hum of the fluorescent lights. She wiped her clammy palms on her skirt, staring at the stranger's profile. He looked perfectly healthy. Did he also have to check his legs for clots every single morning? She bit her thumbnail, unable to look away.

The buzzing of the tattoo needle usually grounded me, but today, it sounded like a warning siren. I sat rigid in the chair, staring blankly at the flash art on the wall. "Crazy," the artist muttered, wiping excess ink from my wrist. "I literally just tattooed Malignant Hyperthermia Susceptible on a guy twenty minutes ago. You two know each other?" My stomach plummeted into a bottomless pit. "No," I whispered, the word barely scraping past my vocal cords. I peered through the glass storefront. A man was lingering by the bus stop, a fresh bandage wrapped around his wrist. My leg started a rapid staccato tap against the footrest. We both possessed the gene that turned general anesthesia into lethal poison. A single hospital trip could end it all. I swallowed a lump the size of a golf ball, shivering despite the warmth of the studio.

David stood at the edge of the hydrotherapy pool, obsessively counting his pulse against his carotid artery. One, two, three. Too fast. Always too fast. He lowered himself into the lukewarm water, his eyes darting around the small enclosure. An older woman was doing leg lifts near the jets. Pinned to her swimsuit was a waterproof Holter monitor, glowing with a faint green light. David’s hand instinctively flew to his own chest, where an identical black disc rested against his skin. The woman noticed his gaze, then noticed his monitor. She offered a grim, knowing smile. David felt the blood rush from his head. He gripped the metal railing, his knuckles stark white. His chest felt constricted, as though the water pressure had suddenly doubled. He tried to take a deep breath, but his lungs refused to expand fully. He just kept recounting his pulse.

I kept checking over my shoulder as I walked down the aisles of the specialty medical supply store. The scent of sterile plastic and rubbing alcohol made my throat itch. I finally found the section for ocular prosthetics. A teenager was standing there, holding the exact same uniquely curved glass conformer I needed for my microphthalmia. I froze, my hand hovering inches from the shelf. My pulse throbbed in my temples. He turned, holding the tiny piece of glass, and caught me staring. I wanted the floor to swallow me whole. My palms grew slick with sweat. I clutched my bag tightly against my chest, my breathing shallow and fast. I had never met anyone else missing the same piece of themselves. I took a step back, bumping roughly into a display rack, desperate to retreat into the anonymous safety of the crowded street outside.

Maya paced the carpeted area near Gate 4B, wearing a path between the charging station and the trash can. She aggressively twisted her silver rings, the metal scraping against her skin. Over the intercom, another delay was announced. The man sitting closest to the podium groaned, pulling a blue autoinjector from his bag to check the fluid window. Maya stopped pacing. Her heart did a painful flutter in her chest. It was a Kineret syringe. She had three packed in her carry-on for her CAPS flare-ups. She stared at the man, a cold prickle of ice washing over her arms. Did his joints burn like fire too? Did his fevers spike without warning? She hugged her arms tightly across her chest, struggling to draw a full breath. She backed away slowly, retreating until her shoulders hit the cold glass of the terminal window, unable to break eye contact.

I stared at the photo on the woman's phone, my fingers gripping the edge of the cafe table so hard my knuckles turned white. It was Mark, wearing the exact sweater I bought him last week, kissing her cheek. My breathing hitched, growing shallow and fast. I felt a cold prickle spread across the back of my neck. "He said he was at a conference in Seattle," I whispered, the words scraping against my dry throat. My knee began bouncing uncontrollably against the table leg, rattling our coffee cups. I scanned her face, then the crowded room, suddenly feeling like the walls were shrinking. How many other lies were there? My pulse hammered in my ears, drowning out the ambient jazz music. I needed to leave, to run, but my legs felt entirely made of lead.

Julian’s thumb hovered over the screen, shaking slightly as he read the direct message again. *I think we need to talk about Liam,* the stranger had written, attaching a screenshot of a dinner reservation. Julian swallowed hard, a sour taste pooling in his mouth. He paced the length of his small apartment, from the window to the door and back, rubbing the back of his neck until the skin burned. He typed a reply, deleted it, and typed it again, his heart drumming a wild rhythm against his ribs. Every time the three little typing dots appeared on the stranger's end, Julian forgot to exhale. He pulled at the collar of his shirt, suddenly finding the room suffocatingly hot. When the stranger's next image loaded—Liam sleeping in a bed Julian didn't recognize—Julian dropped his phone on the rug and squeezed his eyes shut.

The restaurant lobby was crowded, but I couldn't stop staring at the man standing next to the host stand holding the same rare blue orchids I was holding. "Waiting for Sarah?" he asked with a friendly smile, gesturing to my flowers. My stomach plummeted, twisting into tight, heavy knots. "Yes," I croaked out. He laughed, "Me too. Sarah Jenkins? Blonde, loves French cinema?" A cold sweat broke out across my forehead. I shifted my weight from my left foot to my right, wiping my damp palms on my slacks. "Yeah," I mumbled, my eyes darting toward the revolving door. Every time it spun, my chest tightened until it hurt to draw breath. What happens when she walks in? Should I leave? My teeth ground together, and I began peeling the foil off the flower stems piece by tiny piece, awaiting the inevitable collision.

Clara sat frozen on the edge of David’s bed, staring at the silver locket resting in her palm. The woman at the door, who had just used a key to let herself in, froze in the hallway. "Who are you?" the woman asked, dropping her tote bag. Clara’s breath caught in her throat. She looked from the locket—engraved with *To Chloe, forever*—to the woman standing in the doorway. Clara’s hands trembled so violently the locket clattered to the hardwood floor. She quickly knelt to pick it up, her thoughts spinning, unable to form a coherent sentence. She kept pulling her sleeves over her hands, her eyes darting toward the fire escape outside the window. The silence stretched, heavy and suffocating, punctuated only by the erratic, shallow gasps Clara was desperately trying to control.

The fluorescent lights of the ER waiting room buzzed like an angry wasp in my skull. I kept clicking my pen—click, click, click—until the woman sitting opposite me glared. "Are you here for Alex?" she asked, her voice cracking. I froze, the pen slipping from my sweaty grasp. "I'm his fiancé," she continued, twisting a diamond ring on her left hand. My vision blurred around the edges. I pressed my fingertips hard against my temples, trying to slow the sudden, violent thumping in my chest. "I... I live with him," I stammered, the room suddenly spinning. I stood up abruptly, pacing to the water cooler, then back, unable to stand still. I chewed the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper. Every time the swinging doors to the trauma ward opened, I flinched, bracing for an impact I couldn't dodge.

Mateo squeezed his eyes shut as the rideshare navigated the evening traffic. The passenger next to him was talking loudly on the phone. "Yeah, I'm heading to Sam's place now. The one on Elm Street." Mateo’s eyes snapped open. He chewed on his thumbnail, his leg bouncing erratically against the car door. Elm Street. Sam. He watched the stranger hang up and pull out a photo of Sam holding a golden retriever. Mateo’s mouth went bone dry. He gripped the strap of his messenger bag, his knuckles stark white. He checked the map on his phone, watching the little blue dot creep closer to his own boyfriend's apartment. He wanted to tell the driver to pull over, to let him out right there on the highway, but his vocal cords refused to work. He just stared at the passing streetlights, his breathing shallow and rapid.

I threw the tennis ball, watching Buster sprint across the grass, when another dog tackled him in a playful roll. "Sorry! Bella loves other Goldens," the owner laughed, jogging over. I smiled politely until he added, "My girlfriend, Jessica, just adopted her." The leash slipped right out of my hand. Jessica? I looked closely at the man, my heart kicking into a furious sprint. "Jessica Vance?" I asked, my voice rising a full octave. He nodded. My knees felt like they might buckle. I began patting my pockets, hurriedly searching for my car keys, though I knew they were in my jacket. The open space of the park suddenly felt incredibly small, the air thick and unbreathable. I couldn't look the guy in the eye, staring instead at the dirt, wishing the ground would simply open up and swallow me whole.

Priya stood by the punch bowl, her fingernails digging crescent moons into her palms. The new hire, Maya, was excitedly showing off photos of her weekend getaway. "My partner, Greg, took me to the coast," Maya beamed. Priya stared at the screen, her stomach performing a sickening flip. It was Greg. Her Greg. Priya’s throat constricted, making it impossible to swallow the bite of cracker she had just taken. She took a sudden step backward, knocking into a chair. "Excuse me," she muttered, her eyes darting wildly toward the exit signs. She hurried down the corridor, her heels clicking too fast against the linoleum. In the restroom, she locked the stall door and sank onto the toilet lid, burying her face in her trembling hands, her chest heaving as she tried to pull air into her lungs.

The stadium roared around us, but all I could hear was the rushing blood in my ears. The guy in seat 4A leaned over, pointing at my VIP pass. "Crazy, my girlfriend got me the exact same pass," he shouted over the opening act. "Tanya's great." I froze, my plastic cup of beer crushing slightly under my tightening grip. "Tanya Brooks?" I yelled back, my voice cracking. He nodded cheerfully. A cold prickle washed over my scalp. I started bouncing my leg, my eyes scanning the dark stadium aisles, waiting for her to return from the concession stand. I checked my watch every five seconds, the numbers blurring together. I wiped my palms on my jeans, taking short, sharp breaths. The music vibrated in my ribs, perfectly matching the erratic, chaotic drumming of my own heart. I wanted to bolt for the exit.

Arthur watched the dryer spin, mesmerized by the tumbling colors, until a woman beside him reached into her basket. She pulled out a very specific, hand-stitched denim jacket. Arthur’s breath hitched. He had sewn that patch onto Leo’s jacket himself. "Where did you get that?" Arthur asked, his voice shaking. "My boyfriend, Leo," she smiled. Arthur felt all the blood drain from his face. He backed away slightly, bumping into a folding table. He began to rub his hands together vigorously, as if trying to generate heat in his freezing fingers. His eyes flicked from the jacket to the door, then back to the tumbling laundry. He swallowed repeatedly, trying to dislodge the heavy lump in his throat. He abandoned his basket entirely, pacing to the front window, peering out into the street, bracing himself for the sight of Leo's familiar blue sedan pulling up.

I stared at the painting, but the colors were just a smeared blur. The man next to me cleared his throat. "Beautiful piece. My boyfriend, Elias, painted it for me." The wine glass in my hand rattled against my teeth as I took a sudden, desperate gulp. Elias. I looked at the man, my chest tightening as if wrapped in iron bands. I shifted my weight from foot to foot, unable to find a comfortable stance. I began to pick at the cuticle of my thumb until it stung. "Oh," I managed to say, my voice sounding hollow and distant. I looked around the crowded gallery, the chatter of the patrons suddenly echoing like a cacophony in my brain. My breathing grew shallow. I kept checking my phone screen, waiting for a text from Elias, my thumb hovering over his name, trembling violently.

Marcus sat at Gate 14, his leg bouncing so hard it shook the entire row of connected seats. The man sitting beside him sighed, putting down his magazine. "Waiting for someone?" the man asked. "My girlfriend, Nina. Flight from Paris," Marcus replied, his voice strained. The man frowned. "That's funny. I'm waiting for my fiancé, Nina. Also from Paris." Marcus’s stomach dropped like a stone. He gripped the armrests of his plastic chair, his knuckles turning stark white. He stared at the arrivals monitor, the blinking green letters blurring together. A bead of sweat rolled down his temple. He unbuttoned the top of his collar, gasping softly for air that suddenly felt too thin to breathe. Every time the automatic doors slid open, Marcus flinched, his heart hammering violently against his ribs as he awaited the inevitable arrival.
